title: The Israel Architecture
tagline: A library of the documented record, in reading order. Every volume ties each claim to its source.
note: The documented record, told in order, with every claim tied to its source. Tap a note number to see it, a name in a figure for its detail, or the + button for contents, bookmarks and notes.

books.title: The Baseline
books.subtitle: The Ground Before the Flag
books.intro:
Before there was a flag, there was ground. Rome crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt and renamed its province there Syria Palaestina. The land then passed through Byzantine, Muslim, Crusader and Mamluk hands and, from 1516, into Ottoman rule. Through all of it, the land held a continuous if smaller Jewish presence alongside a majority population of Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians. The modern conflict did not begin on a blank map. It began with two documented histories laid on the same territory.

This opening part clears that ground before the story of the state begins. It starts with today's map, because most confusion starts with geography: Israel within its 1949 armistice lines, the West Bank and the divisions drawn in the Oslo era, Gaza, and East Jerusalem. It explains who is meant by "the Palestinians," what the legal words "occupation," "apartheid" and "genocide" mean, who has applied them and who disputes them. Then it turns to the older record: how the story is usually taught, what the name "Israel" first meant in Genesis, a thousand years of Jewish life across the Muslim-majority world, and the departures of 1948 to 1972.

One question runs through every section. It is simple to ask and harder to answer: what does the record actually show, as distinct from the version most readers were handed?

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: Getting Your Bearings
chapters.intro: Before the history, the ground rules: how this book weighs evidence, where the places in the story are, who the Palestinians are in law today, and what the most argued-over words actually mean.

sections.h: How This Book Weighs Evidence
sections.html:
A reader new to this history has every right to suspect that any account of it is opinion dressed up as history. The suspicion is reasonable. The only honest answer is to state the method in advance, so that each claim can be checked against it. Here is that method: what counts as evidence in this book, how the sources were chosen, who produced the work, and how errors are handled.

Every claim rests on one of four levels of evidence, and the prose signals which one is in play. A documented claim rests on a primary record: a law, a court ruling, an official filing, a census, a signed document. A reported claim rests on a named news outlet or a named investigator. A contested claim is one on which credible sources disagree; there, both positions are set out and the author leaves the dispute open rather than settling it. Some questions are stated as unresolved because the record itself does not settle them. How many of Gaza's dead were combatants, a question taken up in later chapters, is one. Where a passage offers a symbolic or interpretive reading rather than a documentary finding, it is labeled as interpretation.

The sources follow one simple principle: each side's own official records are used. Israeli deaths come from Israel's National Insurance Institute and Defense Ministry figures. Palestinian deaths come from the Gaza Health Ministry, United Nations agencies and peer-reviewed studies. Court records and archives come from Israeli, Palestinian, American and international sources alike. Advocacy organizations on every side, among them UN Watch, IMPACT-se, Track AIPAC and the Washington Report, are named as advocacy groups whenever they are cited, so the reader can weigh them accordingly.

This book is the work of Observe The System, an independent research project. No government, party, lobby or donor funds it or reviews it. When a source proves wrong, or has been misread, the claim is corrected and the change is noted.

Every claim carries a citation, and the reader is invited to follow it. Anyone who disagrees with a reading of a document can go to the document itself. That is the point of the apparatus: not to ask for trust, but to make trust unnecessary.

Why might the record differ from what readers learned? Most people meet this history through textbooks, speeches and news headlines. Those are summaries, and summaries leave things out. This book sets the underlying documents beside the summaries so the two can be compared.

The same rules run in every direction. A claim that favors one side gets the same scrutiny as a claim that does not, and the standard applies to this book's own conclusions as much as to anyone else's. Where the evidence is strong, the prose says so. Where it is thin, disputed or absent, the prose says that too.

sections.h: The Map: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem
sections.html:
Much of the confusion in this history begins with geography. Four names recur throughout this book: Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem. They are often used as though they were interchangeable. They are not one place under different names. Each is a distinct territory, with its own history since 1948 and its own legal regime today. Most of the arguments that follow are, at bottom, arguments about where these lines run and who governs on either side of them.

Start with the line itself. Israel, in the narrow sense used here, is the state within the 1949 armistice lines, known as the "Green Line." The West Bank is the territory east of that line. Jordan held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel has occupied it since 1967. In 1995 the Oslo II accord, an interim agreement, divided the West Bank into three zones, explicitly as a temporary arrangement pending a final agreement.[cite:wiki_oslo_areas] Area A, about 18 percent of the territory, went under Palestinian Authority civil and security control. It holds the major cities: Ramallah, Bethlehem, Nablus, Jenin, Tulkarem, Qalqilya, Jericho and most of Hebron. Area B, about 22 percent, came under Palestinian civil control with joint security control. Area C, about 61 percent, stayed under full Israeli control.[cite:anera_areas_abc] Areas A and B together hold some 2.8 million Palestinians.

The zones were meant to be a stage, not a destination. The plan was to transfer these areas gradually to Palestinian control. That transfer never happened, and since 2002 the Israeli army has entered Area A routinely. A temporary arrangement became, in practice, the lasting shape of the territory.

Area C is the key to the land question. Every Israeli settlement outside East Jerusalem lies within it. About 60 percent of Area C is firing zones, military land, state land or nature reserves. Palestinian building there is tightly restricted, and permits are rarely granted.[cite:wiki_area_c] [cite:anera_areas_abc] When later chapters discuss settlement growth or the prospects for a Palestinian state, the land at stake is mostly in Area C.

Gaza is a strip on the Mediterranean coast. Egypt held it from 1948 to 1967, and Israel occupied it from 1967. In 2005 Israel withdrew its settlers from Gaza but kept control of its borders, airspace and coast.[cite:jerusalemstory_area_a] Withdrawing settlers and withdrawing control are two different things, and the difference runs through every later debate about Gaza's status.

East Jerusalem was occupied in 1967 and then annexed by Israel, a step that has not been recognized internationally. Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live there.[cite:minorityrights_palestine] About 737,000 Israeli settlers now live across East Jerusalem and the West Bank together.

Everyday speech blurs these places together. The documents do not. They describe four places under four different rules. A resident of Ramallah, a settler in Area C, a resident of Gaza and a Palestinian in East Jerusalem live under different authorities and different laws. When this book names one of these territories, it means that territory under that rule. Keeping the map in mind is the first condition for reading everything that follows.

sections.h: Who Are "the Palestinians"? One People, Several Legal Situations
sections.html:
When this book says "Palestinians," the word can mean any of several groups whose rights and daily lives differ sharply. The record shows a single people dispersed across several territories and several legal systems. Which law applies to any one person depends largely on where that person was born and now lives.

Begin with the total. The Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated about 14.8 million Palestinians worldwide in 2024.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] Their circumstances fall into several distinct categories.

The first group is the Palestinian Arab citizens of Israel, about a fifth of Israel's population. They vote in Israeli elections and sit in the Knesset, Israel's parliament. Their status has been shaped by the 2018 Nation-State Law and other measures, which later chapters examine in their own right.[cite:jta_nsl_upheld]

The second group lives in East Jerusalem, the part of the city Israel annexed after 1967. Roughly 360,000 Palestinians live there, most of them holding Israeli residency rather than Israeli citizenship.[cite:minorityrights_palestine] They live under Israeli rule, but mostly without the full standing of Israeli citizens.

The third group lives in the West Bank: about 3.4 million Palestinians as of mid-2025. The Palestinian Authority governs them in Areas A and B, and the territory as a whole remains under Israeli military rule. Israeli settlers in the same territory live under Israeli civil law. One territory thus holds two populations under two legal systems.[cite:minorityrights_palestine] [cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees]

The fourth group lives in Gaza, about 2.1 million people as of mid-2025. About two-thirds of them are refugees or the descendants of refugees.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees]

Beyond these four territories lies the largest single category. About 5.9 million Palestinians are registered with UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees. About 40 percent of them are in Jordan, and others are in Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] [cite:minorityrights_palestine] Altogether, about 6.6 million Palestinians live in Arab countries.

The familiar picture of one people in one place under one government stops here. These categories overlap with the map in the preceding section, and they explain why statements about "the Palestinians" so often talk past each other. Say that Palestinians vote in national elections, and it is true of one group and false of others. Say that Palestinians live under military rule, and the same holds. A refugee in Jordan, a resident of Gaza, a West Bank villager, an East Jerusalem resident and a Palestinian Arab citizen of Israel share a national identity. They do not share a legal status.

These differences matter beyond description. Much of the legal debate over Israel's conduct, including whether its policies amount to apartheid, turns on them. The next section takes up that question. For now it is enough to hold the four situations, and the refugee population beyond them, clearly in view.

sections.h: Occupation, Apartheid, Genocide: What the Words Mean and Who Has Said What
sections.html:
Three words recur in nearly every public argument about Israel and the Palestinians: occupation, apartheid and genocide. Some treat them as slurs with no legal meaning; others treat all three as proven in court. Neither is accurate. Each word has a defined meaning in international law. Each has been applied by different bodies with different authority, and each has been disputed by Israel. The first step to weighing what has actually been found is to keep those bodies apart: a court, a United Nations commission, a human-rights organization and a government.

Occupation. In international law, occupation means a state's forces controlling foreign territory. In July 2024 the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion, advised that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible.[cite:icj_press_19jul24] This is a court speaking, though in the form of an advisory opinion.

Apartheid. Apartheid is a crime under international law, defined in the 1973 Apartheid Convention and in the Rome Statute. It means an institutionalized regime of systematic domination by one racial group over another. Three human-rights organizations have concluded that Israel commits apartheid: Human Rights Watch in 2021, the Israeli group B'Tselem in 2021, and Amnesty International in February 2022.[cite:fara_amnesty_explainer] The International Court of Justice, in its 2024 opinion, found that Israeli policies breach the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid.[cite:11kbw_icj_ao] Israel rejects the apartheid label. The wording matters. The organizations concluded that apartheid is being committed; the court found a breach of the prohibition. The findings are related, but they are not the same statement.

Genocide. Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide means specified acts committed with intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part. Several bodies have concluded that genocide, or acts of genocide, have occurred in Gaza. Amnesty International did so in December 2024. Human Rights Watch, also in December 2024, found acts of genocide through the deprivation of water.[cite:ips_amnesty_hrw_genocide] The Israeli organizations B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel reached the same conclusion in July 2025. The International Association of Genocide Scholars passed a resolution to that effect in August 2025, and a United Nations Commission of Inquiry concluded the same in September 2025.[cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:news9_un_coi]

These findings have been challenged. More than 500 scholars called on the genocide scholars' association to retract its resolution, citing how it was adopted. Israel rejects all of these findings. Most important, no court has decided the question. The case South Africa brought at the International Court of Justice is still pending. In 2024 the court issued provisional measures finding that some rights were plausibly at risk, but it did not decide whether genocide occurred.

Side by side, the record looks like this. On occupation, there is a court opinion. On apartheid, there are conclusions by three human-rights organizations and a court finding of a breach of the prohibition. On genocide, there are conclusions by human-rights organizations, a scholarly association and a United Nations commission; a public challenge from scholars; and a court case not yet decided. In every instance, Israel disputes the finding.

A court opinion, a commission's conclusion, an organization's report and a government's denial are different kinds of statement, and they carry different weight. Throughout this book each is named for what it is, so the reader can judge each on its own terms rather than receive them as one verdict.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: The Land Before the State
chapters.intro: Three thousand years in brief, the Ottoman province that was named, counted and governed, and two peoples whose histories in this land are both real.

sections.h: Three Thousand Years in Brief: Judah, Rome, Palaestina, Islam, Crusaders, Ottomans
sections.html:
Both peoples in this history reach back to a deep past, and each is often handed a version of it that erases the other. One erases the Jews from the land for two thousand years; the other has the Palestinians appear only in the twentieth century. The record supports neither.

The story opens with Jewish kingdoms of Israel and Judah in the first millennium BCE. Rome conquered the region in 63 BCE, and in 6 CE it created a predominantly Jewish province, Judaea. Two great revolts against Roman rule failed. The first ended with the destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE. The second, the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 135 or 136, ended in catastrophe for Judea's Jews. Rome killed, enslaved or expelled much of the Jewish population. It rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan colony called Aelia Capitolina and barred Jews from entering it. It also renamed the province Syria Palaestina.[cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] Most scholars read that renaming as an attempt to sever the Jewish connection to the land.[cite:wiki_palestine_region]

The attempt did not fully succeed. A smaller Jewish presence continued without a break, centered religiously in Galilee, where much classical Jewish literature was produced.[cite:encyclo_israel_history] The land itself passed through a long line of rulers: Byzantine Christian rule; Muslim rule from the seventh century; the Crusader kingdoms; the Mamluks in the thirteenth century; and from 1516 the Ottoman Empire, which governed for four centuries.[cite:wiki_palestine_region]

In the sixteenth century, Jewish communities took root in four cities regarded as holy: Jerusalem, Hebron, Tiberias and Safed. They formed what is called the "Old Yishuv," the Jewish population of the land before the Zionist movement. It remained a minority, and its numbers rose and fell over time.[cite:encyclo_israel_history]

Over the same centuries, the majority population became Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians.[cite:wiki_palestine_region] They are the ancestors of today's Palestinians. Their presence is documented across those centuries; they did not appear in the twentieth.

Put together, the two histories do not cancel each other. The record documents an ancient Jewish connection to the land, a continuous if reduced Jewish presence after Rome crushed the revolts, and centuries of residence by the Arabic-speaking majority. Each popular simplification works by pulling out one of these strands. The Jewish tie to the land is in the record. So is the long residence of the people who became the Palestinians.

That is why the modern conflict cannot be read as a contest between a true claim and a false one. It is about how two documented claims to the same ground came to be handled after 1897, and the chapters that follow trace that handling. This section sets only the starting point. By the end of Ottoman rule, the land held a majority of Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians and a Jewish minority whose ties to it reached back to antiquity.

sections.h: Ottoman Palestine: Named, Populated and Administered
sections.html:
For four centuries, from 1516 to 1917, the Ottoman Empire ruled the land that would later become Mandate Palestine. A familiar account holds that the British Mandate, the post-Ottoman British administration, invented the region as a real place. The Ottoman administrative record says otherwise. Palestine was governed through named districts, by named governors, with named cities and a counted population.

One technical point comes first, because it is true. The Ottomans generally named provinces after their capital cities, and they never created a single administrative unit officially called "Palestine." [cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] That is a naming convention. It does not mean the place, its people or its administration were missing. The regional name was far older than the Ottomans. Rome designated the province Syria Palaestina in the second century CE, and the name persisted through Byzantine, Crusader and Mamluk rule. Throughout the Ottoman period it stayed in regular use in European maps, travel accounts and Arabic geographic writing. The technicality sounds authoritative because it is accurate, and that is what makes it an effective talking point. The narrow claim is true. The broad conclusion built on it is false.

The way the Ottomans ran the district shows how much it mattered to them. After an initial separation in 1864, the district of Jerusalem was raised in 1872 to the status of a mutasarrifate. Most Ottoman districts, or sanjaks, were grouped into larger provinces, or vilayets, and reported through a provincial governor. The Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem skipped that layer: its governor, the mutasarrif, answered directly to Constantinople. Only a small number of especially significant districts received this arrangement, and Jerusalem kept it because of the region's religious and strategic importance to the Ottomans and to Western powers. It lasted until the British occupation in 1917. [cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] The status reflected Ottoman imperial priorities, not any foresight about later nationalist politics.

By 1887–88 the territory that became Mandate Palestine was organized as three units. The independent Sanjak of Jerusalem lay in the south. The Sanjaks of Nablus and Acre lay in the north, both attached administratively to the Vilayet of Beirut. Together these three districts map closely onto the later Mandate boundary. [cite:ips_ottoman_palestine] The lines shifted at the margins over the decades, as lines do almost everywhere, but a bounded, governed region existed before the Mandate.

People lived in it. By the late nineteenth century the three districts held approximately 600,000 people, roughly a decade before political Zionism existed as an organized movement. [cite:ips_ottoman_palestine] Nineteenth-century imperial census methods were real but imperfect, so the figure is an approximation, not a precise count. It matters because the demographic record of the Mandate era begins from essentially the same population. Across the change from Ottoman to British rule, the population did not appear from nowhere. It continued.

A British source of the time counted more finely. An 1885 encyclopedia entry on the region listed 753 distinct named places with more than 54,000 houses across the Ottoman districts. [cite:britannica_history_palestine] The cities in the record include Jerusalem, Gaza, Jaffa, Hebron, Nablus, Haifa, Acre, Safed and Nazareth, and every one of them is still a living city today. Populations and settlement patterns shifted over four centuries, as they do everywhere. The basic fact holds: this was a named and inhabited place throughout.

The record, then, supports one narrow claim and refutes a broad one. No Ottoman map labeled a province "Palestine." But the region held elevated status within the empire, three named districts whose combined borders anticipated the Mandate, a counted population of about 600,000, and cities that are still lived in. The British Mandate inherited a place. It did not invent one.

sections.h: Two Real Histories, Not One Winner
sections.html:
Arguments over who belongs to this land usually rest on a single assumption: that only one population has a real, ancient claim, and that the other's national identity is a recent invention without roots. Whichever side it favors, the argument makes the same error. It folds three different questions into one: whether a population was present, whether its culture was continuous, and when it formed a national identity in the modern political sense. The documented record, from the Ottoman period through 1948, treats these as separate questions with separate answers.

The first answer concerns Jewish presence, and it is not in doubt. Ancient Jewish kingdoms existed in parts of the land. Jewish religious, cultural and historical ties to the region are documented across archaeological, textual and religious sources spanning more than three thousand years. Mainstream historians of every political orientation accept this continuity. [cite:substack_historical_record_balfour] Ancient presence alone, however, does not settle modern questions of sovereignty or statehood. Historical presence and modern political legitimacy are related, but they are not the same thing.

The second answer concerns the Arab population, and it is just as well documented. The Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted the population of Palestine, excluding Bedouin, at 381,954: roughly 85 percent Muslim, 11 percent Christian and 4 percent Jewish. The presence of this Arabic-speaking population under Ottoman rule is documented continuously for centuries, and modern genetic and archaeological studies find strong Levantine continuity consistent with long-term local ancestry. [cite:cjpme_historical_demography] [cite:factually_archaeological_evidence] The land was not empty, and its people were not newcomers. Still, a counted and continuous population is not yet a formal national identity.

The third answer concerns national identity, and here the leading Palestinian historian has documented the timeline himself. Rashid Khalidi is Edward Said Professor of Arab Studies at Columbia and a past president of the Middle East Studies Association. In his foundational study Palestinian Identity: The Construction of Modern National Consciousness, he argues that formal Palestinian national identity is modern. In his account it grew out of nationalist currents emerging among Ottoman peoples in the late nineteenth century and sharpened in what he calls the critical years of 1917 to 1923. [cite:wiki_palestinian_nationalism] [cite:cup_khalidi_palestinian_identity] Khalidi is explicit that this modern consciousness drew on a much older regional history and population. He does not treat its late emergence as proof that the people or their culture were invented, and his finding should not be read that way.

Zionism follows the same pattern. Formal Zionist national identity was organized at the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897: a modern political movement built on older religious and cultural material, as earlier sections of this book document. Formal Palestinian national identity, emerging in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, has the same structure. A rule that says "this national identity is recent, therefore illegitimate," applied to one side and not the other, is an inconsistent standard, not a historical finding. The parallel concerns how national consciousness formed. It does not mean the two movements' histories run alike in every other respect.

Taken together, the record supports three facts at once. There is an ancient and continuous Jewish connection to the land. There is a substantial, continuously documented Arab population under Ottoman rule. And there are modern national identities on both sides, formed through comparable political processes in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. None of these cancels the others. The question "who is truly indigenous" casts history as a single contest with one legitimate winner, and the documents support that frame for neither side. Nor do they resolve any present-day question of sovereignty or statehood. What they show is the shape of the history on which those questions rest.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: Words and Names
chapters.intro: Where “Semitic” and “antisemitism” came from, how a word can be used to stop a question, and what the names and symbols at the center of this story actually say.

sections.h: Semitic Is Not a Synonym for Jewish
sections.html:
Much of the modern argument over Israel turns on a single word, and that word has a history of its own. It runs in three stages: a linguist's term from the eighteenth century, a nineteenth-century coinage aimed at Jews, and a twenty-first-century dispute over whether the word should reach political criticism of a state.

The root is Shem, in Hebrew שֵׁם, one of the sons of Noah in the genealogy of Genesis 10. In 1781 the German scholar August Ludwig von Schlözer coined the term "Semitic" (semitisch) for the family of languages that the biblical genealogy traced to Shem. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] It classified languages, not races or religions. It worked the way "Romance languages" does: a family label, named after Rome, that covers French, Spanish and Italian without implying that their speakers are one people. Schlözer grouped Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Ge'ez, Akkadian and Phoenician together. Through most of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the word kept that classroom sense, alongside "Indo-European" and "Sino-Tibetan." Words change meaning over time; that is normal. What matters is tracking how and when this one changed.

The family today includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic, Tigrinya, Maltese, Ge'ez, Syriac and Mehri, as well as extinct Akkadian. By the word's original meaning, all their speakers are Semitic peoples, among them Arabs, Jews, Ethiopians, Assyrians, Chaldeans and Maltese. This is a textbook definition, not a political claim. Peer-reviewed population genetics points the same way for the Levant, finding substantial shared ancestry among many of the region's populations. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000] [cite:behar_2010_shared] [cite:haber_2013_bronze]

That applies directly to Palestinians. They speak Arabic, a Semitic language. According to the population genetics literature, including Nebel and colleagues in 2000 and Behar and colleagues in 2010, they descend from populations that have lived in the region continuously since antiquity, overlapping substantially with the ancestral pool of Levantine Jewish populations. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000] [cite:behar_2010_shared] On linguistic and genetic grounds alike, Palestinians fit the definition of a Semitic people. That fact does not resolve any particular dispute between Israelis and Palestinians. It settles something narrower: the conflict cannot coherently be described as Semites against anti-Semites.

The word "antisemitism" took on its political meaning in 1879. That year Wilhelm Marr, a German journalist and agitator who was a Lutheran, not a Jew, published Der Sieg des Judenthums über das Germanenthum (The Victory of Judaism over Germandom) and founded the League of Antisemites. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] He made "antisemitismus" the name of his movement, a euphemism for Judenhass, Jew-hatred, meant to sound scientific and modern rather than crude and religious. Moshe Zimmermann's 1986 biography, Wilhelm Marr: The Patriarch of Anti-Semitism, documents that the choice was deliberate. The adjective was older. In 1860 the Jewish scholar Moritz Steinschneider had written of "antisemitic prejudices" to attack Ernest Renan's claim that Semitic peoples were inferior. [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] Nothing in Marr's writing or his league's activity shows any concern with Arabic speakers or any other Semitic-language population. From Marr onward, antisemitism meant hatred of Jews, and it still does. That settles what the word means. It does not settle how any particular modern claim should be judged.

The familiar story ends with that settled meaning. The documents go on. The contested shift came much later. The working definition of antisemitism adopted in 2016 by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) carries 11 attached examples, 7 of which describe criticism of Israel or Zionism as antisemitic under certain conditions. In effect, it turned the word toward a new target: political criticism of a state and a political movement. [cite:ihra_definition] On March 25, 2021, more than 200 scholars, including Omer Bartov, Christopher Browning, Michael Rothberg and Noah Feldman, signed the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism. It kept the core definition but stated that boycott of Israel, criticism of settlements and criticism of Zionism as an ideology are not in themselves antisemitic. [cite:jerusalem_declaration] A popular version of the same move circulates in op-eds and online: the claim that opposing Israel denies Jews their right to national self-determination and is therefore discriminatory. It appears in pro-Israel commentary (a 2019 formulation by Bari Weiss is among the most cited), in advocacy organizations' own materials, and in critiques of them. [cite:currentaffairs_snappy_hasbara]

The Jerusalem Declaration has serious critics of its own. Dr. Dana Barnett of the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, and researchers writing for NGO Monitor, have argued that its exceptions could shelter antisemitic framing rather than guard against it. Those exceptions permit comparisons of Israel to settler colonialism or apartheid and treat BDS, the boycott movement, as ordinary non-violent protest. [cite:besa_jda_barnett] [cite:ngomonitor_jda_bogus] Credentialed scholars hold each position in print. Some say the IHRA definition reaches too far into legitimate criticism; others say the Jerusalem Declaration reaches too far in sheltering the real thing. This book does not resolve that dispute.

What the etymology does is clear the ground. Once "Semitic" is understood as a family of languages and their speakers, the conflict appears as what the documents show it to be: a political dispute between a state, a political movement and a displaced population, all of them Semitic in the word's original sense. The next section, [scene:s00b0|on the history of the word "antisemitism"], follows that word from Schlözer to the present.

sections.h: A Word Named by the Haters, Not the Hated
sections.html:
The word's paper trail runs from 1781 to 2015, and it tells a story in four steps. A linguist named a family of languages. Race science turned the label into a "race." A Jewish scholar first wrote "antisemitic" to attack that race theory. Then a German agitator who was not Jewish made "antisemitism" the name of his own movement against Jews. The familiar version says the word is precise, naming hatred of a people called Semites. The documents show a misnomer. Its meaning, though, is not in doubt.

The first step was linguistic. In 1781 the Göttingen historian August Ludwig von Schlözer coined "Semitic" (semitisch) for a family of related languages, borrowing the name of Shem, son of Noah, from Genesis 10. Today that family includes Hebrew, Aramaic, Arabic, Amharic, Tigrinya and Maltese. [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] The term classified languages. It said nothing about blood, race or religion, and it never belonged to one people.

The second step turned grammar into hierarchy. In 1855 the French scholar Ernest Renan published a comparative history of the Semitic languages that treated their speakers, Hebrews and Arabs alike, as a "Semitic race" inferior to the "Aryans." This was the race science of the era: a label made for languages, converted into a ranking of peoples. Historians now regard "Semitic race" as a discredited category, which is one reason the word still confuses. [cite:wiki_renan] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym]

The adjective came next, and a Jewish scholar coined it. In 1860 the bibliographer Moritz Steinschneider wrote of "antisemitic prejudices" (antisemitische Vorurteile) to rebut Renan's claim that Semitic peoples were inferior. In that first use, the target was the whole invented "Semitic race." [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] Within twenty years the word would be seized and narrowed to one people.

The man most associated with that narrowing was Wilhelm Marr (1819–1904), a German journalist and a Lutheran, not a Jew as is sometimes claimed. In 1879 he published The Victory of Judaism over Germandom and founded the League of Antisemites, the first German organization devoted to the alleged Jewish threat. The league called for forcing Jews out of Germany. Marr's Antisemitic Pamphlets of 1881 spread the word further. [cite:wiki_marr_1879] The term's purpose was to make old Jew-hatred sound like modern science. If Jews were a foreign "Semitic race," then no conversion and no number of centuries in Germany could make them German. The word was coined by the people doing the hating, about the people being hated. Marr's biographer Moshe Zimmermann reports that near the end of his life Marr renounced antisemitism in a text he never published. [cite:jvl_marr]

Jews had their own name for the same hatred. In 1882, after pogroms in the Russian Empire, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation. He called the hatred "Judeophobia," an irrational fear of Jews that he described as an inherited disease. The name left no doubt about the target. Pinsker concluded that Jews needed a homeland of their own, which makes the pamphlet one of the founding texts of Zionism. [cite:jvl_pinsker] [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] Marr and Pinsker wrote within three years of each other: one named the hatred to make it respectable, the other named it to answer it.

More than a century later, the institutions most invested in the word acknowledged the flaw in its root. In April 2015 the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance recommended writing "antisemitism" without a hyphen. The hyphen, it reasoned, "allows for the possibility of something called Semitism," lending weight to a discredited racial classification. Style guides followed, and The New York Times dropped the hyphen in 2021. [cite:ihra_spelling_2015] [cite:wjc_nyt_spelling]

Two things are therefore true together. The root is a misnomer: "Semitic" describes languages, Palestinians who speak Arabic are as Semitic as anyone, and many Jews have never spoken a Semitic language at home. And the meaning is settled by use: since the 1880s, "antisemitism" has meant hostility to Jews, and nothing broader. That cuts both ways. The retort "Arabs are Semites too, so I can't be antisemitic" fails, because words mean what they are used to mean, not what their parts suggest. Whether the word should stretch to cover political criticism of a state is a separate, still-contested question, set out in [scene:s00b|the preceding section]. The test lies in the target and the content of what is said, not in the label. [cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] [cite:ihra_spelling_2015]

sections.h: The Shield: When the Word Is Used to Stop a Question
sections.html:
The line that matters can be drawn simply. Hatred of Jewish people is antisemitism, and nothing in this book says otherwise. A question about what a government does is a question about a government, whether that government is Canada's, Mexico's or Israel's. Treating every question about Israel as antisemitic erases that line. The record from 2010 to 2026 shows how the erasure happens, what it costs the person asking, and what is also true on the other side.

Start with the text of the definition most governments and universities cite, the working definition of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance. It contains its own sentence on exactly this point: criticism of Israel similar to that leveled against any other country cannot be regarded as antisemitic. [cite:ihra_text_safeguard] That is the standard the definition sets for itself. What its attached examples add, and what remains disputed, is where criticism of Israel crosses into hostility to Jews.

The definition's lead drafter has said publicly that it is being misused. Kenneth Stern was the American Jewish Committee's antisemitism expert. He has testified that the definition "was not drafted, and was never intended, as a tool to target or chill speech on a college campus"; it was written to help governments collect data on antisemitism. In a December 2019 Guardian op-ed headlined "I drafted the definition of antisemitism. Rightwing Jews are weaponizing it," he called the executive order applying it to campuses an attack on academic freedom that would harm pro-Palestinian advocates and Jewish students alike. [cite:stern_guardian_2019] In 2024 he told NPR that weaponizing it makes students less safe. [cite:npr_stern_2024] [cite:politifact_aaa_2024]

Since then the guideline has moved toward law. A December 2019 executive order directed federal agencies, including the Education Department's civil rights office, to consider the definition when enforcing Title VI, the civil rights provision that office enforces. By August 2024, 35 states and the District of Columbia had adopted it in some form. On May 1, 2024, the House of Representatives passed the Antisemitism Awareness Act, which would write the definition into federal civil rights enforcement, by 320 votes to 91, with members of both parties voting no. The ACLU urged a no vote, warning that the bill would likely chill student speech by wrongly equating criticism of the Israeli government with antisemitism. As of October 2026 the bill is not law; the Senate version stalled in committee in 2025. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] [cite:legiscan_s558]

A label works by raising the price of a question, and the documented prices are concrete. In 2025 Columbia University lost $400 million in federal funding within four days of a federal task-force notice, and about 60 more universities received warning letters. Five days after that notice, Mahmoud Khalil, a recent Columbia graduate who had negotiated on behalf of the protesters, was detained for deportation. In July 2024, after an advocacy campaign, Meta began treating "Zionist" as a stand-in for Jews in narrowly defined hate-speech cases. Each of these cases has its own record, including real failures at Columbia that federal investigators documented. Together they show why many people choose not to ask.

The effect follows from the seriousness of the charge. Being called antisemitic is grave because antisemitism is a grave hatred. That gravity is exactly what gives the label its force when it is aimed at a question about a government. A person who asks risks a job, a place at school, a visa or an online account. So many stop asking, and the version they learned in school goes unexamined. This is what the ACLU and the definition's own drafter warned about. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] [cite:stern_guardian_2019] The effect is documented at the level of institutions, working through rules and penalties. This book does not claim to measure what happens inside any individual's mind.

The other half of the record matters just as much. The charge is sometimes misused; antisemitism is also real and rising. The ADL counted 9,354 antisemitic incidents in the United States in 2024, the most since it began counting in 1979. Federal investigators found that Columbia had no reporting system until the summer of 2024 and left swastika vandalism uninvestigated. Some speech that calls itself anti-Zionist does cross into hatred of Jews, and even the Jerusalem Declaration, written to defend criticism of Israel, lists examples of it. Many of the strongest critics of Israeli policy are themselves Jewish. Misusing the charge and ignoring real antisemitism both do damage, to Jews and to everyone asking honest questions.

Two questions sort almost every case. First: is a statement aimed at Jewish people, or at what a government does? Second, the definition's own standard: would this criticism be fair if aimed at any other country? If the subject is a government's actions, and the same thing would be said of Canada or Mexico, it is a political question, and asking it is not hatred. If the subject is Jews as a people, or the statement holds them responsible for a state, or draws on old tropes, it is antisemitism, whatever it calls itself. [cite:ihra_text_safeguard]

sections.h: Jacob Becomes Israel: What the Text Says
sections.html:
Before the word "Israel" named a movement, a territory or a state, it named a man. The text in which it first appears says something narrower and more personal than the nation or the Promised Land. In the Hebrew Bible, the word begins as a renaming, given to one individual after a single night.

The setting is Genesis 32. Jacob is alone at the ford of the Jabbok river on the night before he is to meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. All night he wrestles with a figure the text calls a man, an angel and, in Jacob's own words afterward, God. When the struggle ends, he receives a new name:

"Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have struggled with God and with men, and have prevailed."

This verse, Genesis 32:28, is the word's first documented occurrence anywhere in the Hebrew Bible.[cite:genesis_32_biblegateway] The word appears 2,362 times across the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, 2,284 times in the Hebrew Bible and 78 in the New Testament, and every later use traces back to this verse. Jacob names the place of the struggle Peniel, "face of God," because, he says, "I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared." Centuries later the prophet Hosea retold the story (Hosea 12:3–4), a sign that later biblical writers understood this episode as the origin of the name.

How the name is built is well established. Yisra'el joins El, the ancient Semitic word for God, to a root related to sarah, meaning to strive, contend or prevail. The standard scholarly reading is "he who struggles with God," or, if El is read as the subject, "God strives." The grammar allows both, and the text does not say which was meant.[cite:wiki_israel_name] El did not belong to Hebrew alone; it was shared across Canaanite, Ugaritic and other Northwest Semitic languages, a point developed in [scene:s00b|the discussion of the word "Semitic"]. The derivation is not contested. Hebrew lexicons, Brown-Driver-Briggs among them, rabbinic commentary and Christian biblical scholarship all hold it.

The text also builds in a contrast. Jacob's original name, Ya'akov, is related to akev, "heel": he was born grasping the heel of his twin, Esau, and the root carries overtones of crookedness and of following from behind. The letters of Yisra'el can also call to mind yashar, "straight" or "upright." Several Hebrew-language sources read this as deliberate: the grasping, deceptive Jacob and the upright, prevailing Israel are the same person, transformed.[cite:wiki_jacob] Before the name belongs to a nation, it describes a change in one man's character, earned through struggle.

From there the name gathers layers. When it is given, it belongs to one person. Generations later it names the descendants of his twelve sons. Centuries after that it attaches to a specific territory. Only in 1948 does it become the name of a modern nation-state. Each is a separate, later development. Each deserves to be tracked on its own, not read backward into the verse as though they had always been one thing.

Reading the verse in its original context makes no claim about how later biblical authors, ancient Israelite communities or modern political movements would use the word. Those uses are real and documented, and this book takes them up elsewhere. What the primary text establishes is the starting point: a personal name, given after a night of wrestling, meaning one who has struggled with God and with men and prevailed.

sections.h: IS-RA-EL: A Symbolic Reading of the Name
sections.html:
The previous section traced the name Israel to its documented roots: El, the Semitic word for God, joined to a root meaning to strive or prevail. This section offers something of a different kind. It sets out one symbolic reading of the name, drawn from esoteric traditions, the inner schools of religious thought. It is an interpretation laid over a documented text, not a finding of linguistics or of the archives, and it should be read that way. Critics dismiss it as mere wordplay with no connection to any religious tradition. They are partly right and partly wrong, and the line between the two is worth drawing carefully.

The reading splits the English spelling of the name into three parts. IS is taken to evoke Isis, the Egyptian goddess whom Hermetic and other inner traditions associate with a receptive, magnetic, lunar principle, what later traditions would call the divine feminine.[cite:wiki_isis_egyptian] RA is taken to evoke the Egyptian sun god, a radiant, generative principle that later traditions would call the divine masculine.[cite:wiki_ra_egyptian] EL is the one part that is genuine etymology: the actual ancient Semitic word for God.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] In this reading, El stands for the unified field above both poles. "Israel," so understood, names neither a place nor a people but a state of being, in which feminine and masculine are brought together under the divine. Its proponents connect this to the transformation that Genesis 32 describes in Jacob.

The limits of this reading need to be stated plainly. It works on the English spelling, not the Hebrew original. It does not claim that ancient Hebrew scribes hid the names of Egyptian gods in the word. It does not displace the documented derivation, which remains the scholarly linguistic record. What it proposes is a symbolic resonance. On this view, transformation traditions across the ancient Near East and Egypt shared a common structural language of polarity, integration and ascent, and the Jacob story reads coherently within that language, whether or not the etymology is literal.

Part of the reading, however, is not new at all. Mainstream Jewish commentary supports the idea that Jacob's story describes an inner transformation open to any person, not only the origin of a family line. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, a widely respected Orthodox authority, wrote of Jacob and Israel as two aspects of one person. He asked readers whether they are Jacob, embarrassed by who they are, or Israel, with the courage to stand upright.[cite:sacks_jacob_israel] What this book adds, and marks as its own interpretive layer, is the specifically Hermetic vocabulary of IS-RA-EL. That vocabulary is not part of mainstream Jewish or Christian commentary.

The traditions themselves also build non-literal reading into their methods. Judaism has PaRDeS, a named four-level method of interpretation: Peshat, the plain sense; Remez, the hinted or allegorical; Derash, the comparative and homiletical; and Sod, the secret or mystical, the level from which Kabbalah grows. One traditional image has the text descending from above while the reader climbs through the four levels from below.[cite:wiki_pardes_exegesis] Islam developed a parallel distinction between tafsir, conventional commentary, and ta'wil, esoteric interpretation, practiced in Shia, Sufi and Sunni scholarship since at least the eighth century CE. The Quran's own account of Khidr refers to an inner meaning behind outward acts.[cite:wiki_esoteric_quran_interpretation] [cite:britannica_tawil] In Christianity, the third-century Church Father Origen helped establish allegorical interpretation.[cite:wiki_aggadah] Scholarship on medieval Catholic exegesis records that in the High Middle Ages a commentary on scripture was thought perfect only if it contained both a literal and an allegorical interpretation.[cite:hnet_tawil_medieval_catholic] In each tradition, the plain sense is named alongside the non-literal one.

The symbolic reading also points to a narrower argument about the modern state's name. Herzl's 1896 pamphlet weighed Argentina alongside Palestine, and in 1903 the Zionist Congress voted on British East Africa. Whichever territory had been chosen, a state called "Israel" would have carried the same scriptural weight, because that weight travels with the word, not with a particular piece of land.[cite:genesis_15_18] On this view, a largely secular political movement attached its project to a name already heavy with religious meaning. This book has found no primary source showing that Herzl, Ben-Gurion or the founders of 1948 consciously intended any such symbolism, and it does not claim they did. The name carries the weight regardless of intent.

The reading, then, is a key for thinking about the name's layered resonance. It is not a documented finding about the name's origin or about anyone's intention, and it should be weighed accordingly.

sections.h: The Star and the Menorah
sections.html:
When a political movement chooses one symbol over another, the choice says something about what the movement takes itself to be. Most people assume that the Star of David is the ancient symbol of the Jewish people, and that it stands on Israel's flag as it always has. The dated record shows two symbols of very different ages, and a choice between them made first by a political congress in 1897 and then by a new state in 1948.

The older of the two is the seven-branched menorah. Exodus 25:31–40 describes it as the lampstand of the Tabernacle, and it later stood in the Temple in Jerusalem. [cite:exodus_25_bible] Its oldest visual record is on the Arch of Titus in Rome, completed in 81 CE, which depicts the sack of the Second Temple. [cite:wiki_arch_titus] It is the oldest continuous Jewish symbol, and it is the emblem of the modern State of Israel, though on the state seal rather than the flag. [cite:wiki_menorah]

The star's history is much shorter. The six-pointed star as a shape is old and appears in many unrelated cultures, but the Magen David, the Shield of David, is medieval as a distinctively Jewish symbol. Its documented use as a Jewish communal emblem appears in fourteenth-century Prague. In 1354 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV granted Prague's Jewish community the right to its own flag, red with a yellow Star of David. Its adoption as the universal Jewish symbol came later still. European Jewish communities drove it between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, wanting an emblem to match the Christian cross and the Islamic crescent. In some traditions it carried Kabbalistic associations, but it was not widely recognized as the Jewish symbol until the modern period. [cite:unpacked_star_of_david_history] [cite:wiki_star_david] Gershom Scholem's 1949 monograph, Magen David: The History of a Symbol, documents how the modern period, and Zionism in particular, fixed the hexagram as the Jewish emblem. Before the seventeenth century, on his account, the symbol of the people would have been the menorah. [cite:scholem_star_david] According to several historians, Herzl himself called the star a "meaningless symbol of Judaism" in this period. None of this makes the star less meaningful to those who hold it now; symbols gain meaning whatever their age. The point concerns the claim of antiquity, which is often overstated.

The flag came out of the movement. In Der Judenstaat of 1896, Herzl proposed a white flag with seven gold stars standing for a seven-hour workday. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] It never caught on. At the First Zionist Congress in Basel in August 1897, a different design flew instead: two blue horizontal stripes on white, with a blue Magen David between them. [cite:basel_program] It closely followed a design that David Wolffsohn had created in 1885 for the Bnei Zion association in Boston, modeled on the colors of the tallit, the prayer shawl. Wolffsohn, who later succeeded Herzl as president of the World Zionist Organization, is credited with proposing it as the movement's banner. [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel]

Why the movement chose the star rather than the menorah is a matter of interpretation. Scholem argued that the star was chosen precisely because it lacked the menorah's religious weight. That left it "available" for a secular political project that needed a Jewish symbol without tying itself to rabbinic authority. [cite:scholem_star_david] The documented record supports a plainer explanation as well. By the 1890s the Magen David was the closest thing to a widely recognized, non-sectarian Jewish emblem, legible across a movement whose members came from many religious and secular backgrounds.

The new state then adopted the movement's banner. When Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, the Provisional Council of State took the Basel flag as the state flag, a choice formalized on October 28, 1948. [cite:declaration_israel_1948] [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] The menorah went on the state seal in 1949. Neither decision was made without debate. The Provisional Council first tried to create a distinct state flag. Its stated concern was that Diaspora Jews who already used the Zionist flag would face accusations of dual loyalty if their movement's banner became a foreign state's flag. It considered and rejected an alternative seven-stars design proposed by Otto Wassisch. In July 1948 Foreign Minister Moshe Sharett cabled Diaspora Jewish leaders for their views, and the answer came back overwhelmingly in favor of keeping the existing flag. The emblem was more contested still. A selection committee rejected 450 proposals from 164 applicants outright, and a second public competition was held. The winning design, by the Shamir brothers, was sent back twice: once to add the word "Israel," and once to replace their modern menorah with the historical version carved on the Arch of Titus. [cite:crwflags_israel_flag_1948] [cite:wjc_flag_unveiled_1948] [cite:nli_emblem_israel_blog]

Both facts hold at once. The choice was considered and consulted on, and it still placed the movement's symbol on the flag and the Temple's on the seal. The movement never hid that the flag was its 1897 banner; the history is public and uncontested. What it shows is that the flag's lineage runs through a nineteenth-century political movement, not through the Temple period.

Some readers go further. One reading holds that a state emerging from a religious tradition might have led with that tradition's oldest symbol, and that leading with the movement's emblem signals which lineage the state understands itself to continue: the political project of Herzl and the Congress. [cite:basel_program] A related reading holds that displaying the flag in synagogues, schools and community centers teaches, below the level of argument, that the political project of 1897 and the religious tradition of millennia are one thing. That is the same conflation traced in [scene:s00c|the section on Zionism and Judaism]. These are interpretations, not documented findings. Many Israelis and Jews elsewhere experience the flag as embracing both histories, and most who display it do so out of a genuine connection to Israel or to Jewish identity, not as part of any messaging campaign.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Peoples and Traditions
chapters.intro: The Jewish lineages, the difference between a religion and a political movement, the long record of dissent from within, the Christian argument over one verse, and centuries of coexistence.

sections.h: The Jewish Lineages: Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi
sections.html:
If "Semitic" names a family larger than any one people, Jewish identity is itself a family of distinct communities. No one disputes that Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish. Two opposite errors nevertheless circulate. The first holds that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Central Asian Khazar converts and have no real Middle Eastern ancestry. The second holds that all Jewish communities are genetically and historically identical, as if two thousand years of separate histories had left no mark. The genetic record supports neither.

Each community has its own history. Mizrahi Jews, the Jews of Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Iran, Syria and elsewhere, never left the Middle East. Their presence there goes back millennia; in Iraq it is traced to the Babylonian Exile of 586 BCE. As late as 1945, Baghdad alone held roughly 140,000 Jews, a third of the city. Sephardi Jews trace their roots to Iberia, where their presence predates the Muslim conquest. Ferdinand and Isabella expelled them in 1492, and most resettled across the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, among existing, related Middle Eastern Jewish populations. Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries under Ottoman rule. Ashkenazi communities formed in the Rhineland in the early medieval period and later moved east into Poland, Lithuania, Russia and Ukraine. By the nineteenth century they were the majority of world Jewry, and they produced most of the Jewish immigration to the United States.

The most thorough genetic study is a 2010 paper in Nature by Behar, Yunusbayev, Metspalu and 18 co-authors. The team compared genome-wide data from 14 Jewish communities across Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia against 69 non-Jewish populations. Most Jewish communities, Ashkenazi included, clustered closer to one another and to Middle Eastern populations than to the peoples among whom they had lived. The paper read this as support for common origins in the Middle East, followed by migrations. [cite:behar_2010_nature] It also found structure within that picture: an Ashkenazi, North African and Sephardi cluster, a Caucasus and Middle Eastern cluster, and a distinct Yemenite cluster. The finding, then, is not that every Jewish community is genetically identical. It is that each carries a detectable shared ancestral signal, with real regional differences layered on top. No single study is beyond revision, but this one remains the most comprehensive of its kind, and its core finding has held up under later attempts at replication.

The Khazar hypothesis has been tested directly. It proposes that Ashkenazi Jews descend substantially from the Khazars, a Turkic people of the Caucasus and southern Russia whose ruling elite is reported to have converted to Judaism around the eighth or ninth century CE. That elite conversion is a separately documented event. The claim that it explains the origin of the whole Ashkenazi population is a much larger one. In a 2013 follow-up, Behar and colleagues compared Ashkenazi genetic data with samples from peoples native to the old Khazar region and found, in their words, "no indication" of a Khazar contribution. Ashkenazi ancestry traces primarily to Middle Eastern and European populations. [cite:behar_2013_khazar] The hypothesis matters beyond genetics because it has a documented history of use in antisemitic argument, to claim that Ashkenazi Jews have no real connection to the land and are not "really" Jewish.

The European share in Ashkenazi ancestry is real and should be stated plainly. It is substantial on the maternal line, the product of roughly two thousand years of intermarriage and conversion in European societies. It sits alongside, not in place of, the shared ancient Levantine origin on the paternal line that the same studies document.

Scripture, read on its own terms, makes the same point about scope. In the genealogies of Genesis 10–11 and 25, Shem's line runs through many generations to Abraham, and then Abraham's line divides. Ishmael is traditionally associated with Arab peoples. Through Isaac come Esau, traditionally associated with Edom, and Jacob, later renamed Israel. By the text's own account, all three lines descend from Shem. [cite:genesis_10_11_bible] [cite:genesis_25_esau_ishmael] "Semitic" was never a synonym for the line of Jacob, which is one branch of the tree. The point is scope, not rank: the text presents all three as branches of one root.

An analogy helps, provided its limits are stated. A Salvadoran, a Mexican and a Peruvian are all Latino, yet each carries a different ancestral mix of Indigenous American, Spanish colonial and other ancestry. A different mix makes no one less Latino. In the same way, Mizrahi Jews carry concentrated, continuous Levantine ancestry, while Ashkenazi Jews carry that same documented root plus substantial European admixture. The comparison illustrates one structure: a shared category containing different histories. It does not claim that Jewish and Latino identity work the same way historically, religiously or genetically.

The Khazar claim returned to public view on February 19–20, 2026, when Tucker Carlson interviewed Mike Huckabee, the U.S. Ambassador to Israel. Carlson asked why everyone in the land should not be genetically tested to find out who Abram's descendants are, saying that "we've cracked the human genome." He singled out Benjamin Netanyahu, citing his family's Polish origin. Huckabee, a committed Christian Zionist, pushed back in the room, calling it a "dangerous conspiracy theory" from "some of the darkest realms of the internet." Reporters at JTA, the Times of Israel, the Jerusalem Post and the Forward identified the underlying claim as the Khazar theory. [cite:jta_carlson_khazar_2026] [cite:toi_carlson_khazar_2026] The episode raised a separate question that deserves its own answer: what threshold of ancestry would make an identity claim legitimate? No geneticist, historian or legal body has ever defined one, for this question or any other. Treaties, borders and citizenship law do not run on DNA percentages, for Israel or for any other nation. Keeping the tested and unsupported genetic claim apart from that broader question is how the discredited version is kept from returning by another door.

sections.h: Zionism Is Not Judaism
sections.html:
In August 1897, in Basel, Switzerland, a political movement was founded. That movement, Zionism, is often treated as the same thing as Judaism, a religion and a set of ethnic and cultural lineages thousands of years old. The record draws a line between the two, and Jews drew it first. Zionism's founder said as much in his own words, and Jewish religious and political bodies across several traditions have kept the distinction alive ever since.

Theodor Herzl was an assimilated Viennese Jew, secular in outlook. He was a correspondent for the Neue Freie Presse, not a rabbi or a religious scholar. He wrote Der Judenstaat in 1896 and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel on August 29–31, 1897. Afterward he wrote in his diary:

At Basel I founded the Jewish State.

"Founded" was his own word, written in a private diary rather than for public messaging. Herzl also gave serious consideration to Argentina and Uganda before Palestine was settled on. At its founding, then, political Zionism treated location as a practical question. [cite:herzl_diaries] [cite:herzl_judenstaat] Herzl's own secularism does not mean every early Zionist was secular; the movement drew both religious and secular support from early on.

The most formal Jewish rejection of a national return came before Zionism existed. In November 1885, twelve years before Basel, American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which declared:

We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron, nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state.

This was the public, signed position of the largest Jewish denomination in America at the time. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] It stood until the 1937 Columbus Platform softened it, and substantial Reform opposition to political Zionism continued even then. The familiar story holds that Judaism had always longed for a return to Zion, and that Zionism simply organized that longing. This document is hard to square with that story. Reform Judaism's institutional position later shifted considerably; the platform records 1885, not the present.

In October 1897, a few months after Basel, Jewish workers in Vilna founded the General Jewish Labor Bund. The Bund rejected Zionism as a political solution. It argued instead for Jewish national-cultural autonomy inside the countries where Jews already lived, with Yiddish as the everyday language, socialist politics, and doikayt, "hereness": building here rather than going there. [cite:wiki_bund] Accounts of its size differ. One figure puts membership above 400,000 across the Russian Empire by 1917, larger than the Zionist movement in Eastern Europe. Henry Tobias's history of the Bund in Russia describes a genuine mass movement with tens of thousands of members in the early twentieth century. Either way, it was no fringe. Its destruction came from the Holocaust and from Soviet suppression, not from losing an open argument with Zionism. The Bund's existence does not make its position the authentic Jewish one. It shows that Jews contested the equation of Jewish with Zionist, at scale, from the movement's first year.

Criticism also came from inside the Zionist idea. Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg (1856–1927), who wrote as Ahad Ha'am, "One of the People," argued for cultural Zionism: a Jewish spiritual and cultural center in Palestine. At the same time he warned against Herzl's political version. His 1891 essay "Truth from Eretz Israel" recorded the Arab population already living in the land and warned that the project would produce conflict: "We are used to believing abroad that Palestine is nowadays almost totally desolate... but in fact this is not the case. It is difficult to find in the land any tillable land which is not already tilled." [cite:wiki_ahad_haam] The warning does not prove his alternative more workable. It shows that the population, and the risk, were seen from inside the movement from the start.

A religious argument followed in 1958, when Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, published VaYoel Moshe. The book rests on the Three Oaths of the Talmud, Ketubot 111a, and holds that Jewish tradition forbids re-establishing sovereignty in the land by human political force before the Messiah comes. In this reading, political Zionism violates a religious commitment rather than fulfilling it. The Satmar community numbers about 130,000 in the United States alone, in Williamsburg, Kiryas Joel and Monsey, with communities in Israel, London, Antwerp and Montreal. It is the largest Hasidic dynasty in the world, and it still teaches this position. [cite:wiki_satmar] It is not the majority Orthodox position, and this book does not present it as one.

Laid on one timeline, the distinction runs from 1885 to the present: the Pittsburgh Platform, Ahad Ha'am's warning in 1891, Basel and the Bund in 1897, Satmar in 1958. [cite:basel_program] In contemporary Jewish life, Judith Butler's Parting Ways, Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism and the organization Jewish Voice for Peace carry the argument on. [cite:butler_parting_ways] [cite:beinart_crisis_zionism] [cite:jvp_org] The distinction matters because collapsing it turns criticism of a political project into what reads as an attack on a people, the move traced in [scene:s00b|the section on the word "Semitic"]. Holding the distinction does not mean Zionists are wrong to see their support as bound up with their Jewish identity, nor that every Jew draws the line in the same place.

Two further arguments extend the point; they are arguments, not findings. The first is a thought experiment built on Herzl's alternatives. Uganda's population spoke Bantu languages. Argentina's spoke Spanish and Indigenous American languages such as Quechua, Guaraní and Mapudungun. None of these is Semitic. Palestine's population spoke Arabic, which is. [cite:wiki_bantu_languages] [cite:wiki_languages_argentina] [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] On this reasoning, the charge that criticizing the state is "antisemitic" found a surface foothold in Palestine only because the people displaced there happened to speak a Semitic language. The argument does not make the conflation any more valid in Palestine than it would have been elsewhere. It explains how the conflation spread.

The second argument concerns selective use. The broad, correct meaning of "Semitic" is often invoked to argue that criticism of Israeli policy cannot coherently be called antisemitic, since Palestinians are Semitic too. On the word's own terms, that argument is sound. [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000] The same breadth is rarely invoked when the subject is Palestinian displacement, such as the roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians displaced in 1948 whom later chapters document. This book does not argue that "antisemitism" should be stretched to cover harm to Arabs; the word has always meant hatred of Jews. Its point is that Palestinian displacement and casualties need no borrowed word. They are documented on their own terms, and they deserve the same seriousness whichever way the "Semitic" argument happens to point.

sections.h: Opposition to Zionism Across Lineages
sections.html:
Zionism was contested inside Jewish life from its first year, as earlier sections showed. A further point deserves plain statement: that opposition was never confined to one community. It is sometimes said that Jewish opposition to Zionism is small and marginal, or that it comes from a single group. The record from 1885 to the present tells a different story. It shows Zionism-critical and anti-Zionist positions in both the Ashkenazi and Mizrahi lineages, two of the communities described in [scene:s00b2|the section on Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews], on religious and secular grounds alike.

The earliest opposition was Ashkenazi and religious. In 1885 American Reform Judaism, a movement founded and led by Ashkenazi immigrants and their American-born successors, adopted the Pittsburgh Platform. It defined Jewish identity as a religious community rather than a nation awaiting territorial restoration. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] The twelve-year gap before Basel matters. The platform was not a reaction against Zionism. It was a position that existed first and simply never adopted Zionism's framework when that framework appeared. Reform Judaism's institutional position shifted considerably over the twentieth century; the 1885 document records its founding stance.

The second current was Ashkenazi and secular. The General Jewish Labour Bund was founded in Vilna in 1897, the same year as the First Zionist Congress. It organized Jewish workers across the Pale of Settlement, the Russian Empire's zone of Jewish residence. It rejected emigration to Palestine and argued for Jewish cultural and political autonomy where Jews already lived. [cite:wiki_bund] Its members were not indifferent to antisemitism. They lived through the same pogroms that gave Zionism its urgency. Their disagreement was over strategy.

The Bund's later history shows how its story ended, which is not the same as showing that its argument was refuted. When the Bolsheviks took power in October 1917, the Bund split. A majority faction, believing it was joining an ally on workers' rights, merged into the Communist Party. A minority led by Vladimir Medem rejected Bolshevik rule as undemocratic and hostile to Jewish national rights. In 1921 the Bolsheviks dissolved the Bund entirely. Remaining members were imprisoned or fled. Mark Liber, one of its leading figures and its representative on the Executive Committee of the Petrograd Soviet during the revolution, was executed in the Stalinist purges in 1937. In Poland the Bund survived independently between the wars and into the Holocaust, and Bundists fought alongside Zionists and Communists in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Survivors who tried to regroup after the war were suppressed again, this time by Poland's new Communist government. [cite:jewishcurrents_bund_rise_fall] [cite:britannica_bund] Within a single generation the organization was dissolved by two governments, one of which its own members had helped bring to power. Suppression by force proves nothing about a movement's ideas; the record documents what happened to the organization, not a verdict on what it believed.

The third current is Ashkenazi, Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, and active today. Neturei Karta, the most publicly visible anti-Zionist Haredi community, rests on the argument of Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum's VaYoel Moshe of 1958. In that argument, the ingathering of exiles and the restoration of sovereignty are meant to come through divine action in the Messianic era, so a state established beforehand by human political and military effort is itself the transgression. [cite:wiki_satmar] Its members still take part in public demonstrations. They are a specific and relatively small community, and most Haredi and Orthodox institutions hold other positions.

A different kind of critique came from Mizrahi Jews inside the state. Scholars including Ella Shohat, Sami Shalom Chetrit and Yehouda Shenhav documented how an Ashkenazi-dominated establishment treated Mizrahi immigrants after 1948: placement in peripheral development towns, discrimination in employment, and the sidelining of Middle Eastern Jewish culture in favor of an Ashkenazi-coded national culture. [cite:chetrit_mizrahi_struggle] This is a critique of the state's conduct from within Mizrahi intellectual life. It is not a claim about Mizrahi opinion as a whole; many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state.

Another strand sat inside Zionism itself. In 1925 Martin Buber and Judah Magnes, with colleagues including Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold, founded Brit Shalom. In 1942 they founded Ihud, in response to the Biltmore Conference's demand for a Jewish Commonwealth. Both groups called for a binational state with full civic equality between Jews and Arabs. In 1947 Buber and Magnes testified against partition before UNSCOP, the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine, to Ben-Gurion's documented fury. Buber called the treatment of the Arab population "the moral acid test of Zionism." Separately, Hannah Arendt's 1944 essay "Zionism Reconsidered" warned that an exclusively Jewish sovereign state risked permanent conflict and dependence on a great-power patron. [cite:wiki_ihud] [cite:britainpalestine_buber_magnes] [cite:researchgate_arendt_zionism_reconsidered] Brit Shalom was a small circle of intellectuals, never a mass movement. It drew fierce hostility from Labor and Revisionist Zionists, some of whom called its members traitors, while Albert Einstein publicly supported it. It dissolved around 1933. Historians tie its failure to the 1929 Hebron violence and the Arab Revolt of 1936–39, which undercut its premise that Arab leaders would accept binational equality. [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] After May 1948 Magnes turned to proposing a confederation between the Jewish state and a future Palestinian Arab state, until his death that October. Ihud's publication, Ner, continued until 1964. [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism] Precision matters here. Buber and Magnes were Zionists who rejected the sovereignty-and-partition model, not anti-Zionists in the sense of the Bund or Neturei Karta.

The dividing line, then, does not run between lineages. Some of the earliest and most organized anti-Zionist traditions were Ashkenazi, and a sustained critique of the state came from Mizrahi scholars. The line runs through Jewish life as a whole, between those who hold the political position of Zionism and those who contest or reject it. This book has no current polling on what share of any community holds which view. What the record establishes is that both support and opposition have had serious, long-standing representation for more than 140 years.

sections.h: "Bless Israel and Be Blessed": Genesis 12:3 and the Christian Dispute
sections.html:
The name Israel carries religious weight within Christianity as well as Judaism, and for a large American constituency that weight bears directly on politics. One position holds that the Bible requires Christians to support the modern State of Israel. The opposite holds that the Bible has nothing to say on the question. The record shows something else: a single verse that Christians read in sharply different ways, with the disagreement running through Christianity itself.

The verse is Genesis 12:3. In it God speaks to Abram, later called Abraham:

"I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you."

The promise of land follows in Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8. The words were spoken to Abraham. The question is whom they address today.

Christian Zionists read the verse as a standing mandate. Groups such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem describe it as the biblical basis for standing with Israel.[cite:icej_cz] [cite:rmc_cz] Many dispensationalist believers go further, viewing Israel's restoration as a precondition for the return of Christ. On this reading, the verse applies to the modern state, and supporting that state is a religious obligation.
