Other Christian traditions read the verse differently. Covenant theology, and the theology known as amillennialism, hold that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and the church, citing Galatians 3:16 and 3:29, and that it does not pass to a modern government.[cite:studylight_gen12] Some scholars also note that the passage stresses blessing to all nations more than it stresses land.[cite:pctii_gen12] On these readings, the Israel of Genesis and the secular state founded in 1948 are not the same thing.

In June 2025 the dispute broke into public view in an exchange between Senator Ted Cruz and Tucker Carlson. Cruz cited the verse. Carlson asked whether the political state led by Benjamin Netanyahu is the same "Israel" as the one in Scripture.[cite:think_gen12] The exchange settled nothing, but it put a theological disagreement in open political view.

Judaism, too, holds differing views on how scripture relates to the modern state. Early Zionism was largely secular, and some Haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, Jews oppose the existence of a Jewish state before the coming of the Messiah. The belief that a religious text mandates support for a particular political state is therefore not held uniformly by Christians or by Jews.

Palestinian Christians, about 1 percent of the population today, are also part of this story; this book treats their history separately.

Whether Genesis 12:3 applies to a modern state is a theological question, argued inside Christianity itself, and this book does not resolve it. What it establishes is narrower. The verse is cited for opposite conclusions, the disagreement is ongoing, and the claim that "the Bible requires it" is one tradition's reading, not a settled fact.

sections.h: Jews and Arabs: A Thousand Years of Coexistence
sections.html:
For more than a thousand years, Jewish communities lived across the Muslim-majority Middle East and North Africa: in Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Sana'a, Fez, Tunis and Casablanca. In some cities they formed a plurality or even a majority. One of the most durable claims about this history holds that Jews and Arabs never lived together in peace, and that an ancient, irreconcilable hatred is the natural and permanent state between them. The documented record does not support it. That coexistence was never utopian, and real violence occurred. But it was neither marginal nor brief.

The best-known chapter is al-Andalus, as Muslim Iberia was called, home to what is known as the Jewish Golden Age of the tenth to twelfth centuries. Its figures included Maimonides (Cordoba, 1135–1204), Judah Halevi, Solomon ibn Gabirol and Samuel HaNagid. Jewish scholars wrote philosophy in Arabic, served as viziers and produced foundational works of rabbinic literature. The period was not free of violence; Granada saw a pogrom in 1066. Yet historians including María Rosa Menocal, David Nirenberg and Mark Cohen document a sustained period of Jewish-Muslim intellectual and civic collaboration without parallel in Christian Europe of the same era.[cite:menocal_ornament]

When Ferdinand and Isabella expelled the Jews of Spain in 1492, Sultan Bayezid II opened Ottoman territory to receive them. Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries. Under the Ottoman millet system, each religious community governed itself under its own leaders, with legal, educational and religious autonomy; the Chief Rabbi of Istanbul was responsible for all Ottoman Jews. Jewish communities lived in Istanbul, İzmir, Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, Cairo and Jerusalem. This was not equality with Muslims. As dhimmi, non-Muslim subjects of a Muslim state, Jews paid the jizya tax and lived under restrictions. But the system sustained four centuries of daily civic life. It produced Sephardic and Mizrahi literature, and the mystical school of Safed associated with Isaac Luria and Joseph Caro. Norman Stillman's documentary sourcebook The Jews of Arab Lands collects the primary evidence.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands]

Baghdad offers the clearest single case. Jews had lived in Mesopotamia continuously since the Babylonian Exile of 586 BCE, more than 2,500 years. This community compiled the Babylonian Talmud between roughly the third and sixth centuries CE. It is one of the two foundational texts of rabbinic Judaism, and it was produced in what became Iraq, not in the land of Israel. By the mid-twentieth century, Baghdad's Jewish population is documented at roughly 90,000 to 140,000, depending on the year and the source, close to a third of the city. Families such as the Sassoons, Kadoories and Basris built commercial networks across the British Empire. Iraq's first finance minister, Sassoon Heskel, was Jewish, and chief rabbis advised the government. In 1917 the community welcomed British forces. Sasson Somekh, a Baghdad-born Jew who later became a professor of Arabic literature at Tel Aviv University, recorded this world in his memoir Baghdad, Yesterday.[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday]

That world ended within a single decade. The Farhud of June 1941, which took place during a short-lived pro-Axis coup, marked a serious rupture. After 1948, legal restrictions, property confiscations and further violence sped up departures, while organized emigration efforts by Israel and the Jewish Agency actively encouraged them. Both forces are documented, and neither explains the exodus without the other. Ella Shohat has documented the second-class treatment many Iraqi Jews then met in Israel: one displacement followed by another.[cite:shohat_sephardim_israel] Today Baghdad's community is functionally gone. The events of 1948 to 1972 are told in full in [scene:s00e2|the account of the exodus and its aftermath].

None of this shows that persecution never happened. It shows that persecution was not the whole story. A community that endured twenty-five centuries in Mesopotamia, and Jewish communities that lived under Muslim rule from Iberia to Iraq for a millennium, do not fit the frame of ancient and permanent hatred. Nor does the record support the opposite simplification, of unbroken harmony. Centuries of integration and specific, dated ruptures belong in the same account. What broke that coexistence, and when, is a twentieth-century story, and it is the subject of what follows.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Two Displacements
chapters.intro: Two great movements of people in the middle of the twentieth century, and why they were not one even exchange.

sections.h: The Exodus of 1948–1972 and Its Aftermath
sections.html:
Between 1948 and 1972, roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries. The familiar account tells this as a single, simple story of rescue: Jews were persecuted throughout Arab lands until Israel gave them refuge. The familiar version stops there. The documents do not. The departures had several causes, operating at the same time and documented separately: violence and legal persecution by Arab states, organized and named Israeli recruitment operations, and, in specific and contested cases, sabotage. What happened to many of the arrivals once they reached Israel is a second, distinct story, and in places a grave one.

The turning point in Iraqi Jewish memory came seven years before Israel existed. On 1–2 June 1941, after the collapse of a pro-Nazi coup in Iraq, rioters in Baghdad killed at least 128 Jews. That is the official count of an Iraqi government commission of inquiry; some estimates run as high as 180. More than 1,000 people were injured, and roughly 900 Jewish homes and more than 1,500 businesses were looted or destroyed.[cite:ushmm_farhud] This event, the Farhud, cannot be explained as a reaction to the 1948 war or the Nakba, the Palestinian displacement of that year. The dates do not permit it.

Law and organization set the Iraqi exodus itself in motion. On 2 March 1950, Iraq's parliament passed a law permitting Jews to leave on condition that they surrender their Iraqi citizenship. A later law required departing Jews to sell their property and liquidate their businesses before going, so that economic loss was built into the exit itself. Israel and the Jewish Agency organized a mass airlift, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah. Shlomo Hillel, an Iraqi-born agent of Mossad LeAliyah Bet, negotiated personally with Iraqi authorities and later described the operation in a memoir, Operation Babylon. Flights ran through Cyprus and Iran via the Near East Transport Company and El Al. Israeli authorities had planned for about 300 arrivals a day; at the peak, 1,400 came. By the end of 1951 more than 107,000 Iraqi Jews had been airlifted, and about 16,000 more had left by other routes. By early 1952, of Iraq's roughly 130,000 Jews, only about 6,000 remained.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:wiki_shlomo_hillel]

Iraq was not the only case. Operation Magic Carpet airlifted approximately 48,000 to 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 1949–50. Operation Yachin, conducted in secret from 1961 to 1964, brought Moroccan Jews. These were organized operations of the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency, not spontaneous flight, though the hardships in the countries of origin were real.[cite:wiki_idf_operations_list] Each country had its own circumstances and its own timeline.

Egypt supplies the documented case of sabotage. In 1954 Israeli military intelligence recruited a cell of Egyptian Jews to plant bombs at Western targets in Egypt, including American and British facilities. The aim was to have the attacks blamed on Egyptian nationalists or the Muslim Brotherhood, and to damage Western confidence in Nasser's government. The operation was discovered, its members were arrested and tried, and Defense Minister Pinhas Lavon was forced to resign.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] That the operation took place is not in dispute. Who authorized it, and at what level, has been argued over for decades. It is a specific case, not a pattern the record documents for every country in this account.

Arrival did not end the story. New arrivals, disproportionately Mizrahi, were housed in crowded transit camps called ma'abarot, first in tents and later in basic shacks. Ashkenazi immigrants of the same period tended to arrive better educated and were more likely to assimilate into the existing, largely Ashkenazi secular establishment. They also qualified for German war-reparations payments, which Mizrahi immigrants, never having lived under Nazi occupation, could not receive.[cite:honestreporting_forgotten_refugees] The gap in starting conditions was structural. Individual lives varied, but the pattern is documented.

Two episodes stand out. Between 1948 and 1954, hundreds of infants and small children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi immigrant families disappeared from Israeli state hospitals and transit camps. Families were often told the children had died, frequently without a body, a death certificate or a burial place. That much is not disputed. What lay behind it is. The Cohen-Kedmi Commission investigated from 1995 to 2001. It concluded that claims of a deliberate, government-organized kidnapping plot were not substantiated, while acknowledging that 42 children remained unaccounted for.[cite:wiki_kedmi_commission] The researcher Shoshana Madmoni-Gerber, drawing on hundreds of family testimonies, has argued that the disappearances reflect a coordinated pattern. The activist Uzi Meshulam, who campaigned for a fuller inquiry, was imprisoned in connection with his campaign.[cite:wiki_uzi_meshulam] [cite:nytimes_disappeared_children] Both positions rest on evidence, and the disagreement remains unresolved.

The second episode is the Ringworm Affair. Through the 1950s, Israeli medical authorities treated scalp ringworm in immigrant children, disproportionately Mizrahi and North African, with X-ray irradiation. One frequently cited figure puts the campaign at roughly 27,000 children; broader estimates run considerably higher. Part of the motive was practical: ringworm was grounds for exclusion under United States and other immigration rules, and irradiation was then a treatment used elsewhere as well. A 2003 Israeli documentary, The Ringworm Children, presented the episode as a grave state-linked scandal.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair]

No single cause cancels the others. Persecution, recruitment and sabotage all operated, and the departure, though large, did not end Jewish life in the region at once or everywhere. Baghdad's community, once very large, is functionally gone today. The full story is neither "they all fled persecution" nor "they were all lured away." It is both, in proportions that varied from place to place, followed by an arrival that was a rescue without being an equal welcome.

sections.h: "An Even Population Exchange"? Two Displacements Compared
sections.html:
Two great displacements marked the years after 1947: the Nakba, the displacement of Palestinians in the war of 1947 to 1949, and the departure of Jews from Arab lands. A common way of resolving them is to set one against the other. In this telling, they amounted to a clean and roughly equivalent population exchange: Jews out of Arab countries, Arabs out of Palestine, the one cancelling the other. Both displacements are real, documented and grievous for the people who lived through them. What does not survive a direct comparison is the claim that they form a single matched exchange. The two differ in mechanism, in duration and in the kind of record they left.

The Nakba displaced roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians within a single concentrated period, the war of 1947 to 1949, a span of roughly eighteen months. Direct military and paramilitary action substantially drove it, including massacres at named places such as Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and al-Dawayima. An identifiable set of forces carried it out: the Jewish armed organizations of the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi, and after independence the Israel Defense Forces.[cite:wiki_nakba] [cite:tandfonline_nakba_education] Later chapters treat these events in full. Here it is the shape that matters: one war, one set of forces, a compressed timeline.

The Jewish exodus had a different shape. As the previous section showed, it unfolded from roughly 1948 to 1972, nearly a quarter of a century, across several countries under separate governments, each with its own triggers. Iraq's Jewish community left largely in an airlift of 1950–51. Egypt's Jews left in two waves, in 1948 and again after the 1956 Suez Crisis. Algeria's Jewish exodus came during that country's war of independence in the early 1960s, more than a decade after 1948. Even the total is disputed: estimates range from roughly 650,000 to 900,000, depending on method and on the end year chosen.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] [cite:hxstem_long_shadow_nakba] The causes varied from place to place, persecution in some cases, organized emigration in others. None of this lessens what individual communities suffered, including the violence documented in [scene:s00e2|the preceding account of the exodus].

A second difference lies in what came after. Israel's government granted citizenship to arriving Jewish immigrants and absorbed roughly 600,000 of them over four years, doubling the country's Jewish population. Most Arab host states, by contrast, have not extended citizenship to Palestinian refugees or their descendants, even after more than seven decades. The continuing existence of UNRWA, a United Nations refugee agency dedicated specifically to Palestinians, reflects that difference.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] More than one side cites this asymmetry for its own purposes. The underlying fact stands either way.

The "clean exchange" framing is rejected from more than one direction. Sources sympathetic to the Palestinian narrative call the comparison "profoundly unfounded," given the different mechanisms involved.[cite:palestineremembered_arab_jews_expelled] Some sources sympathetic to the Israeli narrative reject it too. They argue that the Jewish displacement, sometimes cited as larger in raw numbers, has been comparatively ignored in international discussion.[cite:israelfactcheck_jewish_refugees] The two critiques agree on little else, and their preferred alternatives differ sharply. But both conclude that treating the two processes as one symmetrical event flattens real differences. When parties with opposite sympathies reject the same simplification, the trouble probably lies in the simplification itself.

The comparison establishes something narrow. It does not rank the two displacements or measure whose suffering counted for more. It separates "both real" from "therefore identical." One displacement was concentrated in an eighteen-month war and driven substantially by one identifiable set of forces. The other stretched over nearly twenty-five years across many countries, with causes that differed from one place to the next. To call them an even exchange is to get the shape of both histories wrong.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: How the Story Is Told
chapters.intro: Who shapes what most people learn about this history: classrooms, coordinated campaigns, platform rules, and the historians themselves.

sections.h: How the Story Is Taught
sections.html:
Before turning to the record, take stock of what most readers already carry. For most Americans the story of Israel arrives in a fixed sequence: textbook, teacher, museum, film, news. Each pass reinforces the last. That sequence is usually taken to deliver the true story of an ancient people returning home. What it actually delivers is one framing of a documented modern political project. The framing and the project are distinct, and this book is concerned with the project.

The sequence begins with the textbook. Four publishers, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Pearson, McGraw-Hill and Holt McDougal, reach the great majority of American world-history students in grades 6 through 12. Their coverage of Israel and Palestine follows a pattern that peer-reviewed research has studied, including Sean Yom's 2013 study of American world-history textbooks and, as its mirror image, Nurit Peled-Elhanan's 2012 study of Israeli textbooks.[cite:peled_elhanan_textbooks] The pattern is not one of falsehood. It is one of emphasis. Some events are named: the Holocaust, the 1948 declaration, the 1967 war. Others are compressed: the Nakba, the 1953 CIA coup in Iran, the 1982 Sabra and Shatila massacre. Some terms are used, such as "conflict," "war" and "unrest." Others are avoided, among them "occupation" and "apartheid." Apartheid has been the subject of published findings by B'Tselem, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International since 2021.[cite:btselem_apartheid_2021] [cite:hrw_israel_apartheid] [cite:amnesty_israel_apartheid]

A concrete case shows what emphasis can remove. A textbook may say that Jewish settlers bought land in Palestine, which is true. It need not mention that the Ottoman government passed a Palestine-specific law in 1881–82 barring land purchases by foreign Jews, or that from 1892 it required imperial approval even for Ottoman Jewish citizens. It need not mention that buyers worked around these laws through Ottoman-citizen intermediaries and consular protections. Nor need it mention that in the 1890s the U.S. State Department became involved in a dispute over Russian Jewish emigrants who had become American citizens in order to claim consular protection for such purchases. Both versions cover the topic. Only one describes the mechanism. A reader who knows only that "settlers bought land" has no reason to ask the next question. Whether such omissions are deliberate or simply the product of survey-course compression, the result is the same: not a false belief, but the absence of the facts that would let a reader look further.

Emphasis also shapes who counts as the subject. Jews are not a single lineage. The documented traditions include Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi, Beta Israel, Bene Israel, Kaifeng, Bukharan, Georgian, Yemenite and Karaite communities, and no one disputes that all are Jewish. American curricula typically compress this variety into a single narrative centered on Ashkenazi experience, an imbalance Ella Shohat documented from inside Israel in a 1988 essay.[cite:shohat_sephardim_israel] The compression matters. Political Zionism emerged in 1897 in specifically European Jewish settings. When non-European Jewish traditions vanish from the classroom, it becomes easier to treat "Zionism" and "all Jews" as the same thing, a conflation the record does not support.

The story also travels through the press, and ownership of the press is a matter of record. Robert Maxwell, born Jan Ludvik Hoch in Czechoslovakia in 1923, built a British media empire that by the 1980s included Mirror Group Newspapers, Macmillan, Berlitz and Pergamon Press; he acquired Macmillan in 1988 for $2.6 billion. Seymour Hersh's The Samson Option, Tom Bower's biography and a later biography by Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon describe ties between Maxwell and Israeli intelligence, though the specifics are contested.[cite:hersh_samson] [cite:bower_maxwell] He died at sea on 5 November 1991, near his yacht off the Canary Islands, and was buried on the Mount of Olives with state honors. Spanish and Israeli examinations concluded that he fell overboard; the full sequence of events was never settled. The record establishes ownership. It does not show that any particular story about Israel was directed by an intelligence service, and this book makes no such claim.

Ownership matters more because the textbook system has no independent check. Federal law, 20 U.S.C. § 1232a, bars the Department of Education from any "direction, supervision, or control" over curriculum.[cite:usc_20_1232a] Approval falls to the states, and Virginia's own review documentation places responsibility for accuracy on publishers, who certify themselves.[cite:va_textbook_review] In 2015, after a widely publicized error, the Texas board voted down a proposal to add independent university historians to check textbooks for accuracy.[cite:tx_board_rejects_factcheck] No one in the chain checks the checker, and ownership of a publisher is not screened for anything bearing on accuracy. This book has found no source showing that Maxwell altered Macmillan's textbook content, and does not assert it. The point is structural: the opportunity existed. Errors that enter such a system can also compound. Randall Munroe named the process "citogenesis": an unverified claim is cited, then cited again, until repetition looks like independent confirmation.[cite:cornell_citogenesis_blog] [cite:xkcd_978_citogenesis]

Alongside this undirected emphasis stands an organized effort. Hasbara, Hebrew for "explanation," was formalized as Zionist policy before the Second World War, a step credited to Nahum Sokolow, and it remains the Israeli state's own name for its public diplomacy. Israel quadrupled its 2026 public-diplomacy budget to $730 million, and its foreign minister called the matter an "existential issue." After October 2023, Israel's own National Security Studies institute, INSS, mapped more than 120 civilian "war rooms," 40 organizations building hasbara technology and 100 databases. One scheme reportedly offered roughly $7,000 per pro-Israel social-media post.[cite:nuclearnews_730m_budget] Several sources trace many talking points still in circulation to Frank Luntz's 2009 "Global Language Dictionary," commissioned by The Israel Project.[cite:medium_luntz_kryptonite_hasbara] None of this means that every pro-Israel statement originates there.

For some Jewish students the framing is reinforced in two further stages. Philanthropic funders, the Jim Joseph Foundation among them, support Israel-centered content in Jewish day schools. Later comes Birthright Israel, founded in 1999: a free ten-day trip for those aged 18 to 26, roughly 27 percent funded by the Israeli government, whose first funding guarantee Benjamin Netanyahu made in 1998. More than 800,000 young adults from some 68 to 70 countries have taken it. A 2025 Brandeis University study, funded by Birthright itself, found participants "much more connected to Israel, and much more likely to identify with the political right."[cite:intercept_birthright_2025] [cite:birthright_global_movement] [cite:wiki_birthright_israel]

Repeated exposure to a consistent framing installs a reflex rather than a conclusion: it links Israel with democracy, Palestinians with terrorism, criticism with antisemitism, and the conflict with antiquity. The rest of this book sets those associations beside the record, which rests on archives, court filings, primary documents and named reporting, including court proceedings and federal election data.[cite:icj_south_africa] [cite:fec_gov] Where a claim cannot be sourced, it is not made. Where it is contested, both sides are named.

sections.h: Who Coordinates What Gets Posted
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that pro-Israel content on social media is simply organic enthusiasm, and that any suggestion of coordination is conspiracy thinking. The record for the years 2018 to 2026 is more specific than either the assumption or its opposite. It names firms, contracts, sums of money, a leaked set of instructions, and a meeting attended by a head of government. It also documents influence operations running in the other direction. Influence work around this conflict is not the property of one side.

The most concrete case is STOIC, an Israeli political consulting firm. Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs paid it $2 million to run covert, AI-generated content carrying pro-Israel messaging about the Gaza war, aimed at younger, progressive Americans. FakeReporter, an Israeli watchdog group that tracks misinformation, identified the operation and tied five specific websites to it. The New York Times verified the reporting. Meta said it deleted the associated Facebook and Instagram accounts before they gained traction with real users, and STOIC did not respond to interview requests. [cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] The case shows a funder, a firm and a dollar figure, corroborated from several directions. It does not show that this was the largest such effort, and by Meta's account it was caught before it reached many people.

A second paper trail runs through the Foreign Agents Registration Act, the American law that requires those working for foreign governments to disclose their work. Bridges Partners, a Washington-based firm working with Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs through Havas Media Group Germany, filed documents showing roughly $900,000 invoiced for an "Influencer Campaign" running from June to November 2025. After administrative and production costs, roughly $552,946 remained for payments to influencers, covering an estimated 75 to 90 posts. [cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara] This is a government-mandated disclosure, a stronger kind of evidence than a figure repeated online. It describes one disclosed contract, not the whole public-diplomacy apparatus of which it was a part.

Disclosure filings show that money moved. An investigation by Time Magazine showed what coordination looked like from the inside. It revealed private group chats in which influencers taking part in a pro-Israel campaign were told what specific language to use on X, Instagram and TikTok, and were paid up to $4,250 per post. In a separate case, a Jewish influencer reported receiving a confidential brief from a different campaign, offering $1,500 to promote specific talking points under a non-disclosure agreement. He declined to sign. [cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] The refusal belongs in the record as much as the offer: not everyone accepted the arrangement. Nor does the investigation show that everyone who posted pro-Israel content in this period was part of a paid campaign. Unpaid supporters existed alongside the paid ones.

The effort reached the top of the Israeli government. In September 2025, in New York, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met personally with several American social media influencers to enlist them in amplifying pro-Israel messaging in the United States. [cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] The meeting is documented. What was said inside it, and whether every influencer present agreed to take part, is not part of the public record.

On campus, coordination has also taken the form of deception. The Israel on Campus Coalition, the main convening organization of pro-Israel campus groups, has been reported to gather information on pro-Palestinian students through informants inside Jewish and pro-Israel student organizations, and to pass it to Israel's Ministry of Strategic Affairs. That claim rests on reporting and is less independently verified. A second claim about the same organization is firmer. The coalition secretly ran misleading Facebook pages and ads targeting the Palestinian-American poet Remi Kanazi, and in 2018 Facebook itself removed the pages, citing its policies against misrepresentation. [cite:wiki_israel_campus_coalition] The two claims carry different weight and should be kept apart. Neither shows that such tactics are unique to this organization, or that every affiliated campus group practiced them.

The same record shows coordination aimed against Israel. An Iran-linked network operated fake profiles, bots and groups across WhatsApp, X, Telegram, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram. It spread disinformation, impersonated journalists and rabbis, and worked to stoke tensions among Israelis themselves, including content aimed at Israel's LGBTQ+ community and at ultra-Orthodox Jews. [cite:calcalist_iran_social_media_network] A 2025 report from an independent research organization, "Conflict Amplified: Disinformation and Hate in the Israel-Hamas War," documented disinformation and coordinated hate campaigns from multiple sides of the conflict. [cite:isd_conflict_amplified_2025] The sources do not establish that these operations matched the pro-Israel campaigns described above in size or reach, only that both exist.

Taken together, the evidence describes a real, funded, coordinated messaging apparatus: named firms, contracts disclosed under federal law, private instructions to paid posters, and recruitment by a head of government. It does not support the claim that every pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian post online is centrally directed. The documents settle that coordination exists. They do not settle what any single post means.

sections.h: Content Moderation as a Contested Ground
sections.html:
This section picks up where [scene:s00a|the account of how the story is taught] leaves off, in an arena that is entirely contemporary: what happens to Palestinian and pro-Palestinian content on the major platforms. Two simple stories compete. One says moderation is neutral. The other says it is a secret, coordinated effort to silence one side. The record for 2021 to 2026 supports neither. It is drawn from formal investigations, from reviews the platforms commissioned themselves, from the platforms' own denials, and from findings that run the other way.

The weightiest finding comes from two separate inquiries. In 2021 Meta commissioned an independent investigation by Business for Social Responsibility. It concluded that the company's content moderation "appear[s] to have had an adverse human rights impact on the rights of Palestinian users." In December 2023 Human Rights Watch published a 51-page report, "Meta's Broken Promises: Systemic Censorship of Palestine Content on Instagram and Facebook," documenting 1,050 cases of removal or suppression across more than 60 countries. After the report, Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, demanding accountability. [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] One inquiry was begun by critics; the other was initiated and paid for by the company. When a company's own audit reaches the same conclusion as its critics, the finding carries particular weight. It describes a pattern, not a claim that every removal was politically motivated. Moderation at global scale produces errors of every kind.

A broader dataset brings in other platforms. Sada Social's Digital Rights Index 2024 documented more than 25,000 violations against Palestinian digital content: Instagram 31 percent, TikTok 27 percent, Facebook 24 percent and X 12 percent. [cite:sada_social_digital_rights_index_2024] The Human Rights Watch report, which concentrated on Meta, noted that it received fewer reports about TikTok. Differences of this kind may reflect moderation policy. They may equally reflect the size of each platform's user base, its reporting tools, or the reach of the monitoring organization. The data does not say which, and this book does not decide.

One named case followed a change of ownership. In 2025–26 an Oracle-led group acquired TikTok's American operations, in a deal involving Larry Ellison, whose record of major personal donations to Israeli military-support causes is extensively documented. After the acquisition, a Palestinian journalist and influencer known as Owda was banned from the platform. TikTok's new ownership has not publicly addressed the case. [cite:meo_us_tiktok_ownership_bans] Observers have discussed a link between the ownership change and the ban. That link is plausible but not independently documented. The two facts stand side by side; no causal connection between them is established.

The record also runs the other way. In November 2023 the Anti-Defamation League found specific loopholes in TikTok's moderation, including Photo Mode slideshows and hashtag manipulation, that let antisemitic content slip past automated detection. [cite:adl_tiktok_antisemitism_loopholes] In January 2025 the watchdog CyberWell praised TikTok for improved removal of Holocaust-denial content compared with other platforms. TikTok has formally denied bias, and Reuters reported the company calling Malaysian claims that it suppressed pro-Palestinian content "unfounded." Calcalist, an Israeli technology publication, examined the Human Rights Watch report and identified possible biases in its sampling and choice of platforms. [cite:calcalist_hrw_methodology_critique] That critique deserves to be read alongside the report. None of this cancels the earlier findings. Moderation that fails Palestinian users and moderation that lets antisemitic content through are not mutually exclusive, and on this record both occurred.

Users adapted. Palestinian and pro-Palestinian users began posting images of watermelons, whose red, green, black and white match the colors of the Palestinian flag, because keyword and image filters that flagged the flag did not flag the fruit. That origin is why the watermelon became a globally recognized shorthand for solidarity with Palestine. [cite:wagingnonviolence_watermelon_algorithms] The workaround shows that moderation of flag-related content was something people met often enough to route around. It does not measure how widespread that moderation was.

Held together, the record looks like this. A human rights investigation and a platform's own commissioned review both found an adverse pattern affecting Palestinian users. A credible watchdog found antisemitic content evading moderation on another platform. A platform formally denied bias. A named methodological critique of the most prominent report exists. Several independent and sometimes adversarial sources, among them Human Rights Watch, Meta's own reviewers, Sada Social, the ADL and CyberWell, converge on real but partial and sometimes conflicting findings. That does not mean no pattern exists. It means the honest account ends in complexity, not a clean verdict in either direction.

sections.h: How Historians Argue About 1948
sections.html:
Historians do not agree on what happened in 1948, though it is often assumed that they do. Their names will recur in later chapters, and a reader is better served by knowing in advance where each one stands. This short section maps the camps. It is a guide to the interpreters, not a verdict on them.

Until the 1980s, the dominant Israeli account held that Palestinians largely left on their own or at the urging of Arab leaders. That account changed as Israel declassified its state and military archives. A group of scholars who came to be called the "new historians," Benny Morris and Ilan Pappé among them, used those archives to document expulsions, massacres and the deliberate prevention of Palestinian return. They did not agree with one another about what the documents meant. Morris and Pappé reached sharply different conclusions about how far the expulsions were planned. Walid Khalidi argued that the Haganah, a Jewish armed force of the period, was involved in Deir Yassin at every stage. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] Some material in Israeli military archives, including files on Deir Yassin, remains classified, so parts of the record are still closed to everyone.

The new historians have their own critics. Historians such as Efraim Karsh reject the expulsion-centered account and stress instead the responsibility of Arab leaders and the Arab rejection of partition. [cite:dailyalert_194_karsh] The disagreement is not over whether the archives exist. It is over what they show about intent and responsibility.

A second debate concerns framing rather than events. Scholars such as Joseph Massad describe Zionism as a settler-colonial project. They point to Zionist leaders' own use of the word "colonization," including Vladimir Jabotinsky's 1923 essay "The Iron Wall." [cite:massad_settler_colonial] Others describe Zionism as the national liberation movement of a refugee people with ancient roots in the land, seeking safety after centuries of persecution. Both frames have their advocates, and the choice between them shapes how every later event is read.

The practical rule that follows is simple: read the document first and the interpreter second. Facts drawn from archives are shared ground. Judgments about intent, and the choice of frame, are where scholars divide. The chapters that follow cite the documents and say whose interpretation is whose, so that a reader can tell the two apart. For primary documents and further reading on these debates, see Shlaim's The Iron Wall and Masalha's Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History, among other works. [cite:shlaim_iron_wall] [cite:masalha_four_thousand] [cite:said_question_palestine]

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Lines You've Heard
chapters.span: A field guide to the claims repeated most online
chapters.intro: You now have the ground under the story. This chapter is a field guide to the lines you will meet in comment sections, posts and arguments. Each one is checked briefly against the record, with a verdict and a pointer to the volume that holds the full account. The same standard applies to every line, including the ones aimed at Jews.
chapters.outro:
This opening chapter has cleared away several confusions that shape how the later story is usually told. "Semitic" turned out to be a linguist's term, coined in 1781, for a family of languages that includes both Hebrew and Arabic. "Antisemitism" was a separate word, made into a movement's banner by Wilhelm Marr in 1879, and it means hatred of Jews, nothing broader. Whether that word should also reach political criticism of a state is still argued. The dispute runs from the IHRA definition of 2016, issued by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance, to the Jerusalem Declaration of 2021 and that declaration's own critics. These pages set it out without settling it.

The chapter also separated Judaism, a religion and a set of lineages, from Zionism, a political movement founded at Basel in 1897. It traced Jewish opposition to that movement, and critique from within it or from within the state it produced, through Reform Judaism, the Bund, Satmar, the binationalists and Mizrahi scholars. It placed the Star of David and the menorah in their actual chronology. It established that Ottoman Palestine was a named, administered region of about 600,000 people, and that Jewish continuity, Arab continuity and modern national identity are three separate questions. Finally, it showed that the contest over this history is still being fought today, through paid influence campaigns and through content moderation, with documented conduct on more than one side. With that ground cleared, the story itself can begin.

sections.h: The land and who lived there
sections.html:
Lines about whether Palestine was a real, populated place before 1948, and whose history it holds.

Palestine never existed. There was never a country called Palestine.

False

Palestine was a real, named, populated and governed place long before 1948, even though it was not an independent state. The line leans on one true technicality: the Ottomans named provinces after their capital cities, so no Ottoman unit was officially called "Palestine." [cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] But the region was administered as three districts that map closely onto the later Mandate boundary, and from 1872 the district of Jerusalem reported directly to Constantinople because of its importance. [cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] Roughly 600,000 people lived there by the late 19th century, in cities such as Jerusalem, Gaza, Jaffa, Hebron and Nablus. [cite:ips_ottoman_palestine]

The name itself goes back to 135 CE, when Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina after crushing the Bar Kokhba revolt. [cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] From 1922 to 1948, "Palestine" was a polity in international law, with its own citizenship order (1925), about 70,000 passports, the Palestine pound (1927) and its own stamps. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship]

Read more [scene:s00h|Volume I, The Baseline: Ottoman Palestine] · [scene:s07|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Mandate]

The Palestinian people were invented in the 1960s.

False

Palestinian national identity is documented decades before the 1960s; historians date its emergence to the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods, the same era in which Jordanian, Syrian and Israeli identities formed. On 15 January 1911, two Arab Christian cousins in Jaffa, Issa and Yousef El-Issa, founded a newspaper called Filastin, "Palestine." [cite:wiki_falastin] By 1914 it was openly opposing Zionist land purchases, and it published until 7 April 1948. Israel's own National Library holds 6,692 issues. [cite:nli_filastin_archive]

From 1919, Muslims and Christians organized together in seven Palestine Arab Congresses. Their central demand was a national government answerable to an assembly elected by the country's inhabitants. [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress] Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people in Palestine. [cite:jvl_census_1931] The PLO was founded in 1964, but the people it claimed to represent were already on the record.

Read more [scene:cmt_s06|Volume I, The Baseline: "The Palestinian People Were Invented in the 1960s"] · [scene:fil_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Filastin]

It was a land without a people for a people without a land.

False

Every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country. Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews, about 11%. [cite:jvl_census_1931] At the end of 1946, the UN's investigating committee estimated about 1,846,000 people: some 1,203,000 Arabs (65%) and 608,000 Jews (33%). [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]

The slogan was not Zionist in origin. It first appeared in print in 1843, in a book by Alexander Keith, a Scottish clergyman who had visited Palestine in 1839 and knew it was inhabited. The first Zionist use came in 1901, from Israel Zangwill. [cite:meq_land_without_people] Historians debate whether it meant "empty" or "without a nation." The census figures also refute a slogan from the other side: the claim that Palestinian Arabs privately owned 94% of the land counts large areas of state land as Arab-owned. The 1945 Village Statistics survey separates private ownership from state land. [cite:wiki_village_statistics]

Read more [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War'] · [scene:cen_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Counting the Country]

Jews are the indigenous people of the land, and Arabs are the colonizers.

Half true

The first half of the line rests on real history; the second half does not. Jewish kingdoms existed in the land in the first millennium BCE, and after Rome crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE), barred Jews from Jerusalem and renamed the province Syria Palaestina, a smaller Jewish presence continued, centered in Galilee. [cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] [cite:encyclo_israel_history] That ancient connection is not in dispute among mainstream historians.

But the Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians who became the majority over the following centuries were a resident population, not a colonial one. The Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted 381,954 residents, roughly 85% Muslim, 11% Christian and 4% Jewish, and genetic and archaeological studies find strong continuity with long-term local ancestry. [cite:cjpme_historical_demography] [cite:factually_archaeological_evidence] Formal national identity is modern on both sides: Rashid Khalidi dates Palestinian national consciousness to the late Ottoman period and 1917–1923, just as political Zionism was founded at Basel in 1897. [cite:cup_khalidi_palestinian_identity] Both histories are documented; neither erases the other.

Read more [scene:s00i|Volume I, The Baseline: Indigenous, Colonizer, National Identity] · [scene:ah_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 3,000 Years in One Scene]

Jordan is already the Palestinian state.

False

Jordan is a separate state whose own government rejects the idea that it is the Palestinian state. The line starts from a real event: in 1921–23 Britain separated Transjordan from the rest of the Palestine Mandate under Article 25, exempting it from the Jewish national home provisions. [cite:w_transjordan] [cite:wiki_transjordan_memorandum] But the 1947 UN partition plan divided only the land west of the Jordan River. Many Jordanians are of Palestinian origin because they became refugees in 1948 and 1967, not because Jordan was a partition. [cite:w_black_september]

There is a twist: Jordan's own rulers once made a version of the claim. In 1948 King Abdullah I said Palestine and Jordan were one country, backing Jordan's annexation of the West Bank. [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] On July 31, 1988, King Hussein formally dissolved Jordan's legal and administrative ties to the West Bank. [cite:springer_jordan_palestine_history] Asked whether Jordan should be the de facto Palestinian state, King Abdullah II answered: "Jordan is Jordan." [cite:davidsinger_jordan_palestinian_state]

Read more [scene:cmt_s04|Volume LXII, The Comment Section: "Jordan Is the Palestinian State Set Aside in the Partition"] · [scene:s06a2|Volume II, The Road to 1948: "Jordan Is Already Palestine"] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Jews and Muslims have been fighting over that land for thousands of years.

False

The conflict over the land is about a century old, not thousands of years. It began with modern political Zionism in 1897 and the British Mandate, and the first Palestinian national movement was organized jointly by Muslims and Christians. Before that, Jews, Muslims and Christians lived together under Ottoman rule, where the millet system gave Jewish communities their own legal, educational and religious self-governance, though not equality with Muslims.

Across the Muslim-majority world, Jewish communities lived for more than a thousand years, from the Golden Age of Muslim Iberia [cite:menocal_ornament] to Baghdad, where some 140,000 Jews made up about one-third of the city in 1945. Coexistence was never utopian; there was real violence, such as the Granada pogrom of 1066. And the region was not peaceful before 1948: revolts in Iraq, Syria and Palestine followed the European carve-up of 1916–22. But the documented record does not fit a story of ancient, permanent hatred.

Read more [scene:s00e|Volume I, The Baseline: Semitic Jews Coexisted with Semitic Arabs] · [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War']

sections.h: 1948 and the refugees
sections.html:
Lines about how Israel was founded, how the war went, and why some 700,000 Palestinians became refugees.

Israel was created because of the Holocaust.

Misleading

The Holocaust changed the urgency, the politics and the world's willingness to act, but the plan for a Jewish state, and much of the machinery to build it, existed decades before Hitler took power in 1933. Theodor Herzl published The Jewish State in 1896, weighing Palestine against Argentina. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] The Zionist movement formally rejected a British offer in East Africa in 1905 and kept Palestine as its goal. [cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] Britain pledged support for "a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine in 1917, [cite:balfour_letter] the Allied powers ratified that at San Remo in 1920, [cite:san_remo_wiki] and the League of Nations Mandate approved in 1922 bound Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

By then the movement also had a bank (1899), a land fund (1901) and an organized American lobbying and fundraising base. What the war years did change is real: the Biltmore Program of May 1942 was the movement's first explicit, public demand for a "Jewish Commonwealth." [cite:biltmore_wiki] The Holocaust accelerated statehood; it did not originate it.

Read more [scene:s07a|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Five Dates That Predate the Holocaust] · [scene:us_s08|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Whole Play, Step by Step]

Israel accepted the UN partition plan; the Arabs rejected it and started the war.

Half true

The first half of the line is accurate; the second half compresses the sequence. When the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 on November 29, 1947, by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, the Jewish Agency accepted it, with real reservations about its borders. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected it entirely and vowed armed resistance. [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] [cite:palquest_un_partition_1947] The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine, about 70% of the population, had no vote on the plan, which gave the Jewish state about 55% of the territory. [cite:britannica_res181]

The war did not begin with a single Arab attack. Violence escalated from December 1, 1947, as a civil war inside Mandate Palestine, with documented attacks from both sides: a car bomb in Jaffa killed 26 people in early January 1948, and Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya on February 15, 1948. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] Neighboring Arab armies invaded on May 15, 1948, five and a half months later, the day after Israel declared independence.

Read more [scene:s09b|Volume II, The Road to 1948: "Israel Accepted, the Arabs Rejected and Started the War"] · [scene:s09|Volume II, The Road to 1948: UN Resolution 181]

Palestinians left in 1948 because Arab leaders told them to.

False

No general Arab order to leave has ever been found, and mainstream scholarship no longer defends this account. In 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers reported in The Spectator that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of 1948 Arab broadcasts and found no evacuation orders, but repeated appeals to civilians to stay. [cite:spectator_childers_1961] In 1988 the Israeli historian Benny Morris, working from Israel's own military and state archives, concluded that military attack, expulsion and fear were the main causes of flight. [cite:w_morris_birth]

There is a small kernel: Morris found that some local Arab commanders ordered evacuations of women and children in particular places. But expulsions are documented at Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and elsewhere, and about 500 villages were depopulated as 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced. [cite:morris_1948] Historians still disagree about whether the Haganah's Plan Dalet of 10 March 1948 was a blueprint for removal or a military plan that gave local commanders discretion. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

Read more [scene:np_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: How the Nakba Was Told] · [scene:s10|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Independence, Nakba, and the Czech Guns]

The Nakba is exaggerated; there were no massacres in 1948.

False

Massacres in 1948 are documented, much of the evidence coming from Israeli archives, historians and veterans themselves. On 9 April 1948, Irgun and Lehi forces, supported by the Haganah and Palmach, attacked Deir Yassin, west of Jerusalem, and killed about 110 villagers, many of them women, children and elderly people; a Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies in a cave. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] At Tantura in May 1948, Israeli veterans in their nineties described killings and a mass grave in a 2022 documentary; others deny it, and the number killed cannot be established. [cite:npr_tantura]

One number in this story was inflated: the Deir Yassin toll was long given as 254, and current scholarship puts it at 107–120. Atrocities ran both ways; four days later, a reprisal attack on a convoy to Hadassah Hospital killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The displacement itself is not in doubt: between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians were displaced and about 500 villages depopulated. [cite:morris_1948]

Read more [scene:ma_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy, and Tantura] · [scene:hd_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: How Historians Argue About 1948]

Tiny Israel won the 1948 war against impossible odds.

Misleading

The underdog picture fits only the opening weeks of the 1948 war; after that, the balance reversed. From the Arab armies' invasion on May 15 until the first truce in June 1948, Israeli forces are described as initially inferior in numbers and armament. A contemporaneous US government assessment dated July 1, 1948 put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000, about 35,000 of them used for active operations, and found the Arab armies stronger in artillery and tanks at that point. [cite:frus1948_military_situation]

After the truce, new enlistments and arms, including Czech shipments, let Israel seize the initiative; one historical anthology concludes that for most of the war "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization." [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] By the later stages, Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly 2 to 1. Many of the popular "outnumbered" figures trace back to John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion, who historians note had reason to exaggerate Israeli numbers. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

Read more [scene:s10b|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Actual Military Balance]

Why don't Arab countries just take the Palestinian refugees?

Half true

One Arab state did take most of its Palestinian refugees in, and others chose not to, for stated reasons. Under its 1954 nationality law, Jordan gave citizenship to most Palestinians who arrived after 1948; it hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees] Lebanon, with about 400,000 registered refugees, has never naturalized them, barring them from dozens of professions and, since a 2001 law, from owning property, a policy widely tied to its sectarian power-sharing balance. [cite:fmr_lebanon] [cite:aj_lebanon_property] Egypt and the Gulf offer residency without a path to citizenship.

The Arab League told members not to grant citizenship, to protect refugees' identity and their right of return; critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue this kept refugees in limbo as a political tool. [cite:fmr_lebanon] After October 7, Egypt and Jordan refused to take Gazans, citing the fear that Palestinians who leave would never be allowed back. [cite:pbs_egypt_refugees]

Read more [scene:sq_s20|Volume I, The Baseline: 'Why Don't Arab Countries Just Take the Refugees?'] · [scene:ilb_s03|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Lebanon's Refugee Policy: A Documented Choice]

sections.h: October 7 and the Gaza war
sections.html:
Lines about the attack itself, Israel's response, and how the dead and the hungry are counted.

October 7 came out of nowhere; there was no context at all.

Misleading

The October 7 attack was an atrocity, and it also had a documented context; the record holds both. Hamas fighters killed 1,195 people in Israel, 828 of them civilians and 36 children, and took 251 hostages, the largest single-day loss of Jewish life since the Holocaust. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] It came after 16 years of an Israeli-Egyptian blockade of Gaza, which by 2022 had left 97% of its water contaminated by UN standards and unemployment at 46.6%. [cite:blockade_unrwa] In the West Bank, the UN documented more than 2,150 settler violence incidents in 2023 alone. [cite:gzr_btselem_settlers] That context explains grievances; it does not justify the attack.

Nor was the attack unforeseen inside Israel. Israeli intelligence obtained Hamas's attack plan more than a year earlier and judged it aspirational, and Unit 8200 observers who reported unusual Hamas training were told it was routine. [cite:nyt_jericho_wall_2023] That warnings were dismissed is documented; claims that the attack was deliberately allowed to happen are not established.

Read more [scene:iaa_s12|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: October 7] · [scene:gzr_s06|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: Ten Years of Stories Americans Largely Missed] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas beheaded 40 babies on October 7.

Unsupported

The specific claim that Hamas beheaded 40 babies has not been supported by the record, and it was walked back after spreading. In the first days after the attack, the "beheaded babies" line was amplified by US media and repeated by President Biden before it was retracted. It became part of what reached American audiences while much of the documented context, reported mainly by Israeli outlets, did not.

Debunking that number does not shrink the attack. Hamas killed 1,195 people on October 7, 828 of them civilians and 36 of them children, took 251 hostages, and committed sexual violence documented by UN rapporteur reports and Israeli forensic teams. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] It was the largest single-day loss of Jewish life since the Holocaust. The record supports the atrocity in full; it does not support this particular, widely repeated figure.

Read more [scene:o7_s06|Volume LII, October 7 Architecture: The American Narrative] · [scene:o7_s08|Volume LII, October 7 Architecture: The Record vs. The Narrative] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas are terrorists and Israel has the right to defend itself.

True, with limits

Both parts of the line have a real basis, and the law attaches conditions to the second. The October 7 attack, in which Hamas killed 1,195 people, 828 of them civilians, and took 251 hostages, was a crime. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] Article 51 of the UN Charter recognizes every member state's "inherent right" of self-defense. In 2004, however, the International Court of Justice advised that Article 51 did not justify Israel's separation wall, because the threat came from territory Israel itself occupies. That opinion was non-binding and not unanimous. [cite:icj_wall_op] Israel's defenders argue that Gaza has not been occupied since 2005 and that the right applies against non-state groups like Hamas. [cite:justia_selfdef]

Both sides agree on one thing: the laws of war, including distinction, proportionality and precaution, bind every party, Hamas included. Whether specific Israeli operations met that standard is disputed. Israeli military lawyers say they did; B'Tselem and international law scholars have documented operations they assess as violations. [cite:btselem_casualties]

Read more [scene:sk_s03|Volume LXVI, Street Questions: 'Israel Has the Right to Defend Itself'] · [scene:s20|Volume XIII, October 7 and the Reckoning: Oct 7 · Gaza · Foreknowledge] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

The IDF is the most moral army in the world.

Unsupported

"Most moral army in the world" is a self-description, not a finding any independent body has made, and the documented record of the Gaza war cuts against it. In September 2025 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli authorities "deliberately deprived Palestinians in Gaza of resources indispensable for their survival" and found underlying acts of genocide, findings the Israeli government disputes. [cite:un_coi_sept2025]

Israeli intelligence officers' own testimony adds detail. According to a +972 Magazine and Local Call investigation based on six officers who used it, an AI system called Lavender flagged about 37,000 Palestinians as potential targets at its peak. The officers acknowledged roughly a 10 percent error rate and described reviewing each target for only seconds before authorizing a strike, and said 15 to 20 civilian deaths were accepted per junior operative in the war's early weeks. [cite:972mag_lavender_ai_machine] [cite:aljazeera_ai_assisted_genocide_lavender] Nor is there an outside check that could confirm the superlative: no Knesset oversight committee has access to operational detail.

Read more [scene:s19h|Volume VI, The Machine, Named: IDF and Mossad] · [scene:u82_s05|Volume XXXII, Unit 8200 Architecture: 37,000 Names, Seconds of Review, and a System Built to Find Them at Home] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas uses human shields, so the civilian deaths in Gaza are on Hamas.

Half true

There is documented evidence that Hamas used civilian sites for military purposes, but under the laws of war that does not move responsibility for civilian deaths entirely onto Hamas. In November 2023 the White House said US intelligence, separate from Israel's, indicated that Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad used some Gaza hospitals, including Al-Shifa, and tunnels beneath them to conceal military operations; it called this a war crime. Gaza doctors denied it. [cite:jns_us_intel_hospitals] The record also runs the other way: Israeli soldiers, former detainees and the veterans' group Breaking the Silence described Israeli units sending Palestinians, including a 16-year-old, into buildings and tunnels ahead of troops, a practice nicknamed the "mosquito protocol." The IDF says its directives prohibit this. [cite:cnn_mosquito_protocol] [cite:cbs_human_shields]

Using civilians as shields is prohibited for every party, and a shield's presence does not lift the attacker's duties of distinction and proportionality. Whether specific Israeli operations met those duties is contested. [cite:btselem_casualties]

Read more [scene:hs_s01|Volume LXVI, Street Questions: 'Human Shields'] · [scene:hma_src_s15|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: What the Architecture Has Produced for Civilians] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Gaza's death toll is made up by Hamas.

False

Independent research points to the Gaza Health Ministry undercounting deaths, not inventing them. The ministry is under Hamas's authority, which is why Israel disputes its figures, but the UN has generally treated them as reliable. [cite:gulfnews_lancet_toll] A study in The Lancet in January 2025, cross-checking ministry hospital lists, a ministry online survey and social-media obituaries, estimated 64,260 traumatic-injury deaths by 30 June 2024, against 37,877 reported, an undercount of about 41%. [cite:transcend_lancet_toll] A 2026 household survey in The Lancet Global Health, not relying on ministry records, estimated more than 75,000 violent deaths in the first 15 months, versus about 49,000 reported at the time. [cite:cyprusmail_lancetgh_2026]

As of August 2026, the ministry's count, as reported by UN OCHA, stood at about 73,400 killed. [cite:un_ocha_opt] The real open question is different: the totals do not separate combatants from civilians. Israel says it killed about 20,000 fighters, a figure not independently verified. [cite:yahoo_record_dems_fighters]

Read more [scene:tl_s01|Volume LXVII, Products of the Machine: Is the Gaza Death Toll Reliable? What Peer-Reviewed Studies Found] · [scene:gzr_s03|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: The Numbers Americans Missed: Gaza Death Tolls Across the Last Decade] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

There is no famine in Gaza; the starvation stories are propaganda.

False

Famine in Gaza was formally declared by the body that exists to make that call. On August 22, 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) declared famine in Gaza Governorate, the first ever declared in the Middle East and only the fifth since the system was created in 2008. A declaration requires three thresholds to be breached at once: extreme food deprivation, acute malnutrition and starvation deaths. [cite:ipc_famine_aug2025] The IPC called it "entirely man-made." [cite:gzr_ipc_famine_wiki] WHO had recorded 206 starvation deaths in 2025 by July, and 12,000 children were identified as acutely malnourished in July alone. [cite:gzr_who_famine]

The famine followed more than 60 days in spring 2025 when all humanitarian and commercial supplies were blocked from entering. [cite:ipc_may2025_blockade] Some data points have been challenged: the Times of Israel disputed parts of the IPC's data, though not the existence of severe food insecurity, and an earlier famine claim was revised down. January 2026 brought a brief period when aid met basic food needs.

Read more [scene:gzr_s01|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: Confirmed Famine: The First in the Middle East's Recorded History] · [scene:s19k|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: The Starvation Question] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

The world court has already ruled that Israel committed genocide.

False

The International Court of Justice has not ruled on whether Israel committed genocide; South Africa's case, filed on December 29, 2023, is still pending. [cite:icj_report_un] What the court did, on January 26, 2024, was issue provisional measures: it found that Palestinians' rights under the Genocide Convention were plausibly at risk of irreparable harm and ordered Israel to prevent genocidal acts and allow aid. That is an emergency order, not a verdict, and it did not order a ceasefire. [cite:mee_icj_explainer] Separately, the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants of November 21, 2024 for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant charge war crimes and crimes against humanity, not genocide. [cite:justiceinfo_gaza]

The line blurs courts with other bodies. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (December 2024), the Israeli groups B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel (July 2025) and a UN Commission of Inquiry (September 2025) have concluded genocide or acts of genocide. Israel rejects all of these findings. [cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:ips_amnesty_hrw_genocide]

Read more [scene:arm_s05|Volume XXXIX, The Arms Supply Architecture: The International Legal and Political Context] · [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide'] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

sections.h: Wars, occupation and peace
sections.html:
Lines about who starts the wars, what the occupation is in law, and who walked away from peace.

Israel never starts wars; it only responds.

False

The record shows Israel has opened at least two of its major wars. On June 5, 1967, Israel struck first, destroying most of the Egyptian air force on the ground within hours; its initial claim that Egypt had attacked first was false, and US intelligence knew it at the time. [cite:war1967_adl] The threat was real: Egypt had expelled UN peacekeepers, blockaded the Strait of Tiran and massed 100,000 troops on the border. Whether that justified striking first is still argued by lawyers and historians. Israeli historians such as Tom Segev also document planning that predated the crisis. [cite:segev_1967]

In 1982, Israel invaded Lebanon after its ambassador in London was shot by the Abu Nidal Organization, a rival and enemy of the PLO. Told this by the Shin Bet, General Rafael Eitan replied, "Abu Nidal, Abu Shmidal. We have to strike at the PLO!" [cite:war1982_eitan] Real grievances existed, including 270 PLO attacks despite a ceasefire, but "only responds" does not fit the record.

Read more [scene:iaa_s04|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: 1967] · [scene:iaa_s06|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: 1982] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel gave Gaza back in 2005 and got rockets in return.

Half true

The withdrawal was real, but "gave Gaza back" overstates it. Between 15 and 23 August 2005, Israel evacuated all 21 Gaza settlements and about 8,000 settlers, mobilizing up to 55,000 soldiers and police. [cite:crs_disengagement_2005] But Israel kept control of Gaza's airspace, coastline and most crossings, which is why the UN and the International Court of Justice continued to treat Gaza as occupied, while Israel argued its occupation had ended. [cite:wiki_disengagement]

The purpose matters too. Sharon's top aide described the plan as a way of isolating Gaza and avoiding international pressure for a political settlement. Nothing was handed to a Palestinian government by agreement. Hamas won the January 2006 legislative elections, took control of Gaza in June 2007 after fighting Fatah, and Israel and Egypt then imposed a blockade. Leaving the inside while holding the edges, with no negotiated settlement, produced the arrangement every Gaza war since 2008 has been fought inside.

Read more [scene:dis_s01|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Disengagement] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

There is no occupation; the West Bank is disputed territory.

False

Under international law, the West Bank is occupied territory, and the world's highest court has said so directly. On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice advised that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful, that it must end "as rapidly as possible," and that Israel must stop all new settlement, evacuate settlers and make reparation. Several of those findings passed 14 to 1. [cite:icj_press_19jul24] The court noted that occupation law sets no time limit; it was annexation-like policies and the denial of self-determination that made the presence unlawful. [cite:transcend_icj_ao]

The UN Security Council reached the same view of settlements in December 2016, voting 14 to 0 in Resolution 2334 that they have "no legal validity." [cite:deccan_unsc_2334] Israel rejects these findings, and the 2024 opinion is advisory, not an enforceable judgment. But "disputed" is Israel's position, not the finding of any court or UN body.

Read more [scene:icj_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: The ICJ's 2024 Opinion] · [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide']

The Palestinians rejected every peace offer they were given.

Half true

The record includes real Palestinian and Arab rejections, but "every offer" leaves out the other half. Arab leaders did reject the 1937 Peel plan and the 1947 partition plan. At Lausanne in 1949, Israel offered to take back 100,000 refugees, but "only as an integral part of a general and final peace settlement"; the Arab states demanded return first, and Israel later withdrew the offer. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report]

Camp David in July 2000 is the case most people mean, and its participants disagree. Clinton blamed Arafat for rejecting reported proposals of a state on roughly 91–92% of the West Bank and all of Gaza. Robert Malley, Clinton's own Middle East director at the talks, wrote with Hussein Agha that errors were shared and no offer was ever put in writing. [cite:independent_malley_barak] Palestinian negotiators said the real territory was smaller. The Clinton Parameters followed, and both sides answered with reservations; Taba in January 2001 ended without agreement. [cite:jvl_camp_david_overview]

Read more [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War'] · [scene:cd_s01|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Camp David 2000] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel wants coexistence; peace is up to the Palestinians.

Misleading

The record of Israel's own governments does not support the idea that the only obstacle is on the Palestinian side. On 21 February 2024 the Knesset voted 99 to 9 to back Netanyahu's opposition to "unilateral" recognition of a Palestinian state, and on 11 September 2025, at the Maale Adumim settlement, Netanyahu said "there will be no Palestinian state." [cite:toi_knesset_99] [cite:globalsecurity_two_state] From the signing of Oslo in 1993, the West Bank settler population grew from about 110,000 to about 500,000 by 2025, plus about 250,000 in East Jerusalem. [cite:peacenow_settlement_population]

Former minister Haim Ramon has said Netanyahu told Likud lawmakers in 2019 that letting Qatari money reach Hamas would help "foil the establishment of a Palestinian state"; Netanyahu calls that "a big lie." [cite:alandowty_strong_hamas_netanyahu] [cite:ynetnews_netanyahu_ridiculous_denial] Rabin, who signed Oslo, was killed in 1995 by an Israeli opponent of the deal. Support for two states has also fallen among Palestinians, to 33% by December 2022, so neither side's public is the whole story.

Read more [scene:ts_s02|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Is a Two-State Solution Still Possible? Recognition at 157 Nations, a 99–9 Knesset Vote, and Falling Support on Both Sides] · [scene:hma_s01|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: Netanyahu's Own Reported Words] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel's real plan is a Greater Israel from the Nile to the Euphrates.

Depends on what's said

"From the Nile to the Euphrates" is not official Israeli policy, but the idea of a larger Israel is held by people in the governing coalition. The phrase comes from Genesis 15:18 and is the most extreme of three versions of "Greater Israel"; it is rejected as literal policy even by most religious Zionists. [cite:genesis_1518_text] The more mainstream version is the Likud platform, which says "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty." [cite:likud_charter_platform]

Some statements go further. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich spoke in Paris in March 2023 beside a map that included Jordan, and has said Jerusalem's future is to "extend all the way to Damascus." [cite:smotrich_map_paris_2023] In August 2025, asked if he connects to a pendant map reaching into Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq, Netanyahu replied "very much so," and 31 Arab and Islamic states condemned it. [cite:netanyahu_jewelry_2025] On the ground, Israel annexed the Golan in 1981 but returned Sinai in 1982. "A secret master plan" overstates it; "no one in power wants more land" understates it.

Read more [scene:gia_src_s02|Volume II, The Road to 1948: What Greater Israel Actually Is: Ideology, History, and the Three Versions] · [scene:gia_s01|Volume XXVII, Greater Israel Architecture: The Map He Held Up at the UN] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

sections.h: Democracy, rights and Palestinian politics
sections.html:
Lines about Israel's democracy, the rights of the people it governs, and the record of Palestinian leaderships.

Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.

Half true

For its own citizens, the line holds up on the main international measures, but it leaves out millions of people Israel governs. In its 2024 report, the V-Dem Institute still ranked Israel as the only electoral democracy in the Middle East and North Africa, a region where 98% of people live under autocracies. [cite:globes_vdem] Israel holds competitive elections, has a free press, and Arab citizens vote and sit in the Knesset.

The same report demoted Israel from "liberal democracy" for the first time in about 50 years, citing attacks on the judiciary and a decline in freedom from torture; Freedom House's score fell from 80 in 2017 to 73. [cite:toi_vdem] The Israel Democracy Institute called this "troubling, but not catastrophic." [cite:idi_vdem] Both indices assess Israel without the occupied territories. Palestinians in the West Bank live under Israeli military control but cannot vote in Israel's elections; by one count, about 5.5 million of roughly 15.5 million people under Israel's control lack citizenship. [cite:prio_democracy]

Read more [scene:sk_s02|Volume I, The Baseline: 'The Only Democracy in the Middle East'] · [scene:s19d|Volume VI, The Machine, Named: The Coalition Hostage Architecture] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Arab citizens of Israel have exactly the same rights as Jewish citizens.

Half true

Arab citizens of Israel vote, stand for the Knesset and hold citizenship, but the law has not treated them identically. From 1949 to 1966 most lived under a military administration requiring permits to travel, with curfews and closed zones. Under that regime, on 29 October 1956, a Border Police unit killed 49 villagers at Kafr Qasim returning home after a curfew they had not been told of; the brigade commander was fined one-hundredth of a lira. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre]

The 1950 Absentees' Property Law took the property even of Arabs who never left Israel and became citizens; by 2001 these "present absentees" were estimated at about 200,000 people. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] The law remains in force. In 2018 the Knesset passed, 62 to 55, a Basic Law stating that national self-determination is "unique to the Jewish people," with no equality clause. [cite:jta_nsl_upheld] The Supreme Court upheld it 10 to 1 in 2021, saying individual rights are protected by other laws; supporters say it only states what Israel already is.

Read more [scene:mg_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Eighteen Years of Military Rule Over Citizens] · [scene:nsl_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: The Nation-State Law]

Israel is an apartheid state.

Depends on what's said

"Apartheid" has a legal meaning, and several serious bodies have applied it to Israel, though no court has convicted anyone of the crime. Under the 1973 Apartheid Convention and the Rome Statute, apartheid is an institutionalized regime of systematic domination by one racial group over another. Human Rights Watch and the Israeli group B'Tselem concluded in 2021 that Israel commits apartheid, and Amnesty International reached the same conclusion in February 2022. [cite:fara_amnesty_explainer]

In July 2024 the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion on the occupied territory, found that Israeli policies breach the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid. [cite:11kbw_icj_ao] Israel rejects the label. So the honest answer depends on the wording: "human-rights groups and the ICJ have found apartheid-related violations" is accurate; "a court has ruled Israel guilty of the crime of apartheid" goes further than the record, and "it is a slur with no legal basis" ignores it.

Read more [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide']
