[cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007] Whether this early opposition was political is disputed: a Jewish Agency overview doubts that the local opposition before 1891 had "any political connotations", while Beška finds that the mufti followed Jewish immigration from the 1880s and took an active stance against it. [cite:rs_rd0_jafi_opposition] [cite:rs_rd0_beska_2007]

The Jewish pieces: an old community, new colonies, a movement and its critics. The Jews of Palestine were not newcomers in 1882. Barın puts the Old Yishuv at about 24,000 in 1880, 13,900 of them in Jerusalem; another estimate gives 23,000. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014_pop] [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki] Between 1882 and 1891 new settlements were founded from Rishon LeZion and Zikhron Ya'akov to Rehovot and Hadera. [cite:rs_rd0_firstaliyah_wiki] Behind them stood organized groups: the student pioneers of BILU from 1882, the Hovevei Zion societies that met at Kattowitz in 1884, and the word "Zionism", coined by Nathan Birnbaum in 1890. [cite:w_bilu] [cite:w_hovevei] [cite:w_birnbaum] Herzl's Der Judenstaat of February 1896 came last and gave these groups a program for a state. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] Jewish critics stood on the same board. Reform Judaism's Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 expected "neither a return to Palestine" nor a Jewish state. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] Vienna's preacher Adolf Jellinek answered Pinsker that "We are at home in Europe", and in the 1880s Jerusalem's Orthodox community reported Zionist newcomers to the Ottoman authorities. [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki_dissent]

Put together, the pieces show who could act on Palestine in 1896, and through what instrument. Only the Porte could decide who entered and who bought land. The foreign powers could blunt its decisions through consular protection and treaty. The Paris house and the Jewish Colonization Association had the money to settle people, the restorationists had a voice in London and Washington, and the Jerusalem notables could petition the Porte and, through the mufti's commission, slow sales on the ground. Herzl had a pamphlet.

The years in a ledger. Read year by year, the period from the pogroms to the Dreyfus conviction shows the same pieces moving. In 1881 pogroms broke out in the Russian Empire; of the roughly two million Jews who emigrated in the following decades, the great majority went to America, not Palestine. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] In 1882 Edmond de Rothschild began funding colonies. [cite:wiki_edmond_james_de_rothschild] In 1885 Reform Judaism's Pittsburgh Platform rejected a return. [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] In 1891 Hirsch founded the Jewish Colonization Association with £2,000,000 of capital. [cite:hadassah_mag_hirsch] In 1894 Dreyfus was convicted, and Herzl turned to political Zionism. [cite:wiki_dreyfus]

The ledger's "Who objected" column records the emigrants who chose America and the Reform movement. It leaves blank two objections this chapter documents. In 1882, the year the ledger marks for Edmond's colonies, the Ottoman state forbade foreign Jews to enter and buy land. [cite:rs_rd0_barin_2014] In 1891, the year it marks for Hirsch, Jerusalem's notables petitioned against Jewish immigration and land purchase. [cite:rs_rd0_antizionism_wiki] Read with those two entries added, the ledger shows opposition from the sovereign in the first year of organized settlement, and from Jerusalem's notables within a decade.

What the board does and does not explain. To say the board existed is not to say it decided the outcome. Its pieces could move in different directions, and in 1896 several of the strongest were set against Herzl's project: the Sultan, Edmond de Rothschild, Reform Judaism and the Jerusalem notables, and the Papacy would show in 1904 that it stood with them. What the record supports is narrower and firmer: the structures that would fund, permit, bless or block a Jewish state were older than the movement that asked for one. Some questions remain open in the sources used here. They give no decade-by-decade count of the Arab population of Palestine for this period. They do not total Edmond's spending on the colonies. They do not preserve the text or the signatories of the 1891 petition. And they cannot say how any of these pieces would have moved had the movement chosen Argentina instead.

The next part of this book opens at Basel in 1897 and follows how a political program became a state in fifty-one years, through its bank, its land fund, the Balfour Declaration, the Mandate and Resolution 181, beginning with the First Zionist Congress. Zionism did not build this board. It entered a game whose pieces were already set, and the chapters that follow trace what it did with them.

chapters.label: Stage One
chapters.title: Conceive
chapters.intro:
This stage of the story opens in 1896, when a Viennese journalist named Theodor Herzl published Der Judenstaat, and closes in 1917, on the eve of the Balfour Declaration. In those two decades a political program on paper became a set of working institutions. There was a Congress with elected delegates, an executive and a council. There were national federations in America and Britain. There was a bank incorporated in London with a branch in Jaffa, and a fund that bought land in Palestine and never resold it.

The question here is simple: when, and how, was the project of a Jewish state conceived and given structure? Many people place its origin in the catastrophe of the 1930s and 1940s. The dates point the other way. By 1905 the movement had already weighed Argentina, a Sinai buffer at Suez and a British offer in East Africa. It chose Palestine through its own contested votes.

These years were also years of argument. The Bund, Orthodox rabbis, Ahad Ha'am and the official bodies of British Jewry all opposed or contested political Zionism, and the movement split over East Africa. Herzl, meanwhile, approached the Kaiser, the Sultan, Britain and the Tsar's minister in turn, seeking a charter from whichever power would grant one. Land was bought, mostly from absentee owners, and tenants who held no title paid the price. What follows traces how these pieces were assembled, and by whom.
chapters.outro:
By the end of this stage, the movement launched at Basel had become a working structure. The choice of territory was settled. The Uganda offer was rejected in 1905, and Herzl had explained as early as 1896 why Palestine carried a weight Argentina could not. In Jaffa, the Palestine Office, opened in 1908, coordinated land purchase and settlement with the Jewish National Fund. The Palestine Land Development Company had handled roughly 50,000 dunams by the outbreak of war. Named agents closed the deals.

Across the Atlantic, two separate bases of support had taken shape in the United States. One was Christian, rooted in the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909, and would grow into a large Christian Zionist constituency. The other was Jewish, built through Hadassah, Louis Brandeis and the Zionist Organization of America. By 1918 it had more than 147,000 members and a direct line to President Wilson. During the war, NILI's intelligence and the Jewish battalions in British uniform gave the movement standing in London just as the cabinet weighed the Balfour Declaration.

Opposition was in place too. From 1911, Filastin was reporting Zionist land purchases to every village in the Jaffa district. And one popular claim, that the Federal Reserve's founding was tied to Zionist finance, finds no support in the record.

sections.h: The Country Before the Program: Ottoman Palestine, 1872–1914
sections.html:
When Theodor Herzl and his colleagues spoke of Palestine in the late 1890s, they were speaking of a place that had no border, no government of its own and no single name on an official map. From 1516 to 1917, apart from a period of Egyptian rule in 1831–40, the land was governed as part of the Ottoman Empire. It was administered chiefly as the district of Jerusalem and as parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, and nothing separated it from the territories that are today Syria, Lebanon and Jordan. Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same state, and people and goods moved between them without passports. The national borders that frame every later chapter of this book did not yet exist. Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel were not states. Almost every line that matters in the region's conflicts was drawn between 1916 and 1922, in a window of six years, by Britain and France. Iran, a separate Persian state with its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority, was never Ottoman at all.

Two misreadings of this period are common, and they point in opposite directions. One holds that the Ottomans "occupied" Palestine in the way later settlers did. The other holds that Palestine was an empty backwater of the empire, waiting to be filled. The record supports neither. Ottoman rule was imperial administration: governors, garrisons and taxation imposed over a population that remained, for four centuries, largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, alongside long-established Jewish communities. The Ottomans ruled the country; they did not replace its people. A third misreading, that the Middle East has always been a set of hostile nations permanently at war, fails for a simpler reason. For four hundred years most of the region was one state.

The administrative shape that mattered in Herzl's lifetime dated from 1872. In that year the Ottoman government created the Mutasarrifate, or Sanjak, of Jerusalem as an independent administrative unit. It comprised the districts of Jerusalem, Jaffa, Hebron, Beersheba and Gaza. To its north lay two further sanjaks, Nablus and Acre. This arrangement lasted until Britain occupied Palestine in December 1917, when the Mutasarrifate was dissolved.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] The country that Zionist delegates debated at Basel was therefore, in legal terms, one Ottoman unit centred on Jerusalem plus parts of two others. When later writers speak of "Palestine" in this period, they are describing a region that the Ottoman state itself divided among several administrations.

Inside this imperial frame, religion rather than nationality organized much of daily law. Under the millet system the empire recognized religious communities, Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews, and allowed each to govern marriage, inheritance and schooling through its own religious law, its own courts and its own leaders.[cite:w_ottoman_millet] The arrangement gave communities real autonomy over their internal lives. It was not, however, a golden age, and the record does not present it as one. The order carried heavy taxation and conscription, and it saw periodic violence. Non-Muslims paid special taxes and held a lesser legal status, and revolts were suppressed. The point is not that the Ottoman order was just. It is that it was a different order from the one the twentieth century built: an empire of religious communities, not a map of rival nation-states.

The Jews already living in this country when the Zionist movement was founded had their own long history, and their own institutions, quite separate from the movement that would arise in Europe. Historians call this community the Old Yishuv. According to the National Library of Israel, the Jewish population of the land grew from about 7,000 in 1800 to about 27,000 in 1880.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] It was concentrated in the four cities that Jewish tradition held holy, Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias, and in the nineteenth century most of it lived in Jerusalem. The same four cities appear in the record of the wider Ottoman population as the places where Jewish communities lived among a mostly Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian majority.

The Old Yishuv lived largely on money from abroad. It depended almost completely on the halukka, funds collected from diaspora donors and distributed through kollels, which were organized by the donors' and recipients' country of origin and by Hasidic affiliation. The money therefore moved through channels of family and congregation rather than through any political body, and it sustained a community devoted chiefly to religious life in the holy cities. Before the Ottoman authorities, the Jews were represented by the Sephardi chief rabbi, the Hakham Bashi, a post later titled Rishon LeZion. At the end of the nineteenth century the Ashkenazi kollels united under a single body, the General Committee of Knesset Israel.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] These were the Jews of Ottoman Palestine as the empire knew them: a recognized religious community within the millet order, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, supported by charity, and with no program of statehood.

That began to change before Herzl. The National Library of Israel dates the beginning of a "New Yishuv" to the First Aliyah, the wave of immigration that began in 1881, and describes it as costing the Old Yishuv its leading position among the Jews of the country.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_oldyishuv] The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question counts about 25,000 Jewish immigrants in 1882–1903, and more than 84,000 in 1850–1914, noting that not all of them stayed.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron] The Ottoman Land Code of 1858, which governed how land in the country was held, is examined in the previous stage of this book: [scene:ot_s01|the Ottoman Land Code].

Palestine's Jews were also one community among several in the Ottoman Middle East with deep roots. Jewish life in Mesopotamia, modern Iraq, went back to the Babylonian conquest of Judah in 586 BCE, and the scholars of that community compiled the Babylonian Talmud, still the primary text of rabbinic study.[cite:huc_farhud][cite:ushmm_farhud] That continuous presence predated the Iraqi state of 1932 and the Israeli state of 1948 by millennia; its later history belongs to a different part of this library: [scene:irq_e01|the Jews of Iraq].

How many people lived in Palestine on the eve of the First World War, and how many of them were Jews, is a question on which the sources disagree, and the disagreement is not a technicality. The numbers below are the main ones in the record, with what each source actually counted.

The Ottoman census of 1914–15 recorded 722,000 people: 602,000 Muslims, 81,000 Christians and 39,000 Jews. Roberto Bachi's reconstruction for 1914 gives a smaller total, 689,000, made up of 525,000 Muslims, 70,000 Christians and 94,000 Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_demog_wiki] The gap between the two Jewish figures, 39,000 against 94,000, is larger than the whole Jewish population of 1880. The difference begins with who was counted. The Ottoman register recorded 38,754 Jews, and on the analysis of the historian Justin McCarthy it apparently counted only Ottoman subjects. Many Jews in Palestine were foreign nationals and did not appear in it. McCarthy, adjusting the Ottoman figures, gives a total of 722,143 for 1914–15 and puts the true Jewish figure, including foreign nationals, closer to 60,000. Against this stands the figure long accepted in the literature, 85,000, as summarized by Roger Owen in his review of McCarthy's work.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen] The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question agrees with McCarthy's order of magnitude: about 60,000 Jews at the start of the war in 1914, 39,000 of them Ottoman citizens, against more than 700,000 Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron]

The same pattern appears a generation earlier. For about 1890, Bachi's reconstruction gives 532,000 people, 43,000 of them Jews; the Ottoman census of 1890–91 gives 516,000, with 18,000 Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_demog_wiki] Here the reconstruction is higher on both counts, and its Jewish figure is more than double the census's. The direction of McCarthy's corrections is also on record. He adjusts Ottoman registers chiefly for the undercounting of young children, especially girls, and for categories of people the registers missed, and on the same reasoning he re-estimates the population of 1922 at 823,684, above the official British census total, arguing that modern methods correct the census undercount.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen]

Each side of this dispute has a serious case. Those who prefer the lower Jewish figures point out that the Ottoman register is a contemporary official document and that McCarthy's adjustments are explicit and reproducible. His estimate of about 60,000 deliberately adds back the foreign nationals the register left out, so it cannot be dismissed as an undercount of Jews by design. Those who hold to the higher figures, 85,000 or Bachi's 94,000, rest on the figure long accepted in the literature and on Bachi's reconstruction. They can argue that foreign nationals, the very people the register missed, were numerous enough to lift the total well above 60,000. The sources available here do not set out Bachi's method in detail, so the case for his figure cannot be tested against the record in this book.

What none of the figures disputes is the order of magnitude that mattered politically. On every count, the Jewish population of Palestine in 1914 was a minority, living among a majority of Arabic-speaking Muslim and Christian Ottoman subjects. On every count, too, it had grown several times over since 1800, first through the Old Yishuv's slow increase and then through immigration after 1881. How far it fell during the war that began in 1914 is itself disputed, with one account holding that about a third left and McCarthy arguing the fall was much smaller; that story is told in [scene:rd1_wwi|Palestine at war].[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron][cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen]

The empire that governed all of these people did not survive the war. British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, ending Ottoman rule in the city. The Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that same year.[cite:w_lausanne] Modern Turkey is thus the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine. The layers that followed, oil, the Anglo-French carve-up, installed rulers and revolts, stacked on top of the Ottoman order, and the map below traces them.

Several things this record leaves open should be said plainly. It does not give a single agreed figure for the Jewish population in 1914, and no figure in it can be treated as settled: the range runs from 38,754 to 94,000 depending on who was counted and how. It does not say how many of the more than 84,000 Jewish immigrants of 1850–1914 stayed. Nor does it measure how the Old Yishuv's members themselves regarded the newcomers of 1881 and after, beyond the National Library's judgment that the New Yishuv displaced them from leadership. What it does establish is the country as it was when the program adopted at Basel set its sights on it: an Ottoman land without borders, a majority of Arab Muslim and Christian subjects, an old Jewish community living on charity in four holy cities, and a new wave of immigrants who had begun to change it.

sections.h: Basel, 1897: The Program and Its Opponents
sections.html:
Political Zionism as an organized movement has a precise birthplace and date. It was founded at the First Zionist Congress, which met in Basel, Switzerland, from 29 to 31 August 1897. Its convener and chairman was Theodor Herzl, a journalist born in Budapest and a subject of Austria-Hungary, who had published Der Judenstaat the year before. The Congress adopted a platform, the Basel Program, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its first president. Its founding leadership was overwhelmingly European, and so were its funding and its location.[cite:zionism_founding_1897] The familiar claim that the State of Israel grew from an ancient national presence with no meaningful break therefore needs a qualification at the start. The movement that set out to build a state there was new, and it was organized in Europe in 1897. The Jewish communities already living in the land, the Old Yishuv of the four holy cities, had no such program.

A second familiar claim, that Jews embraced Zionism from the start, does not survive the record of that same summer. The Congress was opposed before it opened, it was opposed by rabbis in Germany and Britain, and in the same season a rival Jewish movement was founded on the opposite premise. The contest inside Jewish life over Herzl's project is one of the clearest pieces of evidence that Zionism and Judaism were not the same thing, and that Jews themselves were the first to insist on the difference.

Herzl had planned to hold the Congress in Munich. It never met there. On 5 June 1897 a notice in the Münchner Neueste Nachrichten rejected holding his congress in the city, and in mid-June, in letters dated 13 June, the board of the Munich Jewish congregation wrote to Herzl rejecting it as well.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The venue moved to neutral Switzerland. In one account, the protest of local Orthodox and Reform rabbis helped push the Congress to Basel, and the German Rabbinical Association refused to support holding it in Munich.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] The documents of June 1897 name the congregation's board and the press notice as the first refusals.

The rabbis' formal protest followed. On 6 July 1897 the board of the Allgemeiner Rabbiner-Verband, the Union of Rabbis in Germany, published a resolution protesting Zionism, on the grounds of loyalty to the state and of religious messianism. Herzl gave its authors a name that stuck: the Protestrabbiner, the "protest rabbis".[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The declaration appeared in English in the London Jewish Chronicle on 9 July 1897, on page 9. It was signed by the Union's executive committee: Maybaum of Berlin, Horovitz of Frankfurt, Guttmann of Breslau, Auerbach of Halberstadt and Werner of Munich. It called the Zionists' efforts toward a state "antagonistic to the messianic promises of Judaism", and it urged Jews to "hold aloof" from the movement and from its Congress.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_protest] The document is more precise than the label attached to it. The rabbis did not object to Jewish agricultural colonization of Palestine. What they rejected was a political state.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_protest] In Britain, the Orthodox Chief Rabbi Hermann Adler sided with the German rabbis and called Herzl's plan völlig unheilbringend, "completely disastrous".[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel]

The Congress met in the Basel Municipal Casino. The figure most often given for its size is 208 delegates from 17 countries, among them 14 women who attended without a vote.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] Herzl presided in top hat and morning coat, and a photograph of him leaning over the balcony of the Drei Könige hotel became one of the movement's most familiar images.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] The size of the gathering is less certain than the famous number suggests. The Posen Library describes some two hundred delegates from seventeen countries.[cite:rs_rd1_posen_congress] The Jewish Virtual Library gives "some 200 participants" without naming the number of countries.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_a] The historian Tobias Grill writes that the delegates came from fourteen states.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel] The sources agree on roughly two hundred people; they differ on the exact count and on whether the delegates came from fourteen states or seventeen countries.

The program that the Congress adopted unanimously on 30 August 1897 was short. Its aim, in a standard English translation, read:[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki][cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest]

Zionism seeks to establish a home in Palestine for the Jewish people, secured under public law.

Another published translation renders the same sentence as "the establishment of a publicly and legally secured home in Palestine for the Jewish people". Both versions turn on one word. The German original uses Heimstätte, a home or homestead, and not Staat, a state.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest] The wording was revised during the Congress itself. According to one reference account, the draft first read rechtlich, "legally" secured, and was changed to öffentlich-rechtlich, "secured under public law"; that account does not give the reason for the change.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki] The difference matters. A home secured merely "legally" could rest on private purchase and contract. A home secured under public law implied recognition by governments.

The program then named four means to the aim. The first was the promotion of settlement in Palestine by Jewish agriculturists, artisans and tradesmen. The second was the organization of all Jews through local and general institutions "according to the laws of the various countries". The third was the strengthening of Jewish national feeling and consciousness. The fourth was preparatory steps toward obtaining the consent of governments, which was needed to reach the aim.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_wiki][cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest] Read against the twenty years that followed, these four clauses work as a plan of construction. Each produced an institution or a line of action, set out below.

The founders said plainly what kind of project this was. Der Judenstaat had framed it as secular nationalism, modeled on the nation-building of nineteenth-century Europe, and Herzl himself was religiously non-observant.[cite:herzl_judenstaat] The First Congress's program, preserved in the Zionist Organization's own archives, deals with political organization, the mechanisms of land purchase and diplomatic outreach, not religious doctrine. Religious authority was contested at the Congress and largely absent from its decisions.[cite:wiki_first_zionist_congress] None of this shows that no delegate had religious motives, or that Zionism never took on religious meaning for its adherents later. It shows what the founding texts say about the founding project, and the texts are still there to be read.

The Congress's most durable product was an organization. The Zionist Organization was built as a standing, congressional-style body of elected delegates with a governing executive, and from 1899 it had its own bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust.[cite:wiki_wzo] Herzl was its first president; Chaim Weizmann would lead it in the period of the Balfour Declaration. It ran the Congresses, managed land purchase through the Jewish National Fund from 1901, and conducted the great-power diplomacy that produced the Declaration in 1917. In 1929 it created the expanded Jewish Agency for Palestine, which became the proto-government of the Jewish community under the British Mandate, running immigration, settlement, defense and diplomacy. When the state was declared in 1948, the Agency's executive effectively became Israel's provisional government. The organization continues today, and the Jewish Agency still administers immigration and diaspora relations with quasi-governmental status, formalized by an Israeli law of 1952.[cite:wiki_wzo] The line from Basel to the state is an institutional one: a durable, public bureaucracy that outlived everyone who built it, and whose working is traced in [scene:zorg_s01|the organization's machinery]. Herzl understood that the members would have to be won. At the Second Congress in 1898 his watchword was to "conquer the communities", meaning the established congregations.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_basel][cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_a]

Herzl's own verdict on the Congress has become part of its legend. After Basel he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State. Perhaps in five years, certainly in fifty, everyone will see it."[cite:herzl_diaries] He was wrong about the five years and almost exactly right about the fifty: the state was declared in May 1948, fifty-one years later. He did not live to see any of it. He died in 1904 at the age of forty-four, exhausted by the diplomacy of offering his project to the Sultan, the Kaiser and the British. The prediction should not be read as more than it was. Herzl foresaw an outcome, not the path to it; nothing in the entry anticipates the Balfour Declaration, the Mandate or the war of 1948 through which statehood actually came.

Opposition to the project came from several directions at once, and the objections were different in kind. The most popular was secular and socialist. The General Jewish Labour Bund was founded in Vilna in October 1897, in the same season as the Basel Congress, and became Zionism's great rival for the loyalty of the Jews of Eastern Europe.[cite:wiki_bund] Against emigration to Palestine it set the idea of doikayt, "hereness": Jews should fight for their rights and build their culture where they already lived, as a national minority with autonomy inside democratic, multi-ethnic states, in solidarity with the non-Jewish working class. It was socialist, Yiddishist and committed to the diaspora. From the 1900s to the 1930s it was arguably the largest and most dynamic Jewish political movement in Poland and the Russian Empire, and in interwar Poland it regularly outpolled the Zionist parties in Jewish community elections. The Bund did not lose its argument with Zionism; it was destroyed. The Bolsheviks dissolved it in 1921, its leader Mark Liber was later executed in the Stalinist purges, its mass base in Polish and Soviet Jewry was murdered in the Holocaust or suppressed under Stalin, and the Polish Bund was suppressed a second time after the war.[cite:wiki_bund] For half a century the most popular Jewish political movement in the heartland of Zionist recruitment was explicitly anti-Zionist.

A second objection was theological. Orthodox anti-Zionist rabbis held that the return of the Jewish people to the land and the restoration of Zion were redemptive events reserved for divine action in the messianic age, not a political program to be forced by secular nationalists ahead of God's time. To many Orthodox authorities, a secular state built in the Holy Land by non-observant socialists was closer to sacrilege than to fulfillment.[cite:neturei_karta] This was a different argument from the Bund's: the Bund wanted Jewish autonomy without a state, while these rabbis rejected human political action as the means of return. The position has been held continuously since 1897, through Satmar Hasidism and, most visibly, the small Neturei Karta group, whose members still appear at Palestinian-solidarity demonstrations with signs distinguishing Judaism from Zionism. It is a minority position within Orthodox Judaism; most Haredi Jews today are not Neturei Karta and have made various accommodations with the state.[cite:neturei_karta] Reform Judaism's opposition and the wider range of Jewish positions in these years are traced in [scene:rd1_currents|Jewish currents for and against].

A third objection came from inside the movement. Ahad Ha'am, "one of the people", was the pen name of Asher Ginsberg (1856–1927), the founder of what came to be called cultural Zionism and political Zionism's sharpest internal critic.[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] He had visited Ottoman Palestine, and in his essay of 1891, "Truth from the Land of Israel", he reported what much of the movement preferred not to see: the land was not empty. It had a substantial Arab population, farming and living on it, who would not simply accept displacement, and he warned that treating them with contempt would poison the whole enterprise. This is Zionist testimony, from 1891, that Palestine was inhabited. Against Herzl he argued that a hurried political and diplomatic state would produce "a state of Jews" but not "a Jewish state": a polity Jewish in population but hollow in spirit, having skipped the slow cultural and ethical renewal he believed must come first. He wanted a spiritual center in the land that would radiate a renewed Hebrew culture to the diaspora, not a nation-state won through great-power maneuvering.[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] Many later readers, Israelis across the political spectrum among them, have found the warning prescient and still invoke it. What the record establishes is narrower and firmer: the warning was made at the founding moment, not in hindsight. It cannot show that his alternative would have produced a better outcome had it been adopted.

The fourth opponent was the movement's greatest existing patron. Baron Edmond de Rothschild (1845–1934), of the Paris branch of the family, had privately funded the struggling agricultural colonies of the First Aliyah in Ottoman Palestine since the 1880s, among them Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov, which was named for his father. His money, sums that would run to tens of millions in today's terms, effectively kept early Jewish settlement alive when it might otherwise have collapsed. Yet Edmond personally opposed Herzl and political Zionism. He distrusted Herzl's public, diplomatic, state-seeking approach and favored quiet, paternalistic philanthropic colonization that would not provoke the Ottoman authorities or make grand political claims, and for years he refused to place his settlements under the Zionist Organization. The two men held incompatible theories of the project, as Simon Schama documents in Two Rothschilds and the Land of Israel.[cite:schama_two_rothschilds] Edmond must be kept distinct from Walter Rothschild of the London branch, who twenty years later was the ceremonial addressee of the Balfour letter and who neither funded the settlements nor wrote the policy. The phrase "the Rothschilds created Israel" fuses two men with opposite roles and opposite views into one imaginary actor, the move by which a documented banking family is turned into an antisemitic hidden hand. The record shows members of one family reaching their own, divergent judgments, not a coordinated plan; his colonies and his first refusal of Herzl are told in [scene:bc_s04|the baron who built the colonies].[cite:schama_two_rothschilds]

Two questions about Herzl himself remain open. The first is what moved him. The usual account, repeated in many references, holds that his catalyst was the Dreyfus Affair: covering for a Vienna newspaper the 1894 degradation of a Jewish French officer, and watching a Paris crowd chant against Jews in the most emancipated society in Europe, he concluded that assimilation had failed as a strategy for Jewish safety and that a national home under public law was the only political answer.[cite:zionism_founding_1897] The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's 2020 biography of Herzl, points to a difficulty: Dreyfus "is not mentioned by name in the Zionist diary of 1895", and Beller uses this to question whether the Affair was the catalyst at all.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_basel] The strongest form of the traditional case is that Herzl was in Paris as a correspondent during the Affair and that its lesson about European antisemitism fits his program exactly. The strongest form of the revision is that the diary in which he worked out his Zionism in 1895 is silent about the case. The record here does not settle which reading is right.

The second question concerns words Herzl never wrote. Fabricated quotations cluster around him, and the best known is a line claiming a Jewish state from the Nile to the Euphrates. It is not in his writings; the attribution has been traced to a misattribution of 1994 and debunked. The Herzl of the record was a secular nation-builder who weighed Argentina and entertained Britain's East Africa offer, not a maximalist with a scriptural map. Keeping the real Herzl distinct from the invented one is part of reading the founding of the movement accurately.

What the record of 1897 does not settle should also be stated. It does not give a single agreed count of the delegates or their countries. It does not explain why rechtlich became öffentlich-rechtlich in the program's aim, only that it did. It does not measure how many Jews in 1897 supported Herzl, opposed him or were indifferent; it records the institutions and named individuals who took positions, and on that evidence the movement began as one current among several in Jewish life, contested from its first summer. It does show that the program asked for a "home", not a "state", in its text, while its convener wrote in private that he had founded a state.

sections.h: The Machinery: How the Zionist Organization Worked, 1897–1917
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that early Zionism was a loose collection of enthusiasts without formal structure, a mood more than a movement. The record shows the opposite. Within two years of Basel the Zionist Organization had a written constitution, an elected parliament, a standing executive, a council of national leaders, national branches in the United States and Britain, and a bank. By 1917 it had a land fund, an office in Palestine and a recognized channel to the British government. What follows is how that machinery was built and how it worked.

Membership was open and cheap by design. Any individual or group that accepted the Basel Program and paid an annual due, called the "shekel", could join.[cite:palquest_wzo] The sources consulted here do not give its amount or the number of shekel-payers in these years. The principle, however, is clear. The organization was built on mass membership by small annual dues, not on the patronage of a single benefactor.

Authority flowed from the Congress. Its constitution, adopted at the Third Congress in 1899, created two governing bodies. The Smaller Actions Committee, with seven members, was the executive, and its chairman was the president of the Congress. The Larger Actions Committee, with 37 members, was a council of national leaders.[cite:palquest_wzo][cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] The Congress itself met every year until 1901 and every two years after that; the Fifth Congress of 1901 made the change.[cite:palquest_wzo][cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] Below the central bodies stood national federations, country-level organizations that recruited members and raised money. The Federation of American Zionists was founded in 1898 and later became the Zionist Organization of America. The English Zionist Federation followed in 1899.[cite:w_zf_gb]

The organization's tools followed one another quickly. The Jewish Colonial Trust, its bank, was established in 1899; the Jewish National Fund, to buy land, in 1901; and the Palestine Office in Jaffa in 1908.[cite:palquest_wzo] The mechanism is worth stating plainly. The Congress, a body of delegates, decided policy. The small executive carried it out between sessions. The federations supplied members and money, and the financial and land instruments turned that money into assets in Palestine. What the machinery could not do is equally plain. It held no governing authority in Palestine, which remained Ottoman territory until 1917, and the consent of governments was still, as the Basel Program itself acknowledged, something to be obtained.

The Congresses between 1898 and 1913 show the organization working out what it was for, often by open argument and recorded vote. The Second Congress, at Basel in 1898, laid the groundwork for the Jewish Colonial Trust. The Third, at Basel in 1899, resolved that the Trust's funds could be spent only in Palestine or Syria, an early decision that bound the movement's money to one region before any territorial alternative had been offered.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] The Fourth Congress met in London in 1900; there religious Zionists led by Yitzhak Ya'akov Reines urged that the organization keep a purely political focus. The Fifth, back at Basel in 1901, established the Jewish National Fund. At the same Congress a group called the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization. It was also this Congress that moved the meetings to every other year.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b]

The organization's sharpest crisis came over territory. The Sixth Congress, at Basel in 1903, voted "295 in favor, 178 against and 98 abstentions" to send a commission to examine settlement in East Africa, a British offer told in full in [scene:s04e|the East Africa offer].[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] Herzl died the next year. The Seventh Congress, at Basel in 1905, voted against a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity. Israel Zangwill's Territorialists walked out, and David Wolffsohn became president.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] The decision settled that the organization's aim was Palestine, and it was taken by a split vote in a Congress, not decreed by a leader.

The next argument was about method. At the Eighth Congress, held at The Hague in 1907, delegates debated "practical" against "political" Zionism. The Congress supported practical work, including a Palestine branch of the organization under Arthur Ruppin, and Weizmann's "synthetic Zionism" gained ground.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] That branch became the Palestine Office, whose work is traced in [scene:s04g|the Palestine Office]. At the Ninth Congress, in Hamburg in 1909, the practical camp challenged Wolffsohn's leadership. At the Tenth, at Basel in 1911, the first session was held in Hebrew, and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn as president. The Eleventh Congress, in Vienna in 1913, backed the founding of a Hebrew University in Jerusalem, which opened twelve years later.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b]

Read together, these meetings trace a shift in the organization's center of gravity. In its first years it sought a charter through diplomacy and built the financial means to use one. After Herzl's death and the East Africa split, it moved toward building in Palestine directly, while the Democratic Faction's push for Hebrew culture surfaced in the first Hebrew session of 1911 and the university resolution of 1913. The movement's leadership changed in the same direction, from Herzl the diplomat, to Wolffsohn, whose leadership the practical camp challenged in 1909, to Warburg.

The First World War cut across this structure. Before the war the organization's head offices were in Germany, and when war came it declared itself neutral. Its effective leadership passed to London, where Chaim Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, and Nahum Sokolow became its de facto leaders.[cite:ismi_israel_yearbook][cite:weizmann_papers_v9] The English Federation, founded in 1899 as one national branch among several, thus became in wartime the movement's channel to the British government.

That channel was contested within British Jewry itself. In May 1917 the community's official representative bodies, the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association, published an anti-Zionist statement in The Times. Days later the English Zionist Federation held a conference in London.[cite:jpost_why_rothschild] The episode explains a detail of the Balfour Declaration that is often misread. Because British Jewry's official bodies opposed Zionism, the government could not address its letter to them. The declaration was instead addressed to Lord Rothschild, for transmission to the Zionist Federation.[cite:jpost_why_rothschild] The declaration itself, and the wider wartime context of competing promises, belong to the next stage of this book: [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

Some things the record here does not settle. It does not give the size of the shekel, the number of members in any year, or the federations' budgets, so the scale of the money that flowed through this structure before 1917 cannot be stated from these sources. It does not show how the 37 seats of the Larger Actions Committee were apportioned among countries, or how far the seven-member executive in practice controlled the Congress rather than answering to it. It does not explain how the neutral organization's German headquarters and its London leaders divided authority during the war. What it does show is enough to answer the claim of formlessness: by 1917 political Zionism was a constituted, voting, dues-paying organization, with branches, instruments and a leadership placed where the decisive government was.

sections.h: Any Power That Would Sign: Herzl's Search for a Charter, 1898–1904
sections.html:
When the delegates left Basel in 1897, the program they had adopted named an aim but no patron. Theodor Herzl's answer to that gap was a single word he used again and again: a charter. By a charter he meant legal backing for Jewish settlement, granted by a great power that could make it stick. The familiar telling of Zionist history has the movement looking to Britain from the start, as though 1917 had been the plan all along. The diplomatic record of Herzl's own years shows something looser and more opportunistic. Between 1898 and 1904 he approached the German Kaiser, the Ottoman Sultan, the British Colonial Secretary, the Russian Interior Minister and the Pope, and to each he brought whatever that power seemed most likely to want.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl]

The reason for this method lay in the structure of the problem. Herzl led an organization with a Congress and a program, but no territory, no army and no standing in international law. Palestine belonged to the Ottoman Empire. Only a sovereign, or a power that could lean on one, could turn a settlement scheme into a legal right. Herzl therefore needed someone else's signature, and he had no fixed view about whose it should be.

He tried Germany first. The introduction came through William Hechler, a Christian restorationist, a believer in the return of the Jews to their ancient land, who had access to the German court. Through him Herzl met Kaiser Wilhelm II three times in 1898: in Istanbul, at Mikveh Israel, an agricultural colony funded by the Rothschilds, and in Jerusalem itself.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl] He did raise the matter with the Sultan. The request failed, and the Kaiser's interest faded after it.[cite:wiki_kaiser_levant_1898]

Herzl then went directly to the ruler of Palestine. He had been pursuing a charter from Sultan Abdul Hamid II since 1896, and his offer had a consistent shape: help in consolidating the Ottoman public debt.[cite:w_herzl] The empire's debts were chronic, and Herzl proposed to put Jewish finance to work on them in exchange for the right to settle. On 17 May 1901 the Sultan finally received him. Herzl made the offer in person. No charter was granted.[cite:avnery_herzl_sultan] [cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress] [cite:w_abdulhamid]

The clearest statement of the Ottoman position comes from Herzl's own diary. It records a message relayed to him from Abdul Hamid II: the Sultan could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people.[cite:w_herzl] The message carries weight precisely because of where it is preserved. It was not written by an opponent of Zionism to discredit Herzl; it was written down by Herzl himself. It answers a claim still heard today, that the Ottoman Empire welcomed the Zionist movement or sold it Palestine. At the level of the throne, the answer was no.

That refusal was matched by policy. From the 1880s the Ottoman government imposed restrictions on Jewish immigration to Palestine and on Jewish land purchase there. The restrictions were real, but they were enforced unevenly. Corruption among officials weakened them, and so did the protection that foreign consuls extended to their own nationals, which could shield a European Jewish immigrant from Ottoman law. Purchases continued through these openings, and through a second Ottoman instrument working in the opposite direction. The Land Code of 1858 required land titles to be registered. Many peasants avoided registering, and large tracts were registered instead to urban notables and absentee owners, whose later sales to the Jewish National Fund led to the eviction of the tenant farmers who worked the land.[cite:w_ottoman_land_code] The Ottoman state thus played two roles at once: the ruler who refused a charter, and the legal order under which land could change hands regardless. How those restrictions were drafted and evaded in practice, and how the absentee estates were bought, is told in [scene:s04j|the land purchase mechanism].

With the Sultan's door closed, Herzl changed both his patron and his offer. In October 1902 he proposed to the British Colonial Secretary, Joseph Chamberlain, a Jewish settlement at El-Arish in the Sinai. He framed it as a buffer protecting British interests at the Suez Canal. Britain tentatively agreed.[cite:unu_water_elarish] [cite:wiki_leopold_kessler] The scheme then ran into the authority that actually governed the ground. In 1903 Lord Cromer, Britain's man in Cairo, vetoed it. The Nile water needed to irrigate a settlement in the Sinai, he said, could not be spared.[cite:unu_water_elarish] The inducement this time was strategic rather than financial, and it failed on a practical question of water rather than on principle.

The most controversial approach came next. In April 1903 came the pogrom at Kishinev, in the Russian Empire, told in [scene:s04e|Kishinev and the East Africa offer]. In August 1903, months afterwards, Herzl twice met the Interior Minister, Vyacheslav von Plehve, a man widely regarded as responsible for the atmosphere that had produced the pogrom. He did so without consulting Russia's own Zionists. The meetings produced a letter in which the Tsar's government agreed to press the Sultan for a charter and to allow Zionist societies to operate in Russia.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl]

Russian Zionists criticized the meetings sharply.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_herzl] The two sides of that quarrel can both be stated in their strongest form. For Herzl, a written commitment to lobby the Sultan, and legal room for Zionist societies inside Russia, were concrete gains that no amount of moral distance would have produced. For his Russian critics, the movement's leader had sat down, uninvited by them, with the minister they held responsible for the climate of Kishinev, and had done so on their behalf without asking them. The record shows the letter and the anger; it does not show that the letter ever moved the Sultan. Weeks later Britain's offer of territory in East Africa split the Sixth Zionist Congress.[cite:wiki_sixth_zionist_congress]

The last of these approaches went to Rome. On 26 January 1904 Herzl had a private audience with Pope Pius X, Giuseppe Sarto, to ask for the Vatican's support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The refusal was direct and on the record.[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] Herzl's diary records the Pope's words: "We cannot give this movement our blessing... We cannot prevent the Jews from going to Jerusalem — but we could never sanction it. The ground of Jerusalem, if it were not always sacred, has been sanctified by the life of Jesus Christ. As the head of the Church, I cannot tell you anything different." Herzl also met the Vatican Secretary of State, Cardinal Rafael Merry del Val, who is described as similarly unreceptive.

Two readings of the Pope's grounds appear in the sources, and they are not identical. One stresses doctrine: the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while the Jews denied Christ, a position later accounts call supersessionist.[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] The other stresses place: the Vatican's specific concern was Jerusalem and the status of the holy sites, which would be complicated by a non-Christian sovereign, rather than Jewish settlement as such. The Pope's own words, as Herzl recorded them, contain both: he would not prevent Jews going to Jerusalem, but he would not sanction the movement, and he grounded that in the sanctity of the city. Either way, the founder of the movement went to Rome and was refused. The Vatican did not recognize the State of Israel until 30 December 1993, forty-five years after its independence; that longer story is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's long refusal].[cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]

Set side by side, the approaches show a pattern. Herzl did not carry one proposal from capital to capital. He shaped each offer to its listener: finance for an indebted empire, a strategic buffer for a Britain anxious about Suez, and, in the Russian case, a movement that would draw Jews out of the empire. Germany, the Ottoman Empire, Britain and Russia were all approached within five years. On this reading, Britain's sponsorship in 1917 was the strategy finally succeeding with one power after failing with the others, not its point of departure.

The long arc of the Ottoman state's dealings with the Zionist movement, and later with Israel, runs from this period of imperial rule through the Treaty of Lausanne, decades of alliance and a later rivalry. The map below follows it; Herzl's audiences sit at its first step, when the empire still ruled the land and could refuse.

On their own terms these approaches produced almost nothing. The Kaiser lost interest, the Sultan granted nothing, Cairo vetoed El-Arish, the Russian letter yielded no charter and a revolt in the movement, and the Pope said no. Herzl died in 1904. What outlasted him was the method itself, the search for a sovereign's signature, and an organization able to keep searching.

Several things the record does not settle. It does not say what, if anything, Herzl offered the Kaiser in return for his intercession, nor exactly what the Kaiser asked of the Sultan. The Sultan's refusal of land is known through Herzl's own diary, as a message relayed to him; the sources here do not give its date or its intermediary, or an Ottoman record of it. The precise terms of the debt offer, how much and from whom, are not documented in this material. Plehve's responsibility for Kishinev is a matter of how he was widely regarded, not a finding of a court. And while the Pope's words survive in Herzl's account, the weight Pius X himself gave to doctrine and to the holy sites cannot be separated from that one record.

sections.h: The People Already There: Herzl, al-Khalidi and the Arab Question, 1895–1905
sections.html:
A common belief holds that the founders of political Zionism imagined Palestine as empty, and that the existence of its Arab population came as a later surprise. The record of the movement's first decade does not support that belief. Herzl, his correspondents and his allies wrote about the people living in the land, sometimes privately and sometimes in print, from the movement's earliest days. What they disagreed about, and what historians still argue over, is what they intended to do about them.

The question had been put to the movement before Herzl came to it. In 1891 Asher Ginsberg, writing as Ahad Ha'am, published an account of his visit to Ottoman Palestine reporting that the land was farmed and lived on by a substantial Arab population, who would not simply acquiesce to displacement; his warning, and his wider quarrel with Herzl, are told in [scene:s04|the Basel section].[cite:wiki_ahad_haam] The historian Steven Beller, reviewing Derek Penslar's biography of Herzl, notes that Ahad Ha'am raised at the time a point Herzl never fully absorbed: Herzl, in Beller's words, "lacked a realistic view about the antagonistic effect" a Jewish settlement would have on the local Arab population.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_arab]

The phrase most often attached to this period has an older and non-Zionist origin. The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration," who had himself travelled to Palestine in 1839 and knew it was populated. Lord Shaftesbury used similar wording in 1853. The first use by a Zionist came in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people."[cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] Historians debate whether the phrase meant a land literally empty or a land "without a nation." Whatever its authors meant, the Ottoman counts of the period, set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|the opening section], show a populated country. The slogan's later career, and the other talking points that grew up beside it, are examined in [scene:sq_s05|three claims checked].

Herzl's own first recorded thoughts on the matter came before the movement existed. In June 1895 he wrote a passage in his diary that has become one of the most argued-over sentences in the history of Zionism. As the Israeli researcher Shaul Arieli quotes it, by way of Edward Said, it reads: "We shall try to spirit the penniless population across the border by procuring employment for it in the transit countries, while denying it any employment in our country."[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer]

Two serious readings of that passage stand against each other, and each has its evidence. Arieli, in a 2025 survey, places it at the head of a chronicle: in his account the idea of moving the Arab population out was a long-standing strand of Zionist strategic thinking, and this 1895 entry is where it begins.[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer] Beller, drawing on Penslar, accepts that Herzl was "quite prepared to remove any local population," but adds two qualifications that matter. Herzl preferred to do it peacefully, through the employment mechanism the passage itself describes rather than by force. And "the context in which he was discussing this was not Palestine": the passage concerned South America.[cite:rs_rd1_beller_arab] The strongest form of Arieli's case is continuity: whatever territory Herzl had in mind, the passage shows that the founder of the movement treated a resident population as something to be moved, and later Zionist thinkers returned to the same idea. The strongest form of Beller's case is context: a private note about an unchosen territory, preferring economic pressure to coercion, is not the same thing as a plan for Palestine. Both scholars quote the same sentence. Neither the exact day of the entry nor its full surrounding text is given in the sources used here, so this book does not go beyond Arieli's quotation.

Four years later the question arrived at Herzl's desk from Jerusalem itself. The writer was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi. According to the reference account of his career, he served as mayor of Jerusalem in 1870–76, 1878–79 and 1899–1906, sat for Jerusalem in the first Ottoman parliament, and had taught at the Oriental Academy in Vienna.[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki] On 1 March 1899 he wrote to Zadoc Kahn, the chief rabbi of France, asking that the letter be passed to Herzl. It was not a hostile letter. Al-Khalidi called the Zionist idea in itself "natural, beautiful and just." But he set two facts against it: Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire, and it was inhabited by others. He closed with a plea: "in the name of God, let Palestine be left alone."[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept]

Herzl answered on 19 March 1899. His reply, as quoted, did not deny that the land was inhabited. His argument was that Jewish immigration would benefit the people already there: "It is their well-being, their individual wealth, which we will increase by bringing in our own." And he asked: "who would think of sending them away?"[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept] [cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_wiki]

How to read that reply is itself disputed. Taken on its own terms, it is a statement of good intent and a prediction: Jewish capital and labor would enrich the country, and no one proposed expulsion. The historian Rashid Khalidi, a descendant of al-Khalidi's family, reads it otherwise. He calls the reply condescending and argues that it did not answer al-Khalidi's central objection, that the people of Palestine would not accept being displaced, whatever the economic benefits offered them.[cite:rs_rd1_khalidi_intercept] The exchange set the founder of political Zionism against a senior Jerusalem notable, and the two men were, in a sense, writing past each other: one about sovereignty and consent, the other about prosperity.

Herzl returned to the argument in fiction. His novel Altneuland, published in German in 1902, imagines Palestine in 1923, run by a cooperative "New Society" in which land is publicly owned. The book has one Arab character, Reschid Bey. According to the standard summary of the novel, Reschid Bey says that Arabs had no reason to oppose Jewish immigration, because the newcomers "developed the country and raised everybody's standard of living."[cite:rs_rd1_altneuland_wiki] The character speaks almost the same argument Herzl had put to al-Khalidi three years earlier. A reader sympathetic to Herzl can see in the novel a sincere vision of a shared, prosperous country without expulsion. A reader persuaded by Rashid Khalidi can see the same objection unanswered: the only Arab voice in the book is one that agrees.

A blunter statement came from Zangwill, the writer who had first given the "country without a people" phrase a Zionist voice. In 1905, as Arieli quotes him, Zangwill wrote that "Palestine itself is already occupied," and that Zionists must be prepared either "to drive out by the sword the tribes in possession as our forefathers did" or "to grapple with the problem of a large alien population, mostly Mohammedan and accustomed to despise us."[cite:rs_rd1_arieli_transfer] The quotation reaches this book through Arieli's survey; its original place of publication is not confirmed in the sources used here. That same year Zangwill broke with the Zionist Organization over the East Africa question and went looking for a territory elsewhere.

Read in order, these documents settle the first question a reader is likely to ask. The founders knew Palestine was inhabited. Keith had seen it in 1839; Ahad Ha'am reported it in 1891; al-Khalidi told Herzl in writing in 1899, and Herzl answered him without denying it; Zangwill, the first Zionist to use the slogan, wrote in 1905 that the land was "already occupied." What they said about it ranged widely: from Herzl's assurance that no one would send the inhabitants away, through Altneuland's picture of shared prosperity, to Zangwill's choice between the sword and the "problem" of a large population. These are the words of individuals, in a diary, a letter, a novel and Zangwill's own statement, not resolutions of a Zionist Congress.

What the record does not settle is the question historians still divide on: what Herzl himself intended for the Arabs of Palestine. Arieli reads the 1895 passage as the start of a continuous strand of thinking about transfer; Beller and Penslar read it as a note about South America by a man who preferred peaceful means. Herzl's 1899 letter denies any intent to send the inhabitants away, and Rashid Khalidi reads that denial as evasion of the real objection. The sources here give the passages these readings rest on, not Herzl's full diary entry or his letter in its entirety, and a reader should weigh the competing readings with that limit in mind. What can be said plainly is that the warning al-Khalidi put to Herzl, that the people of Palestine would not accept displacement, was on paper in March 1899, and that the movement's founder answered it with an economic argument rather than a political one.

sections.h: The Jewish Colonial Trust: A Bank Owned a Pound at a Time
sections.html:
The Basel Program of 1897 named its means but not its money. A movement that hoped to obtain a charter from a great power, and then to settle people on land under it, needed capital of its own, and it needed an institution that could hold that capital, lend it and answer for it in law. The Second Zionist Congress, meeting in 1898, decided to create one. On March 20, 1899, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in Hebrew Otẓar Hityashvuth Hayehudim, was incorporated in London under the English Companies Acts. Its stated aim was to acquire the capital, and the "charter," that would make large-scale settlement in Palestine possible. Its authorized capital was £2,000,000, divided into shares of £1 each.[cite:jct_wiki]

The legal form is worth noticing. Incorporated under English company law, the Trust was not a charity collecting gifts. It was a company selling shares, and the people who bought them became owners of a bank whose purpose was political. It was political Zionism's first financial institution.

A familiar account of Zionist finance holds that the movement was paid for by a few great patrons, with the name Rothschild usually standing in for all of them. The design of the Trust points the other way. Its shares were priced deliberately low, at a single pound, and could be paid for in installments, with plans running to as many as 55 to 80 payments.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:bia_jewish_colonial_trust] The purpose was to let working-class Jews across Europe, and not only the wealthy, become shareholders in the national project. A buyer who could not spare a pound at once could pay it off in small sums over time. The logic is the one a modern crowdfunding campaign uses, applied in 1899: many small commitments in place of a few large ones. Herzl set the example by buying the first 1,000 shares himself.[cite:jct_wiki]

The Trust's founders each brought something different. Herzl supplied the political leadership and the public name. David Wolffsohn, a German-Jewish timber merchant and one of Herzl's closest associates, co-founded the Trust and would hold a remarkable run of offices: he chaired the Anglo-Palestine Company from its founding in 1902 and succeeded Herzl as president of the World Zionist Organization in 1905.[cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] Wolffsohn is also documented as the designer of the two-stripes-and-star flag adopted at Basel in 1897, the design that later became the state flag of Israel.[cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] The third co-founder, Jacobus Kahn, was a Dutch-Jewish banker. His contribution was technical rather than political: he supplied the banking expertise the new institution needed in order to function as a financial body and not merely as a symbol.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The record does not give Kahn a role in the wider movement comparable to Herzl's or Wolffsohn's, and none of the three acted alone; each institution they helped found had other named colleagues.

Measured against its own target, the Trust fell far short. The plan called for 2 million shares. Roughly 250,000 were sold worldwide, raising about £250,000, which is 12.5 percent of the authorized £2,000,000.[cite:jct_wiki] The sources document the shortfall but do not explain it in full. The installment design shows what the founders intended, not why the target was missed, and no account in this book's sources weighs the competing explanations. What the sources do support is that the gap did not make the Trust a failed institution. It continued for decades, and in time became a major shareholder of Bank Leumi, the bank that grew out of its Palestine subsidiary.[cite:jct_wiki]

The sum raised was not the real innovation. The Trust showed that a political movement could be financed by tens of thousands of ordinary owners, each holding a small stake, rather than by the goodwill of a handful of magnates. That model would carry the movement for the next fifty years. Two years later the Jewish National Fund turned it into a physical object, the blue collection box, and after 1920 Keren Hayesod made small-donor fundraising permanent.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:bia_jewish_colonial_trust] The pound share is the direct ancestor of both.

Wide ownership, however, was not the same thing as wide control. By 1899 more than 100,000 people had subscribed for shares, yet lasting control of the Trust sat with a small founding bloc, through a block of "founders' shares" that carried super-voting rights.[cite:jct_wiki] How that mechanism worked, and how long it lasted, is traced in [scene:s04j|the land-purchase pipeline]. The point here is the shape it gave the institution from the start: the cost of the project was spread across a mass of small shareholders, while its direction stayed with the founding leadership of the Zionist Organization.

A bank incorporated in London still had to reach Palestine. On February 27, 1902, the Trust founded the Anglo-Palestine Company as its Palestine-facing banking subsidiary.[cite:encyclopedia_jewish_colonial_trust] This was the point at which fundraising turned into settlement: the subsidiary would finance land purchases directly, run a network of credit cooperatives offering long-term agricultural loans to settlers, and in 1909 lend to the association that built the first neighborhood of Tel Aviv. Its founding, its managers and its branches are the subject of [scene:s04e|the next section]. The parent company in London raised the capital; the subsidiary in Jaffa put it to work.

The library's funding ledger places the Trust at the head of every documented stream of money behind the pre-state architecture. Its first row records the Trust as £2,000,000 authorized and about £250,000 raised in £1 shares, the money that bought "the movement's own bank."[cite:jct_wiki]

A second ledger, which sets each stream beside its value in today's money, gives the same £250,000 for 1899–1901 and converts it to about $47 million in 2025 dollars.

That conversion needs to be read with its method in view. The ledger multiplies each amount by the ratio of the 2025 consumer price index to the index of the year in question, the method of the United States government's own inflation calculator, converting pounds into dollars at the period exchange rate first. For years before 1913 it relies on estimates from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, and it labels those conversions approximate. The ledger also warns against adding its rows together: pounds of 1899 and dollars of 1948 are different units, and the streams partly overlap. The $47 million figure is therefore a rough measure of scale, not a precise sum. By that measure the Trust's raise was modest beside what came later. The ledger's own rows put Keren Hayesod's worldwide income for 1921–1929 at $20.1 million, about $370 million today, and the United Jewish Appeal's 1948 campaign at $150 million, about $2 billion. The Trust's importance did not lie in its size.

The full map of the money behind the state, from the Trust through the land fund, Keren Hayesod and the wartime campaigns, shows where the Trust sits: first in time, and the base on which the later institutions were built. The Trust began the pattern of organized, small-donor finance in 1899, and it began it with a registered company, a stated capital, and shares sold in the open.

Several questions the record does not settle remain. The sources give no full breakdown of who bought the 250,000 shares, by country or by size of holding, and no account of how many installment buyers completed their payments. They do not explain why the £2,000,000 target was missed. And while they document that ownership was wide and control narrow, they do not record whether small shareholders objected to that arrangement at the time. What the record does establish is the structure itself: a London company, a pound share sold on installments, a founding bloc that kept control, and a subsidiary in Jaffa that turned the capital into loans. Those four pieces were the movement's first financial machine, and every later one was built on the same plan.

sections.h: The Jewish National Fund: Land Bought and Never Resold
sections.html:
A bank could lend money, but it could not by itself hold land for a nation. The idea of a fund that would do exactly that was older than the Jewish Colonial Trust. Hermann Schapira proposed a national land fund at the very first Zionist Congress, in Basel in 1897. He died in 1898 without seeing it established.[cite:jnf_wiki] For four years the proposal sat on the Congress agenda, debated and deferred, Congress after Congress.

It came to a head at the Fifth Zionist Congress in Basel in December 1901. With the delegates ready to disperse once more without a decision, Herzl stood before them and pushed the matter to a vote: "After striving for so many years to set up the fund, we do not want to disperse again without having done anything." The motion passed, and the Jewish National Fund was founded on December 29, 1901.[cite:jnf_wiki] Within a month it had its first director, Johann (Yona) Kremenetzky, who ran it from Vienna.[cite:jnf_wiki]

The delay is sometimes read as resistance to the fund's purpose. The record does not show that. The sources describe repeated deferral, and the deferral appears to reflect ordinary institutional delay and competing priorities on a crowded Congress agenda, not organized opposition to a land fund as such. What the sequence does show is that the fund was not an automatic creation of the movement. It existed because its first proponent pressed for it and its leader forced a vote four years later.

The founding resolution was brief and absolute. As the sources give it: "The JNF shall be the eternal possession of the Jewish people. Its funds shall not be used except for the purchase of lands in Palestine and Syria."[cite:jnf_wiki] Two rules followed from it. The fund's money was restricted to a single purpose, the purchase of land, within a defined region. And whatever it bought became, in the resolution's language, the eternal possession of the Jewish people. The resolution as quoted applies that phrase to the fund itself; the sources' own summaries apply it to the land, and the practice that followed treated the land that way.

That practice was the most consequential design choice the fund made. Ordinary land changes hands again and again; a farmer buys it, his heirs sell it, a later buyer sells it on. The JNF built a rule to prevent that. From the start its land was removed from the market permanently. It was leased to settlers on long terms, not sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition once made.[cite:jnf_wiki] Land came into the fund and, by design, did not leave. That single rule is why the fund's totals, tracked across nearly half a century, only ever rose. The sources are careful on one point: the arrangement was not unique in kind. Permanent, inalienable land trusts exist in other places and other contexts. What is documented here is this particular, explicit rule, written into this fund's founding terms.

The money that paid for the land came, as with the Trust, from many small givers. The fund's best-known instrument was not designed at its headquarters. Haim Kleinman, a bank clerk in Nadvorna, in Galicia, put a blue box labeled "Keren Le'umit" in his own office and wrote to the movement's newspaper, Die Welt, proposing that the idea be taken up more widely. Kremenetzky adopted the suggestion, and the first mass-produced boxes were distributed in 1904.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] By the interwar years roughly one million blue-and-white collection boxes sat in Jewish homes around the world.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] The box made physical what the Trust's pound share had begun: a national project paid for in coins, household by household.

Kleinman himself was one of them. He visited Mandate Palestine in the 1930s and planned to settle there, but he perished in the Holocaust before he could do so.[cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] The man whose idea paid for land across the diaspora never lived on it.

Who the box's donors were, and what each of them understood their coins to be for, is a different question. The mass adoption of the box is documented. The intentions of a million households are not, and the record cannot say whether every donor knew of, or would have endorsed, each later use to which the fund's money was put.

The fund's first land was not bought at all. In 1903 Isaac Leib Goldberg of Vilnius, a Russian Zionist leader, gave it 200 dunams east of Hadera, a parcel that later became an olive grove.[cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] From that gift the totals can be followed almost to the eve of statehood. By 1920 the fund held 22,363 dunams. By 1935 its holdings were about 89,500 acres, some 362 square kilometers, with 108 communities on them. By 1940 they reached 516,000 dunams, and by 1947–48 approximately 936,000 dunams.[cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] [cite:jnf_wiki]

The units in that series shift: the 1935 figure is reported in acres and square kilometers, the others in dunams. A dunam is about 1,000 square meters, so 362 square kilometers is roughly 362,000 dunams, which is how the library's land chart plots it. Read in a single unit, the series grows from 200 dunams to about 22,000, then to about 362,000, then 516,000, then about 936,000.

The chart makes the shape of the record plain. Growth was slow for two decades, then steep. The fund's first twenty years added about 22,000 dunams; the five years from 1935 to 1940 added well over 150,000. The record also places the fund within Jewish landholding as a whole. At the moment of statehood, total Jewish holdings in Palestine came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, and the sources describe the JNF's share as more than half of that total.[cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] Taken at face value, the two rounded figures do not quite agree: 936,000 out of 2 million is a little under half. The fund's exact share depends on the precise total, which these sources give only as an approximation.

A common account holds that Zionist land buying before 1948 was sporadic and small. The record shows something different: a single institution, operating continuously for forty-seven years, under one rule, with its holdings rising in every period for which a figure exists. At the same time, the figure needs its context. Even at the end, all Jewish-owned land together amounted to about 7 percent of the country. The land fund was large within Jewish landholding and small within Palestine as a whole. Both facts are true, and a reader who hears only one of them will be misled.

These totals do not show that every dunam was acquired in the same way. The legal framework of the purchases, the sellers, and the tenants who lived on land that changed hands are treated in [scene:s04j|the land-purchase mechanism], which carries this section's numbers into the Ottoman and Mandate land system. The same JNF series appears again, with later figures beside it, in [scene:pm_s01|the ledger of the land's outcomes].

Several matters remain open. The record traces the fund's land but not, in these sources, its full annual income: how much the blue boxes collected in any given year is not documented here, and the library's funding ledger lists the JNF's income series among the totals still unavailable. The 1935 figure is given in a different unit from the rest, which makes the series harder to compare than it should be. And the precise share of Jewish-held land the fund owned in 1947–48 depends on a total that is reported only as roughly 2 million dunams. What is not in doubt is the mechanism: a fund founded by forced vote in 1901, financed by small givers, buying land that it would never sell.

sections.h: A Bank for Palestine, and an Offer for East Africa
sections.html:
In the eighteen months from early 1902 to the summer of 1903 the Zionist movement ran on two tracks at once. On one, it built a bank inside Palestine.
