On the other, under the pressure of a massacre in the Russian Empire, its own Congress voted to look seriously at land in East Africa. The two tracks pulled in opposite directions, and the conflict between them nearly broke the organization apart.

The first track began in London. On February 27, 1902, the Jewish Colonial Trust founded a subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, with initial capital of about £50,000.[cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] Its chairman was David Wolffsohn, the Trust's co-founder and later Herzl's successor. Its manager was Zalman David Levontin, one of the founders of Rishon LeZion in 1882, whom Herzl had recruited personally.[cite:apc_wiki] The parent company in London raised capital from small shareholders; the subsidiary was the arm that would put the capital to work on the ground, as [scene:s04c|the Trust's own history] describes.

The company opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903. From there it financed land purchase and agriculture and supported the credit cooperatives through which settlers borrowed. By 1914 it had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza.[cite:apc_wiki] Its name later changed twice: it became the Anglo-Palestine Bank around 1930, and Bank Leumi in 1950–51.[cite:apc_wiki] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The line runs unbroken from a £50,000 subsidiary of 1902 to one of the major banks of the State of Israel, though the bank's later operations are a different story from its founding years, and are not told here.

What "settlement financing" meant in practice can be seen in a single loan. The Anglo-Palestine Company lent to the Ahuzat Bayit association, which used the money to build the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv in 1909, six years after the Jaffa branch opened.[cite:apc_wiki] One bank, one association, one neighborhood: the record documents the financial link directly. The founding of the neighborhood itself, its lots and its first families, belongs to the story of the Second Aliyah and is told there.

The second track began with a massacre. At Easter, on April 6–7, 1903, a pogrom broke out in the town of Kishinev. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, 49 Jews were killed and more than 500 injured; 700 houses were looted and destroyed and 600 businesses and shops looted; about 2,000 families were left homeless; and the losses were put at 2,500,000 gold rubles.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] The violence had been prepared in print. P. Krushevan's newspaper Bessarabets had incited the population with a steady stream of articles, among them a blood libel.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev]

The same encyclopedia goes further, and its words should be read as its own judgment. Local and central officials, it states, prepared the pogrom, "evidently with the backing of the minister of the interior, V. Plehve," and the town's garrison of 5,000 soldiers did not intervene.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] The word "evidently" marks an inference from the evidence, not a document of instruction, and the role of Plehve rests in this book's sources on this one reference work. Herzl's own meeting with Plehve later that summer belongs to the story of his diplomacy and is told in that section.

The world responded. Protest meetings were held in London, Paris and New York. In the United States a protest petition was handed to President Theodore Roosevelt for transmission to the tsar, and the tsar refused it. The poet Bialik answered the pogrom with his poem "In the Town of Death."[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev] Kishinev was not the end. A second riot in the town in October 1905 killed 19 Jews and injured 56, and some Jewish youth formed self-defense units.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_kishinev]

The pogrom fell inside a movement of people far larger than Zionism. Between 1881 and 1914, according to the historian Shmuel Ettinger, more than 2.5 million Jews left Eastern Europe, about 80,000 a year. About 2 million went to the United States, about 350,000 to Western Europe, and about 300,000 to other overseas countries, Palestine among them.[cite:rs_rd1_ettinger] The proportions matter for everything that follows. The great majority of Jews leaving Eastern Europe in this period chose America. Palestine was one destination within a category of about 300,000. The question in 1903 was urgent and practical: where could people in danger go now?

That question produced the offer. After the Kishinev pogrom, Joseph Chamberlain, Britain's Colonial Secretary, offered Herzl the Guas Ngishu plateau in British East Africa for Jewish settlement.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] [cite:wiki_kishinev_pogrom] The territory lay in what is now Kenya, not Uganda, but the plan has been remembered ever since, inaccurately, as "the Uganda Scheme." The documented record ties the offer's timing to the pogrom. It does not establish what longer-term purposes, if any, Chamberlain or the British government had in making it; the record documents the offer and its trigger, not Britain's wider calculations, which belong to the later story of British policy.

The Sixth Zionist Congress opened in Basel on August 23, 1903, with about 600 delegates, the largest Congress to that date. It was the last Herzl would chair.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] He put the offer before it with careful limits. In his opening address he said of East Africa that "Zion this certainly is not and can never become," and described it as only an auxiliary colonizing measure.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] He also called it a Nachtasyl, a night shelter: a temporary refuge from immediate danger, not a replacement for the Land of Israel.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki]

The question before the delegates was narrow. They were not asked to accept East Africa as the national home. They were asked whether to send a commission to examine it. The Congress voted 295 in favor and 178 against, with 98 abstentions.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] [cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] Another source used in this book gives the vote as 295–177.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The difference is a single vote and does not change the outcome, but it is a disagreement between sources, and the more widely given figure, 295–178, is the one used here.

The numbers describe a divided body. With 98 abstaining, the 295 in favor were only just over half of the 571 delegates who voted or abstained. Then members of the Russian delegation walked out, arguing that the plan violated the Basel Program.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] The sources differ slightly on who left: one describes the Russian Zionist delegation walking out, another speaks of members of the delegation.[cite:uganda_scheme_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] Either way it was a stronger act than a recorded vote against. To leave the hall was to say that the question itself should not have been put.

Both sides had a serious case. Herzl's was a case about time. People were being killed now; a great power was offering land; and a refuge, explicitly temporary and explicitly not Zion, could save lives while the political work for Palestine went on. His opponents' case was about the program the movement had adopted six years earlier. The Basel Program named Palestine. To send a commission elsewhere, in their view, was to break the founding commitment of the organization they belonged to. That the walkout came from the delegation of the country where the pogrom had happened gave their objection particular weight. The record does not show, however, that every Russian Zionist shared the walkout, nor that the rift was never repaired. The movement went on functioning after 1903, and the question was settled two years later.

The familiar account has it that Palestine was always the only place Zionists were seriously prepared to build. The record of 1903 does not support that. Six years after Basel, the movement's own Congress voted to examine a territory in East Africa, as a considered answer to escalating violence and not as a gesture, and the vote split its delegates badly enough that one delegation left the hall. It was the nearest the movement came, after 1897, to turning away from Palestine. At the same time the record limits the point: what passed was an inquiry, framed by its own sponsor as a shelter for the night. Whether the 1903 vote would have led anywhere had Herzl lived is a question no document can answer. How the matter ended, at the Seventh Congress of 1905, is told in [scene:s04f|the next section].

Some things the sources leave unsettled. They do not give the exact date of Chamberlain's offer, beyond placing it after the pogrom. They rest the role of Plehve on a single reference work's inference. They do not say how many of the 98 abstainers sympathized with either side, or what each delegate's reasons were. What they do establish is the shape of 1902–1903: a bank opening its doors in Jaffa while a massacre in Kishinev drove the same movement to vote on whether to look for refuge somewhere else.

sections.h: East Africa Rejected: Palestine Chosen by Elimination
sections.html:
The East Africa question did not end with the walkout of 1903. It ended two years later, by a second Congress vote, and it ended at a price: a permanent split in the movement and the founding of a rival organization that spent twenty years looking for a homeland anywhere but Palestine.

The man who led that rival organization had begun on the other side of the 1903 debate. Israel Zangwill, a British-Jewish writer and Zionist leader, led the "Territorialist Faction" at the Sixth Congress. His argument was not that East Africa should replace Palestine. It was that the British offer should be used as leverage in later negotiations with the Ottomans over Palestine.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth] He was not alone among the movement's prominent figures. Otto Warburg, a German botanist (1859–1938) from a wealthy Hamburg banking family, also supported the East Africa plan at the Sixth Congress.[cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] He is a different man from the better-known twentieth-century biochemist of the same name, and his later career makes the point that support for East Africa in 1903 did not mean indifference to Palestine.

Between the two Congresses the movement lost its founder. Herzl died in 1904.[cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress]

The Seventh Zionist Congress met in Basel from July 27 to August 2, 1905. It did two things. It formally rejected the East Africa offer, closing the question the Sixth Congress had opened, and Britain withdrew the offer. And it elected David Wolffsohn, co-founder of the Jewish Colonial Trust and designer of the movement's flag, as president of the World Zionist Organization in Herzl's place.[cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] One reference work states the decision in broader terms: the Seventh Congress rejected a national home outside Palestine and its vicinity.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_c] The two decisions came at the same meeting, but the record does not link them as cause and effect. The succession followed from Herzl's death and would have come whatever the Congress decided about Africa.

For Zangwill the rejection was final. When the Congress turned the offer down outright, he led 28 delegates out of the hall and founded the Jewish Territorial Organization, the ITO, dedicated to finding land for Jewish settlement anywhere, no longer bound to Palestine.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth] He did not go alone or without means. The ITO had support at the time from two members of the Rothschild family, the brothers Leopold and Baron Nathan Mayer Rothschild, not to be confused with Baron Edmond de Rothschild.[cite:jewishaction_uganda_truth]

The ITO's search was wide. It sent exploratory expeditions to Canada, Australia, Mesopotamia (today's Iraq), Cyrenaica (in today's Libya) and Angola.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] It also ran the Galveston Movement, which directed Jewish immigrants to the United States through the port of Galveston, Texas, instead of New York.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] Zangwill himself, looking back, said that "there was not a land on earth that we did not think about." The search also went to court. Zangwill fought a case in the English courts against the Jewish Colonial Trust; as the sources describe it, the suit sought to restrain the Trust from colonizing anywhere outside Palestine, Syria, Asiatic Turkey, Sinai and Cyprus.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] The sources do not explain the reasoning behind the suit or record its outcome, so its purpose has to be left as they state it. What it shows is that the boundaries of the movement's territory were contested in law as well as in Congress.

None of the expeditions produced lasting settlement. The sources characterize the result in slightly different terms. One calls the Galveston effort a failed attempt to settle Jewish refugees in Texas and says the ITO's search met with little success; another speaks of a single modest, temporary success without naming it. They agree on the larger outcome: the ITO achieved little lasting settlement anywhere.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism] [cite:wiki_jewish_territorial_organization] Zangwill rejoined the mainstream Zionist movement before his death in 1921. The ITO officially disbanded around 1925, four years later.[cite:encyclopedia_territorialism]

Otto Warburg's path ran the other way. Having backed East Africa in 1903, he became the World Zionist Organization's third president, serving from 1911 to 1921, and with Arthur Ruppin founded the Palestine Land Development Company, which he named and led until his death, bringing the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder.[cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] The company's work is told in [scene:s04g|the section on the Palestine Office]. His career shows how contested the movement's direction was in 1903, and how quickly it settled once the Congress had voted.

A common view treats East Africa as a footnote and holds that no real alternative to Palestine ever existed. The record does not bear that out. The alternative was put to two Congresses. It cost the movement a walkout in 1903 and a permanent split in 1905. And after the split, an organized faction with prominent backers and a court case of its own spent two decades looking for other land and did not find it. That is a different finding from "no alternative existed." Alternatives existed, were pursued, and failed.

It is in that sense that Palestine was confirmed by elimination. Its place as the movement's target survived two organized internal challenges: the 1903 vote to examine East Africa, and the ITO's departure in 1905 to search elsewhere.[cite:wiki_jewish_territorial_organization] The phrase needs care, though, in both directions. It does not mean the 1903 Congress chose East Africa: it voted to examine the offer, under a sponsor who said plainly it was not Zion. Nor does it mean Palestine won only because everything else failed. The Seventh Congress rejected East Africa in 1905, while the ITO's search had barely begun; the decision came first, and the failures came after.

What "confirmed by elimination" cannot show is why. The record documents the votes, the walkouts, the split and the search. It does not record a single rationale shared by the delegates who chose Palestine. Some, like the Russian delegates of 1903, argued from the Basel Program, which named Palestine. Others, like Warburg, moved from one position to the other within a few years. A reading that ties the outcome to the Jewish masses' religious and historical attachment to the land is offered in [scene:s04fa|the section on the Uganda counterfactual], and it is a reading, not a documented finding.

The gaps are real. The sources here say nothing about what the East Africa commission reported, or when exactly Britain withdrew its offer. They do not give the vote at the Seventh Congress, only its result. They do not name the 28 delegates who left with Zangwill, explain his suit against the Trust, or identify the "modest success" one of them mentions. What they establish is the sequence: a vote to look in 1903, a vote to refuse in 1905, a split, a search across five continents' worth of possibilities, and, by about 1925, its end.

sections.h: The Uganda Test: Could the Project Have Moved?
sections.html:
This section runs a thought experiment, and it should be read as one. Suppose the Sixth Zionist Congress had gone the other way in 1903, and a Jewish state had been built in British East Africa or in Argentina. What would it have been called, and would the structures later built on the name "Israel" still have worked? No document can answer a question about a history that never happened. What the documents can do is test one assumption that is often made without testing: that geography was incidental, and that the name and the theology later gathered around the state could have attached themselves to whatever territory the movement settled. Put to the record, that assumption does not hold up well. The record does not settle the counterfactual, but it shows which parts of the project depended on one particular place and which did not.

The section is therefore built from documented pieces: what Theodor Herzl wrote in 1896, what the Congress did in 1903 and 1905, what Genesis 15:18 says, and what Cyrus Scofield's prophetic notes require. The argument assembled from them is an argument, offered as such.

What Herzl wrote in 1896. In Der Judenstaat Herzl put the choice of territory as an open question: "Shall we choose Palestine or Argentine? We shall take what is given us, and what is selected by Jewish public opinion." He noted that Argentina's government would "gladly provide" Jews with land.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] His framework was, in the first instance, a political answer to European antisemitism, and Herzl himself was a secular Jew. One account of the text holds that he considered Argentina first and Palestine second, and that when he did prefer Palestine, it was because it would give "the Jewish problem" a solution "not only just, but brilliant," a practical and political reason (Palestine would mobilize Jewish public opinion) rather than a religious one. The Israeli peace activist and writer Uri Avnery went further, judging that Herzl "had obviously thought very little about Palestine as a concrete entity" and had inserted it into his original blueprint as an afterthought.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896]

The same pamphlet also sets the two territories side by side in different terms. Argentina offered practical advantages, fertile land and a sparse population. Palestine was "our ever-memorable historic home... a force of marvelous potency."[cite:herzl_judenstaat] Read this way, Herzl named, seven years before anyone offered him East Africa, the very difference the Uganda dispute would turn on: one territory had only practical merits, the other carried a weight no practical merit could replace. Both readings rest on the same 1896 text. They differ on emphasis: whether Palestine's pull, for Herzl, was mainly its power to rally Jewish opinion or its historic charge. Neither reading claims that every later leader or delegate shared Herzl's reasons. His words are evidence of his own stated view, not of a consensus.

What the Congress did, 1903–1905. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in August 1903 Herzl laid the British offer of land in British East Africa, known as the "Uganda Scheme" although the territory was not in Uganda, before the delegates as a temporary refuge for Jews fleeing persecution. One account gives the vote to send an exploratory commission as 295 to 177.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The account followed elsewhere in this book gives 295 in favor and 178 against, with 98 abstentions, and records that members of the Russian delegation walked out arguing that the plan violated the Basel Program.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_sixth] The sources differ by one vote. The first account describes the minority as mainly Russian and Eastern European delegates who had lived through the worst of the pogroms, and reads their walkout as a statement that they were not looking for any land; they were returning to Zion.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] Herzl died in 1904, and the Seventh Zionist Congress formally rejected the scheme in 1905.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The vote, the walkout and the context of the Kishinev pogrom are told in full in [scene:s04e|the section on 1903].

Zionist historical scholarship describes two broad strands that the dispute brought into the open. "Territorial Zionism," sometimes called Ugandism, held that any safe territory would serve: the purpose was refuge from persecution, and location came second to safety. "Zion Zionism" held that only Palestine, the biblical Land of Israel, Eretz Yisrael, would serve, because the purpose was not refuge alone but national restoration to an ancestral homeland. The debate of 1903–1905 settled the question in favor of Zion.[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The conclusion this account draws is that even secular political Zionism could not override the religious and historical attachment of the Jewish masses to that land; for most supporters, location was not interchangeable.

What the scripture names. The land-promise on which the later theology rests is specific. Genesis 15:18, in one translation, reads:

"On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, 'To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates.'" [cite:genesis_15_18]

Another rendering has "I have given this land" and "the Euphrates river."[cite:genesis_1518_text] Other texts add detail. Deuteronomy 11:24 reads: "Every place on which the sole of your foot treads shall be yours; your territory shall be from the wilderness, from Lebanon, from the river, the Euphrates river, to the western sea." Numbers 34 describes specific borders. Together these passages describe a territory in the Levant bounded by the Euphrates to the northeast, the Nile (or Wadi el-Arish) to the southwest, Lebanon to the north and the Mediterranean to the west.[cite:genesis_1518_text] A promise naming a bounded river-to-river territory is a different kind of promise from a blessing on wherever a people comes to live, and that specificity is what makes the test possible at all. It does not settle how the verse ought to be read. Non-literal, allegorical reading of scripture is an ancient and formally recognized tradition, not a modern alternative to the literal one.[cite:genesis_15_18] The test concerns only the literal reading, because that is the reading later Christian Zionism adopted.

The Scofield test. Scofield's dispensationalism, set out in the notes of his annotated Bible (told in [scene:s05|the section on the Scofield Bible]), arranges prophecy into an ordered sequence. Every step after the second depends on the regathering happening at the place the earlier covenant named, Zion and Jerusalem.[cite:wiki_scofield_bible]

A state in East Africa calling itself Israel would not satisfy "Israel regathered" in the sense the sequence's own logic requires. It would not be a variant of the same prophecy but a different claim, one Scofield's notes never made. On this argument, the 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists who later grew out of his framework exist because the state that formed stood where their theology pointed; move it, and there is a serious case that this constituency, and the sustained American political support it supplied, would never have formed.[cite:wiki_scofield_bible] The argument concerns what the theology's own text requires. It is not a claim about what every believer has consciously reasoned through.

The Greater Israel argument. A second line of argument, made elsewhere in this library, pushes the same logic further. It holds that the idea of Greater Israel, Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the "Complete Land of Israel," is a biblical concept that can exist only because the state was established in the biblical Land of Israel. In Argentina or East Africa, it reasons, five things would have been missing: the biblical land-promise framework, since Genesis 15:18 has no Argentine equivalent; the narrative of return to an ancestral homeland, since Jews had no historical claim to Argentina or East Africa; the concept of the Complete Land of Israel itself; the Revisionist Zionist claim to "both banks of the Jordan"; and the religious-nationalist settler ideology that draws explicitly on biblical texts about Levantine territory.[cite:herzl_judenstaat_1896] [cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] The argument's central step is that the same attachment to the land that made Argentina or Uganda unacceptable in 1903–1905 is the attachment that later generates territorial maximalism, so that the founding choice of Palestine already posed the question of the land's "completeness." As the argument itself puts it, "you cannot have the one without the other."[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] Those later claims belong to later periods and are followed in [scene:gia_src_s01|the Greater Israel question].

A symbolic reading, tested the same way. The opening of this library sets out one symbolic interpretation of the name, reading "Israel" as IS-RA-EL: a state of consciousness a person arrives at, rather than a bloodline or a border. That is an interpretation, not a documented finding, and it is labeled as such wherever it appears. Put to the same counterfactual, even this reading draws its resonance from places named in the text: Jerusalem, the Temple, and Peniel, where Jacob wrestled. A political entity in East Africa that borrowed the word would not carry that resonance by borrowing it.[cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] The literalist theology and the symbolic reading disagree about almost everything. On this one narrow point they converge: the place mattered, not only the word. The convergence goes no further, and it does not mean the symbolic reading endorses any of the literalist theology's other claims.

What would have travelled, and what would not. Fairness requires saying what a move would not have destroyed. The movement's financial and political institutions, among them the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Jewish National Fund, and later bodies such as AZEC, were built to fund and organize settlement, and nothing in their design tied them to one territory. Before Herzl, real settlement infrastructure had in fact been built in Argentina under the JCA. That machinery could have unloaded anywhere. What could not have travelled was the theological and symbolic layer.

If the test holds, it changes how the outcome of 1905 should be understood. Palestine was not merely the sentimental favorite among roughly equal choices. For at least one major source of the movement's eventual support, it was close to a structural requirement: the only site compatible with the theological and symbolic machinery that later supplied decades of American political and financial backing.

The other side. There is a strong case against reading too much into this. The familiar account holds that Zionism was first of all a response to European antisemitism, a movement for Jewish self-determination and safety; that the choice of Palestine was contested inside the movement, with some leaders open to other places; and that the eventual choice reflected the deep historical and religious attachment of most Jews to the biblical Land of Israel. Much of that account is borne out by the same record. The East Africa offer was a real offer of refuge, debated in good faith and voted on; those who walked out in 1903 were delegates from the communities that had suffered the worst pogroms, and what moved them was attachment to Zion, not a program of borders. The same source that builds the Greater Israel argument says plainly that the internal debate "was resolved by religious and historical attachment to the specific land, not by territorial maximalism."[cite:sixth_zionist_congress_1903] That attachment to the land is a precondition of the later maximalist claims is well supported. That the attachment by itself produced those claims is the argument's own inference, and it needs the later history, not the events of 1903–1905, to bear it out. The Scofield test, likewise, bears on the support the state later received from Christians; it does not explain the choice the Zionist delegates themselves made.

What the record cannot settle. No one knows what the founders would actually have named a state in East Africa, or how a Christian constituency would have responded to it, because those things never happened and cannot be documented. The movement did seriously consider East Africa; that is on record. What is offered here is a structural test applied to documented facts, and its answer is narrow: the theological apparatus examined in this book depended on the place, not only on the name. Whether Herzl's own preference was chiefly political or chiefly historic remains a matter of reading the same pages two ways.

sections.h: For and Against: Jewish Currents, 1885–1914
sections.html:
The years between the Basel Congress and the First World War are easy to tell as the story of one movement gathering a people behind it. The record shows something less tidy. Jewish opinion on Zionism in this period was plural, organized and argued in public, and several of its currents were founded expressly to oppose the movement or to contest what it should be. The first wave of opposition, in 1897, came from the German rabbis of the Protestrabbiner declaration, from the Bund and from Ahad Ha'am, and is told in [scene:s04|the section on Basel]. This section follows the currents that took shape around it, from a rabbinical platform in Pittsburgh in 1885 to a newspaper declaration in Berlin in 1914. Some stood outside Zionism and rejected it on principle. Others stood inside the Zionist Organization and fought over its program. A third group opposed both the movement and its religious wing.

Reform in America: "no longer a nation." The earliest of these positions predates Herzl. In 1885 the Reform movement in the United States adopted the Pittsburgh Platform, which declared: "We consider ourselves no longer a nation but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine" nor the restoration of the laws of a Jewish state.[cite:rs_rd1_reform_wiki] The position was put again in the year of the First Congress. In 1897 the Central Conference of American Rabbis resolved: "We reaffirm that the object of Judaism is not political nor national, but spiritual." Isaac Mayer Wise described Judaism as "not tied down to a piece of land here or there."[cite:rs_rd1_reform_wiki] These words come to this book through a reference work quoting N. W. Cohen's study of the subject; the original text of the 1897 resolution has not been checked for this volume. The substance is clear enough. For these rabbis the Jews were a religious community whose object was spiritual, and a national program, in Palestine or anywhere, contradicted that self-definition. Their objection was not to a particular piece of land. It was to the idea that Jews were a nation needing one.

Inside the movement: culture and the Democratic Faction. Within the Zionist Organization the argument was over what Zionism should do besides diplomacy. At the Fifth Congress in Basel in 1901, the Congress that also founded the Jewish National Fund, a group known as the Democratic Faction, among them Leo Motzkin, Martin Buber and Chaim Weizmann, pressed for Hebrew culture and for more democracy inside the organization.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] That December the Congress declared cultural work an essential part of Zionism.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Whether a national movement should take charge of Jewish culture at all was a question on which Zionists themselves divided, and the division soon had an organization of its own.

Mizrachi: religious Zionism, 1902. Three months later, on 4–5 March 1902, a convention in Vilna called by Rabbi Isaac Jacob Reines founded Mizrachi, the religious-Zionist faction within the Zionist Organization.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] Tobias Grill counts 72 delegates at Vilna, 24 of them rabbis.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] The faction grew fast. In its first year it built 210 branches in the Russian Empire, and its first world conference, held at Pressburg on 21–23 August 1904, drew about 100 delegates. Its motto set out the synthesis it stood for: "The Land of Israel for the people of Israel according to the Torah of Israel."[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] Mizrachi worked inside the Zionist Organization, and its motto put the Torah at the center of the national program.

The arrangement held for nine years and then broke at the point where it had started. When the Tenth Zionist Congress, meeting in Basel in 1911, added cultural work to the organization's formal program, all the Mizrachi delegates walked out. A later Mizrachi conference decided not to leave the Zionist Organization; some leaders who disagreed with that decision broke away.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_mizrachi] The episode shows how the organization actually worked. Program was set by majority vote in the Congress; a faction that lost could protest, walk out, or stay, and Mizrachi as a body chose to stay.

Orthodox opposition: Frankfurt and the Wahnjudenthum pamphlet. Religious Zionism had religious opponents from its first year. In 1902–03 Orthodox leaders of the Free Association, based in Frankfurt, declared Mizrachi's principles incompatible with traditional Judaism. A pamphlet by Raphael Breuer published in 1903 carried the title Nationaljudenthum ein Wahnjudenthum!, which branded national Judaism a delusion.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Here the objection ran opposite to Reform's. Reform rejected Jewish nationhood in the name of a spiritual religious community; the Frankfurt Orthodox rejected national Judaism as a counterfeit of the traditional faith, and rejected Mizrachi for trying to reconcile the two.

Agudat Israel, 1912. Orthodox opposition acquired an international organization a decade later. Agudat Israel was founded at Kattowitz in late May 1912 as a worldwide association of Torah-observant Jews. Grill describes it as founded largely as a countermeasure to Mizrachi.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Another account in this library puts the emphasis more broadly: Agudat Israel was founded to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism as a separation from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life.[cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history] [cite:wiki_neturei_karta] The two descriptions do not exclude each other; one names the religious-Zionist faction as the immediate rival, the other names the secular nationalism that faction had joined. Either way, organized Orthodox opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds existed thirty-six years before the State of Israel did. It was not a reaction to the state, which did not yet exist, but a theological position taken toward a movement that controlled no territory at all. The organization's later history, and the more uncompromising current that split from it, are followed in [scene:df_s13|a later volume].

Germany: the Antizionistisches Komitee, 1912–1914. In the same year liberal German Jews organized against Zionism on political grounds. In October 1912 they founded a league to combat Zionism, soon renamed the Antizionistisches Komitee. Its first pamphlet, issued early in 1913, reached about 45,000 copies by July of that year. An appeal of 1913 carried about 300 signatures, and the committee's declaration appeared in the Berliner Tageblatt on 5 February 1914. Before the war it reportedly had more than 1,000 members.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] Its instruments were those of a liberal civic organization: pamphlets, signed appeals and a declaration in a major daily newspaper.

Britain, 1917. The argument outlasted the outbreak of war. About twelve days after the Balfour Declaration, in November 1917, anti-Zionist British Jews formed the League of British Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] The Declaration itself belongs to the next stage; see [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

What the plurality shows. Set side by side, these currents answer a common assumption: that Zionism in its first two decades spoke for the Jews of the world, and that its Jewish critics were a fringe. The record shows at least four distinct positions, each organized and each documented in its own words. American Reform rejected Jewish nationhood as such. Liberal German Jews organized a committee against it. Frankfurt Orthodoxy and then Agudat Israel rejected it as a departure from the faith. And within the movement, secular nationalists and Mizrachi fought over whether culture or Torah would define it. The strongest case on the Zionist side is also in the record. Mizrachi's 210 branches in a single year show that religious Jews in the Russian Empire could be organized for the movement in large numbers, and the decision after 1911 to stay inside the Zionist Organization shows that the movement could absorb deep disagreement without splitting. The strongest case on the other side is that its opponents were not marginal cranks but the established rabbinical bodies of American Reform, leading Orthodox circles in Germany and an international Orthodox association, each stating a principled objection in public.

What the record does not settle. The sources give the founding dates, the counts of delegates, branches, pamphlets and signatures, and the key texts. They do not measure what share of the world's Jews held each position. The figures that exist count organizers and printed copies, not adherents, and they cannot be added up into a census of opinion. Nor does the material here say how these organizations were funded. The 1885 and 1897 Reform texts are quoted through a secondary source, and the AZK's membership figure is reported rather than established. What is established is that the argument existed, that it ran in several directions at once, and that each side made it in its own name.

sections.h: The Second Aliyah, 1904–1914
sections.html:
While the Zionist Organization argued in Basel and Hamburg, a second wave of immigrants was arriving in Jaffa. The Second Aliyah, the immigration of 1904 to the outbreak of war in 1914, was small beside the more than 2.5 million Jews who left Eastern Europe between 1881 and 1914, about 2 million of them for the United States.[cite:rs_rd1_ettinger] And about half of those who came to Palestine did not stay.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] But the years of the wave produced the first collective farm, the first Jewish guards' commune, the first Hebrew high school, and the neighborhood that became Tel Aviv. They also built, in the same years and through the same institutions, a principle of "Hebrew labor" that set Jewish and Arab workers apart. How historians weigh those two achievements against each other is one of the central disputes of the period.

How many came, and how many stayed. The sources do not agree on the size of the wave. The National Library of Israel puts it at about 35,000 immigrants, mostly from Eastern Europe, with a minority from Yemen; the Jewish Virtual Library gives 40,000.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] Both agree that departures were heavy. At least half, by the National Library's estimate, and nearly half, by the Jewish Virtual Library's, left within a few years because of economic hardship. By the end of the period the Jewish community numbered about 80,000.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] That end-of-period total is itself one of several competing counts of the Jewish population in 1914, which range from under 40,000 Ottoman subjects to over 90,000; the reasons the counts differ are set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|the opening section].

The country they found: Rothschild's colonies under the ICA. The newcomers did not arrive in empty institutional space. The farming colonies of the First Aliyah, financed by Edmond de Rothschild, were by then under new management. The Jewish Colonization Association, founded by Baron de Hirsch in September 1891 with a capital of £2,000,000, had taken over the administration of Rothschild's Palestine colonies. The 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia dates that arrangement "since 1899."[cite:rs_rd1_je_ica] The year-by-year ledger compiled for this library places it in 1900; the sources differ by a year. Those colonies were the first employers many of the new immigrants met, and, on Gershon Shafir's account discussed below, they ran on cheap Arab labor.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir]

One arrival: David Ben-Gurion. The best-known immigrant of the wave shows its pattern. David Ben-Gurion, born David Green in Płońsk on 16 October 1886, landed at Jaffa on 9 September 1906, according to Ben-Gurion House, and went that same evening to work in Petah Tikva. Another educational source, the Center for Israel Education, gives his arrival as 7 September 1907; the two dates cannot both be right, and this book does not choose between them. He joined the leadership of Poalei Zion; from 1912 he studied law in Istanbul with Yitzhak Ben-Zvi; and in 1915 the Ottoman authorities expelled him, and he went to Alexandria and then to New York.[cite:rs_rd1_bghouse] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_bg]

Hebrew labor, in principle and in practice. The young immigrants of the Second Aliyah came with an ideal of "Hebrew labor": Jewish farms worked by Jewish hands. The National Library of Israel notes that the ideal met friction in practice, because many Jewish farmers in the older colonies went on employing Arab workers.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] What the workers built next, guards and farms of their own, can be read as an answer to that friction; how far it was an answer, and how far the expression of an ideal held in advance, is the dispute taken up below.

The guards: Bar-Giora and Hashomer. The first answer was armed. In 1907 a small group founded Bar-Giora at Yitzhak Ben-Zvi's home in Neve Tzedek and set up the first Jewish guards' commune at Sejera. In 1909 Hashomer grew out of it under the leadership of Yisrael Shohat. It existed until 1920.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] Hashomer took over the guarding of Jewish settlements from Arab night watchmen, whom the Jewish Virtual Library's account describes as colluding with thieves; that characterization is the account's own, and the material here contains no Arab account of the same events. Hashomer also made it a condition of guarding a settlement that only Jewish laborers be employed there.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] That condition is the mechanism in miniature. A security service the settlements needed was tied to the labor policy the workers wanted, so the guards' bargaining power was used to enforce Hebrew labor where the ideal alone had not.

The farms: Kinneret, Degania, Merhavia. The second answer was settlement on national land. Kinneret Farm, set up in 1908, was the first Zionist instructional farm.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] Nearby, at Umm Juni on land owned by the Jewish National Fund, the first collective took root, though the sources date its founding differently. According to the Center for Israel Education, Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, was founded on 28 October 1910, when the "Hadera Commune," ten men and two women, leased the land from the Jewish National Fund; an earlier group that Ruppin had placed there in 1909 had dispersed. The Jewish Virtual Library dates Degania to 1909.[cite:rs_rd1_israeled_degania] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] The difference is not only one of dates: it turns on whether the dispersed group of 1909 or the commune of 1910 counts as the founding. Ruppin's role came through the Zionist Organization's Palestine Office, whose work is told in [scene:s04g|the section on the Palestine Office]. Two other experiments followed in 1911. The Merhavia cooperative disbanded in 1918, and a women's training farm founded that year trained about 70 young women before it closed in 1917.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] The arrangement at Degania shows the money's path: the land belonged to the Jewish National Fund and was leased to the workers who farmed it rather than sold to them.

The city and the school. The same years produced the first Hebrew urban institutions. The Hebrew Gymnasium, the first Hebrew high school, was founded in Jaffa in 1905; it later became the Herzliya Gymnasium. The idea of a new Jewish garden suburb, Ahuzat Bayit, arose in summer 1906. Its building plots were raffled at Passover 1909 among 60 founding families, and the neighborhood took the name Tel Aviv by majority vote.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] The loan that helped finance it came from the Anglo-Palestine Company, as told in [scene:s04e|the section on the Anglo-Palestine Company].

The Yemenites. The Second Aliyah is usually told as a story of young Eastern European socialists. A significant part of it came from Yemen, and that migration had begun long before. From 1881 to 1882 a few hundred Jews left Sanaa and nearby settlements for Palestine, and migration from Yemen continued almost without interruption until 1914; in that period about 10% of Yemen's Jews left, according to a reference account drawing on the 2003 study by Simon, Laskier and Reguer.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] In 1884 Yemenite families settled in a new neighborhood, Kfar Hashiloach, in Silwan, outside the walls of Jerusalem.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] These early arrivals came independently of the Zionist Organization, which did not yet exist.

In 1911 the organization took a hand. Shmuel Yavne'eli went to Yemen, at his own request, on behalf of the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, to encourage immigration; his journey lasted more than a year.[cite:rs_rd1_ejud_yavneeli] He returned in April 1912. About 1,000 Jews left central and southern Yemen as a result of his efforts, and several hundred more arrived before 1914.[cite:rs_rd1_yemen_wiki] The National Library of Israel calls the Yemenite immigration of 1911–12 "the first planned immigration operation in the history of Zionism," and counts about 2,000 Yemenite immigrants in the Second Aliyah as a whole, about half of them sent to farming settlements.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_yemen] Yavne'eli's own report, written in 1913, gives the scale from the inside: over the past year, he wrote, "some two hundred and fifty to three hundred Yemenite families have settled in the colonies."[cite:rs_rd1_posen_yavneeli]

Why the colonies wanted them is where the dispute begins. On Gershon Shafir's reading, as summarized by Joel Beinin, the planters brought in Yemenite Jews "who were to be paid Arab wages": Jewish workers who would satisfy the national ideal of Hebrew labor at the price of Arab labor.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir] One group's story shows what settlement on those terms could mean. Yemenite families from Sharab reached the Kinneret area in spring 1912 and cleared and farmed land there. According to the Yemenite heritage site Wysinfo, which reproduces the group's letters, their disputes with the neighboring Kvutzat Kinneret over land ended in 1930 with the Yemenites' removal to Marmorek, near Rehovot.[cite:rs_rd1_wysinfo] That ending falls well beyond this period and rests on a single heritage source; a later volume returns to it.

The historians' dispute: land and labor, or ideals. Two readings of the Second Aliyah stand against each other, and each has real evidence behind it. Gershon Shafir's study of 1989, as summarized by Joel Beinin, argues that the First Aliyah colonies relied on cheap Arab labor; that the Second Aliyah workers' "conquest of labor" failed to exclude Arab workers but did split the labor market in two; that the planters imported Yemenite Jews to be paid Arab wages; and that the kibbutz and Hashomer were forged in conflict over land and labor rather than mainly by prior ideology.[cite:rs_rd1_beinin_shafir] On this reading the institutions came first from the economics of a settler frontier, and the ideology explained them afterwards. The record above gives this case its strongest evidence: the farmers' continued hiring of Arab workers, Hashomer's condition that only Jewish laborers be employed, and Yavne'eli's families settled in the colonies.

Against such readings, Anita Shapira argues, as summarized by Rebecca Stein, that the early socialist settlers became conquerors reluctantly, out of "good will and purity of faith."[cite:rs_rd1_stein_merip] On this reading the motive force was a socialist and national ideal, of Jews remaking themselves through their own labor on their own land, and the conflict with the Arab population was a consequence the settlers did not seek. This case rests on the settlers' own convictions, and the material gathered here records what they did, not what moved them, so it cannot by itself decide between the readings. The two readings agree on what happened. They disagree on why, and on whether intention or structure should carry the weight.

What the record does not settle. The size of the wave is known only within a range of 35,000 to 40,000, and the share who left only as "about half." Degania's founding date depends on which group counts as the founders, and Ben-Gurion's arrival is dated to two different years by two reputable sources. The characterization of the Arab watchmen Hashomer replaced comes from one Jewish account; the material gathered here holds no account from the watchmen, the Arab workers displaced by Hebrew labor, or the villages near the new settlements. The Yemenite figures come partly from reference summaries, and the Kinneret group's later removal from a heritage site. And the central question, whether the Second Aliyah's institutions were driven chiefly by ideals or by the competition for land and work, remains a matter of interpretation on which serious historians differ.

sections.h: The Palestine Office: Settlement Gets a Bureaucracy
sections.html:
A familiar picture of Zionist settlement before the First World War shows lone pioneers improvising on the land, with no real organization behind them. Pioneers there were. But by 1908 the movement had also built an office, a land company and a small group of named purchasing agents, and it had set them up to work together. This section describes that apparatus: who set it up, what each part did, and what the record leaves unclear.

The decision came from the top of the Zionist Organization. In 1907 its president, David Wolffsohn, sent Arthur Ruppin to Palestine. In 1908 Ruppin opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa. It became the organization's central operating agency in the country for buying land and coordinating settlement, and it worked directly with the funds of the Jewish National Fund. [cite:ruppin_wiki] The section on how land was bought adds that Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, first came on a pilot study of the prospects for colonization. Ruppin was later called "the father of Zionist settlement." His fuller record, including the documented evidence that he believed Zionism required Jewish "racial purity," is set out in [scene:s04j|the section on how the land was bought]. [cite:haaretz_ruppin_retrospective] [cite:tandfonline_ruppin_weltanschauung] Here the subject is narrower: the institution he founded.

The Palestine Office had three jobs. It coordinated land purchase with the Jewish National Fund, it assisted immigration, and it helped settle the people who arrived. [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The office mattered because of the order in which the movement's tools appeared. The Zionist Organization had founded a bank, the Jewish Colonial Trust, in 1899 and a land fund, the Jewish National Fund, in 1901. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki] The Palestine Office, added in 1908, was the body in the country itself through which money raised abroad was turned into specific purchases and specific settlements. That is why a modest field office in Jaffa holds a central place in the institutional history.

The Palestine Land Development Company was founded beside the office. Ruppin set it up with Otto Warburg, and the sources date its founding to 1908 or 1909. The section on how land was bought gives 1908 and calls the company the office's operational purchasing arm. The company bought land and prepared it physically for ownership by the Jewish National Fund and for use by settlers. By the outbreak of the First World War it had handled approximately 50,000 dunams. [cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] This division of labour defined the structure. The Jewish National Fund was the owner, in whose name land was held. The company was the buyer and preparer, which negotiated, purchased and readied the ground. The office coordinated the two and placed people on the land.

Otto Warburg should not be confused with the better-known twentieth-century biochemist of the same name. He was a German botanist, born in 1859 and died in 1938, from a wealthy Hamburg banking family. At the Sixth Zionist Congress in 1903 he had supported the Uganda Scheme, the British offer of territory in East Africa told in [scene:s04f|the section on the territorialist split]. He later became the third president of the Zionist Organization, serving from 1911 to 1921. With Ruppin he founded the Palestine Land Development Company. He chose its name himself, led it until his death, and brought the Jewish National Fund in as a shareholder. [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] [cite:wiki_otto_warburg_botanist] His record shows how open the movement's direction still was in 1903, and how quickly it settled once the Congress had voted. His support for Uganda did not mean a weaker commitment to Palestine later. His decades of work on the company that prepared Palestinian land for settlement point the other way.

The shareholding is the main financial fact the record gives about the company. Through its stake, the land fund that owned land had a share in the company that bought it. The record does not give the company's capital, its other shareholders or its accounts. Nor does it give the Palestine Office's budget or staff. What can be said is where the money came from at the start of the chain. It was raised by the Zionist Organization's own instruments, the Jewish Colonial Trust's shares and the Jewish National Fund's collections, which are described in their own sections. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki]

Named people stood behind the land totals. In these prewar years Yehoshua Hankin, Arthur Ruppin and Jacob Thon negotiated and carried out land purchases. [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] [cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] Hankin was also the chief negotiator of the Sursock purchases, which are told in the section on how land was bought. Thon is recorded as the company's sole manager from 1907 until his death in 1950. The sources do not fully agree here. A manager from 1907 would predate a company founded in 1908 or 1909. Warburg is said to have led the company until 1938, and the section on land purchase has Hankin becoming its head in 1932. The material does not say how these roles divided. The question stays open. Naming these men turns a dunam total into a historical process with identifiable actors. They did not work alone, however. They worked inside the funding, legal and organizational framework that the neighbouring sections describe.

The relationship to later institutions is direct. The Palestine Office is the institutional ancestor of the Jewish Agency, established in 1929. [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The Jewish Agency became the institutional engine of state-building in Mandate Palestine. [cite:wiki_wzo] The line of descent is documented. It does not follow that every later Jewish Agency practice goes back directly to the methods of 1908. Organizations change, and what runs from Jaffa to 1929 is an institutional line, not an unbroken set of procedures.

The money chain for the whole pre-state period is set out as seven steps in the dashboard panel below. It begins with building a bank in 1899–1902 and buying land through the Jewish National Fund from 1901. It moves through the permanent fundraising of the 1920s and the enlarged Jewish Agency to the war financing of 1948 and the step of 1948–49 that turned donors into state policy. [cite:jct_wiki] [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_palestine_office] The Palestine Office does not have a step of its own in the panel. In this period it was the operating office through which the first two steps reached the ground. The panel's own note is a useful discipline for this section too. It does not claim that any government secretly funded the movement, or that money bought every decision. The record documents private, organized finance.

Two qualifications keep the picture accurate. First, the system did not always run in order. The section on land purchase records that agents such as Hankin sometimes bought land first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish National Fund or the Jewish Agency only afterward. The infrastructure existed, but the financing was not always planned centrally in advance. [cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] Second, the record here describes the structure, not its scale in money. It gives no budget for the office and no figure for what the company paid for its approximately 50,000 dunams. It does not say from whom that land was bought, or what happened to the people living on it. Those questions belong to the section on how land was bought, and the material for this section does not answer them.

The common claim, then, needs correcting on one point and not on others. Settlement before 1914 did involve individual initiative and improvisation. By 1908, however, eleven years after the First Zionist Congress at Basel and forty years before statehood, the movement had a dedicated professional office in Jaffa, a specialized land-development company and named purchasing agents. They connected fundraising abroad to purchase and settlement in Palestine. The pioneers worked within that structure.

sections.h: The Scofield Reference Bible, 1909
sections.html:
In 1909 Oxford University Press published a King James Bible with one man's notes printed beneath the text on every page. A common view holds that Christian support for Israel comes straight from ancient scripture, read plainly. The verses involved are ancient. The framework that links them to a modern political return of Jews to Palestine, and that made such a return a matter of prophecy for millions of American Protestants, has a more recent and more traceable origin. Its main vehicle was this annotated Bible. The research this book draws on argues that before Scofield the framework was "substantially absent" from American Protestant tradition, and that afterward it became a mainstream evangelical framework. Over the following century, on this argument, it produced a political constituency of roughly 30 to 40 million Christian Zionists, which supported the Zionist project in America before American Jewish support consolidated. [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] That is a strong claim. The record supports parts of it more firmly than others, and this section sets out which parts are which.

The ideas did not begin with Scofield. The earlier volume of this library traces [scene:bc_s05|the Christian restorationists] who came before him. The more immediate source was John Nelson Darby (1800–1882), an Anglo-Irish minister who founded the Plymouth Brethren and developed dispensationalist premillennialism in the 1830s. Darby visited America six times between 1862 and 1877 and spread the framework among American Protestants decades before Scofield's Bible existed. [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] That qualifies the claim of absence. Before 1909 the framework was known in America and was held by some of its Protestants. What it lacked was a place in the mainstream. According to the research, standard nineteenth-century American Protestantism was largely amillennialist or postmillennialist. It did not treat a modern political return of Jews as an eschatological necessity, and it did not treat the Church as a separate dispensation from Israel.

The man who carried Darby's framework into the American mainstream had an unusual biography for the purpose. Cyrus Scofield was born in Michigan in 1843, and his family moved to Tennessee. He served in the Confederate Army during the Civil War, from 1861 to 1865. In 1873 President Ulysses S. Grant appointed him United States Attorney for Kansas. He held the post for less than a year and resigned amid financial irregularities. In 1877 he was convicted of forgery in St. Louis and served a prison sentence, which the shorter record describes as brief. In the late 1870s he abandoned his first wife and children and moved to Texas. He was twice divorced. In 1882 he was ordained a Congregationalist minister without formal seminary training and began pastoral work in Dallas. He was not a scholar of Hebrew or Greek. Between 1901 and 1907 he wrote the annotations. He died in 1921, and the book stayed in print after him. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology]

The standard source for this biography, including the forgery conviction, is Joseph M. Canfield's The Incredible Scofield and His Book (1988), which has served as the reference work for some four decades. Canfield also documents where the project's support came from. The research summarizes him as finding that the promotion of Scofield's work, and the money behind the annotation project, came in significant part from figures connected with early American Zionist advocacy. Among them was Samuel Untermyer, a Wall Street lawyer who later became a prominent Zionist. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] That is a documented association. It is not evidence that these backers caused the book's success or wrote its theology. The theology came largely from Darby, and Scofield's work would have found some readers in any case. The research's own account of what produced the book's scale points elsewhere: Oxford's distribution, and what it calls the funding architecture that put the Bible "into every seminary, Sunday school, and pulpit in the American South and Midwest." The material does not say how much the backers gave or how their support was arranged. Without those details, no conclusion beyond the association can be drawn. The biographical record is also no argument against the theology. Scofield's personal history and the framework's later influence are separate facts, each to be checked on its own terms.

The book's form did as much work as its content. Each page carried the King James Version, the standard English Protestant translation of 1611, at the top. Scofield's notes filled a substantial part of the bottom. A reader did not open a Bible and then consult a separate commentary. The commentary was already in place on the page, printed under Oxford's imprint and bound in the same covers as the text. According to the research, the notes did three things. First, they divided biblical history into seven "dispensations," periods in which God deals with humanity in different ways. Second, they introduced a pre-tribulation rapture, the belief that the faithful will be taken up before a time of catastrophe. The research calls this a modern doctrine that is not found in the biblical text. It dates its origin once to the eighteenth century and elsewhere to Darby in the 1830s. Third, they presented the political return of Jews to Palestine as a prerequisite for the Second Coming of Christ. That last point turned a territorial political program into an article of prophecy. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] Scofield had systematized Darby's framework and put it into the vocabulary of American Protestants. The decisive step was placing it in the margins of the Bible ordinary readers already used.

The research describes the effect of that placement as cumulative. Over years of daily reading, text and note merged in the reader's memory, until Scofield's reading became simply "what the Bible says." A claim is hard to examine if the reader never registers it as a separate claim. In plain terms, the label on the book stayed the same, the Bible, while what the reader received under that label now included one man's interpretation. The Reference Bible sold millions of copies through the twentieth century. On the research's account, a mid-century American evangelical who studied the Bible seriously was likely to meet Scofield's notes as the frame for reading it. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] The second edition of 1917 added references to the Balfour Declaration, which had just been issued.

Oxford's part is the step most easily misread. Oxford University Press is one of the two oldest and most prestigious academic publishers in the English-speaking world; Cambridge University Press is the other. [cite:wiki_oxford_university_press] Its name gave a marginal framework an authority it could not have earned on its content alone. A self-published set of the same notes would probably have reached a small readership. Under Oxford's imprint, bound into the scriptural text, it reached millions. The research calls this a transfer of legitimacy, not a conspiracy, and the Press's governance supports that reading. Oxford University Press has never been privately owned. It is a department of the University of Oxford. Since the seventeenth century it has been governed by the Delegates of the Press, 15 sitting academics appointed by the university's Vice-Chancellor, who met fortnightly to approve every title. There was no owner or publishing family whose interests could explain the decision, and no single person positioned to ask why a new theological framework should be bound into scripture. The book went through the same committee process as any other title. Because the underlying text was technically just the King James Version with added footnotes, no special theological review was triggered. [cite:wiki_oxford_university_press] The record shows a gap in review. It does not show that anyone used that gap deliberately, and it does not show any promotional strategy by the Press. The Press did not set out to shape American policy in the Middle East, but its imprint gave the notes an authority its editors had not intended to confer. The Press has never withdrawn the book. Later editions, the New Scofield of 1967 and the Scofield Study Bible III of 2002, were revised but kept the core dispensationalist framework. The research counts 117 years of continuous publication.

The research then sets out what the doctrines meant politically, as later Christian Zionist teaching drew them out. Two of the verses are ancient. Genesis 12:3 reads "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse," and Genesis 15:18 gives the land promise. The research's argument concerns how Scofield's framework applied them to a modern state.

On the research's reading, none of these doctrines had been part of mainstream American Protestant theology before Scofield placed them there. The research summarizes the change this way: the framework was standard by 1950 and taken for granted by 2000. It also argues that the framework leaves no theological role for the people already living in Palestine. Palestinian Christians, members of a community older than most European churches, become an anomaly. Palestinian Muslims become obstacles to the fulfilment of prophecy. These are arguments about the logic of a doctrine, and they should be read as arguments. They are not a census of what each believer holds.

The research also makes a theological critique, and it is presented here as one side of a dispute. Evangelical Protestantism teaches salvation through Christ alone. Scofield's scheme runs a separate track for national Israel, in which an ethnic nation and a literal grant of land carry weight of their own in the history of salvation, alongside the work of Christ. The sequence the notes require runs as follows. Israel is dispersed. Israel is regathered, in unbelief. The regathered nation passes through the Tribulation. Only then does Israel turn to Christ. The Second Coming follows, Christ establishes a millennial kingdom, and Israel stands at its centre. The critique fixes on the fourth step. In a tradition of salvation by grace, it asks, why must a people be regathered in unbelief and pass through catastrophe before conversion? On this reading, the notes never reconcile the two tracks; they simply print them on the same page. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] [scene:s04fa|The Uganda counterfactual] tests the same sequence against a different geography. The material does not give the replies of dispensationalist theologians to this critique. A reader should treat it as a contested theological argument, not a settled finding.

A separate passage is not history at all, and is labeled here as interpretation. One symbolic reading, put forward in this library's opening volume, holds that the confusion dissolves if "Israel" is read not as land but as IS-RA-EL, a "consciousness architecture." In that reading IS stands for Isis, the receptive or lunar principle, RA for the solar or radiant principle, and EL for the unifying divine force. Of the three, only EL is real Hebrew etymology. On this reading "Israel" names a spiritual condition rather than a nation, and Scofield's notes performed a literalizing move, turning a symbol into a flag, a border and an ethnic deed. [cite:wiki_scofield_bible] This is offered as a key for thinking, not a documented claim. The documentary case stands without it.

What followed belongs to later volumes and is summarized here only in outline. Dallas Theological Seminary, founded in 1924, became an institutional home for training pastors in the framework. Between the 1920s and the 1960s, according to the research, Scofield's theology became standard in Southern Baptist and other evangelical denominations and in Bible colleges of the South and Midwest. Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), the best-selling nonfiction book of the 1970s, carried it to a mass readership. In 1979 Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority. Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins's Left Behind novels, published from 1995 to 2007, sold more than 65 million copies. In 2006 John Hagee, pastor of Cornerstone Church in San Antonio, published Jerusalem Countdown and founded Christians United for Israel (CUFI). [cite:hagee_jerusalem_countdown] CUFI claims more than 10 million members, a self-reported figure. It holds an annual Washington Summit and appears in FEC records giving to pro-Israel candidates. [cite:cufi_org] Membership claims of this kind cover a wide range of engagement and do not mean that every member holds the same views. The alliance between these organizations and Israeli leaders is told in [scene:bwm_src_s15|the Christian Zionist network].

The size of the constituency rests on survey figures, and they should be stated exactly. The research cites a 2019 Pew Research Center survey. According to that survey, about 25 percent of American adults identify as evangelical Protestant, and 75 to 80 percent of white evangelical Protestants express strong support for Israel as a biblical requirement. A plurality of white evangelicals were found to support Israel more strongly than American Jews do, 42 percent against 27 percent. The material does not say exactly what question produced those two figures. A related source puts white evangelicals at approximately 25 to 30 percent of the electorate. [cite:pew_evangelical_israel_support] The research also cites a 2022 University of North Carolina Institute of Politics survey, which found white evangelicals to be the largest single religious group supporting unconditional American aid to Israel. The figure of 30 to 40 million Christian Zionist voters is an estimate the research derives from these shares. [cite:wiki_dispensation_theology] It is not a count, and the range is wide.

Two limits keep the account honest. First, nothing in it was hidden. Scofield published openly, Oxford's decisions were public, and Christian Zionist organizations argue their positions in public. To read the chain as a conspiracy would be a category error. Scofield published in 1909, the Balfour Declaration came in 1917, and the state was declared in 1948. He was one factor among many, and nothing here claims that he or Oxford brought the State of Israel about. The research does use the word "manufactured" for the constituency. What the documents support is narrower: a publishing event put a specific framework into wide circulation, and institutions carried it forward for decades.

Second, this is a dispute within Christianity, not a case against Christianity. Mainline Protestant denominations, including the United Methodist, Episcopal, Presbyterian (PC-USA), Evangelical Lutheran and United Church of Christ churches, largely do not embrace Christian Zionism. Roman Catholic tradition does not endorse it, and Orthodox tradition rejects it explicitly. In 2009 Palestinian Christian leaders from across denominations signed the Kairos Palestine document, which calls Christian Zionism a "heresy" from within Christian tradition. The research names the Palestinian Christian Sami Awad, the mainline Protestant scholar Gary Burge and the evangelical Shane Claiborne as public figures whose positions show that the framework can be contested inside the tradition. They show that holding it is not required of Christians. The Christians who reject Scofield's framework do so on grounds within their own traditions.

Some questions remain open. The record establishes the book, its publisher, its author's history, its notes and their place on the page, and the later institutions that carried the framework. It does not measure how far the Reference Bible itself, as distinct from Darby's earlier preaching, the Bible colleges and later popular writers, caused American Christian support for Zionism. It does not show the size or terms of the money behind the annotations. It also does not show what Oxford's Delegates discussed when they approved the book. The constituency figures are survey estimates. The research's account of later American policy, which it partly traces to this constituency, is examined in later volumes against the full record of who decided what.

sections.h: Who Bought the Land, From Whom, and at What Cost
sections.html:
A common account holds that the British government sold Palestinian land to outside Zionist buyers, and that it did so with little scrutiny and little resistance. Almost every part of that sentence fails against the documents. The land was bought in private transactions, overwhelmingly from absentee landowners who had acquired large estates under Ottoman rule. The British, when they came, regulated the process rather than selling into it. And resistance was there from the first large purchase: an Ottoman governor tried to block it in 1910, and two decades later tenants fought an eviction through the courts for years. The mechanism that did the work was assembled before 1917, and its first test came in the Jezreel Valley.

The chain of ownership began before Zionism existed as an organized movement. In 1872 the Ottoman government itself sold the Jezreel Valley, Marj ibn Amir, to the Sursock family of Beirut, wealthy Greek Orthodox Christians.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] From that moment the valley was no longer, in any sense, land the government held; it was the private estate of a family that lived in another city. Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value. The Sursock Purchases alone represent approximately 22 percent of all Jewish land acquired in Palestine through 1948, and 58 percent of all land bought specifically from absentee landlords.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:sursockhouse_rothschild_purchases] The transaction was three separate sales, not one: the Ottoman state to a Beirut family, the family to a Zionist buyer, and, in the legal sense, the extinction of whatever claim the people working the soil might have pressed.

That last step is the hinge of the whole mechanism. Ottoman property law recognized two main categories of land. Mulk was true private freehold. Miri was state land held on a kind of lease, but treated in practice as owned by whoever held the registered rights to it. Most of the agricultural land that tenant farmers worked fell into the miri category, and the registered rights belonged to the landlord, even when the landlord had never once worked the land himself. Families who had cultivated the same fields for generations under hereditary arrangements, paying tithes to absentee owners like the Sursocks, typically held no registered title at all. When the landlord sold, the tenant had no ownership claim to assert.[cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] The sale was lawful, and so was the eviction that followed; under the law of the time they were the same transaction. Nothing about this was a hidden device. It was a documented feature of Ottoman land tenure that predated Zionist land purchase entirely, and the record does not show that it was created for that purpose. What the record shows is that it was used, extensively, once purchase began on a large scale.

It would be wrong, though, to say that no law stood in the way. Starting in 1881–82 it issued a restriction specific to Palestine: foreign Jews could settle anywhere else in the empire, but not there. By March 1883 only Ottoman Jewish citizens could buy land in Palestine at all; foreign citizens were barred outright. In 1892 Sultan Abdul Hamid II went further, requiring imperial approval even for Ottoman Jewish citizens to buy.[cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] [cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization]

The Ottoman authorities explained their reasoning to foreign diplomats, and the explanation survives in American correspondence from the 1890s. American diplomats reported the Ottoman position that individual visitors of any background were welcome, but that the government "does not regard it to its interest to have too large a number of any race or nationality established there." What it opposed was organized, large-scale colonization aimed at a concentrated territorial presence.[cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization] That distinction, between individual presence, which was tolerated, and organized mass settlement toward territorial concentration, which was resisted, was the government's own. It was also an exact description of what Herzl's movement had been organized to achieve.

The restrictions were evaded by three documented routes. First, Ottoman Jewish citizens, who were still permitted to buy, purchased land and later transferred it to Zionist organizations. Second, Jews holding British, French or German passports could sometimes invoke the capitulations, the extraterritorial privileges that European powers had negotiated with the Ottoman Empire, and claim consular protection that Ottoman domestic law could not easily override. Third, and most directly documented, United States State Department correspondence from the 1890s records Russian Jewish emigrants who traveled to America, completed naturalization, and returned to Palestine as American citizens in order to claim American consular protection for residence and land purchase.
