One named case, that of Simon Ben Nachman Lowenstein, was argued over directly between American and Ottoman diplomats.[cite:state_gov_1892_naturalization] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full]

Scholars who have examined the period agree that the restrictions "created real obstacles without constituting an absolute prohibition," and the totals bear that out. After roughly four decades of organized purchasing against these laws, Jewish-held land in Palestine in 1918 came to approximately 418,000 dunams, around 2 percent of the territory.[cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws] [cite:wiki_jewish_land_purchase_full] The law did not stop the process. It slowed it considerably.

Three named organizations did the buying and holding, and it is worth being exact about which did what. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, was the holding body: land went in and, by design, never came back out, held as inalienable Jewish national property. The negotiating was done by the Palestine Land Development Company, led by Yehoshua Hankin, who personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions. The third, the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, or PICA, was founded in 1924 by Baron Edmond de Rothschild, a man who had opposed Herzl personally; it ran a separate, parallel operation on Rothschild money and became the single largest Jewish landowner in Palestine.[cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

Hankin was not an anonymous institutional process but a named individual at the center of the whole mechanism. His working relationship with the Sursock family dated to 1891, and in 1932 he became head of the land development company.[cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] The point of naming him and the companies is not to allege illegality, since the purchases were lawful under the property law of the time, but to document who did the buying and how.

The answer to a reader's obvious question, how the buyers knew where to buy, is bureaucratic. In 1907 the Zionist Organization sent Arthur Ruppin, a German-trained lawyer and economist, to make a pilot study of colonization in Palestine. In 1908 he opened the Palestine Office in Jaffa, and the same year, by this account, founded the Palestine Land Development Company as its operational purchasing arm; other sources date the company to 1909, a discrepancy taken up with the office's founding in [scene:s04g|the Palestine Office and its land company]. Ruppin identified the strategic importance of the Jezreel Valley as early as 1907, years before the large Sursock sales closed.[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] His office coordinated directly with the Jewish National Fund, negotiated with Ottoman and later British authorities on behalf of Jewish immigrants, and, through the land company, handled the surveying, valuing and acquisition of land before settlers arrived. It turned land purchase from an individual pursuit into a coordinated institutional program, and Ruppin became known as "the father of Jewish settlement in Palestine."[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin]

The same documented record contains a second fact about Ruppin, and it has to be stated with equal precision. His Wikipedia biography says that early in his career he "accepted the crude racial views of his age, including the idea that Jews were an inferior race," and that he later "believed that realization of Zionism required 'racial purity' of Jews and was influenced by works of antisemitic thinkers, including some Nazis." A peer-reviewed article in History of European Ideas examines these views at length. Haaretz, in its own retrospective, states plainly: "Arthur Ruppin believed that the realization of Zionism demanded 'racial purity' among the Jews." He is also documented as holding Ashkenazi Jews to be racially superior to Sephardi and Yemenite Jews, a view that, according to the same record, shaped in practice whom his office prioritized for settlement.[cite:wiki_arthur_ruppin] [cite:haaretz_ruppin_retrospective] [cite:tandfonline_ruppin_weltanschauung] Three independent kinds of source, an encyclopedia entry, peer-reviewed scholarship and the mainstream Israeli press, agree on this. The finding is about one individual who held real operational authority over settlement and land selection. It does not show that everyone involved in Zionist settlement shared his views, or that the purchase program as a whole was organized around them. Both facts about Ruppin, the institutional achievement and the racial ideology, are part of the accurate account; neither cancels the other.

The first large purchase in the valley shows the mechanism working, and shows that it was contested from the start. Ruppin recalled, in a memoir written in May 1929, that in February 1910 Hankin concluded an agreement for 9,500 dunams at Fule, al-Ful, the site that became Merhavia. The Jewish National Fund took over 3,500 dunams and the land company the rest.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] The seller was Elias Sursuq, of the same Beirut family; one account describes the land as about 2,500 acres.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Disputes over evicted tenant farmers followed this first significant acquisition, though the sources used here give no count of the tenants concerned.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases]

Ruppin's own account records the opposition. The Turkish government, he wrote, refused to authorize the sale, and "the Governor in Nazareth, a rabid anti-Zionist," declared that he would fight it. Permission was finally obtained through Hankin's friends in Constantinople.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] The governor, according to the biographical record, was Shukri al-Asali, district governor (qaimaqam) of Nazareth from 1910, who tried and failed to stop the sale.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] He did not drop the matter. In 1911 he resigned to win a by-election to the Ottoman parliament for Damascus, and there he argued that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages. He sat until April 1912.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] His argument about dual citizenship was, in effect, a description from the other side of the evasion routes the American consuls had been documenting since the 1890s. On 6 May 1916, by order of Jamal Pasha, al-Asali was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus with a group of Arab nationalists, a wartime story told with [scene:rd1_wwi|Palestine at war], where the dating of those executions is also discussed.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki]

Ruppin's memoir also gives the long arc of prices and quantities, and the figures show how the valley moved from a single deal to a program. Hankin, he wrote, had first reached agreement as early as 1891 for 160,000 dunams at 15 francs a dunam. In 1920 about 70,000 dunams were bought at £3 a dunam for unirrigated land and £6.5 for partly irrigated land, about £300,000 in all. By 1929 about 290,000 dunams had been bought in the Emek and the Acre plain since 1910, for £970,000.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] Elsewhere the record gives a broader benchmark: land sold by absentee landlords to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam by the early Mandate period.[cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] That figure sits at the upper end of Ruppin's 1920 prices, and either way the scale explains why a dedicated financial system existed.

Settlers were not, in the main, buying the land out of their own savings. Individual circumstances varied, and some settlers may have used personal savings alongside institutional support, but the purchases at this scale ran through a purpose-built banking and philanthropic system. The Jewish Colonial Trust, founded in 1899, was the Zionist Organization's overall financial instrument. Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Bank, established in 1902 with Jaffa as its base, did the work on the ground: financing land purchases directly and running a network of credit unions that gave long-term agricultural loans to Jewish colonists. Herzl put the principle in one line: "Settlers in the Land of Israel need credit rather than charity." On the philanthropic side, from 1920, Keren Hayesod raised donations specifically for settlement infrastructure.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] [cite:palquest_wzo_funding] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust]

Ownership of this system and control of it were deliberately separated. The Trust was not the property of one family or a small circle of bankers: over 100,000 people had subscribed for shares by 1899, so many that London's Somerset House needed special accommodation for the shareholder register. But the first 100 shares were designated founders' shares, carrying voting rights equal to all the other shares combined at any general meeting. However widely the rest were held, the founding Zionist leadership kept permanent control.[cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] [cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust] The preparatory committee that launched the Trust was David Wolffsohn, the designer of what became the Israeli flag, Bodenheimer of Cologne, and Rudolf Schauer of Mainz. Zalman David Levontin, whom Herzl personally summoned to a director's seat in 1901 and who had sold his own earlier land holdings to Edmond de Rothschild in 1883, ran the Jaffa branch from 1903.[cite:encyclopedia_levontin] [cite:jewishencyclopedia_colonial_trust] The pattern lasted for decades. As late as 1969 the Trust controlled 88.3 percent of the voting ordinary shares of Bank Leumi, the bank's descendant, while holding only 23.5 percent of its total share capital, a structure that lasted until the late 1980s, when it was sold to private investors.[cite:wiki_jewish_colonial_trust]

The system was not always planned from the center. Purchasing agents like Hankin sometimes bought land first, at personal financial risk, and secured reimbursement from the Jewish Agency or the Jewish National Fund only afterward.[cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

How the sales looked depends heavily on who is describing them, and the two surviving accounts of al-Fula should be read side by side. Ruppin's 1929 memoir presents willing sales by owners who wanted cash, through a buyer they trusted: Hankin, he wrote, "enjoyed the confidence of the Arabs." His account does not mention the tenants on the land at all.[cite:rs_rd1_ruppin_emek] Al-Asali's record describes a sale that the Ottoman district governor tried to block and later raised in parliament as a danger to rural villages.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Both can be true at once: the owners in Beirut may well have wanted cash and trusted Hankin, while the official responsible for the district, and the villagers he spoke for, saw the transaction as a threat. Ruppin's case, at its strongest, is that this was ordinary commerce, lawful and voluntary on both sides of the contract. The case from the other side is that the contract had only two sides because the law left the cultivators off it.

Sellers, too, felt the pressure of their own society. Selling land to Jewish purchasers was regarded by some in the Arab community as a serious betrayal, and in at least one documented case negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen to take responsibility for evacuating the tenants.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

No consultation preceded any of this. There is no documented record of a formal negotiation in which Zionist organizations sought the consent of the existing Arab political leadership, or of the Old Yishuv's leadership, before organized purchase began. Within the movement the warning had been given early: Ahad Ha'am, a committed cultural Zionist, wrote in 1891, in "Truth from Eretz Israel," that the Arab population was being treated as effectively invisible in Zionist planning, years before political Zionism was formally organized (his critique is set out with [scene:s04|the founding Congress and its critics]). What took place was land acquisition and settlement building toward a territorial and political fact, not a negotiated agreement, which is precisely why the Ottoman restrictions existed.

The Jewish communities that had lived in Palestine before organized Zionist immigration were neither uniform supporters of the purchases nor absent from them. The clearest documented window is Avraham Albert Antébi, a Sephardi Jew active in Jerusalem from 1897 to 1916. He ran the Caisse de Prêts, a low-interest loan fund that served both the Old Yishuv, the Sephardi and Ashkenazi communities already in the country, and the settlers of the New Yishuv. That role gave him working relationships with affluent Arab landowners and Ottoman officials as well as with the Zionist institutions. Research on his surviving correspondence, published in Shofar: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Jewish Studies, examines Sephardi reaction to Zionist land purchases and the Arab-Jewish tension that followed, and finds a community financially and socially entangled with every side of the transaction.[cite:shofar_antebi_sephardim] Antébi does not speak for every Old Yishuv resident; views varied by person, community and moment. What his record establishes is that some of the Jews already in Palestine watched the displacement from inside the deals themselves.

The human cost of the Sursock purchases is documented in specific figures. In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted. Under the tenure system described above they were owed no compensation, since they held no registered title to compensate; they were paid roughly $17 a person as a voluntary goodwill settlement. Across the full span of Sursock-linked purchases, an estimated 20 to 25 villages were depopulated.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin] These are the figures for the best-documented single group, not an estimate for every transaction of the period, which varied case by case; nor does the record show that every evicted family received exactly that amount.

Most of that cost fell after 1917, and the later history is told in later volumes, but its outline belongs here because the mechanism built before the war carried it. The main Sursock sales came in 1920–25, negotiated directly with Hankin.[cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] Britain, as the Mandate power, enacted five separate laws between 1920 and 1940 meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale. Analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation."[cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]

Wadi al-Hawarith became the case that tested the system. In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams there at auction from absentee landlords, which the historian Weldon Matthews counts as the third-largest single acquisition of the Fund in the whole Mandate period. The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived on the land refused to leave, and the Fund began formal eviction proceedings. Awni Abd al-Hadi, a significant Palestinian national political figure, represented the residents through a multi-year court battle. The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933, and the response was immediate: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest.[cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith] The case does not show that every sale met organized opposition; many proceeded with less. It shows that resistance existed, was organized, and reached formal legal representation and cross-party protest when the stakes were high enough.

In 1938 the Mandate authorities moved in the opposite direction from their tenant laws. They granted Zionist officials direct permission to copy land-registration and taxation records documenting Arab land ownership, explicitly to facilitate further Zionist acquisition.[cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] Britain was neither seller nor bystander: it first attempted regulation that failed, then took a specific, dated step of facilitation. That does not mean Britain orchestrated the purchase program from the start, or that 1938 was the whole of its policy; its immigration restrictions in the same years, the 1939 White Paper among them, cut sharply the other way. The Mandate's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single coherent policy.

The end point of the land series puts the whole mechanism in proportion. By 1947–48 total Jewish holdings came to roughly 2 million dunams, about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's roughly 26 million dunams, of which the Jewish National Fund held approximately 936,000.[cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] The panel below sets the 7 percent against the rest of the land; its second chart, the 1947 partition plan, belongs to a later volume. The Sursock land, around a fifth of everything acquired, was the single largest component of that total; and the restrictions, the evasions, the bank and the office that produced it were all in place before 1917.

What the record does not settle is substantial. Ruppin's memoir does not count the tenants at al-Fula, and the sources used here give no figure for them or for the price paid in 1910. The documented eviction figures, 1,746 families at about $17 a person, describe one large group of purchases, not the period as a whole, and there is no comparable count for the 418,000 dunams held by 1918. How the owners in Beirut weighed cash against the objections of officials like al-Asali survives only in the buyer's account. And how far Ruppin's racial views shaped individual settlement decisions, beyond the documented fact that they shaped his office's priorities, is not set out case by case in the record this book has.

sections.h: A Newspaper Called Palestine: The Arab Public Sphere Before 1914
sections.html:
It is often said that "Palestinian" was an identity invented after 1948, or even after 1967. The newspapers, parliamentary records and political programs of the years before the First World War answer that claim directly. By 1914 the country had Arabic newspapers arguing about Zionism in print, elected deputies who had raised it in the Ottoman parliament, a governor who had tried to block a land sale, and a paper in Jaffa whose masthead carried the name Filastin, "Palestine." What these sources show, and what they do not, needs to be stated precisely, because the record is richer than the claim allows and more complicated than a simple reversal of it.

The argument began outside Palestine and in French. In 1905 Negib Azouri published Le Réveil de la nation arabe, and in it he set the Arab national awakening beside the Jewish one and wrote of the two movements: "Both these movements are destined to fight each other continually until one of them wins."[cite:rs_rd1_azouri] It was a prediction, not a program, written eight years after the Basel Congress and before any large Zionist purchase in the Jezreel Valley; but it framed the encounter as a contest between two national movements six years after Herzl had answered a Jerusalem notable's warning by writing that the existing population would be enriched by Jewish settlement (that exchange is told in [scene:rd1_arabquestion|Herzl and the Arab question]).

The same year Najib Nassar began the most sustained campaign. From 1905 he wrote against Zionism in two Arabic papers, al-Muqattam in Cairo and Lisan al-Hal in Beirut. In 1908 he founded his own paper, al-Karmil, in Haifa, appearing twice a week.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] It was the year of the Young Turk revolution. The authorities' tolerance of the new paper had limits: they closed al-Karmil for two months in June 1909. In 1910 the Ministry of Justice ordered Nassar tried on a complaint from the Jewish community alleging incitement, and the court acquitted him.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] The episode cuts in more than one direction. It shows an Arab journalist prosecuted for his writing on Zionism; it shows a Jewish community in Palestine using the Ottoman courts against him; and it shows those courts declining to convict.

Nassar did not stop. In October 1911 he collected his articles as a book, Zionism: Its History, Objectives and Importance. In 1913 he called for a non-Zionist national society based in Nablus. In the summer of 1914 he urged Palestinian youth to press Arab landowners not to sell land to Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] That last appeal is the point at which the press campaign met the mechanism described in [scene:s04j|the land purchases]: the sellers were Arab landowners, many of them absentee, and the papers were trying to reach them through public opinion, since the law gave tenants no say.

The 1908 revolution also gave Palestine elected deputies in the Ottoman parliament. Ruhi al-Khalidi was one of three deputies elected for Jerusalem that year. In 1911, with his fellow Jerusalem deputy Sa'id al-Husayni, he raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament, and he stressed that what he opposed was Jewish immigration, not the residence of Palestine's own Jews.[cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] The distinction is worth noticing. It drew the line where the Ottoman government's own restrictions had drawn it since the 1880s: between Jews who were already subjects of the empire and organized settlement from abroad. In the same parliament Shukri al-Asali, the former governor of Nazareth who had tried to stop the al-Fula sale and had resigned to win a seat for Damascus, argued, during a term that ran until April 1912, that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] Ruhi al-Khalidi went further than speeches. He left an unpublished manuscript, "Zionism and the Zionist Question," and died of typhoid in Istanbul in 1913, while serving as deputy to the head of parliament.[cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] The texts of the 1911 speeches, and the month in which they were given, are not established in the sources used here.

Into this setting came Filastin. It was founded in Jaffa on 15 January 1911 by Issa El-Issa and his cousin Yousef El-Issa, Arab Orthodox Christians educated in Beirut.[cite:wiki_falastin] [cite:nli_filastin_archive] It began as a twice-weekly paper, and its first cause was not Zionism at all but the dispute between the Arab Orthodox community and the Greek-led hierarchy of its church.[cite:wiki_falastin] Between 1911 and 1914 its coverage of Zionism shifted. A scholarly study of the paper documents its reporting on land purchases, immigration, violent incidents and the Zionist Congresses moving from cautious ambivalence to open hostility before the war.[cite:academia_filastin_zionism] The editors sent a copy of each issue to every village in the Jaffa district, so that the paper's argument reached the countryside where land was actually changing hands, not only readers in the town.[cite:academia_filastin_zionism] [cite:wiki_falastin]

The record also contains an event that complicates any account in which Arab politics before 1914 revolved around Zionism. The Arab Congress met in Paris on 18–23 June 1913 with 25 official delegates. It adopted ten resolutions, on Arab participation in the central government of the empire, on Arabic as an official language, and on administrative decentralization. Its resolutions did not address Zionism. Two Zionist representatives, Victor Jacobson and Sami Hochberg, attended unofficially.[cite:rs_rd1_arabcongress_wiki] The Congress's agenda was reform within the Ottoman Empire, framed in Arab rather than specifically Palestinian terms, and its silence on Zionism shows that the subject that dominated al-Karmil and, by 1914, Filastin was not yet the first item for the wider Arab reform movement. Why the Congress left it out, and what Jacobson and Hochberg sought there, the sources used here do not say.

Filastin outlived the empire in which it was founded. Under the British Mandate it became one of the most influential Arabic dailies, known for its network of correspondents, and in 1927 Issa El-Issa helped found the Palestine Free Party. The paper appeared in Jaffa until 7 April 1948, shortly before the city fell, and later moved to Jerusalem.[cite:wiki_falastin] [cite:palquest_issa_el_issa] The National Library of Israel's Jrayed archive holds 6,692 issues, from 1911 to 1948.[cite:nli_filastin_archive]

Set against the claim that the identity was invented later, the record is plain on its central point. A paper named "Palestine," carrying a public argument about land and immigration, was printed in Jaffa from 1911, sent to the villages of its district, and preserved in Israel's own national library.[cite:nli_filastin_archive] That documents a Palestinian name in print and a Palestinian public sphere decades before 1948. The fair statement of the other side is that this public sphere operated inside larger frames: its deputies sat in the Ottoman parliament and drew the Ottoman government's own line between subjects and immigrants, and its most ambitious political gathering, in Paris, spoke as Arabs seeking reform within the empire. What the record does not settle is how widely, outside the press and the elected deputies, a distinctly Palestinian political identity was held before the war, how many people read these papers, and what weight the villagers who received Filastin gave it. The sources used here give no circulation figures. They establish the name, the argument and the people making it; they do not measure its reach.

sections.h: The American Machine: Hadassah, Brandeis and the ZOA, 1912–1918
sections.html:
A familiar assumption holds that American support for Zionism became organized and significant only after 1948, or at the earliest after the Holocaust. The institutional record places its foundations three decades earlier. By 1918 the movement in the United States had a national women's organization raising money for medical work in Palestine, a Justice of the Supreme Court as its most influential advocate with direct access to the President, and a merged national political organization reporting more than 147,000 members.[cite:zoa_wiki] [cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] None of this was built in Palestine. It was domestic American institution-building, carried out years before there was a British Mandate to build under.

The first piece was built by women. On 24 February 1912 Henrietta Szold founded Hadassah in New York. Sources give the number of founding members variously, from 38 to 122; on any count it was a meeting of fewer than 130 people.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah] The organization moved quickly from meeting to practice. In 1913 it sent the movement's first two nurses to Palestine, to provide maternity care and to treat trachoma.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah]

Hadassah's significance for the architecture of the movement lies in the channel it created as much as in the clinics it funded. Most of the financial and political machinery traced elsewhere in this stage, the Jewish Colonial Trust, the Jewish National Fund and, from 1918, the ZOA's own fundraising, was built and run by men. Hadassah was a distinct American fundraising channel, financed specifically by American Jewish women and directed to medical and settlement infrastructure in Palestine. It ran alongside the male-led institutions rather than through them.[cite:hadassah_wiki] It did not operate in isolation, however: in 1918 Hadassah became one of the founding member organizations of the Zionist Organization of America, so the two channels were joined institutionally while remaining distinct in organization and purpose.[cite:zoa_wiki] [cite:hadassah_wiki]

Szold's own arc reached far beyond this period. She later directed Youth Aliyah, founded in 1933, which the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum credits with bringing more than 14,000 unaccompanied children to Palestine and Britain between 1933 and 1945.[cite:ushmm_youth_aliyah] That work belongs to a later volume. It is recorded here because it shows the scale an organization founded at a small New York meeting in 1912 would eventually reach, and with the caution that a child-rescue and resettlement operation of that size involved real hardships for the children, a fuller story than a founding-to-scale summary can tell.

The second piece was a single convert. In 1914 Louis Brandeis, who would join the United States Supreme Court in 1916, moved into active Zionist leadership after a meeting with Jacob de Haas, who had been Herzl's secretary.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] The line from Herzl to Brandeis ran, in other words, through one of Herzl's own staff. From 1914 Brandeis led the American movement, and he remained its leader until 1921.

What Brandeis brought was access. He worked with the Reverend William Blackstone on the Blackstone Memorial of 1916 to influence President Wilson. In 1917 he met Balfour, and during the drafting of the Balfour Declaration he worked as a conduit between the British government and the President.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] His direct line to Wilson in those months is documented by multiple historians; the channel itself is not in dispute.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] How the Declaration was drafted, and what Brandeis's part in it was, is told with [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

How much that access mattered is a separate question, and the answer offered most often is an assessment rather than a finding. Nahum Goldmann later argued that without Brandeis "the Balfour Declaration would probably never have been issued."[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] That is one historian's judgment about a counterfactual. It may be right, but no document can prove what Britain would have done without him, and it should be read as an argument, not as settled fact.

Why Brandeis made the turn is a third question, and it remains open. His personal motives for converting to Zionist leadership are contested among historians. Some argue that the conversion was partly career-strategic, a reading that outlets such as Mondoweiss have cited in critical treatments of his role.[cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] No primary source in the record this book has definitively settles his motivation. The distinction matters for how the American story is told: that a Supreme Court Justice had direct access to a sitting President is a documented, checkable fact about influence; why he chose to spend that access on this cause is a matter of interpretation on which historians can reasonably differ.

The third piece was consolidation. In 1918 the Federation of American Zionists, Young Judaea, Hadassah and other bodies merged into the Zionist Organization of America. Brandeis became honorary president and Julian W. Mack president. The new organization reported 147,551 members in 1918.[cite:zoa_wiki]

The size of the merged organization is the figure that the summary of the movement's whole build carries for these years: in the step-by-step account of how the state was built, 1912–18 is "the American machine," made up of Hadassah, Justice Brandeis and the ZOA at 147,000.[cite:zoa_wiki] That compressed row follows directly from the documents above, and it sits between the bank and land fund of 1899–1902 and the promise and endorsement of 1917–22. Its placement makes a point the familiar account misses. The American institutions were not a response to the Balfour Declaration; they were built before it, and one of their leaders was working the channel to the President while it was drafted.

The unity of 1918 did not last. Brandeis and his adherents favored private economic investment over the World Zionist Organization's model of national fundraising, and at the Cleveland convention of 1921 they split away. Louis Lipsky then became president of the ZOA.[cite:zoa_wiki] The movement's most famous American member thus lost the argument over what kind of institution it should be within three years of its founding; the dispute and its consequences belong to the next stage.

Several things remain unsettled. The number of Hadassah's founders depends on which source is counted, from 38 to 122. Brandeis's motives remain contested, and Goldmann's claim that the Declaration would probably not have been issued without him cannot be tested. The record establishes that the 1921 split concerned private investment against national fundraising, but not every argument made on either side. What is not in doubt is the timing: the women's channel, the access to the White House and a membership organization of 147,551 all existed by 1918, thirty years before statehood.

sections.h: The Federal Reserve, 1913: Structure, Need and a Coincidence of Dates
sections.html:
On 23 December 1913 the Federal Reserve Act was signed into law, creating the central banking system of the United States.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act] The date sits in this chapter for one reason. It falls sixteen years after the First Zionist Congress at Basel and seven years before the Keren Hayesod fund existed, and an often-cited repeated claim holds that the two stories are one: that the Federal Reserve was founded by, or to serve, the same financial network that was funding Zionism. A history of the movement's money that said nothing about the claim would leave a silence open to misreading. This section therefore does two things. It sets out what the Federal Reserve actually was and why Congress created it, in the same plain terms this book uses for every other institution. Then it sets out what the record shows about the supposed link, and where the claim comes from.

Most Americans learn the institution's name without learning its structure, and two simple accounts compete to fill the gap. In one, the Federal Reserve is an ordinary federal agency like any other. In the other, it is a purely private bank running the country from behind a public front. Neither matches the documents. The system created in 1913 was a deliberate hybrid. It consisted of twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks. Each was owned by the commercial banks that were its members, and those member banks were required to hold stock in their district's Reserve Bank. Each regional bank historically financed itself from its own earnings rather than from appropriations voted by Congress. Above the regional banks sat a public body, the Board, known at first as the Federal Reserve Board and later as the Board of Governors, whose members are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.[cite:eh_net_federal_reserve_system] Part of the system is owned by banks, and part of it is a presidentially appointed public authority; the two were designed to work together.

The private ownership of the regional banks and their self-financing are unusual facts, and they are stated here as plainly as the sources state them. They do not mean the system escaped public control. Presidential nomination and Senate confirmation of the Board are real mechanisms of democratic oversight. They exist alongside the private regional ownership, not instead of it.[cite:eh_net_federal_reserve_system]

Why Congress accepted so unusual a design begins with the decades before it. Between 1865 and 1913 the United States suffered at least five major financial crises. The Federal Reserve's own historical research states the pattern directly: nationwide banking panics came on average every fifteen years, each forcing financial institutions to suspend operations and each followed by a long, deep recession.[cite:federalreservehistory_jekyll_island] The underlying fault was what economists called an "inelastic" currency. The money supply had no mechanism to expand when demand for money rose, so severe shortages of currency arrived exactly when the economy most needed cash.[cite:history_com_fed_origins] This was a recurring failure in the system's design rather than one bad year. The five crises did not share an identical cause or identical severity, and the sources single out one of them.

The Panic of 1907 is documented as among the most severe financial crises of the era before the Federal Reserve, and as the direct, immediate trigger for its creation. With no central bank able to intervene, the nearest thing the country had to a backstop was the financier J.P. Morgan. He organized a rescue using his own money, his reputation and his private authority, and it stopped the panic from spreading further.[cite:libertystreet_panic_1907_fed] [cite:history_com_fed_origins] The question of what would happen without a central bank therefore has a documented answer: in 1907 a private citizen's fortune stood in for an institution the country did not have. The sources record that the rescue worked as a stopgap. They do not settle Morgan's motives, and this book makes no claim about them.

The plan that answered 1907 was drafted by bankers. In November 1910 Senator Nelson Aldrich gathered a party at the Jekyll Island Club, off the Georgia coast. They travelled by private rail car and used only first names to keep the meeting secret. The Federal Reserve's historians describe the party as five bankers and a former Treasury official, and they give the reason for the secrecy plainly: "the plan was written in secrecy, as the public would never approve of a banking reform bill written by bankers, much less...a central bank." The resulting Aldrich Plan gave private banks substantial control.[cite:federalreservehistory_jekyll_island]

The people at the table are named in the record, along with the institution each belonged to. Aldrich chaired the National Monetary Commission, the body whose work produced the meeting. Henry Davison was a senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.[cite:wiki_henry_davison] Frank Vanderlip was president of National City Bank, documented as the flagship institution of the Rockefeller banking interests.[cite:wiki_frank_vanderlip] Paul Warburg was a partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co. Between them, these three men brought the era's three dominant banking houses to the table, each tied to his house directly by partnership or office. A. Piatt Andrew, Assistant Treasury Secretary, is described as a technical bridge, on good terms with both the Morgan and the Rockefeller spheres but employed by neither.[cite:wiki_a_piatt_andrew] Arthur Shelton was Aldrich's personal secretary, tied to Aldrich himself and with no banking connection of his own. Aldrich's own link to the Rockefeller interests went beyond politics. His daughter Abby married John D. Rockefeller Jr., which made Aldrich the younger Rockefeller's father-in-law; his grandson Nelson Rockefeller was named for him.[cite:wiki_nelson_aldrich] (The named list does not quite match the historians' summary: it holds three bankers from the great houses, a serving Treasury official and a secretary, besides Aldrich himself.)

Bankers drafting the plan for the institution that would regulate banks, at a meeting kept secret, is a genuinely unusual fact. It is not a hidden one. The Federal Reserve's own historical researchers record it and explain it. Nor was the Aldrich Plan simply handed to Congress and passed. Public reaction to it was hostile, and historians are specific about why: "what people were really upset about was the political structure of Aldrich's plan."[cite:richmondfed_jekyll_island] The objection was to how much control the plan gave private bankers.

Congress and President Wilson's administration rewrote that structure before anything became law. In the Federal Reserve Act, private banks received considerably less control than Aldrich had designed. A combination of regional independence and federal oversight replaced a more centralized model. All nationally chartered banks were required to join the system, rather than each bank choosing how far to take part.[cite:richmondfed_jekyll_island] [cite:minneapolisfed_born_of_panic] Congress accepted the final structure because it had first forced the reduction of private banking control that the public and many legislators objected to. The result did not satisfy everyone. Many private banks opposed the provisions that reduced their influence, so the Act was a genuine compromise and not a full victory for either side.[cite:minneapolisfed_born_of_panic]

Taken together, the documented record answers the four questions most readers bring to the subject. The Federal Reserve is neither a standard federal agency nor a purely private bank; it is a hybrid of private regional ownership and public oversight. It was created because the country suffered a banking panic roughly every fifteen years for decades, and 1907 was the severe, specific trigger. Before it, the only real backstop was one financier's personal wealth and standing. And it was accepted not because Congress deferred to the bankers who first drafted it, but because Congress fought to weaken the version they proposed and won.

That leaves the claim this section began with. It usually rests on one man. Paul Warburg, the Kuhn, Loeb partner, was really present at Jekyll Island in 1910 and served on the first Federal Reserve Board, from 1914 to 1918.[cite:wiki_paul_warburg] That is the full documented core of his role. It is a significant role in one institution's founding, and it should be stated without inflating or shrinking it. The record shows no part for him in Zionist fundraising or planning. A person can have one well-documented role in one major institution and no documented role in an entirely different one, and both facts can be stated plainly.

The record also points the other way. Paul Warburg's brother, Felix Warburg, and his father-in-law, Jacob Schiff, were prominent non-Zionists and opponents of Zionism in exactly this period. Schiff put his position on record: "I cannot for a moment concede that one can be at the same time a true American and an honest adherent of the Zionist movement." Felix Warburg held a similar, documented non-Zionist position at the same time.[cite:schiff_zionism_wiki] If the claim is that a single family network was quietly coordinating American central banking and Zionist fundraising, a public, quoted rejection of Zionism by that family's most prominent members contradicts it about as directly as the historical record can. This goes beyond the absence of a connection: it is an opposite position held inside the same family. The quotation documents the position in this period only. Views on Zionism shifted over the following decades across the wider Warburg and Schiff families, and the sources here do not claim that every member held the same view for life. Their opposition was part of a wider current of Jewish dissent from Zionism in these years, set out in [scene:rd1_currents|Jewish positions for and against].

The institutional record was checked as well. The Federal Reserve Act created a central banking system sixteen years after Basel, and there is no documented institutional or financial link between it and the Zionist Organization or its funds: neither the Jewish Colonial Trust, nor the Jewish National Fund, nor the Keren Hayesod, which did not yet exist.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act] A search of the founding documents of the Trust, the Fund and the Federal Reserve shows no connection between them. The absence is itself a finding. It is the result of a search that was carried out, not a gap left by one that was not. It does not mean that no individual moved in both worlds; Paul Warburg's case shows exactly how far such overlap went in a small early-twentieth-century financial world. Two events sixteen years apart, in different countries, sharing a few individuals is not the same as the two events being connected.

The claim has a traceable origin. The specific assertion of a connection between the Federal Reserve and Zionism goes back to Eustace Mullins's tract The Federal Reserve Conspiracy, promoted from the 1950s and recycled since by extremist groups and figures. Mainstream fact-checking and civil-rights research organizations classify "Jewish control of the Federal Reserve" as a documented antisemitic myth, not a contested historical question.[cite:adl_fed_myth] Naming the source explains where the claim came from as well as answering it. It does not mean that everyone who repeats some version of the claim knows or endorses its origin; myths travel independently of their sources. Tested against the documents, the claim fails on each point. The timing is a coincidence. The one documented individual link runs to a man whose own family publicly opposed Zionism. The institutional records show no tie.

Some things the record here does not settle. The sources document that Morgan's 1907 rescue happened and worked; they do not establish his motives. They document the Warburg and Schiff positions in this period, not across the families' whole later history. And this section cannot dispose of every version of the claim that circulates. What it offers is the specific, checkable facts about the Federal Reserve's founding and the specific origin of the myth, so that any other version can be tested against the same documents.[cite:federalreservehistory_fed_act]

sections.h: Palestine at War, 1914–1917
sections.html:
The war reached Palestine before it reached its battlefields. When the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War, the country was still a set of Ottoman districts: the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem, created as a separate administrative unit in 1872, with the sanjaks of Nablus and Acre to its north.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] Its people were Ottoman subjects, but not all of them. A large share of the Jewish community held foreign nationality, and that difference is why the Ottoman register of 1914–15 counted only 38,754 Jews while other estimates run as high as 94,000; the counting dispute is set out in [scene:rd1_ottoman|the Ottoman country]. In wartime, foreign nationality turned from a bureaucratic detail into a matter of who could stay. Over the next three years Palestine's people, Arab and Jewish alike, lived through expulsion, a plague of locusts, famine in the wider region, the hanging of Arab nationalists and the emptying of Jaffa. This section tells that story to the end of 1917.

The first blow fell on the Jews of Jaffa who held Russian citizenship. In December 1914 up to 6,000 Russian citizens, all of them Jewish, were expelled from the city, according to the standard reference account of the period.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] Many went to Egypt. Contemporary reports in the New York Times, cited in a 2021 opinion column, put some 7,000 Jewish refugees from Palestine in British-held Alexandria by the end of January 1915.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] Those figures come to us through a newspaper column rather than an archive, and they are given here as reported.

In 1915 the Ottoman authorities went further. Non-citizens, Jews included, were required to take Ottoman citizenship or leave.[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] The order forced a choice on every immigrant who had kept a foreign nationality. Some of those who left became soldiers. In the same year the British Army formed the Zion Mule Corps from Jews exiled to Egypt, and it served at Gallipoli; that story, and the wider record of Jewish service to Britain, is told in [scene:ww_s01|Services rendered to Britain].[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] [cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion] Political figures were expelled too. David Ben-Gurion, who had been studying law in Istanbul since 1912, was expelled by the Ottomans in 1915 and went to Alexandria and then New York.[cite:rs_rd1_bghouse]

Then came the locusts. From March to October 1915 swarms covered Palestine, Mount Lebanon and Syria. The historian Zachary Foster estimates that they cut the 1915 winter harvest of wheat and barley by 10 to 15 per cent, and destroyed between 60 and 100 per cent of the summer and autumn fruit and vegetables.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki] The Ottoman response was a labor quota. Every male aged 15 to 60 in the cities had to collect 20 kilograms of locust eggs or pay a fine of £4.40. By 21 November 1915, the New York Times reported, 800 people had paid the fine rather than collect the eggs.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki]

The locusts struck a region already under strain, and in Greater Syria, the wider territory of which Palestine was a part, the result was famine. The American University of Beirut's documentary exhibit names four causes acting together. The Allies blockaded the eastern Mediterranean in 1915, cutting off imports. Drought reduced what the land could grow. The locusts took much of the rest. And the Ottoman paper money in circulation lost value.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] The worst-documented losses were in Mount Lebanon. How many died there is disputed. The AUB exhibit says Mount Lebanon lost 20 to 30 per cent of its population.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] A higher figure, nearly half of the inhabitants of the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate, appears in the reference account of the locust plague, but without a source.[cite:rs_rd1_locust_wiki] The sourced range is the one to rely on. For Palestine itself the record used in this book gives no reliable death toll from the famine, and none is offered here.

The war also brought the state's hand down on the Arab political class. On Jamal Pasha's orders a group of Arab nationalists was hanged in Marjeh Square in Damascus. One of them was Shukri al-Asali. From 1910 he had been the district governor (qaimaqam) of Nazareth, where he tried and failed to stop Elias Sursuq's sale of about 2,500 acres of land at al-Fula to Zionist buyers. He resigned in 1911 to win a by-election to the Ottoman parliament for Damascus, and there he argued that Jewish settlers held Ottoman citizenship alongside foreign citizenship and were taking control of rural villages. He sat until April 1912. The sources on his life date his execution to 6 May 1916.[cite:rs_rd1_asali_wiki] The American University of Beirut's exhibit, however, dates the hangings in Damascus and Beirut to 6 May 1915.[cite:rs_rd1_aub_famine] The two accounts differ by a year, and the evidence gathered for this book does not resolve the difference. The al-Fula sale itself belongs to the story of how land changed hands, told in this chapter's section on the land mechanism. What matters here is that an Ottoman official who had opposed a Zionist land purchase in public was put to death by the same Ottoman state, among a group of Arab nationalists.

In the spring of 1917 the war emptied Jaffa. On 28 March 1917 Djemal Pasha (the same Jamal Pasha) ordered the evacuation of Jaffa. The deportation took place on 6 April 1917.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] How many people were driven out is disputed, and three figures circulate. One estimate puts those displaced at about 10,000, of whom 8,000 were Jews. Another puts the number evacuated from Tel Aviv, the new Jewish neighborhood beside Jaffa, at up to 16,000.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] A United States consular report of 1917 gave 8,000 Jews evicted.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] The figures measure different things: the whole city or only its Jewish residents, Jaffa or Tel Aviv. The lower Jewish figures agree with each other, and the highest figure applies only to Tel Aviv.

The deportation did not fall equally. The order covered the city, but Jaffa's Muslim residents were able to return soon afterwards, while the Jewish deportees could not return until the summer of 1918.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] About 1,500 people are thought to have died as a result of the deportation, though the deaths were not properly recorded.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] Reports reached the outside world within weeks. A US consular report, published in the New York Times on 3 June 1917, described looting and killings of deportees; the report survives in that newspaper and is cited in the 2021 column.[cite:rs_rd1_bulut] The evidence here is a contemporary diplomatic report as carried by the press, not a court record, and no primary text of Jamal Pasha's orders is among the sources used for this book.

By the end of the war the Jewish community of Palestine was smaller than in 1914. How much smaller is a real dispute between serious sources. The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question holds that about a third of the Jewish population left Palestine during 1914–18.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_chron] The demographer Justin McCarthy, as summarized by Roger Owen, argues that the fall was much less than the commonly cited quarter, because many of those who fled to Alexandria came back.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen] Both sides have evidence. The expulsions of 1914–15 and the deportation of 1917 were real and large. Return was also real: the Jaffa deportees were allowed back in the summer of 1918, and McCarthy's case rests on returns from Alexandria. The disagreement over the end point is tied to the disagreement over the starting point, since the 1914 baseline itself is disputed between 38,754 and 94,000 depending on whether foreign nationals are counted.[cite:rs_rd1_mccarthy_owen]

Ottoman rule in Palestine ended in December 1917, when Britain occupied the country, and the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem was dissolved.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] By then the British government had already made the commitments that would shape what followed, to the Zionist movement and to others in the region. Those wartime undertakings, and the Balfour Declaration of November 1917 among them, are the subject of Stage Two and are told in [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration and the wartime promises].

Several things the record does not settle. The number of famine deaths inside Palestine itself is not established in the sources this book relies on. The death toll in Mount Lebanon is given as a range, and its upper claim is unsourced. The year of the Damascus and Beirut hangings differs between sources. The size of the Jaffa deportation depends on what is counted, and the deaths it caused were never properly recorded. How far the Jewish population fell between 1914 and 1918 remains disputed. What is not in doubt is that the war brought expulsion, hunger and execution to the country, that famine struck the wider region, and that the expulsions of foreign nationals and the long exclusion from Jaffa fell on Jews in particular.

sections.h: Services Rendered: NILI, the Mule Corps and the Jewish Legion, 1915–1918
sections.html:
A common account treats the Balfour Declaration as a gift: a promise Britain handed over in November 1917 without receiving anything in return. The wartime record complicates that account. While the Declaration was being argued over in London, Jews in Palestine were spying on the Ottoman army for British intelligence, and Jewish volunteers were serving in British uniform, first at Gallipoli and later in the campaign for Palestine itself. Among those volunteers was David Ben-Gurion. These services gave the Zionist movement standing with the British at the moment the cabinet was deciding. What the record does not show is that they bought the Declaration, and the difference matters.

The intelligence work began in 1915. A ring of about 40 members, based mainly in Zikhron Ya'akov and Hadera, formed around the Aaronsohn siblings and Avshalom Feinberg. It took the name NILI. Its members gathered Ottoman military information and passed it to British intelligence, in part through a vessel run by the forerunner of MI6.[cite:wiki_nili] [cite:jc_nili_shindler] The ring's role is serious enough to have been reviewed in the CIA's own professional journal.[cite:cia_review_spies_palestine] NILI worked inside an Ottoman province at war, in a period when, as the previous section shows, the Ottoman authorities were expelling foreign nationals, hanging Arab nationalists and, in April 1917, emptying Jaffa; the risk to its members was real.

Its most consequential member was Aaron Aaronsohn, a noted agronomist. In 1916 he left Palestine to brief the British in person. He influenced British officials including Sir Mark Sykes and William Ormsby-Gore, both of whom were later pivotal in persuading the cabinet to issue the Balfour Declaration.[cite:jc_nili_shindler] This is the most direct documented line in this material between wartime service and the Declaration's authors: a man who had organized espionage for Britain inside Ottoman Palestine was talking, in person, to the officials who would press the cabinet. The line runs through influence on officials, not through any bargain on the record.

The Ottomans broke the ring in October 1917, a month before the Declaration was issued. Sarah Aaronsohn, one of the siblings at its center, took her own life after days of torture.[cite:wiki_nili] [cite:jc_nili_shindler]

The military service had begun earlier still, and it grew out of the wartime expulsions. In 1915 the Ottoman authorities required foreign nationals in Palestine, Jews among them, to take Ottoman citizenship or leave, and some 7,000 Jewish refugees from Palestine were in British-held Alexandria by the end of January 1915, according to contemporary New York Times reports cited in a 2021 column.[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] [cite:rs_rd1_bulut] From Jews exiled to Egypt the British Army formed the Zion Mule Corps in 1915.[cite:rs_rd1_yishuv_wwi] Its 737 volunteers, largely refugees expelled from Palestine, served at Gallipoli that year.[cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion] The men who had been driven out of the country by one side of the war were carrying supplies for the other; how they came to Egypt is told in [scene:rd1_wwi|Palestine at war].

In 1917–18 the service became formal and larger. Five battalions of the Royal Fusiliers, numbered the 38th to the 42nd and known together as the Jewish Legion, fought in Allenby's Palestine campaign. One battalion trained in Nova Scotia, and it included David Ben-Gurion.[cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion] He had been expelled by the Ottomans in 1915 and had gone to Alexandria and then New York.[cite:rs_rd1_bghouse] The Legion's road back to Palestine therefore ran across the Atlantic.

The Legion was not the project of a united movement. Much of the British Zionist leadership opposed forming it. Chaim Weizmann and Ze'ev Jabotinsky were the exceptions who supported it.[cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion] Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, had become with Nahum Sokolow one of the movement's de facto leaders in London, since the Zionist Organization's head offices were in Germany and the organization had declared itself neutral in the war.[cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] [cite:weizmann_papers_v9] That neutrality is a useful corrective. The organization as a body did not offer Britain its services. Individuals and groups did, sometimes against the wishes of their own leaders.

Put together, intelligence from inside Ottoman Palestine and soldiers in British uniform gave the movement standing with Britain at the moment the cabinet was deciding on the Declaration. The record places these services alongside other sources of British goodwill: Weizmann's wartime work as a chemist, and the restorationist sympathies documented in earlier chapters of this book. None of these, on the evidence gathered here, was the single cause. The Declaration's drafting, its addressee, the opposition to it inside the cabinet, and Britain's other wartime undertakings in the region belong to Stage Two and are told in [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

The familiar claim that the Declaration was given for nothing does not survive the record: a spy ring, a mule corps and five battalions were given to Britain's war effort, and one of the spies reached the officials who would argue the case in cabinet. But the opposite claim, that the Declaration was a payment for services, does not survive it either. The sources document influence, standing and timing. They do not document a bargain. The timing also cuts both ways. NILI collapsed in October 1917, before the Declaration was issued, and the Legion's battalions fought in 1917–18; the sources do not date that service closely enough against the cabinet's decision to weigh it. The record gathered here cannot measure how much weight any of these services carried in the cabinet's final decision, and it says so.

sections.h: What Stood by 1917: Five Dates Before the Holocaust
sections.html:
A familiar account holds that the demand for a Jewish state grew out of the Holocaust, that "never again" was its direct cause. That is a claim about sequence, and the calendar can test it. Five documented dates bear on it, and all five fall between 1896 and 1922. Each comes at least a decade before Hitler took power in Germany in 1933, and at least sixteen years before the Holocaust itself. Three of them lie beyond this stage and are told in full in Stage Two; they are named here because the argument needs all five. The second half of this section then sets out what this stage actually built: the structure that stood in Palestine, Europe and America in 1917, and what stood against it.

The first date is 1896. That year Theodor Herzl published Der Judenstaat, The Jewish State, which openly weighed Palestine against Argentina as candidate territories for a political answer to European antisemitism.[cite:herzl_judenstaat] This was a political program, dated and in print, thirty-seven years before Hitler took power. It was not reconstructed afterwards. On the arithmetic alone, the later catastrophe cannot have caused it. That does not mean everything in Zionist history flowed in a straight line from one pamphlet. The chapter that ends here has shown how much was contested: the Basel Program of 1897 spoke of a "home" (Heimstätte), not a state (Staat), and the movement argued for decades over culture, religion, territory and method.[cite:rs_rd1_basel_palquest]

The second date is a pair, 1903 and 1905. The Sixth Zionist Congress voted in 1903 to investigate British East Africa; the Seventh Congress formally rejected it in 1905.[cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] This matters because it shows an active choice. Choosing a place because nothing else is on offer is different from choosing it after seriously weighing a real alternative and turning it down. Palestine's place was confirmed by a contested decision in two stages, and the decision split the movement: the Territorialists who left founded the Jewish Territorial Organization.[cite:wiki_jewish_territorial_organization] It was far from the movement's last internal disagreement.

The third date is 1917. In November that year Britain committed in writing to "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people."[cite:balfour_letter] The commitment came sixteen years before Hitler's rise and twenty-four years before the systematic phase of the Holocaust began. A letter issued that early cannot have been a response to what came later. Nor did it by itself guarantee a state. Decades of uncertain, gradual and contested development lay between the letter and 1948. Its drafting, its addressee and the opposition to it inside the British cabinet are told in [scene:s06|the Balfour Declaration].

The fourth date is 1920. At San Remo the Allied powers formally assigned Britain the Mandate for Palestine and wrote the Balfour language into an international agreement.[cite:san_remo_wiki] The commitment moved from one government's letter to a multilateral agreement, a real change in its legal character and not a repetition of the same promise. It does not follow that every Allied power shared the same enthusiasm or motive; the national interests behind the agreement varied.

The fifth date is 1922. The League of Nations approved the Mandate for Palestine in July 1922, and it came into force in September 1923. Its Article 6 committed Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration and "close settlement by Jews on the land."[cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] This was a binding international legal framework, eleven years before Hitler took power, complete before the word "Holocaust" described anything. It was not applied consistently. Within the same decade Britain's Churchill White Paper narrowed the same commitment, as Stage Two shows.

By the time Hitler took power, then, the movement had a political program thirty-seven years old, a territorial question it had settled twice in its own favor, a great-power commitment, the international ratification of that commitment and a binding legal mandate to build toward it. The Holocaust changed what happened next, and this book does not minimize it. It intensified the urgency and reshaped the world's willingness to act. The clearest evidence of that acceleration is the Biltmore Program of May 1942, the movement's first explicit, public demand for a state, in the form of a "Jewish Commonwealth."[cite:biltmore_wiki] [cite:biltmore_medoff] But Biltmore was the culmination of forty-six years of institution-building and political commitment, not their origin. "Never again" describes why the world finally acted. It does not describe when the planning began.

The strongest form of the opposite view deserves its place. The program of 1896 and the commitments of 1917–22 did not make a state inevitable, and for most of this period the movement was one current among many in Jewish life, opposed by Reform rabbis, the Bund, Orthodox opponents and, in 1917, the official bodies of British Jewry. The Basel Program avoided the word "state." On this reading, it took the catastrophe of the 1930s and 1940s to turn a minority project with institutions into a demand the world would grant. Both things are true, and they are claims of different kinds: one is about when the structure existed, the other about why it succeeded when it did. The documents settle the first. The second is a matter of historical judgment.

What, then, existed by the end of 1917? At the top stood the Zionist Organization founded at Basel. Any individual or group that accepted the Basel Program and paid the annual dues called the shekel could join. Its 1899 constitution created a seven-member Smaller Actions Committee, chaired by the Congress president, and a 37-member Larger Actions Committee of national leaders; the Congress met every year until 1901 and every two years after.[cite:palquest_wzo] [cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] Herzl, its first president, died in 1904; David Wolffsohn succeeded him in 1905, and the botanist Otto Warburg succeeded Wolffsohn in 1911.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_congresses_b] National federations recruited members and raised money: the Federation of American Zionists from 1898 and the English Zionist Federation from 1899.[cite:w_zf_gb] When war came the organization's head offices were in Germany and it declared itself neutral, while in London Chaim Weizmann, a Manchester chemist and president of the English Zionist Federation, and Nahum Sokolow became its de facto leaders.[cite:ismi_israel_yearbook] [cite:weizmann_papers_v9]

Beneath the organization sat its money and land. The Jewish Colonial Trust, incorporated in London in 1899 with an authorized capital of £2,000,000 in £1 shares, had sold only about 250,000 shares, raising about £250,000, but it had proved that the project could be financed by many small shareholders.[cite:jct_wiki] Its subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Company, founded in 1902, opened its first branch in Jaffa in 1903 and by 1914 had branches in Jerusalem, Beirut, Hebron, Haifa, Safed, Tiberias and Gaza; its loan to the Ahuzat Bayit association financed the first neighborhood of what became Tel Aviv.[cite:apc_wiki] The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, held the land it bought as permanent national property, leased and never sold. It began with 200 dunams east of Hadera in 1903, and its blue collection box appeared around 1904.[cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg] [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_blue_box_jnf] In Jaffa, the Palestine Office opened by Arthur Ruppin in 1908 coordinated purchase and settlement, and the Palestine Land Development Company had acquired and prepared roughly 50,000 dunams by the outbreak of war, through named agents including Yehoshua Hankin, Ruppin himself and Jacob Thon.[cite:wiki_palestine_office] [cite:encyclopedia_otto_warburg] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]

Around that structure, and only partly under its control, a settler society had grown. The Second Aliyah, from 1904 to the outbreak of war, brought about 35,000 immigrants by the National Library of Israel's count or 40,000 by the Jewish Virtual Library's, and at least half left within a few years by the first count, nearly half by the second; the Jewish community numbered about 80,000 at the end of the period.[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_jvl_second] It had a Hebrew high school in Jaffa from 1905, the lots of Tel Aviv raffled among 60 families at Passover 1909, and Degania, counted as the first kibbutz, founded on 28 October 1910 on land leased from the Jewish National Fund (another source dates it to 1909).[cite:rs_rd1_nli_second] [cite:rs_rd1_israeled_degania] It had armed guards: Bar-Giora from 1907, and Hashomer, which grew out of it in 1909 and lasted until 1920.[cite:rs_rd1_jvl_defense] In the United States, Henrietta Szold had founded Hadassah in 1912, and in 1914 Louis Brandeis took up Zionist leadership and became the movement's channel to President Wilson.[cite:hadassah_wiki] [cite:brandeis_zionism_wiki] A year after this stage closes, those groups merged into the Zionist Organization of America with 147,551 members.[cite:zoa_wiki] Separately, a Christian constituency had a text: the Scofield Reference Bible, published by Oxford University Press in 1909.[cite:wiki_scofield_bible] And in the war, NILI's intelligence and Jewish soldiers in British uniform had given the movement standing in London.[cite:wiki_nili] [cite:algemeiner_jewish_legion]

Two of the dashboards that accompany this library summarize the same build-out. The year ledger for this period shows that almost every year from 1896 to 1916 added a piece, a bank, a fund, an office, a guard, a newspaper or a lobby, and it keeps a column for who objected. The funding overview compresses the same story into steps: a bank and a land fund in 1899–1902, then an American organization in 1912–18 that it rounds to 147,000 members, against the 147,551 the source gives for 1918. One small difference in the ledger: it dates the Jewish Colonization Association's takeover of the Rothschild colonies to 1900, while the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia says "since 1899".[cite:rs_rd1_je_ica]

Against this structure stood real forces, and the record of 1917 is incomplete without them. The Ottoman state had refused Herzl a charter: his diary records Abdul Hamid II's message that he could not sell even a foot of the land, because it belonged not to him but to his people. From the 1880s the government restricted Jewish immigration and land purchase, though unevenly, and the restrictions were undermined by corruption and foreign consular protection.[cite:w_herzl] [cite:w_abdulhamid] Arab opposition had a public voice. Negib Azouri predicted in 1905 that the Arab and Jewish national movements were "destined to fight each other continually until one of them wins."[cite:rs_rd1_azouri] Najib Nassar's al-Karmil in Haifa campaigned against Zionism from 1908, and from 1911 Filastin in Jaffa sent every issue to every village in its district.[cite:rs_rd1_palquest_nassar] [cite:wiki_falastin] In 1911 the Jerusalem deputies Ruhi al-Khalidi and Sa'id al-Husayni raised Zionism in the Ottoman parliament.[cite:rs_rd1_ruhi_wiki] Arab politics had other priorities too: the Arab Congress in Paris in June 1913 adopted ten resolutions on decentralization and the Arabic language, and none on Zionism.[cite:rs_rd1_arabcongress_wiki]

Jewish dissent was organized as well. The Bund had rejected Zionism since 1897.[cite:wiki_bund] Reform rabbis in America had declared Judaism "not political nor national, but spiritual," and Agudat Israel, founded in 1912, gathered Torah-observant Jews largely against religious Zionism.[cite:rs_rd1_reform_wiki] [cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] In Germany the Antizionistisches Komitee reportedly had more than 1,000 members before the war.[cite:rs_rd1_grill_currents] In May 1917 the Board of Deputies and the Anglo-Jewish Association, the official bodies of British Jewry, published an anti-Zionist statement in The Times; that is why the Declaration was addressed to Lord Rothschild and not to them.[cite:jpost_why_rothschild] And the war itself had cut into everything: the expulsions of 1914–15, the famine in the wider region, the hanging of Arab nationalists and the deportation from Jaffa in April 1917.[cite:rs_rd1_jaffa_wiki] One claim often added to this picture, that the founding of the Federal Reserve in 1913 was tied to Zionist finance, finds no support in the record, as [scene:s04ga|the Federal Reserve section] shows.

The architecture at the end of 1917 was therefore real but small, and it was contested from every side. It had an elected Congress and executive, federations in America and Britain, a bank with a Jaffa branch, a land fund with land, a professional land office, a labor movement with its own guards, an American constituency and now a British promise. It did not have a majority of Palestine's people, the support of many organized Jewish bodies in the West, the official representatives of British Jewry among them, or any power of its own to govern. Ottoman rule ended in December 1917, when Britain occupied the country.[cite:rs_rd1_jerusalemstory] What the record cannot settle is how much of what followed was set by this structure and how much by British policy, Arab resistance and the catastrophes of the next thirty years. The documents show when the machinery existed. They do not show that its outcome was fixed.

chapters.label: Stage Two
chapters.title: Secure
chapters.intro:
In November 1917 Britain made a promise about a country it did not yet govern. Arthur Balfour's letter of 2 November, favouring "a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, was signed while the land was still Ottoman: British forces had taken Beersheba on 31 October and would receive Jerusalem's surrender only on 9 December. [cite:w_sinai_palestine] [cite:w_balfour_decl] Two days later General Allenby entered the city on foot and placed it under martial law, promising that lawful life would go on and that the holy places would be kept by existing custom. [cite:rs_al_nli] [cite:rs_al_proclamation] The people the letter called "existing non-Jewish communities", by one estimate roughly 700,000 Muslim and Christian Arabs and about 90 per cent of the population, had not been asked, and the letter guaranteed them civil and religious rights, not political ones. [cite:balfour_letter] Nor was it Britain's only commitment. Sir Henry McMahon's letters of 1915–16 had pledged British support for Arab independence to Sharif Hussein of Mecca, and the Sykes–Picot Agreement of May 1916 had divided the same lands with France. [cite:w_mcmahon] [cite:w_sykes_picot]

This stage asks how that letter, which had no legal force, was made secure within five years: written into an instrument of the League of Nations, and built into a British government sitting in Jerusalem. The League Council approved that instrument, the Mandate for Palestine, conditionally on 24 July 1922; the League recorded it as in force on 29 September 1923, a date John Quigley disputes. [cite:rs_md_lon1923] [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] It asks with equal weight who resisted, by what means, and with what result. The answer is not one decision but a chain of them, taken in London, Paris, San Remo, Geneva, Cairo and Washington, and contested at each link.

The cast is wide. On the British side stood a War Cabinet that approved the declaration over the written objection of Edwin Montagu, its only Jewish member; Ronald Storrs, governing Jerusalem; Winston Churchill as Colonial Secretary; and Herbert Samuel, appointed the first High Commissioner in 1920. [cite:balfour_letter] [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] The Zionist Organization worked through Chaim Weizmann and Nahum Sokolow, and through a movement that argued with itself: with Louis Brandeis's American faction over who would control the money, and later with Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky over territory. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc168] [cite:sunnafiles_jordan] Palestinian Muslims and Christians organised together in associations and national congresses led by Musa Kazim al-Husseini, while the Husseini and Nashashibi families competed for offices that Britain filled. [cite:rs_mca_palquest_musakazim] [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] Britain installed Hussein of Mecca's sons Faisal and Abdullah as rulers of Iraq and Transjordan. [cite:w_cairo1921] The victorious powers decided, the League of Nations supervised, and in Washington a Congress lobbied by American Zionists acted over the objection of its own State Department. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish]

The sections that follow trace that chain roughly in the order it was forged. They begin with [scene:s06|the three wartime promises] and Britain's reasons for wanting Palestine at all, then with Jerusalem under a military governor before any mandate existed. In Paris in 1919 Faisal signed an agreement with Weizmann on a condition of his own, and an American commission measured local opinion and saw its report shelved. The League's Covenant then supplied the machinery that turned the letter into law, by a route followed in [scene:blg_s01|the account of Article 22], and lawyers still argue over whether Palestine's mandate kept that article's rule. Alongside the diplomacy run the congresses and delegations of the Palestinian national movement, the immigrants of the Third Aliyah, the riots of 1920 and 1921 with the founding of the Haganah and Britain's two inquiries, and the creation of a permanent Zionist fund. Samuel's choice of a Mufti and his new Supreme Muslim Council show the administration building institutions of its own. The Cairo Conference and Hussein's refusal to sign widen the view to the region. The Churchill White Paper and the separation of Transjordan narrowed the promise even as the Mandate's text wrote it into law. The American campaigns end in a congressional resolution. The stage closes with [scene:rd2_council|the Legislative Council that never sat] and with the office of High Commissioner, which governed through the rest of the Mandate with no elected chamber beside it.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1922, and in some parts only during 1923, the promise of 1917 rested on several layers, each laid by different hands and each holding something the others did not.

The legal layer is the most settled. A letter of policy about land Britain did not then rule acquired force through a sequence: the League Covenant, in force from 10 January 1920; the allocation of the "A" mandates at San Remo on 25 April 1920; and the Mandate itself, approved conditionally by the League Council on 24 July 1922, with Balfour's words in its preamble. [cite:rs_a22_frus] [cite:w_balfour_decl] Its articles gave Britain "full powers of legislation and of administration," made the Mandatory responsible for securing the national home, required it to facilitate Jewish immigration, and recognized the Zionist Organization as the Jewish agency. [cite:rs_md_un_origins] [cite:rs_md_avalon] Two edges remain unsettled. The League recorded the Mandate as in force on 29 September 1923, a date John Quigley disputes.
