[cite:rs_hg_palin] Over the days from 4 to 7 April, speeches by Arab religious leaders were followed by attacks on the city's Jews. [cite:jvl_arab_riots_1920s] The toll differs from source to source. Some accounts give five to six Jews and four Arabs killed and some 200 injured. [cite:jvl_arab_riots_1920s] The military court that investigated the events kept its own count. It recorded 5 Jews killed, 18 dangerously wounded and 193 wounded, 216 Jewish casualties in all. It counted 4 Muslims killed, 1 dangerously wounded and 20 wounded, 25 in all, as well as 5 Christians and 7 soldiers wounded. The report gives the overall total as 251. [cite:rs_hg_palin]

The record of those days is not only one of violence. The sheikhs of 82 villages issued a document protesting the attacks on Jews. [cite:jewishpress_nebimusa_palin] The court also found that the attack fell on one community: "the incidence of the attack was against the Jews," it concluded. [cite:rs_hg_palin]

Jabotinsky had organized Jewish self-defense in Jerusalem during the riots. [cite:jvl_arab_riots_1920s] He was arrested with 19 others, most of them former soldiers of the Jewish Legion. A military court sentenced him to 15 years' hard labor and each of his 19 comrades to three years. [cite:rs_hg_ej_jabotinsky] [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] The court of inquiry took a different view of these men from the one the military court had taken. It found the intention of the Jewish self-defense organizers "purely defensive," and it wrote that "the arrest and prosecution of Mr. Jabotinsky was ungenerous." [cite:rs_hg_palin]

What happened to the 15-year sentence is reported in two ways, and both appear on the same reference page. In J. B. Schechtman's account in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the new High Commissioner, Herbert Samuel, amnestied those imprisoned over the Jerusalem riots in July 1920, Jews and Arabs alike. Jabotinsky left Acre prison and in September 1920 had the sentences quashed in London. The Encyclopedia of World Biography entry on that page says instead that the sentence was commuted to one year with banishment from Palestine. [cite:rs_hg_ej_jabotinsky] The two accounts cannot both be right, and this book does not choose between them. An Etzel history site adds that Jabotinsky objected to an amnesty that put defenders and aggressors in the same category, and that he kept pressing until the War Office revoked the sentences. [cite:rs_hg_daat]

Amin al-Husseini was sentenced too. His biographer Walid Khalidi writes that he was sentenced "for having led demonstrations," which places the April events in a different frame: political protest for Syrian unity. [cite:rs_hg_palquest_khalidi] The court of inquiry described an attack directed mainly against Jews and a Jewish self-defense that was defensive. [cite:rs_hg_palin] Khalidi's framing and the court's are both part of the record, and they describe the same days from different sides. Amin al-Husseini's conviction, pardon and rise to religious office are told in [scene:rd2_mufti|the appointment of the Mufti].

Britain's first inquiry was a military Court of Inquiry, known as the Palin court. It was convened on 12 April 1920, heard 152 witnesses, and reported from Port Said on 1 July 1920. [cite:rs_hg_palin] Its findings went further than the riots themselves. It called the Balfour Declaration "the starting point of the whole trouble." It criticized the Zionist Commission for taking on administrative functions that ran alongside the government's own. [cite:rs_hg_palin] It blamed the Zionists, "whose impatience to achieve their ultimate goal and indiscretion are largely responsible for this unhappy state of feeling." The report was never published. [cite:jewishpress_nebimusa_palin]

The Jewish units that had fought in the war were by then almost gone. The Jewish Legion's battalions had numbered over 5,000 men by early 1919. In the second half of 1919 they were cut to one battalion, and by spring 1920, in Schechtman's words, "a mere 300 to 400 men remained." Jabotinsky himself had been forcibly demobilized in August 1919. [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] Meanwhile the labor movement built its own body. In June 1920 an Ahdut ha-Avodah conference at Kinneret accepted the decision of Ha-Shomer to disband. It chose a committee, including Israel Shohat and Eliyahu Golomb, to organize a defense body. That body was the Haganah. [cite:rs_hg_ej_haganah] [cite:wiki_israel_timeline] Its purpose was to defend Jewish settlements. [cite:wiki_israel_timeline]

The Haganah's place in the labor movement is described in different terms. At its founding convention in December 1920, the Histadrut took on matters of guard and defense. Y. Slutsky, writing in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, says the Histadrut "accepted responsibility" for them. P. Atlas, in the Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East, goes further and says the Haganah was placed under the Histadrut's direct control. [cite:rs_hg_ej_haganah] The founding of the Histadrut belongs to the next stage of this book. Slutsky also records how small the force was: through the 1920s, Haganah volunteers "did not exceed a few hundred," and they were armed mainly with revolvers and grenades. [cite:rs_hg_ej_haganah]

The second outbreak began in Jaffa in May 1921. It started after a clash between two rival Jewish May Day marches and spread to Petah Tikva, Hadera and Rehovot. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] On 2 May 1921 Haganah members launched the first reprisal attacks on Arabs. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] The Legion was also caught up in Jaffa. On 1 May 1921 the Legion officer Margolin led armed men into the town without military permission. He was charged with breach of discipline and forced to resign. The last 400 Palestinian Legionnaires joined a mixed Arab-Jewish militia that Samuel created. [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] Samuel also suspended Jewish immigration after the Jaffa riots, which is covered in [scene:rd2_aliyah|the Third Aliyah].

The second inquiry, the Haycraft Commission, was published. Its findings ran in two directions. It found the "fundamental cause" of the violence in Arab "discontent with, and hostility to, the Jews, due to political and economic causes, and connected with Jewish immigration," and with Zionist policy as stated by its exponents. [cite:jvl_haycraft_report] It also found that "the Arab majority, who were generally the aggressors, inflicted most of the casualties." Most Arab casualties came from British forces restoring order. [cite:jvl_haycraft_report]

Put side by side, the two reports do not tell two separate stories. Each holds both halves of the same one. Palin found that the attacks fell on Jews and that the Jewish organizers acted in defense, and still put the political weight on Zionist impatience and on the Balfour Declaration. Haycraft found the Arab side generally the aggressors, and still traced the cause to Arab hostility connected with Jewish immigration and Zionist policy. From its first year, then, Britain's own record held both the attacks by Arab crowds on Jews and the Arab fear of the Zionist program as the cause beneath them. What differed was which report was published. The report that leaned toward Zionist responsibility stayed unpublished in 1920. That was the same year the King–Crane report, discussed in [scene:pc_s01|the Paris Peace Conference], was set aside.

The structure of power was already visible in these thirteen months. Britain's military courts decided who was tried and how severely. Its High Commissioner could amnesty Jews and Arabs alike with a single act in July 1920, and London could quash sentences. [cite:rs_hg_ej_jabotinsky] Its government decided which inquiry the public would read. As Britain cut the Jewish battalions from over 5,000 men to a few hundred, the labor movement built a defense body of its own. [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] [cite:rs_hg_ej_haganah]

Some things these sources leave unsettled. They do not give one agreed death toll for April 1920. The court's own figures, which come closest to a count, sit beside later accounts that differ. The sources do not agree on whether Jabotinsky's sentence was quashed outright or commuted with banishment. They do not settle how directly the Histadrut controlled the Haganah in its first years. They give the reasoning of both inquiries but not, from the material here, why the Palin report in particular was kept unpublished. And they leave open the larger question these two reports first raised, one that every later inquiry would face again: how much weight to give the attacks themselves, and how much the political fear behind them.

sections.h: Keren Hayesod: Fundraising Made Permanent
sections.html:
In the same December of 1920 in which the new Histadrut took on matters of defense, the Zionist movement built the financial institution it needed to use the opening the Balfour Declaration had given it three years before. On 24 December 1920, at a Zionist conference in London, the World Zionist Organization founded Keren Hayesod, the Palestine Foundation Fund. It was to be the organization's central and permanent fundraising arm. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki]

Its originators were Hillel Zlatopolsky and Isaac Naiditch. The fund was registered in Britain in 1921. Its stated ambition was large: the originators contemplated raising £25,000,000 within five years. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] Two features of its design set it apart. First, it was open to non-Zionists as well as Zionists, so a donor did not need to join the movement in order to give. Second, it asked supporters for a self-imposed giving pledge modeled on the tithe, a regular share of income rather than a single gift. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] In 1926 the fund moved its headquarters from London to Jerusalem. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki]

The fund's first public backers suggest a broad intended appeal. Among the named early figures associated with its fundraising were Chaim Weizmann, the president of the Zionist Organization, and Albert Einstein, the most famous scientist of the day. Jabotinsky, who would lead the more militant Revisionist wing, was also among them. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] These three men disagreed on a great deal. Their names on the same fund tell the public that it was meant to reach across the movement's divisions, not to serve one faction. The association does not show that they worked closely together or agreed on strategy. Elsewhere this book records sharp disputes among Zionist factions in these same years. One of the first of those disputes was over this fund. In the spring of 1921 Weizmann and Einstein toured the United States to raise money for it. The tour opened a fight with Louis Brandeis's American faction over who would control the proceeds. That story is told in [scene:us_s01|the first American campaigns].

The money went to more than land. Keren Hayesod financed the absorption of immigrants, settlement, defense and water development. It also financed major enterprises, among them the Palestine Electric Company and the Palestine Potash Company. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] Histories of this period usually give most of their attention to land purchase. That subject is treated in other parts of this book. Keren Hayesod's record shows a second line of investment running beside it. A modern economy needed electricity, water systems and industry as well as land. The fund put the movement's money into all of these.

The mechanism mattered as much as the money. Keren Hayesod made fundraising a standing institution. It had a legal registration, a headquarters, a multi-year target and a regular form of giving. It was built so that donors in many countries would keep paying into it year after year, and so that the money would arrive at one central body, the Zionist Organization. The fund's openness to non-Zionists widened its base. Its move to Jerusalem in 1926 put the money's management in the country where it was spent. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki]

The next step came in 1929. That year Weizmann and Louis Marshall launched the enlarged Jewish Agency for Palestine. It gave non-Zionists equal representation with Zionists, and Keren Hayesod became its financial instrument. [cite:yivo_weizmann_encyclopedia] [cite:israeled_jewish_agency_expands] [cite:britannica_jewish_agency] The fund was now folded into the body that functioned, in the years before the state, as a government in waiting. Marshall died in September 1929, within weeks of the Agency's launch. His successor as leader of the Agency's non-Zionist wing in the United States was Felix Warburg. Warburg became chairman of its Administrative Committee and Weizmann's senior non-Zionist counterpart. [cite:yivo_weizmann_encyclopedia] [cite:israeled_jewish_agency_expands] [cite:britannica_jewish_agency]

Warburg's path tells its own story. In the years before 1929 he had been a prominent, on-record opponent of Zionism. [cite:yivo_weizmann_encyclopedia] [cite:israeled_jewish_agency_expands] [cite:britannica_jewish_agency] A decade later he was one of the senior figures in the pre-state body whose fund this was. His role does not show that he had abandoned his earlier non-Zionist position. The Agency's non-Zionist seats were designed for people who supported the development of Palestine without endorsing political Zionism in full. Warburg's role there was consistent with his earlier position. The principle on which Keren Hayesod had been opened to non-Zionists in 1920 was, by 1929, built into the Agency itself.

This record corrects a familiar story. It is sometimes said that Zionist fundraising was informal and improvised until American donors organized it in the late 1930s. The documents show otherwise. When the United Jewish Appeal was formed in 1939, Keren Hayesod had already been running as a permanent, structured, international fundraising institution for nearly two decades. It had named founders, a stated target, famous early supporters such as Weizmann and Einstein, and a headquarters in Jerusalem from 1926. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki]

Several things remain undocumented here. The sources give the founding target of £25,000,000 in five years, but they do not show whether it was ever reached. They give the categories the fund paid for, from immigration to electricity, but no itemized budget showing how much went to each. The first American tour's takings are recorded in [scene:us_s01|the first American campaigns], but there is no accounting here of the fund's total income in its first decade. Keren Hayesod made giving permanent and gave the movement an institution that outlasted any single campaign. How much money moved through it in these years is not settled by this material.

sections.h: The Mufti and the Supreme Muslim Council
sections.html:
While the Zionist movement built institutions of its own, the British administration was building Muslim ones. In the space of a year, between the spring of 1921 and the first days of 1922, Britain's first High Commissioner, Herbert Samuel, made a man who had been convicted over the riots of 1920 Mufti of Jerusalem, and that man then became president of a new Muslim religious council that Britain had created. Amin al-Husseini became Mufti in May 1921 and president of the Supreme Muslim Council in January 1922. The first was Samuel's appointment; whether the second was an election or an appointment is described differently by the sources. How it made them, and why, is one of the most argued-over episodes of the early Mandate. The documents allow it to be reconstructed in some detail. They do not settle what it meant.

The story begins in April 1920. After the violence at the Nebi Musa festival, described in [scene:ri_s01|the first riots], a British military tribunal convicted Amin al-Husseini in his absence and sentenced him to ten years' imprisonment. He had fled to Syria. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_jvl] Walid Khalidi's biography of him presents the sentence as imposed for having led demonstrations, a political protest for Syrian unity. [cite:rs_hg_palquest_khalidi] Samuel pardoned him, and he returned to Jerusalem later in 1920. [cite:rs_mu_palquest_khalidi] [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] The sources do not agree on when the pardon came. Shira Klein, summarizing the scholarship for the COJS website, dates it to August 1920. The USHMM's Holocaust Encyclopedia says autumn 1920. Khalidi gives no month and says only "later in 1920." [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_palquest_khalidi]

On 21 March 1921 the Mufti of Jerusalem, Kamil al-Husseini, died. He was Amin's brother. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] On 12 April 1921 a Muslim electoral body met to choose three candidates for the office. Amin al-Husseini was not among the three. Raghib al-Nashashibi backed another candidate, Husam al-Din Jarallah. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] One account puts Amin fourth, with "about 7% of the vote." That figure comes from an opinion article by David Storobin, which relies on Joseph Schechtman's book The Mufti and the Fuehrer. It is the only vote figure in these sources, and it has not been confirmed elsewhere. [cite:rs_mu_hnn_storobin]

The day before the election, Samuel had already met Amin. In a note dated 11 April 1921, as published on the COJS website from Elpeleg's 1993 study, Samuel recorded the meeting. Ronald Storrs, by then civil governor of Jerusalem, was present. Samuel recorded Amin's pledge that he and his family would work to keep Jerusalem calm. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_samuel_note] After the vote, Samuel asked Storrs to persuade Raghib al-Nashashibi to drop Jarallah. Jarallah withdrew, and his withdrawal allowed Amin to qualify. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] Amin al-Husseini became Mufti of Jerusalem on 8 May 1921. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein]

Why did Samuel do it? The USHMM's Holocaust Encyclopedia says the British backed Amin because they accepted his assurances of cooperation. They also believed that only he had the credentials and family connections to keep Palestine calm. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] Samuel's own note of 11 April fits that account, since it records exactly such an assurance. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_samuel_note] The Jewish Virtual Library adds a name. It states that the British Arabist Ernest Richmond pressed Samuel to make the appointment, and that Samuel made it with "some trepidation." [cite:rs_mu_jvl] There was also a political balance to strike. Britain had dismissed Musa Kazim al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem in 1920 and put Raghib al-Nashashibi in his place, as described in [scene:pp_s01|the Palestinian national movement]. After May 1921 the mayoralty was held by a Nashashibi and the office of Mufti by a Husseini, the two rival families. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim]

The appointment has been read in three ways. The first reading stresses the overridden vote. Amin was not in the top three, and one account places him fourth with about 7 percent. British officials then induced the withdrawal of a qualified candidate in order to make him eligible. On this view Britain did not merely choose among candidates. It changed the list so that its preferred man would be on it. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] [cite:rs_mu_hnn_storobin] The second reading treats it as an ordinary use of government choice for the sake of order. Officials accepted his assurances and judged him the one figure able to keep the peace. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_cojs_samuel_note] The third, Khalidi's Palestinian biographical account, presents Amin as succeeding his brother in May 1921 and does not discuss the election. [cite:rs_mu_palquest_khalidi]

The office of Mufti was only half of what Samuel created. The other half was a new institution to run Muslim religious affairs. A Muslim conference on the Sharia courts and waqf, the religious endowments, was convened on 9 November 1920. Samuel approved a Regulation on 12 March 1921. It was published in the official gazette on 15 May 1921. Secondary electors met at Government House on 24 August 1921. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order] The result was the Supreme Moslem Sharia Council Order, issued in Jerusalem on 20 December 1921. It created a Council made up of a Rais al-Ulema, the head of the religious scholars, and four members: two for Jerusalem and one each for Nablus and Acre. Each was to serve a four-year term. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order]

Article 8 of the Order set out the Council's powers. It was "to administer and control Moslem Awkaf," the endowments. It nominated the Kadis, the judges of the Sharia courts. It appointed Muftis from three candidates chosen by a special electoral college. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order] The Order thus set down a three-candidate procedure like the one used for the vacancy Amin had filled a few months earlier. On 9 January 1922 Amin al-Husseini became president of the new Supreme Muslim Council, which controlled the Sharia courts and the waqf funds. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm]

How Amin reached the presidency is itself disputed. Klein describes him as elected, and to a presidency for life. Khalidi describes him as appointed president of a council that the High Commissioner instituted. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] [cite:rs_mu_palquest_khalidi] The Order's own text cuts against the idea of a life term on paper, since it sets four-year terms for the Council's members. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order] What the documents do show is the mechanism. A British High Commissioner created the body by Order, set its membership and its electoral rules, and the man he had already made Mufti became its president. Through Article 8 that body received control of the waqf, the nomination of the Sharia judges and the appointment of Muftis. These functions now came under a single council, created by the mandatory government.

The contrast with the national movement is plain. In these same months the Palestinian national movement's executive body, the Arab Executive of the Palestine Arab Congresses, went unrecognized by Britain. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim] The Supreme Muslim Council, by contrast, was a body Britain created and whose powers it defined, and the Mufti Samuel had chosen stood at its head. Control of the waqf funds and the Sharia courts went to the Council, and so to the man at its head. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_smc_order]

Several questions remain open. The full vote count of 12 April 1921 is not established. The only figure, Amin's 7 percent, comes from one opinion article relying on one book. Samuel's note records Amin's pledge, but it does not by itself show how much weight Samuel gave it against Richmond's urging or against the balance between the families. The month of the pardon is reported three ways. Whether the presidency of the Council was won by election or by appointment, and whether it was meant for life or for four years, is described differently by the sources and is left open here. The record establishes the sequence: the vote, the withdrawal, the appointment and the Order. Whether that sequence was a manipulation or a judgment about public order is a question each reader has to weigh from the evidence above.

sections.h: Kings by Appointment: Cairo, 1921, and the Sharif Who Would Not Sign
sections.html:
By 1921 Britain had to decide who would rule the Arab lands it now held. The wartime promises had been made: to Sharif Hussein of Mecca, to France and to the Zionist movement, as set out in [scene:s06|the three wartime promises]. The peace conference had handed out the mandates. What remained was to choose the men who would sit on the new thrones. The common picture of the region's monarchies is of dynasties that grew from deep local roots and popular choice. The record of 1921 shows something different. Two of the new rulers were chosen at a single British conference in Cairo. The third ruler in the story, Hussein, the father of both, refused the settlement that his sons accepted. By one account, the refusal cost him British support when his kingdom was invaded.

The decision was taken in March 1921. Winston Churchill, the Colonial Secretary, met British officials at Cairo. There they agreed to install Hussein's son Faisal as king of Iraq and another son, Abdullah, as emir of Transjordan. [cite:w_cairo1921] Faisal came to Iraq after losing a kingdom elsewhere. His Arab Kingdom of Syria, proclaimed in Damascus in March 1920, had been defeated by French forces at Maysalun on 24 July 1920. Iraq itself had risen in revolt against Britain in 1920. [cite:w_maysalun] [cite:w_iraq_revolt_1920] Abdullah's emirate, and the way Transjordan was separated from the rest of the Palestine Mandate, are the subject of [scene:s06a2|the separation of Transjordan].

The instrument was simple. A British minister and his officials agreed on names in Cairo, and the names became kings. The populations of Iraq and Transjordan did not elect them. When Iraq gained formal independence in 1932, it was under a treaty that preserved British bases. Across the region, rulers whom Britain had chosen or backed now held most of the thrones.

The same pattern reached beyond the Arab lands. In February 1921, a month before the Cairo meeting, an officer named Reza Khan led the Persian Cossack Brigade into Tehran in a coup that had the support of British officers, among them General Edmund Ironside. He became prime minister, in 1925 was made Shah and founded the Pahlavi dynasty. Iran's parliament survived, but with sharply reduced power. [cite:w_1921_persian_coup] Iran's later history belongs to another volume. Set beside Cairo, the coup can be read as part of the same pattern: much of the region's leadership in these years was installed, not elected.

Faisal's reign in Iraq also opened a chapter in the history of Iraq's Jews that later volumes follow. The mandate-era state founded in 1921 gave Iraq's Jews full citizenship, with the right to vote and to hold office. Jews became prominent in commerce, law, journalism and government service. [cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:unpacked_farhud] Iraqi Jewish historians remember Faisal's reign as tolerant and call it a "Golden Age." [cite:unpacked_farhud] Iraq's Jewish community was the oldest and, at the time, one of the largest Jewish communities in the Middle East outside Palestine. By the 1940s it numbered roughly 135,000, about 3 percent of Iraq's population, with 90,000 in Baghdad alone. [cite:ushmm_farhud]

Both of the usual summaries flatten that history. One says that Jews and Muslims in Iraq always lived in harmony. The other says the community was persecuted from the start. The record shows a real period of civic inclusion that ended at a datable point. After independence in 1932, Iraqi nationalist sentiment increasingly cast the country's Jews as pro-British and pro-Zionist, running together Jews, Zionism and British influence. That shift laid the ground for what followed, which later volumes take up. [cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:unpacked_farhud]

The father of the two new rulers would not accept the settlement. In 1919 Sharif Hussein declined to ratify the Treaty of Versailles. He did so in protest at the mandates imposed on Syria, Palestine and Iraq. Faisal had represented him in Paris. [cite:rs_hu_britannica] According to the PBS account of his life, he refused to recognize the Paris settlements at all. [cite:rs_hu_pbs]

Britain then tried to bind him by a separate treaty. The British India Office file that records the effort, IOR/L/PS/10/881, runs from 25 May 1921 to 25 August 1925. It covers two linked questions: the subsidy Britain paid Hussein, and the negotiation of an Anglo-Hejazi treaty. [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f426] T. E. Lawrence negotiated for Britain. On 28 November 1921 he telegraphed the Colonial Secretary with a proposal to revise draft Article 4 of the treaty. The new wording would "clear away all agreements" that Hussein cited but could not produce. [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f230] In December 1921 Lawrence and Emir Abdullah signed a treaty text. On 27 February 1922 Hussein threatened to abdicate. [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f111] [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f230] The Foreign Office considered making two demands of him before he could be invited to Britain: that he ratify the Treaty of Versailles, and that he accept the British treaty. [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f230]

The negotiation dragged on into 1923. On 19 April 1923 Curzon sent Jeddah a revised draft, initialled by himself and by Hussein's agent, Dr Naji al-Asil. It differed from the earlier text chiefly in a new Article 2 and in Articles 3 to 5, which dealt with "the disputed land frontiers of the Hedjaz." [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f111] Britain also changed the money. Instead of a continuing subsidy, it offered Hussein a single final payment of £50,000. [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f111]

Why did Hussein refuse? The British file shows that he refused and what was on the table. It does not, in the material here, give his reason in his own words. Jordan's official Arab Revolt centennial site gives one. It states that he refused the 1921 treaty because it required him to recognize the mandate over Palestine, and with it a Jewish national home. [cite:rs_hu_arabrevolt] That account comes from the Hashemite royal house's own heritage site. No British document in these sources names Palestine as his reason, so the explanation rests on the Jordanian account alone.

The refusal had a cost. According to PBS, his rejection of the Paris settlements and of the Anglo-Hashemite treaty cost him British support when Ibn Saud invaded. [cite:rs_hu_pbs] In March 1924 Hussein proclaimed himself caliph. In September 1924 an Ikhwan attack on Taif caught him unprepared. He abdicated on 5 October 1924. [cite:rs_hu_britannica] After his abdication Britain declined to resume treaty talks with his son King Ali, "so long as present unsettled conditions in the Hejaz continue." [cite:rs_hu_qdl_f426] Hussein lived in exile in Cyprus until 1930 and died in Amman in 1931. The Jordanian site gives the date as 3 June 1931 and says he was buried at the al-Aqsa compound. [cite:rs_hu_britannica] [cite:rs_hu_arabrevolt]

Hussein's refusal bears directly on the old question of whether Britain kept its wartime promises to him. Three positions are on the record, and each has documents behind it.

The first is that the promises were kept. Its strongest witness is Lawrence himself. As Rick Richman has set out in the Jewish Review of Books, Lawrence wrote that the Cairo settlement was "fulfilling (I think) our promises in letter and spirit." In January 1921 he told Churchill that Faisal had agreed to "abandon all claims of his father to Palestine." [cite:rs_hu_jrb_richman_2020] On this reading Britain gave the thrones of Iraq and Transjordan to two of Hussein's sons, and, on Lawrence's account, a Hashemite prince had given up the claim to Palestine. Faisal had also dealt directly with the Zionist movement in 1919, as told in [scene:rd2_faisal|the Faisal–Weizmann Agreement].

The second is that the promises were broken. The Hashemite account says plainly that "the Allies did not keep their promises," and it presents Hussein's refusal to sign a treaty recognizing the Palestine mandate as the expression of that view. [cite:rs_hu_arabrevolt] The Palestine Arab Delegation made the same case on the text of the correspondence. In its reply to the British government in 1922, it argued that McMahon had written "districts," not "vilayet." It argued that the area he reserved was Lebanon, and that "Palestine thus comes within the scope of the promise." [cite:rs_hu_cmd1700]

The third is the British government's official position, stated in the same 1922 parliamentary paper. It held that "the whole of Palestine west of the Jordan was thus excluded from Sir H. McMahon's pledge." [cite:rs_hu_cmd1700] That paper, the Churchill White Paper, is the subject of its own section.

Each position is strongest on its own ground. Lawrence's case rests on what the Hashemites received. Hussein's sons ruled two states, and one of them had, on Lawrence's account, agreed to give up the Palestine claim. The Arab case rests on the wording of the letters and on what the Sharif himself refused to sign. The British case rests on a reading of the wartime correspondence that the Arab Delegation disputed word by word in the same year. Hussein's refusal does not settle what McMahon meant. It does show that the man to whom the promise was made refused to recognize the Paris settlements and never ratified the treaty Britain offered him.

The record leaves several gaps. No British document in this material states Hussein's own reason for refusing, so the Palestine explanation rests on the Jordanian account. The sources here do not give the final fate of Curzon's 1923 draft beyond Hussein's abdication the following year and Britain's refusal to negotiate with his son. Lawrence's report that Faisal agreed to give up his father's claim is Lawrence's own account. Nothing here records Faisal saying so himself. And the meaning of McMahon's "districts" was argued in 1922 by the two sides that had most at stake, and it remains disputed.

sections.h: The Separation of Transjordan and the Claim That "Jordan Is Palestine"
sections.html:
At Cairo in March 1921 Britain chose Abdullah to rule Transjordan. [cite:w_cairo1921] That was the first of four steps by which the territory was separated from the rest of the Mandate: Abdullah's installation in March 1921; the Churchill White Paper of June 1922; the League Council's approval of a British memorandum on 16 September 1922; and completion by 1923. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] [cite:rs_md_transjordan] [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] The legal instrument was a clause written into the Mandate itself. Article 25 of the Mandate for Palestine let the Mandatory, with the consent of the League Council, postpone or withhold the application of the Mandate's provisions in the territories lying between the Jordan and Palestine's eastern boundary, provided nothing was done in conflict with Articles 15, 16 and 18. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The British government had formulated this arrangement in 1921: Transjordan would fall within the Mandate's scope, but be exempted from the provisions dealing specifically with the Jewish national home. [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] [cite:wiki_transjordan_memorandum] How Abdullah came to his throne belongs to the story of [scene:me_s05|the Cairo Conference]; this section follows the legal instrument and what was later built on it.

The memorandum of September 1922. The formal act came less than two months after the Mandate text was approved. On 16 September 1922 the Council of the League of Nations approved a British memorandum, submitted under Article 25, declaring that a list of the Mandate's provisions "are not applicable to the territory known as Transjordan." [cite:rs_md_transjordan] The list is precise. It excluded the second and third recitals of the Preamble; part of Article 2; Articles 4 and 6 in full; the part of Article 7 dealing with Palestinian citizenship for Jews; part of Article 11; and Articles 13, 14, 22 and 23. [cite:rs_md_transjordan] In the same document Britain accepted "full responsibility as Mandatory for Transjordan." [cite:rs_md_transjordan]

Read against the Mandate's own articles, the exclusions took in the main national-home provisions. Article 4 had created the recognized Jewish agency; Article 6 required the Administration to facilitate Jewish immigration and encourage close settlement by Jews on the land; Article 2 carried the Mandatory's responsibility for securing the national home; Article 11 allowed arrangements with the Jewish agency for public works. [cite:rs_md_avalon] East of the river, none of that applied. What remained was British responsibility as Mandatory over a territory under Abdullah's rule. The full reading of the Mandate's articles is in [scene:s07|the Mandate text].

Some accounts associate the separation with the Churchill White Paper of June 1922, describing it as the decision by which British Mandate authorities divided Transjordan, the territory that would become the modern state of Jordan, from the part of the Mandate designated for Jewish settlement. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] The League document places the formal step in September, under Article 25. The two fit as successive stages of one policy: the British policy paper of June 1922, then the League's approval in September of the instrument that gave it legal effect, with the separation complete by 1923. Neither was the whole of it. The White Paper's other terms are treated in [scene:s06a|the Churchill White Paper].

Who could act, and who could not. The mechanism concentrated the decision in two places. The Mandatory proposed; the League Council consented. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_transjordan] The separation, roughly three-quarters of the Mandate's land, was carried out by British administrative decision, not by war and not through negotiation with the Zionist leadership. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] On that account the Zionist Organization, the body Article 4 recognized as the Jewish agency, was not a party to the act that switched Article 4 off east of the river.

The Revisionist answer: two banks of the Jordan. The decision produced a political movement defined in part by its refusal to accept it. Jabotinsky founded Revisionist Zionism in the early 1920s, explicitly rejecting the 1922 decision to separate Transjordan from the territory available for Jewish settlement, and made "a Hebrew majority in the Land of Israel on both banks of the Jordan River" a core part of the movement's program. [cite:sunnafiles_jordan] The grievance had a precise origin: a specific, dated British administrative act, not a vague sense of loss.

The program was carried in song and in symbols. While visiting Paris in 1929, Jabotinsky wrote "The East Bank of the Jordan," whose refrain, "the Jordan has two banks, this one is ours and that one too," became an anthem of Betar, the Revisionist youth movement. [cite:jabotinsky_org_etzel] [cite:sunnafiles_jordan] Betar, which traced its beginnings to Riga in the 1920s, grew to more than 70,000 members by the mid-1930s. [cite:grokipedia_betar] The Irgun, a Revisionist paramilitary organization active from 1931 to 1948, adopted in the late 1930s an emblem showing a map of the whole Mandate territory, both banks of the Jordan included, with a hand holding a rifle superimposed on it and the Hebrew words "Rak Kach," "Only Thus." [cite:wiki_irgun] One reading treats the emblem's design as a statement about method as well as territory: paired with the rifle, the slogan said the territorial claim would be achieved by force rather than negotiation, consistent with Jabotinsky's "Iron Wall" doctrine, which held that Arab opposition could be overcome only through unyielding strength. [cite:peoplesworld_greater_israel] The emblem's visual content and slogan are corroborated across several independent sources; what they document is the position of a historical organization, not the policy of any later Israeli government. [cite:wiki_irgun]

The lineage did not end in 1948. Betar is the direct ideological ancestor of Israel's Likud party, itself a Revisionist successor organization. [cite:grokipedia_betar] In 2023 the politician Smotrich, whose Religious Zionism party sits further to the right within the same broad tradition, delivered a both-banks statement in Paris with a map of that territory displayed, a visual echo of the Irgun emblem roughly ninety years later. [cite:grokipedia_betar] [cite:wiki_irgun] Ninety-four years separated the two Paris moments, Jabotinsky's song and Smotrich's speech. Both places and dates are documented; nothing in the record connects the two beyond coincidence, and no source suggests Smotrich chose Paris to echo Jabotinsky. No source suggests Smotrich chose the city to echo Jabotinsky, and this book does not suggest it either. The coincidence matters only as evidence of how deeply the idea is embedded in the movement's own history. [cite:jabotinsky_org_etzel]

"Jordan is already Palestine." From the separation grew a second argument, the reverse of the Revisionist one. The claim runs that the 1921 partition of Mandatory Palestine already gave the Arabs their homeland, so that Jordan is in effect the Palestinian state and a second one would be redundant. It is often treated as a purely pro-Israel argument. The documented record is more complicated, because Jordan's own rulers made versions of the same claim, for their own reasons, before Jordan's government formally reversed course.

In 1948 King Abdullah I declared that "Palestine and Jordan are one, for Palestine is the coastline and Transjordan the hinterland of the same country." [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] In 1959 the Jordanian prime minister Hazza Majali stated: "We are the government of Palestine, the army of Palestine, and the refugees of Palestine." [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] King Hussein made comparable statements at several points. [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] These were not concessions to Israeli arguments. They were Jordanian claims, made to support the Hashemite Kingdom's annexation of the West Bank and its influence over Palestinian politics. [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] They show that the idea did not originate as an outside talking point; they do not show that it was ever permanent or unanimous Jordanian policy.

The reversal was formal and dated. On 31 July 1988 King Hussein announced the dissolution of Jordan's legal and administrative ties with the West Bank. [cite:springer_jordan_palestine_history] With that act Jordan's own government renounced any continuing claim to represent or administer Palestinian territory or population, the opposite direction from the claims of 1948 and 1959. The record cited here documents the act and its completeness; it does not set out every strategic consideration behind its timing, or the regional politics of 1988 around it.

The present position is on record from Jordan's head of state. Asked in a televised interview whether Jordan should be considered the de facto Palestinian state, King Abdullah II answered: "Jordan is Jordan." [cite:davidsinger_jordan_palestinian_state] A large share of Jordan's population is of Palestinian origin, from the displacements of 1948 and 1967. [cite:davidsinger_jordan_palestinian_state] That demographic fact is real and remains a significant factor in Jordanian society and politics. It does not change the government's position that this population is not a separate Palestinian polity within Jordan's borders.

The dispute. Two arguments have been built on the same administrative fact, and they point in opposite directions. The Revisionist argument treated the separation as a loss to be undone: the national home had been promised a territory, and three-quarters of it had been removed by a British decision. The "Jordan is Palestine" argument treats the same separation as a settlement already made: the Arabs of the Mandate received the larger share in 1921–23, so the Palestinian question was answered then. The historian Bernard Wasserstein has documented that, in later ideological use, the separation came to be called "the myth of Palestine's first partition." [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] His phrase does not deny the administrative fact, which is documented. It flags the gap between that fact and the political conclusion later drawn from it.

The strongest form of the case for the claim rests on the documents of 1921–23: the national-home provisions were written for the whole Mandate, Article 25 withdrew them east of the river, and Arab rule was established there. The strongest form of the opposing case rests on the documents of 1988 and after: whatever weight the 1921 separation carries, a state's sovereign status is not conferred by outside argument, and Jordan's own government has formally, explicitly and repeatedly rejected the role of Palestinian state since 1988, most recently in its king's words. That Jordanian monarchs once made the claim themselves complicates any reading of it as a one-sided talking point. That Jordan then withdrew it, formally, is the documented end point of that history.

What the record leaves open. The material here does not say why Britain chose 1921 for the Article 25 formula, or record the reactions of Transjordan's own population to the memorandum. It does not set out the full reasoning behind Jordan's 1988 timing. The administrative history of 1921–23 is settled; its political meaning has been asserted and rejected by different parties at different times for different reasons, and it remains contested.

sections.h: The Churchill White Paper of 1922: The First Narrowing
sections.html:
The policy paper that marked the second stage of that separation said a good deal more. On 3 June 1922 the Colonial Secretary, Winston Churchill, published a command paper titled "Palestine: Correspondence with the Palestine Arab Delegation and the Zionist Organisation." Historians call it the Churchill White Paper. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It was made up of nine documents, with Churchill's own memorandum as an enclosure, and it was an official British clarification of what the Balfour Declaration meant, put on the record five years after the declaration itself. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It appeared seven weeks before the League Council's conditional approval of the Mandate text in July 1922.

Why 1922. The paper was drafted partly in response to the Jaffa riots of May 1921, in which dozens were killed on both sides. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] Those riots pushed Britain toward its first restatement of policy; their course and Britain's inquiry into them are told in [scene:ri_s01|the first riots and the first inquiries]. [cite:wiki_jaffa_riots_1921] A major narrowing of policy thus came within roughly a year of serious violence. The record does not show that the riots were the only cause, and Britain's wider strategic and administrative concerns were almost certainly in play as well.

What the paper said. The White Paper reaffirmed the Balfour Declaration. In the same breath it set limits on what the declaration meant. Palestine, it insisted, was not intended to become "as Jewish as England is English." [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] That sentence did not withdraw the promise of a national home. It narrowed what the promise could be taken to mean, and it did so in Britain's own official words.

The second limit concerned immigration. The White Paper laid down the principle that Jewish immigration should be limited by the country's economic capacity to absorb new arrivals. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] This was the first formal mechanism under the Mandate for limiting immigration, seventeen years before the 1939 White Paper imposed a harder, fixed numerical ceiling. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] The 1922 rule was a standard rather than a number. It tied the flow of immigrants to an economic judgment about what the country could take. How the rule had been foreshadowed in Herbert Samuel's statements of 1921, and how immigration actually moved under it in the early 1920s, belongs to the story of the Third Aliyah.

The third limit was territorial. The White Paper is associated with the separation of Transjordan, the land east of the Jordan River and roughly three-quarters of the Mandate's total area, from the part of the Mandate open to Jewish settlement. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] It was one stage of that separation, not the whole of it. Abdullah had been installed in Transjordan in March 1921; the League approved the memorandum that formally excluded the national-home provisions on 16 September 1922; and the separation was complete by 1923. [cite:w_cairo1921] [cite:rs_md_transjordan] [cite:wiki_borders_of_israel] Those stages, and the arguments later built on them, are traced in [scene:s06a2|the separation of Transjordan]. The separation was the largest territorial reduction in the whole pre-1948 history, and it came by administrative decision, not by war and not through negotiation with the Zionist leadership. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922]

How it was received. The paper's own title shows that it was framed as an answer to two parties at once, the Palestine Arab Delegation and the Zionist Organisation. The Arab Delegation, then in London, had demanded a "national independent Government" and refused the Balfour Declaration as a basis for discussion; the White Paper gave it neither, and its exchanges with the Colonial Office are set out in the account of the Palestinian national movement. [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] The Zionist leadership accepted the paper without treating it as a triumph, and Chaim Weizmann and others believed the absorptive-capacity principle could still allow a Jewish majority to be built; that acceptance, and the Arab refusal of the 1922 constitution, are treated in [scene:rd2_council|the Legislative Council]. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] Acceptance did not mean agreement. The record of the Mandate years shows continuing tension between the Zionist Organization and Britain over exactly this kind of step-by-step retreat, and real Zionist objection to the territorial decision, even though it was never reversed. The sharpest objection came from Jabotinsky, who built the Revisionist movement in part on rejecting the separation of Transjordan. [cite:sunnafiles_jordan]

What happened to immigration anyway. The policy limited growth; it did not stop it. By the figures given in one account of the White Paper, the Jewish population of Palestine grew under the absorptive-capacity rule from about 80,000 in 1922 to roughly 380,000 by 1936, nearly a fivefold increase in fourteen years. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] The 80,000 is a round estimate; the British census of October 1922 counted 83,794 Jews. [cite:rs_ta_report1922] The same pattern of a formal restriction followed by continued growth recurs with the harder cap of 1939.

Reversal or narrowing. The familiar account holds that the Balfour promise stood unchanged from 1917 until Britain suddenly reversed it in 1939. The documents tell a different story. Within five years of making the promise, Britain narrowed its meaning, attached an economic test to immigration, and set in motion the removal of roughly three-quarters of the territory from the area open to Jewish settlement, seventeen years before the better-known reversal. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] Whether 1922 should be called the first reversal or only a narrowing is a matter of judgment, and the record supports both readings in part. The case for "reversal" rests on scale: the territorial reduction was larger than any later one before 1948, and the immigration rule was the first formal mechanism for limiting immigration. The case for "narrowing" rests on the paper's own words: it reaffirmed the declaration, kept immigration open, and left the national home in force west of the Jordan, where the Jewish population then grew almost fivefold. On either reading, the 1939 White Paper was not the first time Britain redefined its promise. It was the second.

What the record leaves open. The growth figures show that the absorptive-capacity rule did not prevent large-scale immigration. They cannot show what immigration would have been without it: growth might have been faster with no cap at all, and the record here makes no counterfactual claim. Nor does it show that "economic absorptive capacity" was applied consistently or predictably in the years that followed. The weight of the Jaffa riots against Britain's other motives in drafting the paper is likewise unsettled; the riots are documented as a direct contributing factor, not as the sole cause.

sections.h: The Mandate for Palestine: The Text and the Polity It Created
sections.html:
The document that wrote a British wartime letter into a League of Nations instrument ends with a place and a date: "Done at London the twenty-fourth day of July, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-two." [cite:rs_md_avalon] Behind that line lay two years of diplomacy. At the San Remo Conference in April 1920 the victorious Allies assigned Palestine to Britain, and in July 1922 the Council of the League of Nations approved the text under which Britain would hold it. [cite:san_remo_wiki] [cite:mandate_text] How a letter of policy became an instrument of the League, and the argument over whether that instrument honored the League's own Covenant, is told in [scene:blg_s01|By What Right?]. This section reads the instrument itself: what its articles said, when it actually took effect, what kind of state apparatus it brought into being, and what it gave and withheld.

The League of Nations, founded in 1920 under the Treaty of Versailles, was the authority in whose name the arrangement was made. [cite:san_remo_wiki] The mandate system was Woodrow Wilson's attempt to separate a temporary trusteeship, meant to lead toward self-government, from outright colonial annexation. In practice, mandates were administered essentially as colonies. [cite:san_remo_wiki] [cite:mandate_text] That judgment concerns Palestine; the record summarized here does not show that every mandate across the world was run the same way. The League itself did not survive the Second World War, and its successor, the United Nations, inherited its records. [cite:san_remo_wiki]

What the articles said. Article 1 gave the Mandatory, Britain, "full powers of legislation and of administration." [cite:rs_md_un_origins] Everything else in the text operated inside that grant.

Article 2 set out the Mandatory's core obligations, and it set out three of them in one sentence. Britain was responsible for conditions that would secure the Jewish national home; for the development of self-governing institutions; and for "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine." [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] The national home and the protection of rights were both binding. The text did not say how they were to be weighed against each other if they collided.

Article 4 provided that "an appropriate Jewish agency shall be recognized as a public body" to advise the Administration, and it recognized the Zionist Organization as that agency for as long as its constitution was deemed appropriate. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] The League later recorded that in 1929 the Zionist Organisation was replaced in this role by the "Jewish Agency for Palestine." [cite:rs_md_lon1945] The articles summarized here name no equivalent public body for the Arab majority. Britain's later offer of an "Arab Agency" analogous to the Jewish Agency, with members chosen by the High Commissioner, and its rejection in October 1923, belong to the story of the Legislative Council of 1922–23. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency]

Article 6 turned the national home from a principle into a working instruction. The Administration was to "facilitate Jewish immigration under suitable conditions" and to encourage close settlement by Jews on the land, while ensuring that other sections of the population are not prejudiced. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_lon1945] Read closely, in the article that governs immigration and settlement the majority of the country's people appear in that form: as other sections of the population, protected against prejudice but not named.

Article 7 provided the basis for a Palestinian citizenship, and part of it concerned the acquisition of Palestinian citizenship by Jews. [cite:rs_md_transjordan] Three years later, that article became the legal ground of the Palestinian Citizenship Order, discussed below.

Article 11 dealt with the country's wealth. It allowed the Administration to place natural resources and public works under public ownership or control, and to make arrangements with the Jewish agency for such works, with the profits that could be distributed capped. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The clause named the Jewish agency as a body that could be brought in to develop public resources, and it limited the profits that could be taken out of them.

Article 22 made English, Arabic and Hebrew the official languages of Palestine, and required that any Arabic inscription on stamps or money be repeated in Hebrew, and any Hebrew inscription in Arabic. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The rule is small, but it fixed in law that the coins and stamps of the new polity would speak to both communities at once.

Article 25 concerned the lands east of the river. It let the Mandatory, with the consent of the League Council, postpone or withhold the application of provisions of the Mandate in the territories between the Jordan and Palestine's eastern boundary, so long as nothing was done that conflicted with Articles 15, 16 and 18. [cite:rs_md_avalon] Britain used that power within two months of the text's approval. The memorandum of September 1922 that removed the national-home provisions from Transjordan, one stage in a separation completed by 1923, is the subject of its own section, with the long political afterlife of that separation.

Set beside the letter it absorbed, the Mandate shows what changed in five years. The 1917 declaration expressed a government's favour and promised its best efforts. The 1922 text made the national home a legal responsibility of the governing power, added an immigration duty and a recognized Jewish public body, and widened the protected group from "existing non-Jewish communities" to "all the inhabitants." It also added a promise the letter had not contained: self-governing institutions, with no date and no form specified.

When the Mandate took effect, and the dispute over it. The approval of July 1922 was conditional. The League Council approved the terms of the Palestine and Syria mandates together, pending an agreement between France and Italy over Syria. [cite:rs_md_lon1923] At its meeting in Geneva on 29 September 1923, the Council took note that the France–Italy agreement had been reported and that the two mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force." [cite:rs_md_lon1923] The United Nations later used that date. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj]

That date has been challenged. John Quigley, writing in July 2026, argues that the Council only noted, in the future tense, that the mandates would enter into force, and that the Secretary-General, Drummond, changed the tense in the circular that reported the meeting. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] Quigley adds a second argument: Britain lacked title to the territory at that point, because the Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, entered into force only on 6 August 1924. [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] The case for the conventional date rests on the League's own record, circular C.L.101.1923.VI, which states that the mandates had "automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and on the United Nations' later reliance on it. [cite:rs_md_lon1923] [cite:rs_md_quigley_oj] The case against rests on the minutes' wording and on the sequence of the Ottoman peace treaty. The dispute is about the legal moment the Mandate began, not about whether Britain governed: British administration of Palestine was already in place, under a High Commissioner, from 1920.

The government the text created. Britain administered Palestine under the Mandate until 1948. It issued passports, minted the currency, printed the stamps, ran the police and the courts, operated the railways and the ports, and staffed a civil service that employed Arabs and Jews alike, all under a High Commissioner headquartered in Jerusalem. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Beneath him sat a postal system and a customs and taxation apparatus that functioned for the whole of the Mandate's span. The Mandate had a legal text, published borders and recognized standing in international law. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

The first High Commissioner, appointed in 1920 by the Cabinet that had issued the Balfour Declaration, was Sir Herbert Samuel, a British Jew and a committed Zionist. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] One reading holds that his appointment embedded the declaration's contradiction in the administration itself: a single government was charged at once with fostering a Jewish national home and safeguarding the rights of an existing Arab majority, two obligations that, on this reading, could not both be honored. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] His tenure and those of the six men who followed him are traced in [scene:s07a2|the High Commissioners].

Citizens, passports, money. The Palestinian Citizenship Order of 1925, which came into force on 1 August 1925, gave legal form to a Palestinian citizenship under Article 7. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] Under it, about 70,000 brown passports were issued over the years of the Mandate, each stamped "BRITISH PASSPORT / PALESTINE." [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] The word "British" on the cover is what later led casual observers to misremember them. The holders were citizens of Palestine, Arab and Jewish. They used the documents to cross borders, conduct trade, study abroad and perform the hajj. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] The Palestine pound was minted from 1927 and circulated as legal tender; Palestine issued its own postage stamps, ran its own courts, and registered its own births, deaths, marriages and land titles. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

The historian Lauren Banko's study The Invention of Palestinian Citizenship, 1918–1947 traces how this status was built. It was not an informal identity but a specific legal status created by British administrative order, with its own bureaucratic history, population records, and legal disputes over who qualified. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship] Many of the passports survive. They are held today by the descendants of Palestinian families in Ramallah and Haifa, in the refugee camps of Lebanon and Jordan, and across the diaspora, as evidence that their grandparents were citizens of a recognized polity. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship]

The people of the polity. By one general account of the Mandate, its population at the start was roughly 90 per cent Arab and 10 per cent Jewish, about 600,000 Arabs and 60,000 Jews. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] An account of the 1922 White Paper puts the Jewish population at about 80,000 in 1922. [cite:wiki_churchill_wp_1922] Both are round estimates. The one count from these years is the British census of October 1922, which recorded 757,182 people: 590,890 Muslims, 83,794 Jews and 73,024 Christians. [cite:rs_ta_report1922] Its figures are set out with [scene:rd2_aliyah|the Third Aliyah]. The census total is well above the first estimate, and its Jewish count is close to the second. By 1947, the last full year of the Mandate, the figures had moved to roughly 1.3 million Arabs and 600,000 Jews. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Jewish growth came substantially through waves of immigration from Europe between the wars, heaviest in the 1930s as antisemitism in Europe intensified. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] The start and end points are documented here; the year-by-year course of that change, and the immigration and land machinery that drove it, belong to later chapters.

Land ownership moved more slowly than population. The Jewish National Fund, founded in 1901, and the other Zionist institutions had acquired about 9.8 per cent of Mandate Palestine by purchase by 1948. [cite:jnf_wiki] The same source's further point is that most of the territory of the state that emerged in 1948 came not through purchase but through the war and displacement of that year. [cite:jnf_wiki] The two measures are taken against different wholes, Mandate Palestine in one case and the territory of the new state in the other, so they should not be read as a single sum. What the comparison does establish is that fifty years of organized, funded purchase left Jewish institutions owning under a tenth of the country's land on the eve of statehood.

The claim and the record. A familiar line holds that Palestine was an empty desert until Jewish pioneers made it bloom. The administrative record of the Mandate answers the first half of that sentence directly. The territory Britain governed had a High Commissioner, a treasury, a passport office, courts, a postal service, a registry of births and land titles, a currency, and a population numbering in the hundreds of thousands. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] [cite:san_remo_1920] The Mandate text itself legislated for "all the inhabitants of Palestine" and for "other sections of the population" whose rights were not to be prejudiced, wording that presupposes people already living there. [cite:rs_md_avalon] None of this asserts a modern nation-state before 1948, or settles any present political claim. It establishes something narrower: that a functioning civic polity called Palestine, with a documented citizenry, existed for a quarter-century before 1948. That matters for what followed. If the land was empty, no one was displaced; if it had citizens, the events of 1948 require a different accounting.

The record also supports the strongest form of the Zionist reading of the same document. The Mandate was not a British favour that could be quietly withdrawn. It was an instrument approved by the Council of the League of Nations that wrote the national home into binding articles: Britain was responsible for securing it, was obliged to facilitate Jewish immigration and close settlement, and was required to work with a recognized Jewish public body. [cite:rs_md_avalon] [cite:rs_md_un_origins] For the Zionist movement, that was international legitimacy in the most formal sense then available. The Arab leadership's reading pointed to what the framework did not give: in February 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation demanded a "national independent Government" and said the Balfour Declaration could not be a basis for discussion, and the Colonial Office replied that "the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge." [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] Both readings rest on the same articles. On one reading, the disagreement is over which of Article 2's obligations governed when they could not all be met at once.

What the record leaves open. The passport count is an approximation, and the record does not give the number that survive today. It does not resolve present arguments about citizenship, return or statehood; it shows only that a formal, legal Palestinian citizenship existed under British administration decades before 1948. The two estimates of the Jewish population at the Mandate's start, 60,000 and about 80,000, are not reconciled with each other or with the census count of 83,794. Whether the Mandate entered into force on 29 September 1923 remains, as of the scholarship cited, contested. And the text never answered its own central question. It bound Britain to a national home, to self-governing institutions and to the rights of all inhabitants, and it named no rule for choosing among them. The documents of 1922 that tried to supply such a rule, the Churchill White Paper and the Transjordan memorandum, are where the next sections turn.

sections.h: The First American Campaigns: Weizmann, Einstein and the Fight Over the Money
sections.html:
The Mandate's text was settled in London and Geneva, but much of the money and some of the political backing for the national home were being sought in the United States. American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to the years after the Second World War, as a response to the Holocaust. The organized American campaign began a generation earlier. By the spring of 1921 the Zionist movement was running national fundraising tours across the United States, and by January 1922 one of its leaders was sitting with the President. It was also, in those same months, fighting an internal battle over who would control the money it raised. American Jewish opinion was not yet its own: much of the established community still kept its distance.

The United States had figured in Zionist and British calculations from the start. Among the motives the British War Cabinet weighed in 1917, when it approved the Balfour Declaration, was the hope of winning sympathy in Russian and American Jewish communities, to help keep Russia in the war and bring America into it. [cite:cohen_palestine_great_powers] What changed after the war was that the movement now needed money on a new scale. At a London conference on 24 December 1920 the Zionist Organization founded the Keren Hayesod, the Palestine Foundation Fund, as its central and permanent fundraising arm, open to non-Zionist donors as well, with an original five-year target of £25,000,000. [cite:keren_hayesod_wiki] The fund's structure and what it went on to finance are told in [scene:s04i|the account of the Keren Hayesod]. America was where a large part of that money would have to come from.

In March 1921 Chaim Weizmann invited Albert Einstein to accompany him to the United States. The two toured the country for two months that spring, raising money for the new Keren Hayesod and for the Hebrew University. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] [cite:hnn_isaacson_einstein] The movement was sending the world's most famous scientist on a national fundraising tour. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252]

The tour also brought into the open a struggle over control. The Einstein Papers document it. Weizmann wanted the Keren Hayesod centralized under the Zionist Executive. The American faction led by Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis and Judge Julian Mack wanted American control of the money and businesslike management of how it was spent. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc168] [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] At stake was who would decide how American donations were spent: the world movement's executive, or the American organization that raised them. The sources record each side's position; they do not set out the full arguments each made for it.

The dispute came to a head at the 1921 convention of the Zionist Organization of America in Cleveland. Weizmann's side won, and the Brandeis group withdrew from the leadership of American Zionism. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc168] [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_intro] Weizmann's centralized model for the fund had prevailed.

The campaign did not stop with the split. In November 1921 a second delegation arrived for a Keren Hayesod tour: Nahum Sokolow, who with Weizmann had drafted the Balfour Declaration, Otto Warburg and Jabotinsky. [cite:balfour_letter] Their tour raised nearly $5 million. On 13 January 1922 Sokolow met President Warren Harding for nearly an hour. [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] Within months, Congress would take up a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration, the subject of [scene:us_s02|the next section].

None of this meant that American Jewry as a whole had embraced Zionism. Much of the established community remained non-Zionist. Paul Warburg avoided the cause, and when Einstein invited about fifty non-Zionist notables to take part, few responded. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252] The campaign of 1921 and 1922 was the work of an organized movement within American Jewish life, not the voice of that community entire, and the distance kept by many of its leading figures is as much a part of the record as the money raised.

So the common account needs correcting on two counts. American support for a Jewish national home did not begin after 1945: by 1921, twenty-seven years before statehood, the movement had a national fundraising operation in the United States, a public figure of Einstein's standing on tour, a fight over control of the proceeds, and an audience with the President. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252] But that support was not yet broad, even among American Jews.

The record here leaves several things open. It does not say what Sokolow and Harding discussed, or whether the meeting bore on the congressional resolution that followed. It does not break down the nearly $5 million by source or show how it was spent, nor does it give the sums raised by the spring tour itself. And it records the outcome of the Cleveland convention, not the vote or the arguments made on its floor.

sections.h: Congress Endorses Balfour: The Lodge–Fish Resolution of 1922
sections.html:
Official American support for a Jewish homeland is usually dated to 1948 and President Truman's recognition of the new state. The first formal endorsement by the United States government came twenty-six years earlier. On 21 September 1922 President Warren Harding signed a joint resolution of Congress favouring a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. It had been requested by American Zionist leaders, opposed by the State Department, and passed by the House and, by unanimous consent, the Senate.

The initiative came from the American Zionist movement, then in the middle of the fundraising campaigns described in [scene:us_s01|the previous section]. American Zionist leaders approached two Republicans, Senator Henry Cabot Lodge of Massachusetts and Representative Hamilton Fish III of New York, and asked them to introduce a resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration of 1917. The Jewish Virtual Library credits a significant lobbying effort by the American Zionist community, and in particular the work of Rabbi Simon Glazer. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] Nahum Sokolow had met Harding for nearly an hour on 13 January 1922, during the Keren Hayesod tour that raised nearly $5 million. [cite:israeled_sokolow_harding] The record used here does not say whether that meeting touched on the resolution.

The resolution met objection from two quarters. The State Department opposed it, and so did the New York Times. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] It passed regardless. The House approved it on 30 June 1922, and the Senate followed by unanimous consent on 13 July. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] The Senate's passage came eleven days before the Mandate for Palestine, which wrote the Balfour Declaration into an instrument of the League of Nations, was done at London on 24 July 1922. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The Mandate itself is examined in [scene:s07|the section on the Mandate text].

Harding signed the measure on 21 September 1922 as Public Resolution 67-73. Its text favoured "the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," repeating the phrase the Balfour Declaration had used in 1917. [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:balfour_letter] It also carried a condition: that nothing should be done which might prejudice "the civil and religious rights of Christian and all other non-Jewish communities in Palestine." [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] The condition belongs in any account of the resolution as fully as the endorsement does. Congress, like the British government before it, favoured a national home for one people and stated in the same text that the rights of the communities already living in the country were not to be prejudiced.

Inside American Jewish life the resolution mattered too. The World Jewish Congress notes that it helped legitimize Zionism within American Jewry by giving it a "stamp of approval" from the non-Jewish world. [cite:wjc_lodge_fish] That carries weight against the background of the previous year, when much of the established American Jewish community still kept its distance from the cause, and when Einstein's invitation to about fifty non-Zionist notables drew few replies. [cite:einstein_papers_vol12_doc252]

The episode shows how this resolution was made. The initiative did not come from the State Department, the arm of government responsible for foreign policy, which opposed it. It came from an organized domestic movement that approached members of Congress directly and won passage in both houses, after which the President signed. The resolution was lobbied for and passed over the objection of the foreign-policy bureaucracy. [cite:jvl_lodge_fish] [cite:wjc_lodge_fish]

What it committed the United States to is a narrower question than its importance might suggest, and the record used here answers it only in part. The text says what Congress favoured and on what condition. The sources do not show that it obliged the government to take any particular action, and they do not describe any action taken under it. Nor do they give the grounds on which the State Department and the New York Times objected, or the House vote count. What is documented is the sequence, the words of the text with their condition, and the fact that the first official American endorsement of a Jewish national home came in 1922, not 1948.

sections.h: The Council That Never Sat: The Legislative Council of 1922–1923
sections.html:
The Mandate obliged Britain to do two things that pulled against each other. Article 2 made the Mandatory responsible for conditions that would secure the Jewish national home and for the development of self-governing institutions, while also "safeguarding the civil and religious rights of all the inhabitants of Palestine." [cite:rs_md_avalon] The first test of how those duties would be reconciled came in 1922, when London offered Palestine a constitution with a partly elected legislature. Within a year the offer had failed. The record of that failure is more specific than either side's later shorthand: a share in government was offered, on terms that the Arab leadership refused and the Zionist leadership accepted, and its rejection left the High Commissioner ruling without any elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate.

The negotiation began before the text was final. Through the first half of 1922 the Palestine Arab Delegation in London, the body sent by the Fourth Palestine Arab Congress, corresponded with the Colonial Office about the draft constitution [cite:rs_mca_jvl_congress]; its rejection of the draft in February and the Colonial Office's replies are told in [scene:pp_s01|the account of the Palestinian national movement]. Two of the delegation's specific objections bore directly on the council. An earlier draft had included two nominated members, and the Colonial Office agreed to drop them. The delegation went further: it demanded that every member be elected, and it objected to a quorum of ten. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] By the arithmetic of the final text, the ten official members would by themselves have made a quorum of ten.

The Zionist side answered the same correspondence differently. On 18 June 1922 the Executive of the Zionist Organisation assured the government that its activities "will be conducted in conformity with the policy therein set forth," meaning the policy of the statement now known as the Churchill White Paper. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] According to the historian Shira Klein, the Zionist leadership did not treat the White Paper as a triumph. Weizmann and others accepted it because they believed its principle of "economic absorptive capacity" could still allow a Jewish majority to be built over time. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] The White Paper itself, and the immigration rule at its centre, are examined in [scene:s06a|the section on the Churchill White Paper].

The constitution was issued in London as the Palestine Order in Council on 10 August 1922, and Herbert Samuel, as High Commissioner, proclaimed it in force on 1 September 1922. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] Article 19 set out the Legislative Council: twenty-two members plus the High Commissioner, of whom ten were to be official members and twelve unofficial, elected members. Article 30 set the quorum at ten. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] The two nominated seats were gone, as the Colonial Office had conceded. The quorum of ten, to which the delegation had objected, remained.
