The twelve elected seats were divided by community: eight Muslim, two Christian and two Jewish. The historian Philip Mattar has set that allocation against the population. Palestinian Arabs, by his reckoning, were allotted 43 percent of the seats while forming 88 percent of the population. [cite:rs_lc_mattar] The figure explains the shape of the dispute that followed. Even if every Muslim and Christian seat had been filled, the ten Arab members would have held ten places in a chamber of twenty-three.

The two sides' reasons for accepting and refusing are the heart of the matter, and each deserves its strongest form. The Arab leadership's case was that the council was built on the Mandate and on the Balfour Declaration, which the delegation said could not be a basis for discussion; that it gave the Arabs a minority of the seats although they were the large majority of the people; and that it fell short of what they had asked for, a national government with control over immigration. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_mattar] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] In February 1922 the delegation had already demanded a "national independent Government," and the Colonial Office had replied on 1 March that "the creation at this stage of a national Government would preclude the fulfilment of the pledge" to the Jewish people. [cite:rs_mca_cmd1700] To take part in the council, on this reading, was to accept the frame that made the Arab majority a minority in its own legislature. The Zionist leadership's case was that the framework, whatever its limits, kept the national-home commitment intact and tied immigration to the country's economic capacity rather than to Arab consent. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_whitepaper] Both readings rest on the same documents. They differ on what those documents were for.

The Arab answer came at the Fifth Palestine Arab Congress, meeting in Nablus in August 1922, which resolved to boycott the elections to the Legislative Council. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] [cite:rs_lc_albright] According to the Jewish Virtual Library's account, the congress opened on 22 August and also resolved to reject the new constitution. [cite:rs_mca_jvl_congress]

The boycott was tested in the primary elections of late February 1923. Voting was in two stages, and the primaries chose secondary electors. Of 809 secondary electors expected, no more than 213 were chosen. The Muslim districts, expected to yield 663, produced only 107. [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] The 1947 Yale study of the Mandate by Albright and others records the pattern by community. Jews and Druze took part fully. Muslims filled about one-sixth of their allotment and Christians about one-third. The polling was extended on 7 March 1923, and even then the result was too unrepresentative for a council to be formed. [cite:rs_lc_albright]

Britain then tried twice more within the year. It first proposed a nominated Advisory Council in place of the elected one. The Arab nominees refused their seats, and the idea collapsed. [cite:rs_lc_albright] It next offered an "Arab Agency," a body meant to parallel the Jewish agency recognised under Article 4 of the Mandate, but with its members chosen by the High Commissioner. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency] That offer was rejected in October 1923. The president of the Arab Executive, Musa Kazim al-Husseini, wrote that the Arabs' "sole object is independence." [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_arabagency] [cite:rs_mca_palquest_musakazim] One difference between the two agencies is plain in the documents: the Zionist Organization had been named in the Mandate itself as the Jewish agency, while the Arab body would have been the High Commissioner's own selection. Britain reported the episode to the League. Its report on the administration for 1923 lists a White Paper of November 1923 on the "Proposed Formation of an Arab Agency" and "Papers relating to the Elections for the Palestine Legislative Council." [cite:rs_lc_report1923]

By the end of 1923 Britain was governing with an advisory council made up of British officials only. The High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] One asymmetry follows from the documents: with no legislature, the Arab leadership held no elected place in government, while the Zionist Organization kept the advisory standing that Article 4 of the Mandate gave it as the recognised Jewish agency. [cite:rs_md_avalon]

The idea did not die at once. A council was proposed again in 1930, under Passfield, and again in 1935, when Britain offered a council of twenty-eight members: fourteen Muslims and Christians, eight Jews, five officials and one commercial member. That proposal was suspended amid Jewish opposition and Arab division, and the idea died with the revolt of 1936–39. [cite:rs_lc_mattar] The terms had shifted since 1922. The 1935 council would have given Muslims and Christians fourteen seats to the Jews' eight, and this time the opposition recorded on the Jewish side was part of the setting in which the proposal was suspended.

Several things the record here does not settle. The sources give the turnout by community, not the reasons of individual voters who stayed away. It does not establish whether a council of this shape, had it sat, could have changed policy on immigration or land, since no such council ever met. The formal instrument by which the 1923 elections were set aside, and the exact membership of the Advisory Council Britain then proposed, are not established in the sources used here and are left out rather than guessed at. Nor do the sources detail the 1930 proposal beyond its date. What the record does show is the sequence: a constitution offered on terms one side accepted and the other refused, three British attempts in a single year to find some form of Arab participation, and, from the end of 1923, a High Commissioner who governed with officials alone.

sections.h: Who Ran Palestine: The High Commissioner and the Seven Who Held the Office
sections.html:
The council's failure left one office at the centre of Palestine's government. The Mandate is often written about as though "the British government" ran Palestine as a single, faceless machine. The documents show something more particular. From 1920 to 1948 the country was governed day to day by a sequence of seven appointed High Commissioners, with acting commissioners filling the gaps between them, and each of them made decisions that can be dated and traced. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine] Herbert Samuel opened the office in 1920. His successors, Plumer, Chancellor, Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham, presided in turn over the riots of 1929, the Arab Revolt, the years of the 1939 White Paper, the Jewish armed campaign against British rule, and the withdrawal of 1948. What follows describes the office itself, the first man to hold it, whose decisions fall inside these years, and, more briefly, the six who came after.

The office drew its power from the Mandate itself. Article 1 gave the Mandatory "full powers of legislation and of administration." [cite:rs_md_un_origins] Britain exercised those powers through a High Commissioner based in Jerusalem, at the head of a civil government that ran everything from passports and currency to police, courts and railways, and that employed Arabs and Jews alike. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] Above him stood London and, more distantly, the League of Nations. The Colonial Office conducted the negotiations over Palestine's constitution in 1922, and the Mandatory reported to the League on its administration. [cite:rs_lc_cmd1700] [cite:rs_lc_report1923] Beside the administration, Article 4 of the Mandate recognised the Zionist Organization as the "appropriate Jewish agency," a public body to advise it. [cite:rs_md_avalon]

What the office lacked tells as much as what it held. The constitution of 1922 placed the High Commissioner at the head of a Legislative Council of twenty-two members, ten of them officials and twelve elected. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] That council never sat. After the boycott of the 1923 elections, Britain governed with an advisory council of British officials only, and the High Commissioner ruled without an elected legislature for the rest of the Mandate. [cite:rs_lc_albright] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] How that happened is told in [scene:rd2_council|the account of the Legislative Council]. Its effect on the office was lasting: for the rest of the Mandate, the "full powers of legislation and of administration" that Article 1 gave the Mandatory were exercised in Palestine through the High Commissioner without any elected body beside him.

The first man to hold this office had a direct link to the Balfour Declaration. Herbert Samuel was a British Cabinet minister and an advocate of Zionism, and a memorandum he wrote in 1915 influenced the Balfour Declaration itself. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel] He was appointed in 1920 by the same British Cabinet that had issued the declaration, and by many accounts he was the first Jewish governor of the land since Roman times. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel_hc] [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] The appointment was itself a point of contemporary debate. It sharpened Arab suspicion that the Mandate was built to deliver the Balfour promise, and it placed inside a single administration the double charge of fostering a Jewish national home while safeguarding the rights of the Arab majority. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki] He served until 1925, and the administrative and legal foundations he laid framed the work of every administration after him. [cite:wiki_herbert_samuel] [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

Samuel's record in office does not fit either of the simple portraits drawn of him. According to J. B. Schechtman's account in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, one of his first acts, in July 1920, was an amnesty for those imprisoned over the Jerusalem riots of that April, Jews and Arabs alike. [cite:rs_hg_ej_jabotinsky] He also pardoned Amin al-Husseini, whom a British military tribunal had convicted in his absence after the same violence. [cite:rs_mu_ushmm] [cite:rs_mu_jvl] What became of Jabotinsky's sentence under the amnesty is disputed, as told with [scene:ri_s01|the riots of 1920 and 1921]. Samuel lent his name, as Honorary President, to the Pro-Jerusalem Society of Ronald Storrs, Jerusalem's military governor until 1920 and its civil governor from that year. [cite:rs_al_ashbee1921] [cite:rs_al_openjerusalem] In 1921 he made Amin al-Husseini Mufti of Jerusalem, after recording Amin's pledge to keep the city calm and after Storrs, at his request, secured a rival candidate's withdrawal. [cite:rs_mu_cojs_samuel_note] [cite:rs_mu_cojs_klein] On 20 December 1921 the Supreme Moslem Sharia Council Order created the council over which Amin would preside. [cite:rs_mu_smc_order] Whether the Mufti's appointment was a manipulation of an election or a judgment about public order is set out in [scene:rd2_mufti|the account of the Mufti's appointment].

The violence of 1921 tested the office early. After the Jaffa riots, on 15 May 1921, Samuel temporarily prohibited Jewish immigration, and on 3 June he tied future immigration to the country's economic capacity, the principle the 1922 White Paper would write down. [cite:rs_ta_cojs_whitepaper] He created a mixed Arab-Jewish militia, which the last 400 Palestinian Legionnaires of the Jewish Legion joined. [cite:rs_hg_jvl_legion] On 1 September 1922 he proclaimed the Palestine Order in Council in force, the constitution under which the Mandate was to be governed. [cite:rs_lc_order1922] When the Legislative Council it created failed in 1923, the office he handed on governed with officials alone. [cite:rs_lc_albright]

Taken together, these acts resist a simple portrait. A Zionist by conviction, chosen by the Cabinet that issued the Balfour Declaration, Samuel suspended Jewish immigration after Jaffa and backed as Mufti a man he had pardoned. The documents support neither the portrait of a governor who simply served the national home nor its opposite.

The six who followed him inherited the office he had shaped and held it through crises that belong to later chapters of this book. They are told here only as the record gives them, to show how the office ran in practice.

Field Marshal Herbert Plumer, who came to the post from command of the British Expeditionary Force's Second Army, served from 1925 to 1928. He was named without consultation with the World Zionist Organization, yet he was regarded as committed to fairness toward Zionist aspirations. When he died in 1932, a Jewish Telegraphic Agency obituary described his tenure as "the only period when complete tranquility existed in Palestine." [cite:jta_plumer_obituary] [cite:toi_diaries_1929_officials] That is a contemporary judgment of comparative calm, set against what came before and after, not a claim that those three years were free of tension.

Sir John Chancellor served from December 1928 to September 1931, a period of what has been described as "tremendous tension." It began with a dispute at the Western Wall on Yom Kippur 1928 and culminated in the Hebron Massacre of 24 August 1929. Chancellor was not in the country when the massacre happened. He was on home leave in England through the critical period of July and August 1929. Harry Luke served as acting High Commissioner throughout, and Chancellor returned to Jerusalem only on 29 August 1929, five days after the killings. [cite:toi_diaries_1929_officials] [cite:encyclopedia_hc_palestine] Two facts stand side by side here, and both are real: his absence during the acute crisis, and his responsibility as head of the administration whose wider policies formed its setting. The episode also shows how the office worked when its holder was away. Authority did not lapse; it passed to an acting commissioner, who carried it through the massacre itself.

Arthur Wauchope held the office from 1931 to 1938, through years of rising Jewish immigration and the outbreak of the Arab Revolt of 1936–39. Historians generally regard him as more sympathetic to Zionist settlement than his successors, and his approach has been called relatively conciliatory. He resigned as the revolt intensified. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine] The record used here gives his general reputation and the crisis that ended his term, not an itemised account of his decisions.

Harold MacMichael, from 1938 to 1944, administered Palestine as the 1939 White Paper was put into effect and through the early years of Jewish paramilitary resistance. In 1944 Lehi, also known as the Stern Gang, attempted to assassinate him in an ambush on his motorcade. He survived, wounded; his wife was seriously injured. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

The shortest tenure, and the one most often left out of popular accounts, belonged to Field Marshal John Vereker, 6th Viscount Gort. He served from November 1944 to November 1945 and retired because of ill health after barely a year. He died the following year, 1946. [cite:wiki_john_vereker_gort] His brevity is itself the notable fact. The record does not attribute major policy shifts to him, and this book does not claim any.

The last was Alan Cunningham, from 1945 to 1948. He presided over the most violent period of Jewish paramilitary resistance, including the bombing of the King David Hotel, and over the chaotic British withdrawal from Palestine in May 1948. [cite:wiki_hc_list_palestine]

Naming all seven matters because twenty-eight years of rule did not run on a single setting. Each administration made its own choices within the broader policy framework: how firmly to enforce limits on immigration, how to respond to violence coming from more than one direction, and even whether to be present or on leave when a crisis broke. [cite:encyclopedia_hc_palestine] Treating the period as one undifferentiated British policy erases a calm three years under one man, an absence during a massacre under another, and an assassination survived under a third. The opposite error is just as real. No one High Commissioner's character explains the Mandate's outcome. Each worked inside a much larger structure: a Mandate held by Britain under the League, directed from London, and from 1923 governed without an elected chamber in Palestine.

Some of what a reader would want to know is not in the record used here. It does not name every acting commissioner who filled the gaps between tenures, beyond Harry Luke in 1929. It does not show, for any of the seven, how much of what he did was his own decision and how much followed instructions from the Colonial Office. It does not give the content of Samuel's 1915 memorandum, only that it influenced the Balfour Declaration. And for Wauchope, MacMichael, Gort and Cunningham it gives a reputation and a few dated events rather than a full account of their administrations; those belong to the later chapters in which their crises fall.

chapters.label: Stage Three
chapters.title: Build
chapters.intro:
Between 1922 and 1936 the Zionist project in Palestine changed character. It stopped being chiefly a matter of declarations and diplomacy and became a matter of building. The British Mandate, the arrangement under which Britain now governed the country, supplied the frame. Inside it the movement assembled the working parts of a state that did not yet exist: a labor federation with its own bank, construction firm and health fund; a Jewish Agency widened to take in wealthy American non-Zionists; a banking channel chartered in London; an electricity monopoly whose grid followed Jewish settlement. Over the same years Britain counted the country's people and investigated its violence. Once it tried to slow the pace of immigration and land transfer, and within months it reversed itself.

These were not years of unity. Inside Palestine, Jewish opponents of Zionism made their case to the British, and in 1924 one of their spokesmen was shot dead in Jerusalem. The movement itself split. The Revisionist break of 1925, the departure of the movement's right wing, produced both the paramilitary organizations of the 1930s and 1940s and the institutional line that later became Likud. In 1929 violence at Hebron removed a Jewish community that had lived there for centuries; organized Jewish life in the city did not resume until 1968. And from 1933 Germany cast its shadow over everything. There a democracy was voted out of existence, a transfer agreement with the new regime divided the Jewish world, and the Nuremberg Laws gave persecution the form of statute.

The chapters that follow ask a single question. In the years when the state-in-waiting took shape, what was actually built, by whom, and on what terms?
chapters.outro:
By the mid-1930s Palestine held the institutions of a state, but no state to hold them. The Histadrut, the Jews-only labor federation, ran its own construction firm, bank and health fund, and it was training the men and women who would govern. The Jewish Agency, enlarged in 1929, had brought wealthy American non-Zionists into its governance. The Anglo-Palestine Bank carried the movement's money. A seventy-year electricity monopoly had produced a grid that followed Jewish settlement. In the United States, a Zionist executive had founded the American Palestine Committee in 1932 to organize prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans. In the 1940s it and a parallel council for clergy, both organized from within the Zionist political office, would claim thousands of members.

Nor was the movement unified. Jabotinsky's Revisionists had seceded in 1925 and left entirely in 1935. The Irgun had broken with the Haganah's policy of restraint in 1931. And Jewish dissent from Zionism had been met, at least once, with a killing.

Britain, for its part, had counted a country that remained largely Arab and had investigated the violence of 1929. It had then seen its attempt to limit immigration and land transfer reversed within four months. Jewish immigration rose sharply, to over 60,000 in 1935. In Germany, democracy had been voted away and the Nuremberg Laws had made exclusion a matter of statute. The movement's own Congress, meanwhile, had chosen to continue the transfer agreement with the Nazi state. The pieces of the state-in-waiting were in place, and so were the pressures that would test them.

sections.h: The Histadrut and "Hebrew Labor"
sections.html:
In December 1920, in Haifa, the two labor Zionist parties of the day, Ahdut HaAvoda and Hapoel Hatzair, joined forces to found the General Federation of Hebrew Workers in the Land of Israel, known by its Hebrew short name, the Histadrut [cite:wiki_histadrut]. It began small. Membership stood at about 4,400 in 1920 and about 8,400 in 1922, in a country where, by a Zionist historian's estimate, there were roughly 50,000 Arab workers [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss]. Those workers were outside the federation by rule, not by accident: from its founding, membership was restricted to Jews [cite:wiki_histadrut].

Labor Zionism is often remembered as a socialist workers' movement, committed to class solidarity across national lines. The Histadrut was socialist in its language and its ownership of enterprises. But it was not a union of the country's workers. It was a union of one community's workers, and much of its work in the 1920s and 1930s was to build that community's separate economy. The question this section answers is how a trade union came to be, in practice, a government-in-waiting.

The decisive figure was David Ben-Gurion, elected secretary of the federation at the end of 1921 [cite:wiki_histadrut]. In the account of the historian Zeev Sternhell, Ben-Gurion turned the Histadrut into a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional class union [cite:wiki_histadrut]. Its campaign in the labor market went by the name "Hebrew labor," avoda ivrit. The Histadrut pressed Jewish employers, especially citrus growers and builders, to hire only Jewish workers [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The demand was made of Jewish employers; the workers it was meant to exclude were Arab. This was separation in the labor market long before there was any separation in law.

The federation did not stop at organizing workers. From December 1920 it also took responsibility for defence, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control; through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. How that militia grew after 1929, and how part of it broke away, is told in [scene:s07e2|the armed line].

The Histadrut also owned the places where its members worked. It built the construction and public-works company Solel Boneh. In association with the World Zionist Organization it founded the Workers' Bank, Bank Hapoalim. It ran the Kupat Holim health fund, on which many Israelis later depended for their health insurance, and it gathered industrial holdings that later became Koor Industries [cite:wiki_histadrut]. A union that ran a bank, a building contractor, a health system and its own militia was, in effect, a parallel economy with its own means of protection. The scale it eventually reached shows what this structure made possible: by 1989 the Histadrut employed about 280,000 workers [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss].

Land was the other half of the same design. The Jewish National Fund held land that could not be resold to non-Jews and leased it on terms requiring Jewish labor; that clause is set out in [scene:rd3_land|the land section]. Taken together, the land fund and the labor federation meant that the Yishuv had separate economic institutions decades before 1948: land that stayed in Jewish hands, a labor market organized for Jewish workers, its own bank and its own health system.

How to read this is disputed, and both readings deserve their strongest form. The movement described itself as socialist, and its defenders hold that the description was sincere. Pinhas Lavon, the Histadrut's secretary-general in 1960, described its founders as young people seeking work in a country "which rejected its inhabitants." On this reading the Histadrut was what young immigrants built in order to find work at all, and its enterprises were a means of employing them.

The critical reading starts from the same facts. On Sternhell's account, under Ben-Gurion the Histadrut became a national instrument for realizing Zionism rather than a conventional union; its socialism served the national project, not the other way round [cite:wiki_histadrut]. Critics including the BDS movement go further, describing the pre-state Histadrut as a national-exclusivist rather than a socialist body, and "Hebrew labor" as national exclusivism in place of worker solidarity [cite:bds_histadrut_critique]. That is their characterization; it is not a finding of this book. What is not in dispute is the membership rule. A labor federation that excluded the majority of the country's workers from the day of its founding cannot be described, on the record, as practicing class solidarity across national lines, whatever its members believed about themselves.

The Histadrut was also a school for government. Ben-Gurion went on to chair the Jewish Agency from 1935 and became prime minister in 1948. He was followed by two Histadrut veterans, Levi Eshkol and Golda Meir [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss]. The membership rule outlasted independence. Arab workers were admitted to full membership only in 1959, eleven years after the state was founded. By 1983 about 170,000 of the federation's 1.6 million members were Arab [cite:wiki_histadrut] [cite:marxists_histadrut_union_boss].

The record leaves some questions open. The sources give no year-by-year membership series between 1922 and the 1950s, so the federation's growth through the period of this chapter cannot be traced here. Nor do they measure how far "Hebrew labor" actually succeeded: how many Jewish employers complied, how many Arab workers lost work in Jewish-owned groves and building sites, or what the policy cost employers in wages. The campaign is documented; its economic effect, in numbers, is not.

sections.h: The Electricity Concession and the Grid
sections.html:
Land, labor and arms are the usual measures of how the Yishuv was built. Electricity belongs beside them. On 12 September 1921 the Mandate government signed the Auja (Yarkon) Concession. It granted the Jaffa Electric Company of Pinhas Rutenberg the exclusive right, for 70 years, to generate, distribute and sell electricity in the Jaffa district, using hydroelectric turbines on the Auja [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. It was a monopoly over a whole district, granted by the governing power to a single company.

The common view of the Mandate's public works is that they were neutral economic modernization, of benefit to everyone in the country. The concession tests that view. Its terms, the politics of its approval and, above all, the shape of the network it produced show something more particular: infrastructure that followed Jewish settlement and helped bind it together.

The concession had a legal footing in the Mandate itself. Article 11 allowed the administration to arrange with the Jewish Agency to construct or operate public works [cite:zaoerv_mandate_article11]. Rutenberg also had backing at the top. The High Commissioner, Herbert Samuel, and the Colonial Secretary, Winston Churchill, both supported him [cite:jc_turnberg_rutenberg]. The point of the arrangement, in mechanical terms, was that the British administration did not have to build or run a power system itself; it could grant the right to a concessionaire, and the Mandate named the body with which such arrangements could be made.

The grant did not pass unopposed. In 1922 the House of Lords passed an amendment to stop the concession. The House of Commons then overturned the Lords by a large majority, in a vote led by Churchill [cite:jc_turnberg_rutenberg]. The Lords had tried to stop the monopoly; the elected chamber chose to keep it. A challenge came from abroad as well. Euripides Mavromatis, a rival Greek concessionaire, contested the monopoly before the Permanent Court of International Justice. The sources used here record the challenge but not its outcome, so this book does not state one.

What was built did not match what was promised. The hydroelectric plant on the Auja was never built. When the grid switched on in 1923, it ran on diesel, in Tel Aviv [cite:jstor_electrifying_conflict] [cite:military_wiki_rutenberg]. The concession had also brought Rutenberg irrigation rights in the Auja valley, and those rights ended up benefiting only Jewish settlers [cite:jstor_electrifying_conflict] [cite:military_wiki_rutenberg]. A concession justified by a public river and a public need produced a diesel network in the Jewish city and water for Jewish farms.

In 1923 Rutenberg founded the Palestine Electric Corporation. It built the country's only hydroelectric plant, not on the Auja but at Naharayim, on the Jordan. In 1961 the corporation was renamed the Israel Electric Corporation [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. The name change marks the continuity: the company founded under the Mandate became the national electricity company of the state, without a break.

The money in this arrangement moved through rights rather than cash. The Mandate government granted a monopoly over a whole district's electricity for 70 years; the concessionaire gained a protected market and, with it, the irrigation rights in the valley. The sources do not give the sums invested, the tariffs charged or the company's revenue, so the financial size of the monopoly cannot be stated here. What they do show is who gained the water and where the power went.

The fullest study of where the power went is the historian Fredrik Meiton's prize-winning work on electrification in Palestine. Meiton finds that the centralized grid knit Jewish settlements together while marginalizing and bypassing most Palestinian Arab communities [cite:mesa_meiton_award] [cite:wiki_israel_electric]. Another historian writes that the Yishuv's economic separatism "was given a tremendous push" by the 1921 monopoly. On this reading, electricity was statecraft: a network laid along the lines of Jewish settlement drew a map of a future state in copper and diesel, decades before any partition line was proposed.

The other reading deserves its strongest statement. The familiar account holds that the Mandate's development of Palestine was neutral economic modernization that benefited everyone, carried out by the means the Mandate text itself provided, a concession under Article 11. On this view a grid had to begin somewhere, and where it began says more about where it could be built first than about whom it was meant to serve. Parliament debated the concession openly and approved it by a large majority. Nothing in the sources shows that Arab communities were barred from connection by rule. The findings of Meiton and the second historian concern the shape and effect of the network, not a written policy of exclusion.

That is also where the record runs out. The sources here do not say how many Arab towns or villages were connected by 1936, or on what terms; whether the bypassing Meiton describes was planned or followed from where the company chose to build; or how the Mavromatis case ended. What is documented is the monopoly, the parliamentary fight that kept it, the plant that was never built, the diesel grid in Tel Aviv, the irrigation rights that served only Jewish settlers, and a company that passed intact from the Mandate to the state.

sections.h: Counting the Country
sections.html:
Every later argument about Palestine, about immigration, land and partition, rests on numbers, and the most important of them were gathered by the British administration in the years this chapter covers. Two slogans have grown up around those numbers, one on each side. The first says Palestine was "a land without a people." The second says Palestinian Arabs owned 94% of the land. Neither survives the Mandate's own statistics. This section sets out what the counts show, so that the arguments that follow can start from them.

Britain's first census of Palestine, taken in 1922, counted 757,182 people. Of these, 83,794 were Jews, about 11% of the population [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The second census, in 1931, found Jews at 17% of the population, Muslims at 73% and Christians at 9% [cite:jvl_census_1931]. In nine years the Jewish population had doubled. Yet the growth of the non-Jewish population over the same years was larger than the entire Jewish population [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The 1931 census also asked where people were born: 42% of Jews had been born in Palestine and 58% abroad [cite:jvl_census_1931]. The Yishuv of 1931 was, by a clear majority, a community of immigrants, though a substantial share was native-born.

The line above traces the Jewish share of the population across three counts: about 11% in 1922, 17% in 1931 and about 33% at the end of 1946 [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. The first two points are British census results. The third is an estimate, made by the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP). UNSCOP put the population at the end of 1946 at about 1,846,000: roughly 1,203,000 Arabs (65%) and 608,000 Jews (33%) [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. Over almost the same span, British records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946 [cite:ssrn_mandate_immigration]. How those arrivals were distributed year by year, and why two published series for the same years disagree, is taken up in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section].

These three figures frame the period. The 757,182 people of 1922 are the country as Britain found it when the Mandate began; the 376,415 recorded Jewish immigrants of 1920–1946 are the arrivals that changed its composition; and the roughly 1.85 million of late 1946 are the country UNSCOP had in front of it when it made its recommendation [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:ssrn_mandate_immigration] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. Even at the end of 1946, after a quarter-century of immigration, about two in three of the inhabitants were Arabs.

There is a second count from these years, and it does not match the census. In 1937 David Horowitz of the Jewish Agency's Economics Department prepared the Agency's economic case for the Peel Commission. According to that paper, the Jewish population in 1922 was 84,000, or 13 percent, against a non-Jewish population of 565,000 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. The Jewish figure is close to the census count of 83,794. The non-Jewish figure is far below the census, so the two together make a smaller total and a higher Jewish share. The Agency's paper does not explain its base in the sources used here. It is advocacy, and it is examined as such in [scene:us_s06|the economy section]; the census figure of about 11% is the one this book uses.

Land was counted too, and here the numbers have been bent in both directions. The Village Statistics of 1945 was compiled for the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry and later used by UNSCOP. It classified land by ownership, by use and by tax category [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. In 1947, the United Nations partition plan allotted about 56% of the territory to the proposed Jewish state, at a time when Jews owned under 7% of the land; the proposed Jewish state would also have contained a large Arab minority [cite:historyskills_partition]. How the Jewish share of land was assembled in these years, through the purchases of the Jewish National Fund and others, is told in [scene:rd3_land|the land section]; the partition plan itself belongs to a later chapter.

With these figures, both slogans can be tested. "A land without a people" is refuted by every census the British took. The 1922 count found three-quarters of a million people, and the 1931 and 1946 figures found the Arab majority still growing [cite:jvl_census_1931] [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]. The country was inhabited, and mostly by Arabs.

The counter-slogan fails in a different way. The claim that Palestinian Arabs privately owned 94% of the land counts large areas of state and public land as Arab-owned [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. The 1945 survey keeps those categories apart: land in private ownership is one column; land held by the state is another [cite:wiki_village_statistics]. Jewish ownership of under 7% does not mean Arab private ownership of the remainder. The honest comparison, for anyone making either case, uses the survey's own categories.

What do these numbers not settle? They do not tell us how the land not privately owned by Jews or Arabs was divided between state land and other public categories in any given year; the sources here give the distinction, not the totals. The 1946 population figure is an estimate, not a count, and the sources do not give its margin of error. And the gap between the census and the Jewish Agency's 1937 figures for 1922 is not explained in the material used here. The direction of the record is nonetheless clear. Palestine between 1922 and 1946 was a populated, majority-Arab country with a fast-growing Jewish minority, which owned a small share of the land, much of the rest of which was held by the state rather than by private Arab owners.

sections.h: How the Mandate Became Law, 1923–1925
sections.html:
By the summer of 1922 Britain had governed Palestine for nearly five years. Its forces had taken Jerusalem in December 1917, and the text of the Mandate had been approved by the Council of the League of Nations. Yet two legal steps were still missing. The state that had ruled the country for four centuries had not yet given it up, and the Mandate had not yet formally entered into force. Between 1923 and 1925 both gaps were closed, or so the standard account holds, and the Mandate government then defined, for the first time, who was a citizen of Palestine. Each step has a date, a document and, in at least one case, a serious scholarly challenge.

The first step was taken at Lausanne. The peace treaty between the Allies and Turkey was signed there on 24 July 1923 [cite:rs_rd3_lausanne_fcdo]. In it the new Republic of Turkey, founded that year, renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces of the Ottoman Empire [cite:w_lausanne]. The treaty made modern Turkey the empire's successor state, not a claimant to Palestine [cite:w_lausanne]. Professor John Quigley stresses a further point about the wording: the renunciation was not made in favour of Britain or of the Allies [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Turkey gave up its rights; it did not hand them to anyone. The treaty did not take effect at once. It entered into force on 6 August 1924 [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026].

The map above follows Turkey's long relationship with the land and, later, the state, from four centuries of Ottoman rule through Lausanne to the present. For this chapter only its second step matters: the renunciation that closed the Ottoman claim.

The second step was the Mandate's entry into force, and here the record holds two accounts. The League Council had approved the mandates for Palestine and Syria on 24 July 1922, on a condition: they would take effect once France and Italy reached a final agreement over Syria [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. One scholarly source gives a different date for that approval, 12 August 1922 [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]; the UN's document gives 24 July [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. At the Council's meeting of 29 September 1923, according to the minutes as reproduced by the United Nations, the mandates for Syria and Palestine "had thereby automatically and simultaneously entered into force," and the British representative, Sir Rennell Rodd, said the question was "finally settled" [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force]. On this account, 29 September 1923 is the date the Mandate became law. Britain, the League Secretariat and, in 1947, the United Nations all treated it as such [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force].

Quigley disputes it. He argues that the Council minutes used future-tense wording and that the Council took no resolution. In his reading, the past-tense formula, that the mandates had entered into force, was supplied afterwards by the League's Secretary-General, Eric Drummond, in his Circular Letter 101. If that is right, the 29 September 1923 date has no legal force, and since Lausanne did not take effect until 6 August 1924 and gave Britain no title in any case, Britain held Palestine without title [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Quigley's argument was published in July 2026; it is a challenge to the standard date, not yet a settled finding.

Each side has a real case. The standard date rests on a primary document, the minutes, and on the conduct of every body that mattered at the time: Britain administered the Mandate, the League supervised it, and the UN in 1947 started from that date. Quigley's case rests on the same kind of evidence read more closely: the tense of a verb, the absence of a resolution, and the question of who changed the wording. It asks whether a legal status can rest on a secretariat's paraphrase. The practical history of the Mandate did not wait on the answer; the legal question remains open in the sense that the argument has been made and not, in the sources used here, answered.

The third step was to decide who belonged. The Palestinian Citizenship Order was issued on 24 July 1925 and took effect on 1 August 1925. It made Palestinian citizens of Ottoman subjects habitually resident in Palestine on that date [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]. Two groups stood outside that rule. The first were Arabs who had emigrated abroad: because the Order tied citizenship to residence on 1 August 1925, it denied them citizenship [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. The second were immigrants, who could acquire citizenship by naturalization.

How naturalization worked in practice is known mainly through one study. According to Nadia Abu Alia and Asem Khalil, the Government of Palestine reportedly accepted about 100 of some 9,000 naturalization applications in one period, using an "absolute discretion" clause. By 1946, on their figures, about 130,000 foreigners had acquired Palestinian citizenship by naturalization, 99 percent of them Jews [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil]. The two figures describe different things: the first a single period of tight refusal, the second the cumulative total over two decades. The sources do not say which period the first figure covers or whose applications were refused.

The historian Lauren Banko reads the Order as a turning point and a double standard at once. It was, she notes, the first Mandate legislation to treat the Arab population as citizens rather than as "ex-enemy Ottoman subjects" [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. But it treated Jewish citizenship and the naturalization of immigrants in sharp contrast to Arab citizenship, in Banko's account, and Palestinian Arabs answered it by invoking Ottoman-era principles of descent and birthplace [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast]. The two principles pulled in opposite directions. Descent and birthplace would have reached the emigrants abroad; the Order's rule, residence on a fixed date with naturalization for those who arrived, did not reach them but was open to newcomers. Banko's reading is that this asymmetry was the point of contention, and the naturalization figures, in which 99 percent of those naturalized by 1946 were Jews, show which way it ran in practice [cite:rs_rd3_banko_podcast] [cite:rs_rd3_abualia_khalil].

The Mandate text's own provisions on nationality, passports and currency are set out in [scene:s07|the Mandate text] and are not retold here. Some things remain unsettled. Whether the Mandate ever validly entered into force is argued, not decided. The sources do not give the number of Arab emigrants who lost a claim to citizenship under the 1925 Order, nor the year-by-year breakdown of naturalizations, nor, for the reported period when about 100 of 9,000 applications were accepted, who the applicants were. What is documented is the sequence: a treaty that ended the Ottoman claim without transferring it, a League record whose wording is contested, and a citizenship law that, by 1946, had naturalized about 130,000 people, almost all of them Jews.

sections.h: The Revisionist Line, 1923–1935
sections.html:
Zionism is often described as a single political movement that divided into parties only after the state was founded. The institutional record shows otherwise. Its deepest split, between the movement led by Chaim Weizmann and the one led by Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky, opened in the years of this chapter and was documented step by step: a youth movement in 1923, a secession in 1925, a second and final break in 1935. The organization Jabotinsky built is the direct ancestor of Herut and then Likud. It also produced the armed groups, the Irgun and later Lehi, that operated alongside and often against the Haganah and the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism] [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization].

Jabotinsky was a Russian-Jewish writer and Zionist leader [cite:wiki_jabotinsky]. He was not religious, and his claims to the land were territorial and historical rather than biblical [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. In 1923 he founded Betar, a youth movement built on discipline and military training. Its watchwords were hadar, pride or dignity, and armed self-defense, and it spread through Poland, the Baltic states, Palestine and the Americas [cite:wiki_betar].

The same year he set out the argument on which his politics rested, in an essay called "The Iron Wall." Its claim was that the Arabs of Palestine would never voluntarily accept a Jewish majority, and that Zionism could therefore proceed only from a position of overwhelming military strength [cite:wiki_iron_wall_essay] [cite:theconversation_israels_iron_wall]. Its central sentence reads:

Zionist colonization, even the most restricted, must either be terminated or carried out in defiance of the will of the native population.

A follow-up essay, "The Ethics of the Iron Wall," argued that this approach was itself moral [cite:wiki_iron_wall_essay] [cite:theconversation_israels_iron_wall]. The essay is notable for what it conceded as much as for what it proposed. It did not pretend the land was empty or that its people would welcome the project; it said plainly that they would not, and drew the conclusion that consent could not be the basis of the plan.

Among the young men drawn to the movement was Benzion Netanyahu, born Mileikowsky in Warsaw in 1910, who had emigrated to Palestine in 1920. In the 1930s he edited the Revisionist newspaper Ha'Yarden [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:wiki_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:tabletmag_bibi_fathers_footsteps]. His later role belongs to a later chapter: in 1940 Jabotinsky sent him to the United States, where he served as Jabotinsky's personal secretary until Jabotinsky's death that year and then ran the movement's American operations for eight years [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:wiki_benzion_netanyahu] [cite:tabletmag_bibi_fathers_footsteps]. His son, Benjamin Netanyahu, told a Jabotinsky memorial audience in 2023 that one hundred years after the "iron wall" was set down in Jabotinsky's writings, Israel was "continuing to successfully implement these principles" [cite:counterfire_netanyahu_shadow]. He has also, separately, dismissed the idea that his father's formation under Jabotinsky shaped his own views as "psychobabble" [cite:jewishjournal_benzion_netanyahu]. Both statements are his own, and they sit in tension; this book records both and does not choose between them.

The organized break came two years after the essay. In April 1925, in Paris, Jabotinsky founded the World Union of Zionist-Revisionists, known by its Hebrew acronym Hatzohar [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism] [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. Its first president was Vladimir Tiomkin [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The founding is described as a secession from the World Zionist Organization that Weizmann led [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism]; yet the Revisionists went on sending delegates to Zionist Congresses for the next decade, so in practice the break of 1925 created a rival faction rather than a separate body [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. Its founding platform called for transforming Palestine and Transjordan into a Jewish commonwealth within the British Commonwealth, in direct opposition to the mainstream's gradualist strategy [cite:wiki_revisionist_zionism].

The heart of that platform was the claim to "both banks of the Jordan," a Jewish majority on both sides of the river, covering what is now Israel, the West Bank, Gaza and the whole of Jordan [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. Jabotinsky argued that Britain's separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate in 1922 was an arbitrary partition, which denied Jews the territory they would need to absorb millions of future immigrants [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. He put the geography in one sentence, writing in 1929–1930:

What does the word Palestine mean? Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center.

The movement's anthem made the same point in a line: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well" [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925]. This was the first of several versions of what would later be called "Greater Israel," and the most limited of them: a territorial claim to the whole of the original Mandate area, not a biblical one. How later religious-nationalist versions differ, and how the idea is used today, is traced in [scene:gia_src_s02|Greater Israel and its three versions]; the history of the "two banks" claim from 1922 to 1948 is told in [scene:ijr_src_s04|Two Banks of the Jordan].

In 1925 the Revisionists were a small faction. They had four delegates at the Fourteenth Zionist Congress that year [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. Six years later they were a major force. In 1931 they won 17 percent of the vote for the Yishuv's elected assembly, the Asefat ha-Nivharim, and became its second-largest party. At the Seventeenth Zionist Congress in Basel the same year they had 52 delegates, and proposed a resolution for a Jewish state on both sides of the Jordan [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists].

Growth brought internal conflict. In 1933, at Katowice, Jabotinsky suspended the party's executive. A plebiscite of the membership backed him, and his opponents, led by Meir Grossman, seceded to form the Jewish State Party. At the Eighteenth Congress the Jewish State Party had seven delegates to the Revisionists' 46 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The Revisionists' quarrel with Labor Zionism turned violent the same year, after the murder of Chaim Arlosoroff, and the attempt to settle it through agreements with Ben-Gurion in 1934 failed; that story is told in [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|1933–1935].

How large was the movement by the mid-1930s? The figure most often quoted is 600,000, and it is used in two different ways. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, more than 600,000 Jews in 24 countries signed a Revisionist petition addressed to the British king and Parliament in 1934 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. That is a count of signatures. Other accounts present the same figure as the membership the broader Revisionist movement claimed by 1934 [cite:wiki_betar]. A signature on a petition and a membership are not the same thing, and the first reading rests on the more specific source. Even as a membership figure, it was the movement's own claim, and it would include a wide range of commitment. A smaller figure, for Betar alone, is given as over 70,000 by the mid-1930s in the account of the "two banks" claim cited above. The difference between 70,000 and 600,000 is the difference between a disciplined youth movement and a mass petition.

The final break came in 1935. That year the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" that barred independent political action by member parties [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. The Zionist Executive formally rejected Jabotinsky's platform [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization]. A Revisionist plebiscite chose secession, and the constituent assembly of the New Zionist Organization met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Jabotinsky as its president [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. He resigned from the World Zionist Organization altogether [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization] [cite:wiki_hatzohar]. Where the 1925 secession had left room for a working relationship with the mainstream, the 1935 break did not. The New Zionist Organization ran its own political and fundraising work, parallel to and in competition with the Jewish Agency and, later, the American Zionist Emergency Council [cite:wiki_new_zionist_organization] [cite:wiki_hatzohar]. The "713,000" was the movement's own description of its electorate; the sources do not say how those votes were counted.

The Revisionist case, in its own terms, was coherent and was argued openly. Its premise was that the Arab population would never consent to a Jewish majority, so that any plan built on consent would fail; better to say so, and to build the strength on which the project could proceed without that consent. Its territorial claim held that Britain had cut the Mandate in two in 1922 without right, and that a state confined to the western bank could not take in the millions of Jews who would need it. Its method, a militarized youth movement and open political demands such as the 1931 resolution for a state on both banks, was set squarely against the mainstream's gradualist strategy.

The critics' case is in the same record. The Zionist leadership's answer is on record in what it did: the General Council's discipline clause barred exactly the independent political action the Revisionists practiced, and the Executive rejected their platform. Within the movement itself, Grossman's followers broke away in 1933 over Jabotinsky's suspension of the executive. And the Iron Wall essay is, on its face, a statement that the project would be carried out against the will of the people already living in the country. Read from the side of the population it named, it was not only an analysis of their opposition but a program for overriding it by strength. Both readings start from Jabotinsky's own words.

Jabotinsky held his position to the end of the period and beyond. In 1937 he testified before the Peel Commission against any partition of Palestine, insisting on Jewish rights to the entire Mandate territory, Transjordan included. He died of a heart attack in 1940 while visiting Betar in the United States [cite:wiki_jabotinsky]. The line he founded continued as an institution. Herut was founded on 15 June 1948 by Menachem Begin, a former Irgun commander, as a challenge to Hatzohar, which was then succeeded by and merged into Herut after the state was established. Herut joined the Liberal Party in 1965 to form Gahal, which in 1973 became the founding core of Likud, the party that has led or co-led Israeli governments for most of the past five decades, including under Netanyahu [cite:wiki_herut] [cite:wiki_hatzohar] [cite:wiki_gahal] [cite:wiki_likud]. That is a documented chain of foundings and mergers. It is not a claim that Likud's platform today is Jabotinsky's; parties change over a century.

Some questions the record here does not answer. The sources do not give a verified membership figure for the Revisionist movement or for Betar in any year; the 600,000 and the 713,000 are a petition count and a claimed electorate, and the 70,000 for Betar comes from a single account. They do not set out the specific policy disputes behind the Executive's rejection of the platform in 1935 beyond the discipline clause. And they do not show how much money the New Zionist Organization raised in its parallel campaigns. What they do show is that by September 1935 organized Zionism had two rival centers, each with its own leader, program and electorate, thirteen years before the state.

sections.h: Jacob de Haan and the Orthodox Opposition, 1919–1924
sections.html:
On the evening of 30 June 1924, Jacob Israël de Haan left evening prayers at a synagogue on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem and was shot three times. He died soon after. No one was charged [cite:w_dehaan]. The killing is widely described by historians as the first political assassination inside the Jewish community of Palestine, and its victim was neither a British official nor an Arab leader. He was a Jew, a former Zionist sympathizer, and in the years before his death the most effective political voice, in English, of the Jewish community that rejected the Zionist movement's claim to speak for it [cite:w_dehaan].

A common account of these years holds that Jewish opposition to Zionism before 1948 was marginal, peaceful, and faded away on its own. De Haan's career does not fit that account. The opposition he represented was organized, it had a leadership, it took its case to the British authorities and to Arab rulers, and it was met, at least once, with a bullet.

A poet and lawyer in Jerusalem. De Haan was born in the Netherlands in 1881 and was a poet and a lawyer by training. He arrived in Palestine in 1919 as a newspaper correspondent, and he taught law in Jerusalem at the Mandate government's law classes [cite:w_dehaan]. He came with some sympathy for Zionism. He moved from that sympathy to the other side of the question entirely, into the Haredi camp, the strictly Orthodox community of the old Yishuv [cite:w_dehaan].

The "old Yishuv" was the name for the Orthodox Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Safed, Hebron and Tiberias, which had lived in the country for generations before political Zionism existed [cite:w_dehaan]. Its leadership, including Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, rejected a secular Jewish state on religious grounds, and objected to the Zionist Organization speaking in its name. That objection had an organizational form older than the Mandate. Agudat Israel (also spelled Agudath Israel) was founded in 1912 as a worldwide movement to strengthen Torah-observant Judaism, and specifically to separate it from the emerging secular Jewish nationalist movement, which its founders regarded as a danger to Torah-observant Jewish life [cite:w_dehaan] [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history] [cite:wiki_neturei_karta]. Its opposition to political Zionism on religious grounds was thus organized thirty-six years before the State of Israel was founded. It was a theological position, not a reaction to any later political dispute [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history].

This was the community de Haan came to represent, and he became its most effective political voice in English. He wrote for British newspapers and lobbied Mandate officials directly [cite:w_dehaan].

The argument. De Haan's case was narrow and precise. The Zionist Organization, he argued, was one political movement among Jews. It was not the representative of all the Jews in Palestine [cite:w_dehaan]. For the old Orthodox community, whose presence in Jerusalem long predated the Zionist movement, that distinction was the whole point: a secular national movement should not speak in the name of religious Jews who rejected its aims. De Haan pressed that distinction on British officials, and argued to them that the Zionist Organization did not speak for all Jews in the country [cite:w_dehaan].

The method of this opposition is worth stating plainly. It was a claim about representation, and de Haan carried it to two audiences: the Mandatory power, whose officials he lobbied, and Arab leaders, with whom he sought a separate understanding [cite:w_dehaan].

The approach to the Hashemites. His most provocative act was diplomatic. He sought a separate understanding between Orthodox Jews and Arab leaders, on the premise that Jews who did not seek a state need not be in conflict with the Arab majority [cite:w_dehaan]. In 1924 this led him to meetings with the Hashemite leadership in Transjordan [cite:w_dehaan]. He was then preparing to travel to London with an anti-Zionist Orthodox delegation, to put the community's case at the seat of the Mandatory government [cite:w_dehaan]. He was killed before he could go.

The sources in this book do not record what was said at the Transjordan meetings, what, if anything, was agreed, or what the London delegation intended to ask for. They establish the direction of his effort, not its content.

The killing and sixty years of silence. After the shooting on Jaffa Road, each side looked to the other. The Zionist leadership publicly condemned the killing. Orthodox leaders blamed Zionist circles [cite:w_dehaan]. No one was charged, and for sixty years the question of who had ordered the killing remained formally open [cite:w_dehaan].

The silence broke in 1985. Avraham Tehomi, by then elderly, said on Israeli television that he had shot de Haan, and that he had done so on the orders of the Haganah, the underground defense force of the Jewish community [cite:w_dehaan]. Tehomi was no peripheral figure. He was the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, and he then led a group that seceded from it and, together with Revisionist groups, formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi; he returned to the Haganah in 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi]. That later history is told in [scene:s07e2|the armed line].

The dispute over the order. Tehomi went further than naming the Haganah. He named Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later Israel's second president, as the man from whom the order had come [cite:w_dehaan]. Here the record thins, and the two parts of the confession have to be weighed separately.

The first part, that the shooting was a Haganah operation, carried out by the man who was speaking, is the documented core of the case. It is a confession by the gunman himself, and it is what allows historians to treat the killing as an act of the organized Jewish community's armed wing rather than a private crime [cite:w_dehaan].

The second part rests on Tehomi alone. Ben-Zvi had died in 1963, twenty-two years before the interview, and could not answer. No second witness or document in the sources places the order with him, and some historians dispute his involvement [cite:w_dehaan]. Tehomi's account of his own act and of the organization behind it is a confession; his account of who stood above him is an accusation against a man who could no longer reply, given six decades after the event, with nothing else in the sources to support it. The honest conclusion is the narrower one: the record establishes the gunman and the organization he said he served, and it does not establish a single, settled chain of command above him [cite:w_dehaan].

What the case shows. Three things are established. Organized Jewish opposition to Zionism existed inside Palestine in the early Mandate years, with a leadership, an international organization behind it and a public spokesman. It was argued openly, to the British and to Arab leaders. And the Zionist movement's own armed wing, by its gunman's admission, killed its most effective spokesman [cite:w_dehaan]. The familiar picture of a dissent that was marginal and peaceful and simply faded is incomplete on each count.

This opposition was also distinct from the other Jewish dissent of these years. The binationalists of Brit Shalom, founded in 1925, argued from inside Zionism about the form a national home should take; the old Yishuv rejected the national project itself on religious grounds. Their story is told in [scene:rd3_brit_shalom|Brit Shalom and the Hebrew University].

Orthodox opposition did not end with de Haan's death. Its later history lies outside this chapter, but its next turn is documented: in 1938 Neturei Karta split from Agudath Israel to preserve a more uncompromising anti-Zionist position, after Agudath Israel began making practical accommodations with Zionist institutions [cite:britannica_neturei_karta]. The split itself shows that Agudath Israel, which had organized the old Yishuv's refusal, had by then begun to accommodate the institutions it once opposed. The 1912 founding marks where the organized religious objection began, not a full history of how each of its branches moved afterward [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history].

What remains unsettled is considerable. The sources do not say who, if anyone, above Tehomi gave the order, if Ben-Zvi did not. They do not record why no one was charged in 1924, what the British authorities established about the crime, or what the Hashemite leadership said to de Haan. They do not show whether his London delegation would have changed anything. They establish a spokesman, an argument, a killing and a confession, and they leave the decision behind the shot where Tehomi left it, resting on his word alone.

sections.h: Immigration, 1923–1936: The Fourth and Fifth Aliyot
sections.html:
Between 1923 and 1936 the number of Jews entering Palestine each year rose and fell steeply. In 1925 more than 33,000 arrived; in 1928 barely 2,000. In 1935 more than 60,000 came, the highest figure of these years. The swings were not random. They followed pressures and decisions outside Palestine, in Poland and in Washington among them, and they passed through a British administration that counted the arrivals and set an allotment for those who came as workers. This section follows the two great waves of these years, the Fourth Aliyah of the mid-1920s and the Fifth Aliyah of the 1930s, and sets out what the official figures show, and where they disagree.

The Fourth Aliyah, 1924–1929. The Jewish Virtual Library, summarizing the standard account, puts the Fourth Aliyah at 82,000 Jews who came to Palestine between 1924 and 1929, of whom 23,000 left again [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. It attributes the wave to two pressures that operated together. One was in Poland: an economic crisis and anti-Jewish policies there pushed Jews to leave [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The other was in the United States. The Jewish Virtual Library points to stiff American immigration quotas, and the Center for Israel Education ties the rise in immigration to Palestine directly to the US Immigration Act of 1924, which limited annual immigration from each country to 2 percent of its residents in the 1890 census [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_cie_1924_act].

Most of the Fourth Aliyah's immigrants were middle class, with modest capital [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The town whose growth tracks the wave most visibly is Tel Aviv. It had about 15,000 inhabitants in 1922 and about 34,000 in 1925; by 1931 it had 45,564 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

The wave broke quickly. The Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, suffered an economic crisis in 1926–1928 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah]. The annual figures show its scale. Recorded Jewish immigration, which stood at 33,801 in 1925, fell to 13,081 in 1926, 2,713 in 1927 and 2,178 in 1928 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. Many of those who had arrived left: the 23,000 departures are part of the Fourth Aliyah's own total [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah].

The British inquiry that followed the violence of August 1929 drew a lesson from those years. The Shaw Commission, reporting in March 1930, criticized what it called "excessive" immigration in 1925–26, and quoted Sir John Campbell's view that the crisis of 1927–28 had come from immigrants arriving "in excess of the economic absorbing power of the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest]. The phrase mattered. It tied the permitted level of immigration to an economic test, the country's capacity to absorb newcomers, and that test ran through the British arguments over immigration that followed. The argument that followed Shaw, through Hope Simpson and the White Paper of 1930, is told in [scene:pf_s01|From inquiry to reversal].

The Fifth Aliyah. The low point did not last long. Recorded immigration was 5,249 in 1929, 4,944 in 1930 and 4,075 in 1931, and then it climbed: 9,553 in 1932, 30,327 in 1933, 42,359 in 1934 and 61,854 in 1935, before falling back to 29,727 in 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. The Jewish Virtual Library dates the Fifth Aliyah from 1929 to 1939. It states that nearly 250,000 Jews arrived in that wave by 1940, of whom 20,000 later left; that 174,000 settled in the four years 1933–1936 alone; and that the Yishuv reached 450,000 by 1940 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fifth_aliyah].

The steepest climb began in 1933. The emigration of Jews from Nazi Germany in these years, and the Transfer Agreement that let some of them bring capital, are told with their own numbers in [scene:hv_s01|the Haavara Agreement]. The sources used here do not break down the annual totals by country of origin, so they cannot say what share of the 1933–1936 arrivals came from Germany and what share from Poland and elsewhere.

Tel Aviv again shows the effect most plainly. A town of 45,564 in 1931 had about 120,000 people by 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv]. It received municipal status on 12 May 1934 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

How the gate worked. Not every immigrant entered on the same terms, and the 1935 peak shows how the categories fitted together. A State Department memorandum of 6 November 1936, written by Paul Alling for Assistant Secretary Moore, cites Palestine Government statistics for that year. Of the 61,854 Jews who entered in 1935, 14,653 came under the labour schedule and 13,076 were their dependants. Alling estimated that the remaining 44,000 entered in other categories, such as capital holders, professionals and skilled artisans [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. The figures as reported do not reconcile exactly: 61,854 less the workers and their dependants leaves about 34,000, not 44,000, and the memorandum as summarized does not explain the difference. What the breakdown does show clearly is that in the peak year fewer than one immigrant in four entered as a worker on the schedule; the rest came as dependants or, on Alling's estimate, in categories defined by means or occupation.

The labour schedule was the part of immigration that came in fixed allotments. Alling lists them for half-year periods, and his figures show how they moved. The allotment was 5,500 for April–September 1933 and rose to 8,000 for April–September 1935. For October 1935–March 1936 it was cut to 3,250 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531].

Two series, and a gap between them. Readers who look up the annual figures for these years will find more than one set. The memorandum by J. Rives Childs of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, dated 3 June 1939, gives recorded Jewish immigration year by year, compiled from the British returns [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. A second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for most years [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The two are set side by side below.

The pattern of the differences is itself informative. For 1928 to 1931 the two series agree exactly. For the mid-1920s the Porath figures are a few hundred to about a thousand higher each year. For 1932 to 1935 they are higher by roughly three to seven thousand a year, with the widest gap in 1933, 37,337 against 30,327. In 1936 the order reverses, and the Porath figure is slightly lower [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The sources do not explain the difference. It may reflect how arrivals who were not recorded at entry, or who registered later, were counted in one series and not the other, but that is a possibility, not a documented finding [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. This book uses the State Department figures as the recorded series and gives the Porath figures beside them where the difference matters.

A third figure does not fit cleanly with either. The Jewish Virtual Library's total of 82,000 for the Fourth Aliyah is higher than the sum of either annual series for 1924–1929, while its 174,000 settlers for 1933–1936 falls between the two series' totals for those years [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fourth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_fifth_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The wave totals and the annual returns may rest on different definitions; the sources do not say.

Immigration and natural increase. The same 1939 memorandum carries a finding that bears on one of the most argued questions of the Mandate. It cites a Consul General's report dated 10 January 1939, that the Jewish population had risen sixfold since 1920, almost entirely through immigration, while the Arab population had risen by about 57 percent, almost entirely through natural increase [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. Two populations grew in these years by two different mechanisms. The Jewish community grew because people came; the Arab population grew because births exceeded deaths.

The finding also explains why the level of Jewish immigration, and the Shaw Commission's test of the country's "absorbing power," carried so much weight: on the consul's account, immigration was the means by which the Jewish share of the population changed. The consul's report is one official observer's assessment, made in 1939. The question of Arab immigration into Palestine in the 1930s, its scale and its sources, has not been researched for this book, and the prose here makes no claim about it beyond what the consul wrote.

What the record leaves open. The documents establish the shape of these years clearly: a surge in 1925, a collapse in 1927–28, a slow recovery, and a steep climb from 1932 to the peak of 1935. They establish the main forces behind the first wave, Polish economic and political pressure and the narrowing of American immigration, and they establish that fewer than one in four immigrants in the peak year entered as a schedule worker. They do not settle the exact number who came in any given year, because the two published series differ and neither source explains why. They do not break down the 1930s arrivals by country, or say how many of the 1935 immigrants without a schedule place held capital and how many were professionals or artisans. And the 44,000 in Alling's memorandum does not square with the numbers it is drawn from. These are the limits within which any account of the Fourth and Fifth Aliyot, including this one, has to work.

sections.h: Bringing In the Non-Zionists: The Enlarged Jewish Agency, 1924–1929
sections.html:
It is often assumed that American Jewish leadership was Zionist from the start, and that the money which built the Jewish national home flowed from a settled consensus. In the 1920s that was not so. Much of the wealthiest American Jewish leadership was non-Zionist, and a non-Zionist relief body ran its own appeals in competition with the Zionist fund [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. Bringing those leaders and their money inside the movement's institutions took Chaim Weizmann the better part of five years. When it was done, in Zurich in August 1929, the Jewish Agency had become a body in which Zionists and non-Zionists sat in equal numbers, and the institution that would govern the Yishuv until 1948 rested on a funding base that reached well beyond committed Zionists.

Two appeals, one constituency. The problem first showed itself as a fight over fundraising. The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, a non-Zionist relief body chaired by the banker Felix Warburg, ran its own campaigns. The Zionist Organization of America saw them as a rival to the Keren Hayesod, the movement's permanent fund, and the two clashed. To protect the Keren Hayesod, the ZOA created a United Palestine Appeal under Rabbi Stephen Wise [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. Two appeals were now asking the same American Jewish public for money, one Zionist and one not.

The stakes were large, because the United States had already become the movement's main source of funds. From April 1921 to December 1929 the Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million worldwide, about $370 million in today's dollars. More than half of it, $11.0 million, came from the United States [cite:jta_kh_decade] [cite:bls_cpi]. Over the fund's first twelve years, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised [cite:jta_kh_12yr]. The money paid for the core of the movement's work in Palestine: before 1948 the fund's mandate covered immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works [cite:jvl_kh].

The country breakdown shows how lopsided the base was. After the United States came South Africa with $1.5 million, Germany with $0.98 million, Romania and Britain with $0.88 million each, Poland with $0.82 million and Canada with $0.74 million [cite:jta_kh_decade]. No other country gave even a seventh of the American total. And this was the Zionist fund alone; the non-Zionist Joint Distribution Committee under Warburg raised its money separately [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. The longer-run story of who paid for the pre-state enterprise, through 1948, is told in [scene:gf_s01|the Global Funding Ledger].

Weizmann and Marshall. Weizmann's answer was to stop competing with the non-Zionists and bring them in. From December 1924 to February 1925 he was in the United States, launching the annual Keren Hayesod campaign and negotiating an expanded Jewish Agency with Louis Marshall, president of the American Jewish Committee [cite:einstein_papers_vol15_doc625]. The offer was institutional: the non-Zionists were to be brought inside the Jewish Agency itself, as partners in its governance, rather than courted as donors to a rival appeal.

The negotiation took more than four years. It ended at Zurich in August 1929. There the Sixteenth Zionist Congress ratified the agreement, and the Council of the enlarged Jewish Agency held its first meeting, with Albert Einstein, Léon Blum and Herbert Samuel present [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf].

How the enlarged Agency was built. The structure agreed at Zurich divided power deliberately. The Council's membership was split equally between Zionists and non-Zionists. Louis Marshall became chairman of the Council and Lord Melchett its associate chairman. Felix Warburg, who had chaired the rival relief appeal, became chairman of the Administrative Committee, the body that ran the Agency's affairs. And the Keren Hayesod was recognized as the Agency's main financial instrument [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf]. The two money streams that had competed for the same donors were now tied to the same institution.

Weizmann's papers record what he believed he had won. Marshall and Warburg assured him that his "financial troubles are over" [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14] [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14_pdf]. Whether they were is another matter, and the sources here do not show how much non-Zionist money actually flowed through the enlarged Agency in the years that followed.

The partnership lost its chairman almost at once. Marshall died weeks after Zurich, in September 1929. One summary of these events places his death in the same month that the riots in Palestine began; the violence in Jerusalem, Hebron and Safed in fact began in August 1929, weeks before he died, and is told in [scene:s07a4|Hebron, 1929].

How the British inquiry read it. The enlargement was not only an internal Jewish matter.
