The Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the August violence, found the fundamental cause of the outbreak in Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future. Among the immediate causes it listed the incidents at the Wall from September 1928 to 16 August 1929, the Jewish demonstration of 15 August, an inflammatory press, and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The two descriptions of Zurich sit uneasily together. For Weizmann and his partners, the agreement ended a quarrel among Jews over relief and fundraising, and consolidated the movement's support. The Commission, by contrast, placed it beside the Wall incidents among the immediate causes of the violence. The record supports both: it was an act of Jewish communal organization, and a British inquiry judged it to have helped bring on the outbreak of 1929. The sources here do not record the Arab leadership's own statements about Zurich.

A government in waiting. The importance of 1929 lies in what the Agency became afterward. By that year the body that would run the pre-state Yishuv had brought wealthy American non-Zionists inside its governance, widening its funding base well beyond committed Zionists, nineteen years before 1948. In the sequence of institutions shown below, from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel, the Jewish Agency stands between the British Mandate and the American political effort of the 1940s, and Zurich is where it took the form it would hold.

The record leaves several things open. It does not say how much non-Zionist money the enlarged Agency actually received, or how Warburg's Administrative Committee used it. It does not show how far the non-Zionist half of the Council shaped the Agency's political decisions, as distinct from its finances. And the structure was tested at once: within weeks of Zurich, the Agency faced the crisis of August 1929 and lost the chairman around whom the partnership had been built. What the record does establish is the turn itself. American Jewish leadership was divided on Zionism in the 1920s, and the movement's central institution was built, deliberately, to include those who did not share its creed.

sections.h: 1925: The Hebrew University and Brit Shalom
sections.html:
On 1 April 1925 Arthur Balfour stood on Mount Scopus above Jerusalem and opened the Hebrew University. Chaim Weizmann presided, as chairman of the university's board [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]. In the same year, and prompted by a lecture given at that same opening, a small group in Jerusalem founded an association around a question the rest of the movement answered differently: if Jews and Arabs were both to live in Palestine, on what terms would they share its government? The association was Brit Shalom, and its answer was a binational country in which neither people ruled the other [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

The university on Mount Scopus. The university had been a long time in the making. Twelve foundation stones were laid on Mount Scopus on 24 July 1918, and Albert Einstein gave the first lecture there in 1923 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]. At the opening in 1925, Balfour performed the ceremony and Weizmann presided. Judah Magnes became the university's chancellor, and later its president. The first degrees were awarded in 1931 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ].

Balfour's presence was itself an event in Jerusalem. A report in the Detroit Jewish Chronicle of 10 April 1925 described "excitement" among the city's Arabs at a rumour that he would visit the Omar Mosque, and stated that no incidents occurred [cite:rs_rd3_djc_1925_04_10]. That is the extent of what the sources used here record about the Arab response to his visit. Accounts of wider protests have not been verified for this book and are left out.

The founding of Brit Shalom. Brit Shalom was founded in Jerusalem in 1925 on the initiative of Arthur Ruppin. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the immediate prompt was a lecture by Professor Joseph Horowitz at the university's opening [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. Ruppin chaired the association until 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. Its early members included Ruppin, Jacob Thon, Joseph Lurie, Yitzhak Epstein, Haim Margolis-Kalvaryski and Rabbi Binyamin [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

Its program was simple to state and radical in its implications. Brit Shalom sought a binational arrangement in which Jews and Arabs would share the administration of the country equally, regardless of their numbers [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The last three words were the heart of it. Brit Shalom proposed to separate political power from population: parity of government whichever people was the larger. For Jews, then a minority in the country, it meant giving up any claim to rule by majority should they become one. For Arabs, then the majority, it meant sharing power equally with a minority.

Its members were, in the precise sense, Zionists. They did not reject Jewish settlement or a Jewish national home in Palestine. What they rejected was the model of Jewish sovereignty, and later of partition. In that they were a different current from the Orthodox opposition of the old Yishuv, which rejected the national project itself on religious grounds and whose spokesman was killed in Jerusalem the year before Brit Shalom was founded; that story is told in [scene:dh_s01|Jacob de Haan and the Orthodox opposition] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Who belonged, and the dispute over Magnes. Brit Shalom never had more than 200 members [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. It functioned more as a small study circle of academics and intellectuals than as a political party, and it never grew into a mass constituency among either Jews or Arabs [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom]. Its character changed over time. According to the Encyclopaedia Judaica, after 1929 Central European intellectuals influenced by Martin Buber predominated, among them Hugo Bergmann, Hans Kohn, Gershom Scholem, Ernst Simon and Robert Weltsch [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. It did have prominent public support. Albert Einstein, who had given the university's first lecture, publicly backed it, a fact rarely mentioned alongside his name [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom].

The sources disagree about who founded it, and the disagreement concerns its best-known associate. One account used elsewhere in this library calls Martin Buber and Judah Magnes "both founders of Brit Shalom (1925)," and names Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold among the colleagues who founded it with them [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. The Encyclopaedia Judaica gives a different picture. It credits the initiative to Ruppin and lists different early members; it places Scholem among those who predominated after 1929; it describes the later members as influenced by Buber rather than naming him as a founder; and it states that Magnes, though he advocated binationalism in this period and his name was often linked to the association, was never a member of it [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom].

The two accounts can be partly reconciled. Magnes advocated binationalism in these years, which may be why his name was so often linked to the association; that is an inference, not a documented finding. Buber's influence on its later members is common to both accounts. But on the narrow question of membership the sources conflict, and this book does not resolve it. The Encyclopaedia Judaica is the more specific of the two, naming founders and dates; the other account reflects how the association has commonly been remembered.

Attack and decline. Brit Shalom drew open hostility from the rest of the movement. Most Zionist parties attacked it [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The opposition came from both of the dominant currents, Labor and the Revisionists, and some of its opponents explicitly called its members traitors [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom].

The decisive blow came from events. The violence of August 1929, in Hebron above all, undermined the premise on which the association was founded: that Arab political leadership would accept binational equality [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. The killings in Hebron and Safed, told in [scene:s07a4|the Western Wall and August 1929], made the argument for parity far harder to make among Jews, and the sources here record no Arab political body that took up the offer. Ruppin left the chair in 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The association carried on for a few more years, with the Buber circle now predominant. Its monthly, She'ifoteinu, appeared from 1930 to 1933. By 1933 Brit Shalom had virtually ceased to exist [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom], about eight years after its founding [cite:wiki_brit_shalom].

The arguments, for and against. The sources record the hostility to Brit Shalom more fully than the reasoning behind it. Its own case is documented in its program: parity in government, fixed regardless of numbers, so that neither people would rule the other [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_brit_shalom]. The case against it, as historians reconstruct it from events, is that it depended on an Arab political partner willing to accept binational equality, and that the violence of 1929 showed no such partner in view [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism]. Its opponents inside the movement went further and treated the proposal as betrayal [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom]. The record does not decide whether the binational idea could have worked. It shows that it was never tested, because the association never won a constituency large enough to test it, among Jews or among Arabs.

The binational idea outlived the association. Buber and Magnes went on to found Ihud in 1942, Hannah Arendt warned against an exclusively Jewish sovereign state in 1944, and Buber and Magnes testified against partition before the United Nations commission in 1947. [cite:wiki_ihud] [cite:researchgate_arendt_zionism_reconsidered] [cite:britainpalestine_buber_magnes] That later history lies outside this chapter and is told in [scene:s00b3|Opposition to Zionism across every lineage].

Several questions remain open. The sources do not settle who founded Brit Shalom or whether Magnes ever joined it. They do not record any formal Arab response to its proposals, or name an Arab group with which it negotiated. They give no membership figures beyond the ceiling of 200, and they do not say what Joseph Horowitz argued in the lecture that prompted its founding. What is established is that in 1925, alongside the institution meant to crown the national home, a group of Zionists at the center of the movement proposed sharing the country on equal terms, were attacked for it by most of their own movement, and had all but disappeared within eight years.

sections.h: Money, Currency and the Mandate Economy, 1922–1936
sections.html:
New states, it is often said, need years to build a financial system: a currency, a central bank, the machinery of public credit. When Israel declared independence in 1948 it did not start from nothing. It inherited a currency managed by the Mandate, and a banking network that the Zionist movement had built and run for half a century before the state existed. The pieces that mattered were in place by the 1920s and 1930s, the years of this chapter. This section follows them: the Palestine pound and the board in London that issued it, the movement's own banks, the growth of the Mandate's revenue and spending, the case the Jewish Agency made about the economy it had helped to create, and the oil pipeline that reached Haifa in 1934.

A currency managed from London. In 1926 the British Colonial Secretary appointed a Palestine Currency Board, and from 1 November 1927 the board issued the Palestine pound [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_pcb_notes]. The pound was fixed at par with sterling and divided into 1,000 mils [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. The arrangement is worth stating plainly, because it explains who could act. The board was appointed by the Colonial Secretary, and the currency it issued was tied one for one to the British pound. It was a currency managed from London. No body in Palestine, Jewish or Arab, issued the country's money or set its value. The Palestine Currency Board's notes stayed in circulation until 18 August 1948 [cite:wiki_palestine_pound] [cite:israelmint_pcb_notes].

The movement's own banks. Alongside the Mandate's currency ran a separate financial structure, owned by the Zionist movement. The Jewish Colonial Trust was chartered in London in 1899. Its operating subsidiary, the Anglo-Palestine Bank, was founded in 1902, was London-based, and was owned through the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_israeli_pound] [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. Together they carried the movement's finance for half a century. Their founding belongs to an earlier volume of this library; what matters here is that by the 1920s the Yishuv, the Jewish community in Palestine, had a bank of its own that operated in the Mandate's currency but answered to the movement's institutions.

The structure had a clear shape. The money that built the national home came from abroad, as donations to the movement's funds and as the capital that immigrants brought with them. It moved through institutions chartered in London and denominated in a currency pegged to sterling. It was invested in building, citrus and industry. The figures for that investment come mainly from the Jewish Agency itself, and they have to be read as what they are.

The Agency's case, 1937. In 1937 David Horowitz of the Jewish Agency's Economics Department prepared Economic and Social Transformation of Palestine for the Agency's case before the Peel Commission [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. It is an advocacy document, written to persuade a British commission, and its figures are the Agency's own. They are reported here as Horowitz gave them.

According to Horowitz, "LP 80,000,000 have been invested by Jews in economic enterprise" over sixteen years. Annual Jewish investment in building, he wrote, rose from LP 900,000 in 1924 to LP 7,000,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. He gave citrus exports rising from £200,000 in 1921 to £2,700,000 in 1934, and the area under citrus growing from 30,000 dunams in 1922 to 260,000 in 1935. Industrial output, in his figures, rose from under LP 1,000,000 in 1921 to over LP 8,000,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937].

He gave the population too. In his account there were 84,000 Jews in 1922, 13 percent of the population, and 375,000 in 1935, 28 percent; the non-Jewish population was 565,000 in 1922 and 975,000 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. His Jewish figure for 1922 is close to the census count of 83,794. His share is not. The 1922 census counted 757,182 people in all and put Jews at about 11 percent [cite:jvl_census_1931]. Horowitz's 13 percent rests on a smaller non-Jewish base of 565,000, and the source does not explain how that base was drawn. The country as the census counted it is described in [scene:cen_s01|the opening section of this chapter].

The Mandate's own accounts. The Mandate government grew along with the economy. Horowitz gave government revenue as LP 2,371,000 in 1922–23 and LP 5,452,000 in 1934–35, and expenditure rising over the same years from LP 1,900,000 to LP 3,200,000 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. On his figures the administration took in more than it spent in both years, and its revenue more than doubled while its spending grew by about two-thirds. The cost of holding the country militarily was a separate account. The British garrison cost £1.5 million in 1923–24 [cite:league_report_garrison], more than three-quarters of the civil spending of 1922–23, and it was paid by Britain. The full ledger of what the Mandate cost Britain, to its end in 1948, is told in [scene:gf_s02|Charity for an Army].

The rows of that table for these years tell the story in brief: Mandate civil spending of £P1.9 million in 1922–23 and £P3.2 million in 1934–35 [cite:horowitz_1937]; the garrison's £1.5 million in 1923–24 [cite:league_report_garrison]; and, set beside them, the Agency's estimate of £P80 million of Jewish capital invested between 1921 and 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. The figures come from different payers and different kinds of account, and they are shown side by side for scale, not added together.

Who gained: the dispute. Horowitz went further than investment totals. He argued that Arabs gained directly from Jewish economic activity: from Jewish contributions to government revenue, from land prices that had risen 400 to 500 percent, and from falling death rates in the districts of Jewish immigration. He set daily wages of 10–15 piastres in Palestine against 2–3 in Iraq and Egypt [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. This is the strongest form of the Zionist economic case, and it was made in the movement's own words, to a British commission, for a political purpose.

A British official had reached a different conclusion seven years earlier. Sir John Hope Simpson, reporting in October 1930, found that Jewish National Fund leases required Jewish labour only, that a landless Arab class was forming, and that families displaced by land sales had not been resettled [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal_l]. On his account the benefits of Jewish investment did not flow freely across the population; the institutions that directed it were built to employ Jews, and some of the cost fell on Arab cultivators who lost their land. His figures, and the Agency's rebuttal of them, are set out in [scene:rd3_land|the section on land and labour].

The two positions are not strictly contradictory, since one speaks of average wages, prices and revenue and the other of the people displaced and excluded. But the sources used here do not measure how gains and losses were distributed among Arabs, and neither Horowitz's figures nor Hope Simpson's settle that question. Each was produced for a purpose, the first to argue for the national home before Peel, the second to advise the British government on land and immigration. The record supports neither the claim that Jewish investment benefited everyone nor the claim that it benefited no one.

Oil to Haifa. One more flow of these years ran through Palestine without passing through either the Mandate's budget or the movement's banks. The Iraq Petroleum Company built a pipeline from Iraq to the Mediterranean between 1932 and 1934. At Haditha it split into two branches, one to Tripoli and one to Haifa [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. The transit agreements with Palestine, Transjordan, Lebanon and Syria had been signed between 5 January and 25 March 1931 [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. The first oil reached Haifa on 16 October 1934, and official opening ceremonies were held in January 1935. The line could carry four million tons a year [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline]. Palestine had become a transit country for the oil of a neighbouring state, with a terminal on its coast. The arrangement lasted until 1948, when Iraq stopped sending oil to Haifa [cite:rs_rd3_gulbenkian_pipeline].

Where it led. The banking structure built in these years carried the state through its birth. Before independence the Anglo-Palestine Bank's chairman, Eliezer Hoofien, persuaded the American Bank Note Company in New York to print new notes. Because neither the state's name nor its currency had been decided, they were denominated in "Palestine pounds." According to Israel's state mint, the notes were not marked "legal tender," and the printer's name was left off, to get around the need for the US Secretary of State's approval to print foreign currency [cite:israelmint_aplb_series] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes]. They reached the country secretly in July 1948 and became legal tender by law on 17 August 1948, the day before the Mandate's notes went out of circulation [cite:israelmint_aplb_series] [cite:jhom_anglo_palestine_notes] [cite:wiki_palestine_pound]. On 1 May 1951 the bank's assets passed to Bank Leumi le-Israel, and the currency became the Israeli pound [cite:wiki_israeli_pound].

The common assumption, then, has it backwards for this case. The state did not have to build a financial system after 1948. One already existed: a London-chartered bank that had operated for decades, inside a currency system the British had set up in 1926–27. What 1948 required was a change of name and of sovereign, and the first notes for that change were printed in New York.

What remains open. The record here is strong on structure and weaker on totals. The investment, output and export figures for 1922–1936 come from a single advocacy document, and no independent series in the sources checks them. The sources do not give the Anglo-Palestine Bank's own balance sheets, its lending, or how much of the Agency's £P80 million passed through it. They do not say how the Currency Board's reserves were held, or what the peg to sterling cost or gained the country. And they do not measure how the gains of the Mandate economy were divided between Jews and Arabs, or among Arabs themselves, which is the question on which Horowitz and Hope Simpson most sharply disagree.

sections.h: The Wall and August 1929: Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed
sections.html:
A common account of Mandate Palestine dates organized violence between Arabs and Jews to the Arab Revolt that began in 1936. The record puts a turning point seven years earlier. In the last week of August 1929, violence that began in Jerusalem over the Western Wall, which Muslims call al-Buraq, spread to Hebron and Safed. It left a precise death toll, ended one of the oldest continuous Jewish communities in the country for nearly four decades, produced Britain's first major inquiry of the Mandate years, and, in the judgment of historians, made the political reputation of the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929] [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini].

The dispute had a specific starting point. In September 1928, on Yom Kippur, Jewish worshippers set up a portable screen at the Wall to separate men from women, and its removal opened the conflict [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. The ground mattered because of who owned it. The Wall belonged to Muslim religious authorities, and Jews prayed there. Through 1928 the tension built on both sides. A documented Arab campaign asserted Muslim rights over the site, and documented Jewish activity pressed for prayer arrangements there; each community treated the dispute as central to its larger claim [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. Hajj Amin al-Husseini is documented as leading the 1928 campaign asserting Muslim rights over the Wall [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]. The record shows real escalation from both directions in the year before the riots. It does not settle which particular acts bear more of the blame.

The final days before the outbreak are dated precisely. On 15 August 1929 a few hundred Jewish youths, Betar members among them, marched to the Wall and raised a flag. On 16 August a Muslim demonstration went to the Wall beat Jews who were there and burned prayer notes [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. In the days that followed, according to the historians cited here, rumor and organized propaganda inflamed the city, and the Mufti's activists distributed inflammatory material [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929] [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini].

The outbreak came on 23 August in Jerusalem. The Shaw Commission, which investigated it the following year, found that it began there as an attack by Arabs on Jews, that it "was not premeditated", and that it was not a revolt against British authority [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The country had almost nothing to stop it with. Only about 150 British police and 1,500 local police served the whole of Palestine [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The British command at the time is part of the story of the High Commissioners in [scene:s07a2|the High Commissioners].

The worst of the killing was in Hebron. There, on 24 August 1929, it began at about 9 a.m. Eight American students of the Slobodka Yeshiva were among the dead [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. Sixty-seven Jews were killed in the city [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. The sources differ on how the count fell across the two days. Human Rights Watch gives 67 Jews killed and dates the massacre to 23 August; the EBSCO reference account records one yeshiva student killed on 23 August and 64 killed at the Heichal residence on 24 August [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. Those two EBSCO figures add to 65, not 67, and the sources used here do not reconcile the difference.

Hebron also produced the best-documented account of rescue in the whole week. According to Human Rights Watch, the Zionist Archives list 435 Hebron Jews who found refuge in 28 Arab homes. Norman Bentwich wrote that many Jews were saved by their Arab neighbours [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The figure of 435 rests on that one archival list as reported by Human Rights Watch; it is not, in the sources here, independently counted. It belongs in the record beside the death toll, because both happened in the same streets on the same morning.

After the killing the British authorities evacuated Hebron's surviving Jews. A community present in the city for centuries was removed within days, and organized Jewish life there did not resume until 1968, thirty-nine years later [cite:wiki_hebron_massacre_1929]. Many episodes of violence in these years were followed by some return. This one was not: the change was immediate, total and lasting. The circumstances of the 1968 return, and what came after it, belong to a much later part of this book.

The violence reached Safed on 29 August 1929. Between 18 and 20 Jews were killed there and about 80 wounded, and some 200 Jewish homes were burned [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jewishcurrents_safed].

By the end of the week the dead numbered 133 Jews and 116 Arabs, according to the EBSCO reference account and the Jewish Virtual Library. Most of the Arab deaths were caused by British police and military fire during the suppression [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom]. The Jewish toll is itself disputed. The Jerusalem Story lexicon of the Institute for Palestine Studies gives 113 Jews and 116 Arabs, and adds that the Mandate probably under-reported Palestinian casualties [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. The two accounts agree on the Arab figure and differ by twenty on the Jewish one; neither source, as used here, explains the gap.

The reckoning took several forms, and Britain's own report to the League of Nations for 1929 records the first of them. Collective punishments were imposed on towns and villages that took part in attacks on Jews at Hebron, Safad, Motza, Artuf and Beer Tuvia, with fines totalling £P17,840. The courts moved quickly. By the end of December 1929, 791 Arabs and 66 Jews had been tried summarily; 17 Arabs and 1 Jew had received capital sentences, and 7 death sentences had been confirmed on appeal [cite:rs_rd3_lon_report_1929]. These were measures of the Mandate administration, and Britain reported them to the League as the mandatory power answerable to it.

On 17 June 1930 three Arab men were hanged in Acre for their part in the riots. Twenty-five other death sentences, two of them on Jews, were commuted. This account rests on a single general reference, and the identities of the three men are not established in the research for this book, so they are not named here. Palestinians remember the day as "Red Tuesday" [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_1930].

The Shaw Commission reported in March 1930. On the question that has divided accounts ever since, the Mufti's role, it was precise. It found no evidence that Hajj Amin al-Husseini had incited the outbreak, but held that he "must accept a share in the responsibility". It found premeditation not proved against the Arab Executive [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. On causes, Shaw distinguished two levels. The fundamental cause was Arab hostility rooted in disappointed political aspirations and fear for their economic future. The immediate causes included the incidents at the Wall from September 1928 to 16 August 1929, the Jewish demonstration of 15 August, an inflammatory press, and the enlargement of the Jewish Agency in 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d], whose making is told in [scene:us_s03|the enlarged Jewish Agency]. What London did with Shaw's findings, and with the land inquiry that followed, is the subject of [scene:pf_s01|the Passfield White Paper and its reversal].

The ownership question at the Wall itself went to an international body. A commission of three members, none of them British, sat in Jerusalem from 19 June to 19 July 1930 under the approval of the League Council: Eliel Löfgren of Sweden, Charles Barde of Geneva and J. van Kempen of the Netherlands. It reported in December 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_wall_1930]. It found that the Wall and the pavement before it are Muslim property, and that the Wall is "sacred to both Parties". Jews were to have free access for their devotions, but could bring only the appurtenances permitted under the Turkish regime, and screens separating men and women were barred [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_wall_1930]. The commission thus ruled on the very object, a screen, that had opened the dispute in September 1928. It confirmed Muslim ownership and Jewish access together, and held both sides to the arrangements of the Ottoman years.

The three main readings of August 1929 rest on different evidence, and each has a strong form. In the Palestinian account, preserved in the Jerusalem Story lexicon under the name "al-Buraq Uprising", the trigger was a provocation: Betar-led demonstrators raised the Zionist flag at a site under Muslim authority, and the response grew from a real fear that the holy places would be taken over [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq]. The march of 15 August is documented in every account, and Shaw named it among the immediate causes, so this reading rests on the inquiry's own findings as well as on Palestinian memory. In the Jewish account, the cause was a Muslim campaign over the Wall led by the Mufti, and incitement that ended in massacres of unarmed communities [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_prayer_pogrom] [cite:rs_rd3_jewishcurrents_safed]. Its evidence is equally concrete: the Mufti's documented 1928 campaign, the inflammatory material his activists distributed, and the fact that the dead of Hebron, eight American yeshiva students among them, were killed in another town, a day after the outbreak in Jerusalem. The British inquiry stood between the two. It found no premeditation, a share of responsibility on the Mufti, and the 15 August demonstration among the immediate causes, while naming an Arab attack on Jews as the form the outbreak took [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d].

Behind the question of the Mufti's role in the riots lies a larger one about what the riots did for him. Historians cited in this research, notably Oren Kessler in a 2024 account, describe 1929 as the event that made al-Husseini's political reputation among Palestinians, the platform on which his leadership of the 1936–39 revolt was later built [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]. That reading moves the start of his rise seven years earlier than the date most popular accounts use. It does not make 1936 less important to his career. It says what came before it and made it possible.

Several things the record does not settle. The first is the Mufti's direct part. That his activists distributed inflammatory material before the riots is documented. Whether he organized the violence itself, or capitalized on tensions that moved beyond his control, is a question historians still debate; Shaw's "share in the responsibility" was a judgment, not a finding of organization [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. The second is the count. The Jewish dead of the week are given as 133 or 113, the Hebron dead as 67 across one day or two, and the Arab dead, most of them killed by the forces of order, may have been under-recorded [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_buraq] [cite:rs_rd3_hrw_hebron] [cite:rs_rd3_ebsco_wwriots]. The third is the rescue: the 435 sheltered in Hebron rest on one archival list as reported by one organization. What is not in doubt is the sequence, from a screen at the Wall in September 1928 to a commission's ruling on screens in December 1930, and the cost paid in between, chiefly by people who had taken no part in the quarrel over the Wall.

sections.h: Palestinian Politics, 1928–1935: From Congress to Parties
sections.html:
A familiar claim holds that the Palestinians had no leaders, no national organization and no political demands before 1948. By 1928 they had already held seven national congresses, and their central demand to Britain was an elected government. From 1919, Muslims and Christians organized together through Muslim–Christian Associations; the congresses chose an Arab Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini, called for "a national government responsible to a representative assembly", and rejected the Balfour Declaration and mass Jewish immigration [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress] [cite:jerusalemstory_arab_executive]. That earlier history, from the first congress of 1919 to the delegations of 1921–22, is told in [scene:pp_s01|the Palestinian national movement]. This section takes up the story at the last of those congresses and follows it to the party system that stood on the eve of 1936. It is a story of choices made by Palestinians, among themselves and against one another, under a mandatory power that never recognized their Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim].

The Seventh Palestinian Arab Congress met in June 1928. Its importance lay in who attended. Raghib al-Nashashibi's opposition bloc took part, and Nashashibi himself joined the Arab Executive that emerged from it [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. Rivalry between the factions aligned with the Husseini family and those aligned with the Nashashibis had divided Palestinian politics since the British dismissed Musa Kazim al-Husseini as mayor of Jerusalem in 1920 and appointed Raghib al-Nashashibi in his place [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:wiki_musa_kazim]. The 1928 congress briefly brought the two camps into one front [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. Nashashibi held the mayoralty throughout: re-elected in 1927, he served until 1934, when Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi was elected [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi].

Two months after the violence of August 1929, Palestinian organization widened. On 26 October 1929 the first Palestine Arab Women's Congress met in Jerusalem, with about 300 delegates. Salma al-Husseini led it; Wahida al-Khalidi and Amina al-Husseini organized it. The congress called for repeal of the Balfour Declaration and an end to Jewish immigration, and it elected a fourteen-member executive [cite:rs_rd3_jerusalemstory_womens]. Its demands matched those of the national congresses. What was new was that women had built their own national body to press them.

The Executive's next move was diplomatic. In 1930, while London weighed the findings of its inquiries into 1929, an Arab Executive delegation went to London. Nashashibi travelled with it in March 1930, and Jamal al-Husseini sat on the delegation that negotiated there in April and May [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi] [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]. The sources used here do not record what the delegation obtained. The policy London published that autumn, and its withdrawal in February 1931, are told in the section on the Passfield White Paper.

In December 1931 the rivalry took international form. The General Islamic Congress opened in Jerusalem on 7 December 1931 with 130 delegates from 22 countries, according to an account in Middle East Eye, and Hajj Amin al-Husseini, the Mufti, was among its main organizers. It resolved to defend the holy places, to boycott Zionist goods, to found an Islamic university in Jerusalem and to form a company to buy Palestinian land [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931]. The same account records Britain's response: High Commissioner Wauchope questioned the Mufti about the delegates' political speeches; Britain deported Abd al-Rahman Azzam and refused entry to the former caliph Abdulmecid II; and the university project stalled for lack of funds in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931]. The Mufti's congress did not speak for all Palestinians. In the same month Nashashibi held a rival conference in Jerusalem to counter it [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi].

Land was a recurring concern. In 1932 the Executive launched a "Piaster Project", a fund to keep land in Arab hands [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. Like the Islamic Congress's land company, it answered the purchases described in [scene:rd3_land|land and labour, 1922–1933].

The sharpest challenge to the Executive came from inside the national movement. In August 1932 eleven founders, among them Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim, Awni Abd al-Hadi and Muhammad Izzat Darwaza, officially announced the Istiqlal (Independence) Party. It called for full Arab independence and Arab unity, and named British imperialism as the main enemy [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. That was a change of target. The congresses had petitioned Britain; Istiqlal treated Britain itself as the adversary, and it attacked the established leadership for inaction in 1932–33 [cite:fhfpal_musa_kazim]. Its reach was limited. According to a reference account drawing on Porath, Khalidi, Kedourie and others, the party never built a large membership; its influence peaked among young educated Palestinians in early 1933 and then fell, partly through Husseini hostility and partly for lack of funds [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. Its founders remained active: until June 1933 Awni Abd al-Hadi was representing the tenants of Wadi al-Hawarith in court, and Istiqlal joined the protests when the eviction order came [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith].

Open confrontation with the government came in October 1933, called not by Istiqlal but by the Arab Executive. Following its call for protest demonstrations, disturbances broke out in Jerusalem on 13 October, in Jaffa, Haifa and Nablus on 27–28 October, and in Jerusalem again on 28–29 October. The Murison Commission, which investigated them, found that they were "aimed against the Government and not against the Jews" [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. Its count was exact. One policeman and 26 members of the public were killed; 56 police and 187 members of the public were injured. All the public deaths were by gunfire, 15 of them at Jaffa, where police fired 102 rifle and 43 revolver rounds [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. Musa Kazim al-Husseini, the Executive's president, was injured by British forces at the Jaffa protest [cite:wiki_musa_kazim] [cite:fhfpal_musa_kazim].

The commission reported on 4 January 1934 and found that the police had acted with restraint [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. The two readings of October 1933 rest on the same report. In Murison's own judgment, the police acted "with restraint and forbearance" and no officer departed from regulations. The protesters' case draws on its other findings: the demonstrations were political protest against government policy, called openly by the national leadership, and every one of the 26 civilian dead was killed by police gunfire, while one policeman died [cite:rs_rd3_murison_palquest]. The commission found that the force used was lawful and measured. Its figures show who bore the cost of that force. A reader can hold both findings at once; the report does not resolve them into one verdict, and neither does this book.

Musa Kazim al-Husseini died in March 1934, and the Arab Executive dissolved that year [cite:wiki_musa_kazim] [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. Over fifteen years the congresses and their Executive had sent petitions and delegations asking for an elected government; Britain recognized the Zionist Organization's Jewish Agency but never recognized the Palestinians' own Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. Its end left the field to parties built around the old rivalries.

Nashashibi moved first. Having lost the mayoralty of Jerusalem to Hussein Fakhri al-Khalidi in 1934, he founded the National Defense Party in early December 1934. Its program rejected the Balfour Declaration, Jewish immigration and land sales, and called for parliamentary government; Nashashibi was close to Emir Abdullah [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. The Husseini camp answered within four months. The Palestine Arab Party was officially established on 27 March 1935, and Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti, was unanimously chosen as its leader [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]. By the end of 1935, five Arab parties stood where one Executive had been. Late that year they formed a united front, which the American consul general in Jerusalem, Leland Morris, described in April 1936 as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. How that front met the High Commissioner's offer of a legislative council, and how it held, is the subject of [scene:rd3_council_1935|the legislative council of 1935–36].

The structure that emerged had two poles and a third force. The Husseini pole ran through the Mufti, who held religious office and had organized the Islamic Congress, and through the Palestine Arab Party under Jamal al-Husseini, who was close to him. The Nashashibi pole ran through the National Defense Party, which held to the same rejection of the Balfour Declaration but looked toward parliamentary government and stood close to Emir Abdullah. Istiqlal, small and short of money, named British imperialism as the main enemy. The united front of late 1935 joined them without dissolving them.

Who could act in this structure, and through what, is part of the story. The Palestinian leaders had no recognized channel to government. They had congresses, delegations, the press, demonstrations, and from 1934 parties; the mandatory power had police, deportation and the power to refuse entry. The Islamic Congress shows both sides of that balance. It could gather 130 delegates and pass resolutions on land, boycott and a university; the High Commissioner could question its organizer and Britain could expel a delegate, and the university project stalled in 1935 for lack of funds [cite:rs_rd3_mee_congress_1931].

Several questions the record does not settle. The sources do not say what the 1930 London delegation won or lost in its negotiations. The figures for the Islamic Congress and for Istiqlal's decline come from secondary accounts and are attributed as such. The sources do not name the two smaller parties of the 1935 front, or show how far the front reconciled the Husseini and Nashashibi camps rather than suspending their rivalry. And the Murison report leaves open the question at the center of October 1933: whether a police force that fired 145 rounds at Jaffa and killed 15 people there acted with restraint, as the commission found, or whether the toll itself is the better measure. What the record does show is a political movement with named leaders, recorded demands and organized institutions, making its own choices, and divided against itself, through the years before 1936.

sections.h: How Weimar Fell, 1929–1933
sections.html:
The German emigration that reached Palestine from 1933, and the Transfer Agreement that moved part of its capital there, began with the collapse of a democracy in Berlin. That collapse is often told as the work of an unstoppable wave of popular fanaticism. The documented record supports a narrower and more specific account: an economic catastrophe, a real but already declining surge of support for the Nazi Party, a decision taken by a small number of conservative politicians who believed they could control Hitler, and then a fire, an emergency decree, and a legislature that voted away its own authority. Each step can be dated, and at several of them people with power chose.

The first step was financial. The Weimar Republic's recovery in the mid-1920s had been built in large part on a steady flow of American loans. The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 led to the recall of those loans and plunged Germany back into economic catastrophe and mass unemployment [cite:ushmm_nazi_rise_to_power] [cite:history_weimar_republic]. The money ran in one direction and then reversed: American lenders supplied the capital that carried the stabilization, and when they withdrew it, the cost came due in Germany as mass unemployment, borne by a republic that had depended on that capital. The timing of Nazi support followed the money. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum's Holocaust Encyclopedia, genuine popular support for Hitler and his party began to accumulate from late 1929 onward, not before, while the economy still functioned [cite:ushmm_nazi_rise_to_power].

That connection has limits, and the record marks them. Economic hardship does not by itself explain Nazi support. Millions of Germans lived through the same conditions and did not become Nazis, and the more immediate causes of what followed were political decisions, not economic forces acting alone.

The second step is the one most often left out. The Nazi Party's electoral high point came in July 1932. By November 1932, three months before Hitler became Chancellor, its vote share had fallen to roughly 33 percent [cite:historycollection_weimar_collapse]. Hitler did not come to power at the crest of a rising wave. He came to power after the wave had begun to fall. That decline is the strongest evidence for the view that the Republic might have survived this particular crisis given more time. It is evidence, not proof. Historians treat survival as a real possibility; no one can show it would have happened.

The third step was a decision. Franz von Papen, an aristocrat and former chancellor, brokered the arrangement that made Hitler Chancellor. According to the accounts cited here, Papen assured his associates that he had Hitler's measure and could control him from within the cabinet, using him, in the phrase historians use, as a "battering ram" against the political left [cite:historycollection_weimar_collapse] [cite:britannica_third_reich]. Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 [cite:history_weimar_republic]. This was not a popular revolution. A small circle of men who held real institutional power chose to hand him the office, on the calculation that they would remain in control. The record shows a catastrophic misjudgment about whether he could be controlled. It does not show that Papen or his circle intended, or foresaw, what came after.

The fourth step supplied the emergency. In February 1933 the Reichstag building burned, and the regime used the fire to push through the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil liberties and made possible the mass arrest of political opponents [cite:history_weimar_republic]. Who set the fire remains a question historians dispute. Its political use does not depend on the answer: whatever its origin, the fire provided the pretext for the decree, and the decree cleared the way for the next step weeks later.

The fifth step ended the Republic in law. In March 1933 Hitler introduced the Enabling Act, which allowed him to pass laws without the approval of Parliament or the President. To secure its passage he forcibly prevented the Communist members of Parliament from voting [cite:history_weimar_republic] [cite:britannica_third_reich]. With its enactment the Weimar Republic's twelve-year democratic experiment ended, not by a street coup but by a legislature voting away its own constitutional authority [cite:history_weimar_republic]. The mechanism is precise. The instrument was a statute passed through the legislature's own procedure; the members who could have opposed it were, in the Communists' case, physically kept from the vote, and the remaining members voted under the climate of intimidation that followed the February decree. The record does not show that every member who voted for the act did so freely.

Two readings of these years meet in the evidence. One emphasizes the depth of the economic collapse and the real popular support the Nazi Party won from late 1929; on that reading the Republic was gravely weakened from below, and the support was genuine. The other emphasizes the decline of November 1932 and the deal that followed; on that reading the decisive act was taken from above, by men who were not swept along by a mass movement but believed they could use one. The record supports both parts, in sequence. Popular support was real and was falling; the appointment was an elite choice; the dismantling of the constitution was carried out through law, under coercion. What it does not support is the familiar picture of a democracy overrun by a fanaticism no one could have stopped.

The record leaves several things open. It does not settle who set the Reichstag fire. It cannot show that the Republic would have survived had Hitler not been appointed when he was; the decline of late 1932 makes that possible, not certain. And it does not show what Papen and his allies expected beyond their belief that they could control the man they empowered. The regime installed by these steps is the one that appears, within months, as a party to [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement of 1933], and two years later as the author of [scene:hol_s02|the Nuremberg Laws of 1935].

sections.h: Inquiry and Reversal: The Passfield White Paper and the MacDonald Letter, 1930–1931
sections.html:
British policy in Palestine is often described as moving in one steady direction from the Balfour Declaration to the White Paper of 1939. Between March 1930 and February 1931 it moved twice. After the violence of August 1929, two official inquiries concluded that Jewish immigration and land purchase were feeding Arab fears and creating a landless Arab class. In October 1930 London published a policy built on those findings. Four months later the Prime Minister, in a letter to the leader of the Zionist movement, explained it in terms that removed its restrictions. It is the clearest case before 1939 of a British decision on Palestine reversed within months under political pressure, and the immigration figures of the following years show what the reversal allowed.

The first inquiry was the Shaw Commission, sent to investigate the 1929 violence. It reported in March 1930. It concluded that the fundamental cause was Arab fear, economic and political, of being displaced through Jewish immigration and land purchase, and it recommended that Britain clarify its policy on both [cite:w_shaw] [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_d]. Its findings on the Mufti and on the riots themselves are told in [scene:s07a4|the Wall and August 1929]. On land it found that the Land Transfer Ordinances of 1920 and 1921 had failed, that the 1929 Protection of Cultivators Ordinance did not stop evictions, and that a landless class was forming, "a potential danger to the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e].

The second inquiry went deeper. Sir John Hope Simpson surveyed land and agriculture across the country; his report, Cmd. 3686, carries a covering letter dated 22 August 1930 and was published in October 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. He found that a large share of rural Arab families had too little land to live on, that evictions after land sales were producing a landless class, and that without development there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement [cite:w_hopesimpson]. It is the most detailed British land study of the Mandate period [cite:w_hopesimpson]. In 104 surveyed villages, 29.4 per cent of families held no land, and he put the land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside" [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. His full figures, and the Jewish Agency's challenge to them, are set out in [scene:rd3_land|land and labour, 1922–1933].

On the basis of these two reports, the Colonial Secretary, Lord Passfield, issued a White Paper in October 1930. It made immigration depend on Arab as well as Jewish unemployment, and it tightened control of land transfers [cite:w_passfield]. It was the first serious attempt to slow the machinery of settlement the Mandate had set running. The mechanism lay in two levers the Mandatory already held: the rate at which immigration certificates were issued, and the approval of land transfers. The White Paper proposed to tie the first to the condition of the whole labour market, Arab included, and to hold the second more tightly.

The response was immediate. Chaim Weizmann resigned as president of the Jewish Agency in protest. Senior Conservative and Liberal politicians attacked the policy in Parliament and the press as a breach of the Mandate, and the press campaign was intense. In a closely watched by-election at Whitechapel, a constituency with a large Jewish electorate, Labour's majority shrank [cite:w_passfield]. The pressure fell on a minority Labour government [cite:w_passfield]. Nothing in the record requires a hidden hand to explain the outcome. A government without a majority faced an opposition, a press campaign and an electoral warning, all in the open, and gave way.

On 13 February 1931 Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald sent Weizmann a letter, which was read into the record of the House of Commons [cite:w_passfield]. Its text shows exactly how the reversal was done. The letter did not repeal the White Paper. It presented itself as the "authoritative interpretation" of it, and then interpreted it point by point. On immigration, it stated that the government did not contemplate "any stoppage or prohibition of Jewish immigration", and tied any limits to the principle of absorptive capacity, described as "purely economic considerations". On land, it said the 1930 policy did not bar further Jewish land purchase and referred only to "temporary control of land disposition and transfers"; the duty to settle landless Arabs was confined to those displaced by land passing into Jewish hands. On labour, it accepted the Jewish Agency's right to affirm the preferential employment of Jewish labour, while saying that the Mandatory must take account of any resulting displacement of Arab labour or rise in unemployment [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]. And it restated the Mandate itself: "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine", a double undertaking to which equal weight was to be given [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal].

The two sides read the letter in opposite ways, and each reading has a solid basis in the documents. The Zionist reading, which leading opposition politicians had also put in Parliament before the letter was written, was that the White Paper had breached the Mandate, and that the letter corrected the breach [cite:w_passfield]. The letter's own language supports that reading on its terms. If the Mandate was an undertaking to the Jewish people as a whole, not only to the Jews already in Palestine, then a policy that measured immigration by the local labour market alone weighed only one side of a double obligation. The Arab reading was summed up in the name Arab leaders gave the document: the "Black Letter" [cite:w_passfield]. Its evidence is the sequence itself. A policy founded on two official inquiries was withdrawn within four months, through a letter to the head of one party to the dispute, after a campaign waged in Parliament, the press and a by-election.

The letter's effect on Arab trust is documented by Arab officials of the Mandate government itself. On 30 June 1936, 137 Arab senior government officials told the High Commissioner that the Arabs had lost faith in official pledges. They cited the 1931 letter, issued as an interpretation of the 1930 White Paper, as a cause, and recommended that immigration be stopped [cite:rs_rd3_officials_memo_1936]. Five years after it was written, men who served the Mandate administration still cited the letter when they explained their loss of faith in British commitments.

Immigration then rose steeply. Recorded Jewish immigration, as compiled by the United States State Department from British returns, was 4,075 in 1931, 9,553 in 1932, 30,327 in 1933, 42,359 in 1934 and 61,854 in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]. A second series, printed from the historian Yehoshua Porath, gives higher figures for the later years; both are set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|immigration, 1923–1936]. The 1935 figure was the highest of the Mandate years. The letter did not by itself produce that rise. From 1933 the Nazi takeover in Germany drove Jewish emigration on a new scale. What the letter did was keep in place the rules under which that emigration could enter Palestine. The Arab Revolt began the following year.

Several questions the record does not settle. The sources do not show which pressure weighed most with MacDonald: the parliamentary attack, the press, the Whitechapel result, or Weizmann's resignation. They do not separate the letter's effect on immigration from the effect of events in Germany; the two arrived together, and any attempt to apportion the rise between them goes beyond the evidence. Nor can they say what the White Paper would have achieved had it stood, since it was never applied as written. What they do show is a documented sequence: London commissioned two inquiries, adopted their findings, and, under open political pressure, withdrew them through an act of interpretation, leaving the earlier rules on immigration and land in force for the 1930s.

sections.h: Land and Labour, 1922–1933
sections.html:
Two opposite simplifications surround the land of Mandate Palestine. One holds that the British government sold the country's land to Zionist buyers with little scrutiny or resistance. The other holds that Jewish land purchase was small and sporadic before 1948. The record of the 1920s and early 1930s answers both. The land was not, in the main, sold by Britain. It was bought, privately and lawfully, from landowners, most of them absentees, by Zionist institutions that held it permanently and leased it on condition that only Jews work it. The Mandate tried to protect the tenants who lost their land and failed, and its own inquiries of 1930 measured the result. Resistance was real and documented, in courts and in protest, though it rarely stopped a sale once begun [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith].

The legal ground for all of it was older than the Mandate. Under Ottoman law, tenant farmers who had worked land for generations usually held no registered title; when the registered owner sold, the tenant had no ownership claim to assert, so a lawful sale and a lawful eviction could be the same transaction [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine] [cite:israelfactcheck_ottoman_land_laws]. How that law worked, how the Ottoman restrictions on Jewish purchase were met and circumvented, and how the purchasing institutions were built before 1914 are told in [scene:s04j|the land purchase mechanism].

The largest single seller was a family, not a government. The Sursocks of Beirut, a wealthy Greek Orthodox Christian family, had acquired great tracts of the Jezreel Valley under Ottoman rule; the Ottoman government itself sold them Marj ibn Amir in 1872. Between 1901 and 1925, and mainly in the 1920s, the family sold roughly 60,000 to 75,000 dunams to Zionist purchasing organizations, for a fraction of the land's later value [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:sursockhouse_rothschild_purchases]. The main sales fell between 1920 and 1925. The Sursock purchases alone account for about 22 percent of all the land Jews acquired in Palestine up to 1948, and 58 percent of all the land bought from absentee landlords [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases].

The buyers were three institutions with distinct roles. The Jewish National Fund held purchased land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people. The Palestine Land Development Company did the actual purchasing, led by Yehoshua Hankin, who had worked with the Sursock family since 1891, personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions, and became head of the company in 1932. The Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, founded in 1924 by Edmond de Rothschild, became through parallel acquisitions the largest single Jewish landowner in Palestine [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. By the early Mandate years land sold by absentee owners to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam. Purchasing agents such as Hankin sometimes bought first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish Agency or the Fund afterward [cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] [cite:palquest_wzo_funding]. The banks and campaigns that supplied the capital are described in the section on the Mandate economy.

What a purchase cost the people living on the land is documented for one group of sales. In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted. Under the tenure system they were owed no compensation, but they were paid about $17 a person as a goodwill settlement. Across all the Sursock-linked purchases, an estimated 20 to 25 villages were depopulated [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. The sources do not date this group of evictions within the sale period, and the figure of $17 describes that group only, not every transaction. Selling land to Jewish buyers was seen by some Arabs as a serious betrayal. In at least one documented case, negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen as responsible for the evacuation [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin].

The Jewish National Fund turned each purchase into a permanent holding. Its land was leased long-term rather than sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition; its founding resolution called the land "the eternal possession of the Jewish people" [cite:jnf_wiki]. The Fund's own history, from its founding in 1901, is told in [scene:s04d|the Jewish National Fund]. Its holdings in these years show the scale. It held 22,363 dunams in 1920. By 1935 it held about 89,500 acres, some 362 square kilometres, across 108 communities [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg].

The chart of the Fund's holdings shows how the 1920s and early 1930s changed its course. From a first gift of 200 dunams in 1903, it took seventeen years to reach 22,363 dunams in 1920. In the fifteen years that followed it grew to about 362,000 dunams by 1935, more than sixteen times the 1920 figure, and the curve kept rising, to 516,000 dunams in 1940 and about 936,000 by 1947–48 [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg]. Because Fund land was never resold, the line could only climb. The 1935 point is the 89,500 acres of the sources expressed in dunams, and should be read as an approximation.

The Mandate's role was that of regulator, not seller, and as regulator it failed. Between 1920 and 1940 Britain enacted five separate laws meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale. A documented analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation" [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. The Shaw Commission said the same in 1930 about the laws then in force: the Land Transfer Ordinances of 1920 and 1921 had failed, the Protection of Cultivators Ordinance of 1929 did not stop evictions, and the evictions were creating a landless class, "a potential danger to the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. Later in the decade British policy moved the other way: in 1938 the Mandate authorities allowed Zionist officials to copy land-registration and tax records of Arab ownership in order to facilitate further purchases [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. Britain's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single policy, and its restrictions on immigration in 1939 cut in the opposite direction.

The case that tested the system came at the end of the 1920s. In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams at Wadi al-Hawarith at auction from absentee landlords; the historian Weldon Matthews counts it as the third-largest single acquisition the Fund made in the whole Mandate period. The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived there refused to leave, and the Fund began legal proceedings to evict them. Awni Abd al-Hadi, a leading Palestinian national figure, represented the residents through a court battle that lasted several years. The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933. The response was organized and crossed party lines: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith]. The case was decided in the Mandate's own courts, under its own law. It shows that resistance reached formal legal representation and cross-party protest when the stakes were high enough. It does not show that every sale met such opposition; many went through with less.

The fullest measurement of all this came from Sir John Hope Simpson. His report, Palestine: Report on Immigration, Land Settlement and Development (Cmd. 3686), carries a covering letter dated 22 August 1930 and was published in October 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. It is the most detailed British land study of the Mandate period [cite:w_hopesimpson]. He adopted the Director of Surveys' estimate of 8,044,000 metric dunams of cultivable land, including 1,500,000 in the Beersheba region, and found that only 40 per cent of the hill country was cultivable, not the 66.6 per cent that had been assumed. He put Jewish-held land in June 1930 at about 1,250,000 Turkish dunams. Deducting about 900,000 metric dunams of Jewish holdings, he left 5,644,000 metric dunams for non-Jewish cultivators [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The two Jewish figures are in different units, Turkish and metric dunams, and the report as summarized here does not reconcile them further.

His village figures carried the human finding. In 104 surveyed villages, 6,940 of 23,573 families, 29.4 per cent, held no land at all. His own enquiry into 688 Arab families displaced by land sales found that only 379 were cultivating land again; the other 309 had joined the landless. He estimated the land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside" [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. Without development, he concluded, there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement [cite:w_hopesimpson].

Hope Simpson also examined labour, and here he quoted the movement's own documents. The Jewish National Fund's draft lease required the lessee to cultivate "only with Jewish labour", on penalty of ten Palestinian pounds for each breach and repossession of the land after three breaches. The Jewish Agency's constitution of 1920 committed it to colonization "based on Jewish labour". And fewer than one in three of the immigrants who had arrived since 1921 had settled on the land [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The clause had a plain consequence for the purchase chain: a tenant evicted from land the Fund bought could not be hired back to work it, because the lease forbade the lessee to employ him. Shaw had added two further findings: the allocation of labour-schedule immigration certificates by political creed was indefensible, and Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. The labour movement's own doctrine of "Hebrew labour" is described in the section on the Histadrut.

The Jewish Agency contested Hope Simpson's numbers. In 1931 it published a memorandum, The Statistical Bases of Sir John Hope Simpson's Report, to challenge the report's figures [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The two positions stand side by side. Hope Simpson held that without development there was no margin for settlement, that at most 100,000 dunams were available, and that a landless class was forming [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The Agency held that his statistical foundation was unsound [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The research for this book has not verified the memorandum's specific arguments, so they are not summarized here. On the Agency's side, the strongest evidence in the record used here comes from a British inquiry: Shaw's finding that Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits. What London did with these findings is told in [scene:pf_s01|the Passfield White Paper and its reversal].

Several things the record does not settle. The total number of Arab families displaced by land sales in these years is not established; Hope Simpson's 688 families were those his own enquiry traced, and the 1,746 Sursock-linked families are one group of sales. Whether there was room for more settlement in 1930 is a question on which Hope Simpson and the Jewish Agency disagreed, and the Agency's arguments have not been examined here. The full Jewish holding in 1930 is given in two units that the summarized report does not reconcile. What is documented is the mechanism: a private sale by an absentee owner, a purchase by a Zionist company, a permanent holding by the Fund, a lease that barred non-Jewish labour, and protective ordinances that the Mandate's own inquiry found had failed to protect.

sections.h: The Armed Line: The Haganah, the Irgun and the Jaffa Barrels, 1920–1935
sections.html:
A familiar picture of the Mandate years shows one Jewish defence force, the Haganah, acting under a single political direction until it became the army of the new state in 1948. The record for these years shows something less tidy. By the end of 1931 there were already two Jewish armed organizations in Palestine, the Haganah and the Irgun, and by 1940 there would be three. They were divided by documented disputes over strategy and politics, they went through periods of open hostility toward one another, and even at the declaration of statehood they had reached only a partial, negotiated coordination. This section follows the line from its small beginnings in the 1920s to the arms shipment found in the port of Jaffa in 1935, and then points forward to where it led.

The starting point was modest. When the Histadrut, the Jewish labour federation, was founded in December 1920, it took responsibility for defence, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control. Through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was a volunteer body of the labour movement, not an army. In 1924 its senior commanders drew up a "Constitution of the Haganah," a first attempt to give the organization written rules. The labour camp was not of one mind about it. In 1926 former members of Ha-Shomer formed a separate underground of their own inside the Gedud ha-Avodah [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. Even before the Revisionist split that is the usual subject of this story, the Yishuv's armed structure was divided.

The violence of August 1929 changed the Haganah's position. In that month its volunteers helped defend the Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa. The massacres of that August happened where the Haganah was absent or weak: in Hebron, in Safed and at Motza [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The lesson the movement drew was organizational. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's account describes the result as a shift toward wider organization and toward public control of the force [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

That shift took formal shape in 1931. A national command of six members was set up, with parity between the labour movement and everyone else: three members came from the Histadrut, Eliyahu Golomb, Dov Hos and Meir Rutberg, and three were non-labour members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The mechanism matters. A defence force that had answered to one party's federation now answered to a body in which labour held half the seats and the non-labour parties held the other half. The commander who opposed public control was removed [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

Not everyone accepted the arrangement. A group led by Avraham Tehomi, who had been the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, seceded. Together with Revisionist groups it formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi, also known as Etzel [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi]. Tehomi is the same man whose 1985 account of the 1924 killing of Jacob de Haan is weighed in [scene:dh_s01|the de Haan section]. He did not stay with the organization he founded: he returned to the Haganah in 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi].

The Irgun's founders were officers aligned with Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist movement, and the point of principle on which they broke was havlagah, the Haganah's policy of restraint in the face of Arab attacks, which they rejected [cite:wiki_irgun]. Through the 1930s and 1940s the Irgun conducted an armed campaign against British rule and against Arab civilian targets. From 1943 it was commanded by Menachem Begin, who later became Israel's sixth Prime Minister [cite:wiki_irgun]. That is a direct, documented personal line from the command of this organization to the country's highest office. The source establishes the founding rationale and the line of command; it does not, on its own, give a full operational history of the Irgun, and this section does not attempt one.

The two positions can be stated in their own terms, as far as the sources record them. The Haganah's leadership held to restraint and, after 1931, to a command shared equally between labour and non-labour members, removing the commander who opposed that public control. The Irgun's founders rejected restraint in the face of Arab attacks and left rather than serve under that command. Both answers came out of the same experience of 1929, which had shown how few defenders there were and what happened where there were none.

Between 1931 and 1935 the Haganah built itself into something more permanent. It had urban branches in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa, each with memberships "in the hundreds," it ran annual officers' courses, and it had workshops producing hand grenades [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was still small. It was also now an organization that trained its own officers and made some of its own weapons.

The clearest single episode of these years came at the port of Jaffa in 1935. Rifles and ammunition had been shipped from Belgium hidden in barrels of cement. British authorities seized 537 barrels at Jaffa, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. One account, drawing on the Palestine Post and the Peel report among other sources, gives the contents as 25 Lewis machine guns, 800 rifles and 400,000 rounds, found in 359 of the drums, and says they were consigned to a merchant in Tel Aviv who was never identified. The same account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. Those details rest on that one account and are given here as its report.

The sources do not agree on when the shipment was found. The account just cited, relying on Palestine Post reports and the Peel report, dates the discovery to 16 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on the Haganah dates it to 18 November 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. This book has not resolved the difference. The earlier date sits before the reported strike of 26 October; the later one would fall after it. Neither source, as gathered here, names who in the Yishuv ordered the shipment.

One claim about these years does not hold up as stated. A compiled account of Zionist intelligence before 1948, drawn on elsewhere in this library, says that the first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine was established under the Haganah in 1929. The same account also dates the founding of the Shai, the Sherut Yediot or Information Service, the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm, to 1940 [cite:shai_wiki]. The two statements may describe different bodies, an informal service in 1929 and a formal one in 1940, but the account does not say so, and this book has not been able to confirm a founding date for any Haganah intelligence body in 1929. The claim is reported here as unconfirmed. The Shai's wartime and American story belongs to a later period and is not told here.

Where the line led is told in later chapters, but its shape follows from what was built in these years. In 1940 the Irgun split in turn. Avraham Stern led a faction out to form Lehi, Lohamei Herut Israel, "Fighters for the Freedom of Israel," often called the Stern Gang, rejecting the Irgun's decision to suspend operations against the British during the Second World War [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. Stern's group is documented as having explored contact with Fascist Italy and, most controversially, Nazi Germany, in search of any power willing to oppose British rule in Palestine. The episode was widely condemned at the time, including within the broader Zionist movement. The record shows exploratory contact, not a completed cooperation or alliance [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. That story is told in [scene:lh_s01|Lehi].

In 1944 and 1945, in what became known as the "Hunting Season," the Haganah, under Jewish Agency direction, moved against members of the Irgun and Lehi through surveillance, exposure to the British authorities and detentions, in an attempt to suppress their independent operations and keep political control unified [cite:wiki_hunting_season]. The source documents the pattern rather than every operation. And at independence, when the Haganah became the core of the Israel Defense Forces and the Irgun and Lehi were formally absorbed, the merger was contested. In June 1948 the Altalena affair, an armed confrontation between the new army and Irgun forces over a weapons shipment, left sixteen Irgun members and three soldiers dead; the ship was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on Ben-Gurion's direct order. Begin's refusal to let the clash become a civil war, in his words "there will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates," is documented as decisive in preventing a wider fight [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. Most of the roughly 940 passengers aboard were inducted into the army without incident, so the flashpoint was not the whole of the integration [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. The wreck was found intact on the Mediterranean seafloor in 2026, 78 years later [cite:jpost_altalena_wreck_2026]. That ending is told in [scene:mil_s01|1948].

The reason to tell this line in a chapter about building institutions is a matter of consistency. This library gives full weight to the internal divisions on the political side: the Bund, Reform Judaism's early ambivalence, Neturei Karta.
