[cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] From the summer of 1945, Palestine was handled in London as a question of foreign policy, and the man most identified with British policy on it, by Zionists, by Americans and by later historians, was Bevin.

His reputation in this story is unusually divided. To many Zionists of the period, and to some of his own colleagues, he was a man who disliked Jews. To his biographer and to Attlee, he was an opponent of a Jewish state, not an enemy of Jews. To a third school, his policy followed from what the Foreign Office took to be Britain's interests in the Middle East, and his personal feelings mattered little. All three readings rest on documents. Before weighing them, it helps to set out what Bevin actually said and did in his first eighteen months.

The general reference works are sparing. Britannica's entry on Bevin offers only one judgement on Palestine: that his plans of 1947–48 "for a federal Jewish-Arab nation or other partition of Palestine collapsed" in the face of the Arab-Israeli conflict. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] The detail lies in his own statements, in American diplomatic reports, and in the scholarship that has tried to explain him.

The statement of 13 November 1945. Bevin's first major act on Palestine came on 13 November 1945. He announced a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship," to examine the position of the Jews in Europe and the question of Palestine. Until it reported, he said, there would be "no interruption of Jewish immigration at the present monthly rate." The text did not state what that rate was. Looking further ahead, he spoke of a trusteeship agreement that would "supersede the existing mandate." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] The statement also set out the terms in which London saw the problem. Bevin reminded his audience that the Arabs of Palestine had "90,000,000 co-religionists in India," a reference to the weight Britain gave to Muslim opinion across its empire, and he said that Palestine "does not by itself provide sufficient opportunity" for solving the Jewish problem. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] In other words, Palestine was to be one part of an answer for the Jewish survivors of Europe, not the whole of it, and any answer had to reckon with opinion far beyond Palestine.

The committee itself, its twelve members, its hearings and its report are the subject of [scene:aac_s01|the next section]. What matters here is that the inquiry was Bevin's chosen instrument. It brought Washington into a decision that had been Britain's alone, and it bought time.

The same day, Bevin spoke privately to the American ambassador in London, John Winant. Winant's telegram, received in Washington on 14 November 1945, reported that Bevin said he would be willing to "stake his political future on finding solution for Palestine problem," and that he "made a plea against approaching this subject in spirit of racial antagonism." [cite:rs_rd5_frus_winant_1945] The telegram is a primary American record, not Bevin's own text, but it shows how he wished to be understood by the government he most needed to persuade: as a minister who had staked his career on a settlement and who wanted the question kept out of racial politics.

His public words that day did not always match that wish. According to the historian Raphael Langham, Bevin told the House of Commons on 13 November, "We cannot accept the view that the Jews should be driven out of Europe." At a press conference the same day, he warned that if Jews "want to get too much at the head of the queue" there was a danger of an antisemitic reaction. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The first sentence stated a principle: the survivors had a future in Europe and should not be treated as people to be removed from it. The second turned the survivors' claims into the cause of the hostility they might meet. Langham calls the remark "unfortunate." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

"Too many Jews in New York." The pressure Bevin resisted came above all from the United States, where President Truman was pressing for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine. At the Labour Party conference in June 1946, Bevin said of that pressure that "They did not want too many Jews in New York." Langham calls it "a gratuitous sneer." It angered Truman and provoked protests in the United States. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The remark was an antisemitic jibe from a sitting Foreign Secretary. It suggested that American support for Jewish immigration to Palestine was a way of keeping Jews out of America, and it was made at a party conference, in public. Whatever conclusion one reaches about Bevin's policy, the sentence itself needs no softening.

The London conference and the American visit. In September 1946 Britain convened a conference at Lancaster House in London. According to Langham, Bevin told the Arab delegation there that no solution could ignore Jewish claims. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] This sits awkwardly beside the remarks above, and that is part of what makes him hard to read: the same minister who sneered at American motives told the Arab states that Jewish claims had to be part of any settlement. Two months later he travelled to the United States, in November and December 1946. During that visit, Langham writes, Bevin reportedly came to the view that Britain would have to give up the Mandate. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The decision itself, taken in Cabinet in February 1947, belongs to [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain's exit], the subject of a later section.

The mechanism. In these months Bevin held the levers that mattered for Palestine: the rate of Jewish immigration, the choice of forum, and the timing of any settlement. The November 1945 statement used each one. It kept immigration at the existing rate rather than opening the gates or closing them, it moved the question into a joint inquiry with the United States, and it pointed toward trusteeship rather than either a Jewish or an Arab state. The parties most affected could not set any of these terms. Jewish refugees in Europe could not choose where to go; the Jewish Agency and the Arab leadership could argue before the inquiry but could not decide; and Washington, though it pressed hard on immigration, did not govern Palestine. What Bevin could not control was the American response, and his June 1946 remark shows how much that pressure grated.

The dispute over his motives. Why did Bevin oppose a Jewish state? Historians have given three answers, and Langham sets them out side by side. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

The first answer is personal hostility. Two contemporaries who dealt with him said so plainly. Christopher Mayhew wrote that "Ernest detests Jews," and Chaim Weizmann said Bevin was "blinded by his hatred of the Jews." The historian Peter Weiler takes a more careful line: he finds that Bevin "held antisemitic views" but sees "no evidence that they shaped his policy." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is the remarks themselves, which are on the record and were made in public. Its weakness, as Weiler's own wording shows, is the step from a man's prejudices to the reasons for his decisions.

The second answer is that Bevin was an anti-Zionist, not an antisemite. His biographer Alan Bullock wrote that he "was not moved by hatred of the Jews." David Ben-Gurion, who had every reason to think the worst of him, said, "I prefer to consider Bevin simply as an anti-Zionist." Attlee defended him in the same terms in the House of Commons in 1949. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is that it comes in part from Bevin's opponents, Ben-Gurion above all, and that it fits his statement to the Arab delegation in September 1946. Its weakness is that the remarks of November 1945 and June 1946 are hard to describe as political opposition to Zionism alone.

The third answer is strategic interest. A Foreign Office briefing attributed to Harold Beeley stressed Middle East oil, communications and the Suez route as Britain's interests in the region, and Langham cites the historian W. Roger Louis on Britain's Middle East position. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] On this reading, Bevin's policy was the Foreign Office's policy: Britain needed the goodwill of the Arab states and of Muslim opinion, the "90,000,000 co-religionists in India" whom Bevin himself had invoked, and a Jewish state imposed against that opinion would put those interests at risk. The strength of this case is that it explains the policy without needing to explain the man, and that it matches the reasons the government gave in its own papers. Its weakness is that it says little about why the remarks were made.

Langham's own conclusion leans toward the third answer. Bevin, he writes, was probably not motivated by antisemitism when he made policy, and "genuinely thought it was in the best interests of Britain." But his opposition hardened over time into anti-Zionism, and Langham leaves open whether, in that later stage, Bevin crossed into antisemitism. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] That conclusion keeps two things apart that are often run together: what a man said about Jews, which in Bevin's case included antisemitic remarks stated in public, and why his government did what it did, which the documents tie to British strategic interest.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here do not show what "the present monthly rate" of immigration was in November 1945, since Bevin's text gave no figure. They do not show what Bevin said to American officials during his visit in late 1946, only Langham's report that he came to think the Mandate would have to be given up. Nor can any document settle what Bevin felt, as against what he said and did. The remarks are a matter of record; the motive behind the policy remains a matter of judgement, and the historians who have studied him most closely still disagree.

sections.h: The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, 1945–1946
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that no international body heard the Arab case, or the case for a shared state, before the United Nations voted to partition Palestine in November 1947. The record shows otherwise. Eighteen months before the vote, a joint British and American committee heard the Jewish Agency, Arab spokesmen, Jewish advocates of a binational state, Christian and Jewish organizations, and the refugees themselves. It then produced a unanimous report that rejected both a Jewish state and an Arab state. What happened next is the more important part of the story. Washington took the one recommendation it wanted and left the rest; London set a condition that stalled even that one; and the follow-up plan pleased no one.

Twelve members, two governments. The committee was announced in November 1945 by the Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, as a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship" (the announcement and its context are told in [scene:rd5_bevin|the section on Bevin]). [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] It was created as Washington pressed London to admit Jewish displaced persons to Palestine, and it was built to share the question between the two governments. It had six American and six British members. The Americans included Bartley Crum and James McDonald; the British included Richard Crossman. [cite:w_aac]

Hearings on three continents. Between January and March 1946 the committee held hearings in Washington, London, the displaced-persons camps of Europe, Cairo and Jerusalem. [cite:w_aac] It took evidence from governments, the Jewish Agency, Arab states and the Arab Office, Christian and Jewish organizations, and refugees in the camps. It was, in the judgement of the account this book follows, the most complete hearing of competing cases before 1947. [cite:w_aac]

Three of the cases put to it deserve naming. The Jewish Agency's leaders presented the Zionist case. Arab representatives presented theirs, among them the Arab Office, where the historian Albert Hourani gave testimony that the record describes as notable. [cite:w_aac] The sources used here do not give the substance of what Hourani said, so this book does not paraphrase it. The third case came from Jews who opposed a Jewish state. Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, and the Ihud association argued that Arabs and Jews should share one state with political parity. [cite:w_aac] Their testimony shows that a Jewish alternative to partition was argued, in person, before an official body. It was not a position invented afterward by critics of the state that emerged.

The April 1946 report. The committee reported unanimously in April 1946. It recommended four things. First, the immediate issue of 100,000 immigration certificates for Jewish refugees. Second, the repeal of the 1940 land regulations, which restricted land transfers. Third, the continuation of the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship. And fourth, as a principle of the future constitution, that Palestine should be neither a Jewish state nor an Arab state, with neither people dominating the other. [cite:avalon_aac]

The report was a package. The 100,000 certificates answered the plight of the survivors in Europe; the repeal of the land regulations removed a restriction that bore on Jewish land purchase; trusteeship and the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle were meant to stop either community from turning numbers or land into domination of the other. Unanimity mattered: the six Americans and six Britons had agreed on all of it together.

What Washington kept, and what London required. President Truman publicly endorsed the 100,000 and was silent on the rest. [cite:w_aac] The admission of refugees was popular with American voters. The constitutional recommendation against a Jewish state was not something he endorsed. Prime Minister Attlee answered by tying any admissions to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups in Palestine. [cite:w_aac] The British condition was not abstract. At the time, the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi were acting together against British rule, as told in [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]. By making the 100,000 depend on disarmament, London made the one recommendation Washington wanted depend on something the Jewish armed groups would not concede.

Morrison–Grady. The two governments tried once more. In July 1946 a follow-up Anglo-American plan, known as Morrison–Grady, proposed provincial autonomy for Palestine under continued outside rule. Zionist and Arab leaders both rejected it, and Truman declined to back it. [cite:w_morrisongrady] With that, the joint Anglo-American attempt to settle Palestine was finished. The question went to the United Nations the following year. [cite:w_morrisongrady]

The mechanism. The episode shows how the decision was structured in 1946. The committee could hear anyone and recommend anything, but it could decide nothing. The two governments could decide, but each took from the report what served its own position. Washington, which did not govern Palestine, could press on the one point that cost it nothing at home and had public support. London, which governed Palestine and carried the cost of policing it, could attach conditions. The people heard by the committee, whether the Jewish Agency, the Arab Office, Magnes and Ihud, or the refugees in the camps, had a hearing but no hand in what followed. The binational option that Magnes argued, and that the report's "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle partly echoed, had no government willing to carry it.

The two readings. One reading of this record is that the hearing was real and the outcome was a failure of politics: the committee did its work, and the governments that commissioned it then ignored most of it. Another reading, found in the source this book follows, puts it more sharply: what survived into American policy was the part with domestic political value. [cite:w_aac] Both readings start from the same facts. They differ on how much weight to give Truman's own reasons, a question taken up in [scene:wh_s01|the section on the White House]. What neither reading supports is the claim that the Arab and binationalist cases went unheard before 1947. They were heard; they were not adopted.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here name only three of the twelve members, and do not record the committee's internal debates or how it reached unanimity. They do not give the content of Hourani's testimony or of the Jewish Agency's. They do not say what, if anything, London said about the land regulations, trusteeship or the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle once the report was published, beyond its disarmament condition on the 100,000. And they do not show whether any of the 100,000 certificates were issued as a result of the report.

sections.h: Black Sabbath: Britain Cracks Down
sections.html:
On Saturday, June 29, 1946, British troops and police fanned out across Mandate Palestine, the territory Britain then governed. It is often said that relations between Britain and the Jewish community there soured gradually, without a single sharp turning point. The record identifies one. That day Britain launched Operation Agatha, a coordinated raid across the country. Because it fell on the Jewish Sabbath, the community it struck named it "Black Sabbath."

The scale was enormous. Roughly 17,000 British troops and police searched Jewish settlements, kibbutzim and offices at the same time. More than 2,700 people were arrested, among them senior officials of the Jewish Agency, the body that represented the Jewish community. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The operation was a direct response to mounting attacks on British installations by the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi. Its targets, however, went beyond the armed groups. By arresting the Agency's own senior officials, Britain struck at the institutions of the mainstream Zionist leadership itself. The sources give the operation's overall scale and its targeting of the leadership. They do not list every site searched or every person detained.

Part of what was at stake was paper. British forces seized a large cache of documents from the Jewish Agency's headquarters in Jerusalem. The material was believed to include evidence linking the Agency's mainstream leadership to Haganah operations. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] If that link could be shown, it would undo the careful separation the movement had kept between its political leadership and armed resistance. The same kind of separation had been built, on the other side of the Atlantic, into the procurement network described in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting]. The sources do not specify what the seized documents contained. They document what the documents were believed to contain, and why that mattered.

The operation's two names tell their own story. "Agatha" was the official British codename, and there is no reason to think it carried any special meaning; codenames of the period were typically assigned without symbolic intent. "Black Sabbath" was the name given by the community whose settlements and institutions were searched. It records how the event was lived and remembered. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

The raid's most important consequence followed quickly, along a line that can be traced. The Irgun believed the seized documents were being processed at the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. The hotel's southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the British government in Palestine, and served as regional British military headquarters, while hotel business went on in the rest of the building. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] To Irgun planners, the building was both a symbol of British authority and the place where the evidence against the Jewish Agency's leadership was kept. Irgun intelligence assessed that the Agatha documents were held in the Secretariat wing specifically. The documented objective of what followed was to destroy that evidence and to strike the administration that had just carried out the mass raid and arrests. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

Irgun planning for the attack began in direct response to Black Sabbath. The bombing took place on July 22, 1946, twenty-three days after the raid. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The chain ran from raid to seizure, from seizure to an intelligence assessment, from that assessment to the choice of target, and from there to the attack.

Tracing that chain is not the same as excusing what came at its end. Ninety-one people died in the bombing, many of them with no connection to the administrative work being targeted. Nor was retaliation for Black Sabbath necessarily the only motive; the attack's planning and stated objectives are examined more fully in the next chapter. Explaining why an act happened and judging it are separate tasks. This chapter attempts only the first.

sections.h: The King David Hotel Bombing
sections.html:
On July 22, 1946, explosives tore through the southern wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. The bombing is sometimes remembered, where it is remembered at all, as a minor incident in a British office building. The record does not allow that description. The attack killed 91 people. It was carried out by an organization whose commander later became Prime Minister of Israel. It hardened British opinion toward leaving Palestine. And on its own documented merits, it stands among the most consequential single events of the Mandate, the period of British rule.

The attack came three weeks after the Black Sabbath raid. The Irgun, an underground militia commanded by Menachem Begin, detonated explosives in the basement of the southern wing, the part of the building that housed the British Mandate Secretariat and the military command. The explosives were reportedly hidden in milk churns. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The 91 dead included British, Arab and Jewish civilians and administrative staff. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] It was the deadliest single attack on the British during the entire Mandate period. The sources give the total toll and its spread across communities. They do not provide a full list of the victims.

As the previous chapter showed, the target was chosen for specific reasons. The Secretariat wing was the administrative and military center of British rule. Irgun intelligence believed that documents seized from the Jewish Agency, the body representing the Jewish community of Palestine, during Operation Agatha were being processed there. The bombing was meant both to destroy that evidence and to strike the administration that had carried out the raid.

Whether the people in the building were adequately warned is a question the record has not resolved. By the Irgun's own account, warning calls urging evacuation were placed about 25 minutes before the detonation, to the hotel switchboard, to the French consulate and to the Palestine Post newspaper. British investigators and later historians have disputed whether any warning reached the hotel's management in time to act, or whether it was dismissed as a hoax. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Both accounts are documented. Neither has displaced the other, and this book does not choose between them.

The man who commanded the Irgun at the time had a long political future. Menachem Begin later served as Israel's Prime Minister, from 1977 to 1983. [cite:wiki_menachem_begin] The line from commanding this operation to holding the country's highest office is a matter of record. Begin's own later justifications and public statements about the bombing are not covered in the sources used here, and nothing should be inferred about them from this account.

Within the Jewish political leadership, the reaction was public. The Jewish Agency, whose seized documents had helped bring about the attack, publicly condemned the bombing. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The condemnation laid bare the tension between the mainstream political leadership and the armed groups. The sources document the public statement, not the private views of individual officials or the internal debate behind its wording.

In London the effect was significant. The bombing is documented as having markedly hardened British public and parliamentary opinion toward leaving Palestine altogether. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] In that way it contributed to Britain's decision in 1947 to hand the whole question to the United Nations. It was not the only cause; Britain faced several pressures at once. But it was one significant factor among them.

The future of Palestine was moving from a British problem to an international one. When the United Nations took up the question in 1947, the Jewish Agency was ready with a prepared case, and the other party chose not to appear. That story is told in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair].

sections.h: The Jewish Agency's Campaign at the United Nations
sections.html:
In August 1946, more than a year before any United Nations committee reported on Palestine, the Jewish Agency, the body that represented the Jewish community there, put a detailed partition map on paper. American recognition was one track toward statehood. Admission to the community of nations through the United Nations was another, and the two were separate. The Agency worked both, and its work on the second began before the United Nations had any committee on Palestine at all.

The usual account holds that the United Nations arrived at partition on its own, through the neutral fact-finding of its eleven-member committee. The documents complicate that picture. The Agency's August 1946 proposal drew boundaries for a Palestinian rump state that bear a notable resemblance to the territory that later became the West Bank. [cite:jewishagency_1946plan] This was formal, prepared diplomatic work, set down well ahead of any international process that might adopt something like it.

Nor was the proposal a one-off tactical move. Historical accounts of the United Nations process note that by 1946 partition had become the Jewish Agency's openly avowed policy. [cite:unscop_testimony] The Agency did not adopt partition in reaction to an initiative from New York. Its position was public and settled before the formal process began. It entered that process years into a coordinated, prepared diplomatic campaign, not responding to a fresh proposal from outside. [cite:unscop_testimony]

Two limits on this argument should be stated plainly. First, resemblance is not adoption. The sources show that the 1946 boundaries resemble a later territorial outcome. They do not show that the United Nations committee copied its lines from the Agency's map. Second, a settled commitment to partition did not mean that every detail of the Agency's later presentation at the United Nations matched the 1946 document. What was fixed by 1946 was the principle, not every line on the map.

Even within those limits, the timing matters. When the United Nations committee began its work in 1947, one party to the dispute arrived with a worked-out plan and a stated policy. Who else would present a case, and how, was still an open question. That imbalance shaped the hearings that followed, taken up in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair]. It also placed the diplomatic groundwork for what became Resolution 181 inside the Jewish Agency's own planning, alongside the procurement network in the Americas and the political channels in Washington described in earlier chapters.

In the same summer that the Agency set out its proposal, however, its relationship with Britain, the governing power in Palestine, reached a breaking point. Weeks before the August 1946 submission, Britain had raided the Agency's own offices and arrested its senior officials. The consequences of that raid would soon dominate events on the ground.

sections.h: Inside the White House: Niles, Clifford and the Yom Kippur Statement
sections.html:
On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur, Harry Truman issued a statement on Palestine that would echo through the next two years. A common account holds that his Palestine policy was made on its merits, by the State Department. The record tells a different story: a policy shaped in significant part inside the White House, by named advisers, with timing that critics at the time tied to the electoral calendar.

The first of those advisers was David K. Niles. He served in the White House from 1942 to 1951, under Roosevelt and then Truman, and he was one of only two Roosevelt aides Truman kept on. Niles was entrusted with minority affairs. He was also a committed Zionist and an important channel through which American Zionists reached the White House. [cite:wiki_david_niles] [cite:hnn_clark_truman] A second adviser, Max Lowenthal, counseled the special counsel Clark Clifford on Palestine. Truman's old friend and former business partner Eddie Jacobson offered a third, separate channel, described in [scene:s08|the previous chapter].

The clearest test of how these influences worked came with that October statement. Its date was the eve of Yom Kippur, and it fell a month before the midterm elections. In it Truman regretted the adjournment of the London conference on Palestine and urged immediate large-scale immigration. He also said that the United States could support a solution along the lines of a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine." [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] [cite:nuremberg_yomkippur] It was a public signal that an American president could support a Jewish state, given the year before the question went to the United Nations.

The British reaction was sharp. Prime Minister Attlee was furious. Truman wrote to him that he "very much" regretted any embarrassment. [cite:frus_truman_attlee_1946]

Observers at the time drew their own conclusions about the timing. On 7 October, James Reston wrote in the New York Times that the President "went against his advisers' foreign policy and chose to follow the promptings of those who were primarily interested in retaining Democratic majorities in Congress." [cite:palestinestudies_christison_truman] Truman rejected that reading. In a statement in February 1947 he called the impression that partisan and local politics drove American policy "most unfortunate and misleading," and said his position had been consistent since 1945. [cite:jvl_truman_feb1947]

The two accounts can be weighed, but these sources cannot fully settle them. What is on the record is who had access to the President and when he chose to speak: a Zionist aide in the White House, an adviser counseling Clifford, a personal friend with an open door, and a statement issued on the eve of a religious holiday a month before an election. What remains contested is motive. Named sources argue both sides, Reston on one and Truman's own statement on the other. The honest answer may be that conviction and electoral interest worked together rather than against each other.

The statement also had a precedent of its own. Earlier in 1946, an official Anglo-American inquiry had heard Zionist, Arab and binationalist cases and produced recommendations that Washington used only in part. That inquiry, and what the White House chose to keep from it, is the subject of the next chapter.

sections.h: Moscow Said Yes First
sections.html:
On 14 May 1947, a full year before Israel declared independence, the Soviet Union stood up at the United Nations and signaled that it could accept a Jewish state. Its vote for partition that November was no last-minute surprise. It had been announced six months earlier, before Washington had committed to anything. Popular memory casts Israel as a creation of American support, with the Soviet bloc hostile from the start. The diplomatic record runs almost the other way.

That day the Soviet representative at the United Nations, Andrei Gromyko, addressed a special session of the General Assembly. He told the delegates that the USSR preferred a single Arab–Jewish state with equal rights for both peoples. If that proved impossible, he said, partition into two states was a justifiable alternative. [cite:israeled_gromyko_speech] [cite:israeled_gromyko_timeline] The statement reversed decades of Soviet opposition to Zionism. Analysts at the time and since have read the motive as a wish to remove British influence from the region. The USSR and its satellites voted for partition in November 1947.

The spring of 1948 showed how firm that commitment was. In March, the United States moved to retreat from partition toward a trusteeship for Palestine. Moscow did not follow. At the Security Council the Soviet Union stood behind partition, and Gromyko argued that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce bloodshed. [cite:yated_stalin_israel] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] At the moment American policy wavered, the Soviet position held.

Recognition followed the same pattern. Truman recognized the new state on 14 May 1948, the day of independence, but his recognition was de facto, an acknowledgment of the state as a working reality. On 17 May, three days later, the Soviet Union became the first state to grant Israel full legal, or de jure, recognition. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] In the same months, arms from Soviet-bloc Czechoslovakia reached the new state while an American embargo was in force, a supply line taken up later in this part of the book ([scene:cz_s01|the Czech arms]).

The convergence did not last. In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against UN Resolution 194 on the return of refugees, and from the 1950s Moscow turned toward the Arab states. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] That later turn helps explain why the earlier record faded from popular memory.

The sources support a narrow conclusion, and it should be stated no more broadly than they allow. In 1947 and 1948 both Washington and Moscow backed the new state. Moscow did so earlier and, when the United States hesitated, more firmly, apparently to push Britain out of the region. It was a rare Cold War convergence of two rival powers acting for different reasons, not an alliance of shared purpose.

sections.h: UNSCOP and the Empty Chair
sections.html:
In 1947, eleven members from as many countries set out to recommend what should become of Palestine, and one of the two parties declined to speak to them. The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine, known as UNSCOP, is often described as an impartial international body that investigated the problem and reached its recommendation independently. How its hearings actually worked complicates that picture. The committee did not weigh two prepared cases against each other. It heard one, at length, while the other side stayed away.

The General Assembly established UNSCOP in May 1947, at Britain's own request, after London had handed the question to the United Nations. Its eleven members came from Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia. [cite:unscop_ecf] On its face it was a genuinely international body spanning several continents, not a proxy for the United States or Britain.

Its work, however, was boycotted entirely by Palestinian Arab representatives. As a result, the committee heard testimony almost exclusively from Zionist representatives. [cite:unscop_ecf] The Arab Higher Committee for Palestine, the leading Palestinian Arab political body, refused to take part because it regarded the whole framework as illegitimate. In its view, any United Nations body that set out to decide Palestine's future without first affirming the self-determination rights of the existing majority was biased before it began. The Jewish Agency, by contrast, engaged fully. It supplied detailed logistical help, including its own proposed itinerary for the committee's site visits in Palestine.

David Ben-Gurion presented the Agency's case, testifying as its head. He told the committee plainly that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable political outcome. [cite:unscop_testimony] The map the Zionist side presented was substantially the 1937 Peel Commission map, with the Galilee, the Negev and West Jerusalem added. [cite:unscop_testimony] It was less a new proposal than an extension of an earlier one, and it came after more than a year in which partition had been the Agency's avowed policy, as described in [scene:s07h|the previous chapter on the Agency's campaign]. One historical account says the Agency's presentation overwhelmed the committee "with data, logic, and cogent analyses of every central and tangential issue," while the boycotting side offered nothing to weigh against it. [cite:unscop_testimony] The imbalance did not arise because the Arab position was weak. It arose because that position was never formally put before the committee for comparison.

The limits of this point matter. The record does not show that Arab perspectives were absent from every channel open to the committee. UNSCOP traveled through the region and could observe conditions directly, and it would be wrong to claim its members heard nothing of Arab objections. What the record does establish is more specific: no formal, prepared Arab case was presented to UNSCOP to set against the Jewish Agency's. That is a narrower claim than saying the process was rigged, and it is the claim the evidence supports.

UNSCOP issued its report on September 3, 1947. It was not unanimous. A seven-member majority recommended partition into a Jewish state and an Arab state joined by an economic union. A three-member minority proposed a federal state instead. [cite:unscop_wiki] The report, produced after hearings shaped by the boycott, became the direct basis for the revisions made by the United Nations Ad Hoc Committee and for the General Assembly vote of November 29, 1947. [cite:unscop_wiki]

The empty chair was a choice, made by the Arab Higher Committee on grounds of principle. Its consequence was that the record on which partition was built held one side's data, maps and arguments. Between the report and the vote, the decisive pressure would shift to Washington, where the government's own experts were warning against the course the President was taking.

sections.h: The Warnings: State, the Pentagon and Oil
sections.html:
On September 22, 1947, the State Department's senior expert on the Middle East put a blunt warning on paper: partition of Palestine was "not workable." Within weeks, two more parts of the American government had said much the same. A familiar explanation holds that the strategic costs of supporting partition were not understood until much later, a blind spot born of limited information or the slow communications of the era. The documents do not support it. Before the United States backed partition, the State Department's regional experts, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense each warned in writing that it would damage American strategic interests, citing oil access and Soviet opportunism. The oil industry lobbied against it directly. The warnings were heard, and they were set aside.

The first came from Loy Henderson, director of the State Department's Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs. Henderson had served as American ambassador to Iraq in the mid-1940s and had seen at first hand how Arab governments were reacting to the Palestine question. On September 22, 1947, he sent Secretary of State George Marshall a memo warning that partition was "not workable" and would lead to "untold troubles" in the future. His views, he wrote, were shared by "nearly every member of the Foreign Service or of the department who has worked to any appreciable extent on Near Eastern problems." [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] The memo was not buried. Under Secretary Robert Lovett was impressed enough to read it aloud to President Truman himself. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994]

The military reached the same conclusion through its own channels. On October 10, 1947, the Joint Chiefs of Staff filed a memorandum titled "The Problem of Palestine." It warned that dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states would let the Soviet Union displace American and British influence in the region and would endanger American access to Middle East oil. The next day, October 11, 1947, the United States announced its support for partition. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] The gap between a formal military warning and a decision against it could hardly have been narrower. The surviving record documents both the warning and the decision, but no stated internal reasoning that connects them.

The Secretary of Defense made the same case in public. James Forrestal had earlier been Secretary of the Navy and now oversaw the new Department of Defense created under the National Security Act of 1947. He told a House committee that oil was "the life blood of a war machine," and warned that the Arab world's response to partition would threaten the pipelines carrying oil out of the Persian Gulf. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] His public testimony and the Joint Chiefs' internal memo made one argument through two channels.

Private industry added its own pressure. A 1947 memorandum submitted to President Truman, published under the title "Oil and the State Department policy on Palestine: the documentary evidence of how ARAMCO attempts to destroy the partition resolution of the United Nations," documents a direct lobbying campaign against partition by the Arabian American Oil Company, known as ARAMCO. [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] ARAMCO held the core American oil concession in Saudi Arabia, the relationship that also lay behind Roosevelt's meeting with Ibn Saud in 1945. A region inflamed against the United States threatened that concession's value. The campaign and the government warnings ran in parallel. The sources treat them as separate efforts, not one coordinated one, and do not reproduce ARAMCO's internal communications.

None of this changed the outcome. Truman had heard Henderson's memo directly. According to multiple historical accounts, he was worried about the 1948 election, and Clark Clifford urged him to endorse partition to secure Jewish-American votes in key swing states. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The United States backed partition. In the months that followed, Palestine descended into the violence the warnings had predicted. On February 24, 1948, George Kennan, the State Department's Director of Policy Planning, warned that only foreign troops could now stop it. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman]

Two cautions apply. Historians still debate how much of the later violence was inevitable and how much turned on other factors, so Henderson's predictions should not be treated as correct in every detail. And no one can show that a different decision would have produced a better result by every measure. What the record does establish is that this was not a failure of information. It was an informed decision that weighed documented strategic risk against domestic political considerations, and chose the latter.

sections.h: The New CIA's First Major Warning
sections.html:
On 28 November 1947, one day before the United Nations voted on partition, a ten-week-old American intelligence agency put its judgment in writing: partition would mean war. The familiar version of events holds that American intelligence either never assessed partition or supported it. The documents say otherwise. The newest agency in Washington assessed it formally and warned against it on the eve of the vote.

Before 1947, American foreign intelligence ran first through the Office of Strategic Services, or OSS, created in 1942 and led by William J. Donovan, whom Roosevelt appointed. [cite:w_oss] The OSS was dissolved in October 1945. Its analysts and operatives fed the agencies that followed, beginning with the interim Central Intelligence Group in 1946. [cite:w_oss] The National Security Act of 1947 then created the Central Intelligence Agency, effective 18 September 1947, together with the National Security Council and the structure that became the Department of Defense. [cite:w_nsa1947] Truman appointed the first Director of Central Intelligence, Rear Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter. [cite:w_hillenkoetter]

The agency was barely ten weeks old when it delivered its estimate on Palestine. Its Office of Reports and Estimates issued ORE-55, "The Consequences of the Partition of Palestine," dated 28 November 1947. [cite:cia_ore55] The summary opened with a prediction: if the General Assembly adopted partition, armed hostilities between Jews and Arabs would break out. The United Nations would then be morally bound to enforce its decision. Jewish forces would initially prevail, because of superior organization and equipment. And by backing partition, the United States had already lost much of its prestige in the Arab world; an imposed partition would put American commercial and strategic interests in serious danger. [cite:cia_ore55] The declassified estimate is held in the CIA's own reading room. [cite:cia_ore55]

The estimate did not stand alone. It echoed warnings already on file from Loy Henderson at the State Department, from the Joint Chiefs of Staff and from Defense Secretary James Forrestal, described in [scene:s07j|the previous chapter]. Within roughly ten weeks, four separate parts of the American government had warned in writing against American sponsorship of partition: the State Department's Near East office, the Joint Chiefs, the Secretary of Defense and the new CIA.

The case on the other side came from the President's domestic political advisers, led by Clark Clifford and David Niles. Their view prevailed, both in the partition vote and later in the recognition of Israel eleven minutes after its declaration of independence. The record shows that the warnings were made and read. It does not show them shaping the outcome.

The estimate is worth a closer look, both for what it predicted and for how it framed the risks. It predicted war. It also predicted that the Jewish side would hold the early advantage, because of organization and equipment. The concerns it set out were American interests: prestige in the Arab world, commerce and strategy. That was the language of the State Department and the Pentagon as well, and it was the language that lost.

A question often asked about this period is whether Washington understood what it was backing. On the evidence of ORE-55, it did. American intelligence assessed partition, in writing, and predicted war and damage to American interests. The decision was taken anyway.

sections.h: Objections at the Time
sections.html:
In 1948, as the partition debate played out, a rabbi's organization, a CIA officer and a former college dean all went on record against the campaign for a Jewish state. A familiar assumption holds that no one in the United States questioned lobbying on behalf of a foreign state until much later, in the era of AIPAC. The familiar version misses these voices. Objections were raised as events unfolded, by Jewish organizations, by a CIA officer and by a Christian committee, and a foreign parliament protested as well. The objections were made and published. They were also outweighed.

One organized opposition came from the American Council for Judaism. Founded in 1942, it was led by Lessing Rosenwald with Rabbi Elmer Berger. The Council argued that Judaism was a religion, not a nationality, and it opposed partition. In 1948 it objected to United Jewish Appeal funds being used "for political and foreign governmental purposes." [cite:djn_1948_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman] Its weight should not be overstated. The Council's own historian documents it as a small minority that mainstream Jewish organizations opposed, and Zionist sources describe it as a fringe group. [cite:kolsky_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman]

A more mainstream body also stopped short of endorsing a Jewish state. At the 1944 congressional hearings, the American Jewish Committee proposed an international trusteeship for Palestine instead of a Jewish commonwealth. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] Together, the two bodies show that American Jewish opinion in these years was not one position. Jewish institutions argued openly for alternatives to statehood.

Criticism also came from inside the national-security world. In 1948 Kermit Roosevelt Jr. published a 24-page pamphlet, "The Partition of Palestine: A Lesson in Pressure Politics." [cite:ptsem_kr_pamphlet] Roosevelt would later serve as the CIA's field commander in the 1953 coup in Iran. [cite:w_kermit_jr] That same year, with Virginia Gildersleeve, former dean of Barnard College, he formed the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land. The committee warned that "extreme Zionist pressure" risked disrupting national unity. [cite:mosaic_cia_zionism] [cite:w_kermit_jr] Its argument concerned the political process in Washington, the same concern Reston had raised in the New York Times in 1946.

Objections came from abroad too. Iraq's parliament protested the congressional resolutions of 1944. [cite:djn_1944_marshall]

None of these objections changed the outcome. The pattern matches the one traced in the preceding chapters on [scene:s07j|the warnings] and the CIA estimate. Concerns were stated clearly, on the record and in time, and then set aside. Formal action on foreign agents came only much later, with a 1962 order under the Foreign Agents Registration Act and the Fulbright hearings of 1963.

These critics matter for two reasons. First, they refute the idea that lobbying for a foreign state was an unthinkable subject before recent decades; the question was posed in print in 1948. Second, the critics included Jewish organizations as well as Christian and governmental voices, so the debate cannot be reduced to one community against another. It was an argument among Americans about how their government was making a decision. In the years before 1948, one side of that argument consistently won.

sections.h: Resolution 181: The Three-Day Vote
sections.html:
On November 29, 1947, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, recommending the partition of Mandate Palestine, the territory Britain then governed. The final tally was 33 in favor, 13 against and 10 abstentions, enough to clear the two-thirds threshold the Assembly required. [cite:un_unispal_186560] [cite:avalon_res181] [cite:britannica_res181] The familiar account ends with that number and calls it the peaceful, democratic creation of a state by international consensus. The procedural record does not stop there. The vote that succeeded on November 29 was not the first count. An initial tally had found 25 in favor, short of two-thirds, and the Assembly President, Aranha, arranged a three-day postponement. [cite:un_181_records] [cite:un_181_text]

Those three days are the hinge of the story. A resolution that lacked the votes, then passed after a pause, had a specific window in which something changed. The record does not explain every delegation's reasoning. It does document several of the forces at work inside that window.

The first was the American executive. The Truman administration pushed for a yes vote, while the State Department and the Pentagon opposed the push, warning of Arab anger and of the stakes for Cold War oil strategy. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The most senior internal objection came from James Forrestal, the first Secretary of Defense and formerly Secretary of the Navy. His diaries, published after his death as The Forrestal Diaries (1951), record his distaste for what he called the "bullying" and "coercion" of small states to secure their votes. They also record his conviction that Middle East policy was being driven by domestic political calculation rather than national interest. [cite:un_unispal_186560] A private diary written at the time, not for an audience, is a primary source of unusual weight. It shows a sitting cabinet officer objecting to his own government's methods. It does not, however, itemize which tactic was used on which country by which official.

The second force is visible in the states that moved. Haiti, Liberia and the Philippines shifted from a no vote or an abstention to yes during the postponement. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The historian Michael Cohen, in Palestine and the Great Powers (1982), documents the shift and ties it to a broader pattern of pressure on smaller, economically dependent nations. Liberia is the best-documented case. The Firestone Tire and Rubber Company held a rubber concession there of roughly 1.1 million acres, which made the company, in effect, the Liberian economy. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Cohen connects that dependency to Liberia's change of vote. Liberia's own ambassador complained that the American delegation had threatened aid cuts to several countries in the same period. These were two separate pressures, one corporate and one diplomatic, converging on one small state. The sources do not describe a single coordinated operation, and the exact mechanics of the Firestone leverage are less fully documented than the economic relationship itself. Firestone had no stake in Palestine. Its importance is what it shows: a great power's commercial hold over a small client could be turned into that client's vote on an unrelated question.

The Philippine and Haitian shifts are less fully documented. According to the sources, the Philippines reversed course after American intervention. Its representative, General Carlos Romulo, later wrote of being recalled and overruled by his own president: "This particular chapter in history had been exceedingly unpleasant to me." Haiti is reported to have changed position after direct communication from the American executive. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Cuba offers a contrast. Its delegate said publicly that Cuba would vote against partition "in spite of the pressure that has been brought to bear upon us," which suggests the same campaign reached states that resisted it. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition]

The third force came from Moscow. The Soviet Union and its bloc voted yes, and the documented motive was anti-British: partition would end the Mandate and weaken Britain's position in the Middle East. [cite:un_unispal_186560] The same logic would lead the USSR to supply arms to the new state through Czechoslovakia in 1948. Soviet-Israeli relations cooled substantially within a few years, which fits a vote driven by strategy rather than lasting alignment.

One group had no part in any of this. The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine had no vote in the General Assembly and no direct voice in the decision that divided its territory. The plan allocated 55 percent of the Mandate to the Jewish state, with about 30 percent of the population, and 45 percent to the Arab state, with about 70 percent, and made Jerusalem an international zone. [cite:britannica_res181] This book does not weigh every argument made at the time for that formula. But the structural fact is plain: the people most affected were the object of the resolution, not participants in it.

Resolution 181 was a real international act with genuine legal weight. It was neither the serene consensus of the familiar account nor a secret plot. It was a contested vote, carried after a three-day postponement by a convergence of different self-interests: an American White House overriding its own State Department and Pentagon, a Soviet Union seeking to push Britain out, and small dependent states moved at the margin. [cite:un_181_records]

Forrestal's warnings were overruled. He left office in early 1949, and weeks later he died in a fall from a high window at Bethesda Naval Hospital, where he was being treated for depression and exhaustion. The death was ruled a suicide; some historians consider the ruling contested. [cite:un_unispal_186560] His opposition is documented. This book builds no theory on the circumstances of his death.

sections.h: Acceptance, Rejection and the Two Escalations
sections.html:
In the days after the partition vote of November 29, 1947, one side said yes, the other said no, and the fighting began. A single sentence has long served as the summary: Israel accepted, the Arabs rejected and started the war. In its fuller form, the familiar account holds that the Arab side rejected a peaceful UN compromise and at once launched a war against a state that had only accepted it. That sentence joins two separate questions. The first is who accepted and who rejected Resolution 181. The second is how the fighting actually began. The record gives each its own answer.

On the first question the familiar account is accurate, and it deserves to be said plainly. The Jewish Agency, which represented the Jewish community of Palestine, accepted Resolution 181, reluctantly and with real misgivings about the plan's narrow borders. The Arab Higher Committee, the leading Palestinian Arab body, and the Arab League rejected the plan entirely and vowed armed resistance. Their spokesman, Jamal Husseini, told the United Nations that the partition line would be "nothing but a line of fire and blood." [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] [cite:palquest_un_partition_1947] On who said yes and who said no, the record is one-sided.

The second question is where the compressed story slips. Violence escalated sharply from December 1, 1947, within days of the vote. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] It took the form of a civil war inside Mandate Palestine between Jewish and Arab communities and their armed forces. It was not yet a war between states. Documented attacks in these months ran in both directions. In early January 1948, a car bomb at the former Ottoman government house in Jaffa killed 26 people. On February 15, 1948, Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya near Haifa, part of a documented pattern of Jewish paramilitary attacks on Palestinian towns and villages in the war's first months. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] [cite:aljazeera_remix_partition_transcript] These came well before the massacre at Deir Yassin, treated separately in this book ([scene:ma_s01|Deir Yassin and the massacres of 1948]). None of this means Arab forces and communities had no hand in starting or continuing the violence. It means the violence of these months was two-sided.

The invasion by the armies of neighboring Arab states was a second, distinct escalation. It came on May 15, 1948, the day after Israel's declaration of independence. The war ended in 1949 with Israel's territorial gains reaching far beyond the lines of the UN plan. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] The invasion was real and significant, and its territorial consequences are documented. But it followed five and a half months of civil war already under way. It was not where the war began.

The documented sequence has three parts: a one-sided vote; a two-sided civil war, with attacks from both communities; and, five and a half months later, an invasion by Arab states. Each part is separately documented. The distortion comes from stitching them into one unbroken line from the vote to the invasion, so that the civil-war phase, with attacks such as Qisarya and Deir Yassin, drops out of view.

None of this argues that the Arab League's rejection was justified, or that the later invasion was unprovoked. Nor does it offer a final judgment on which side bears greater responsibility for the outbreak of war. It establishes the shape of the sequence. Told in either direction, as a purely defensive story or a purely aggressive one, the compressed version leaves out a real and documented phase of the conflict. The reader is better served by the full order of events.

sections.h: Golda's Tour: The Money That "Made the State Possible"
sections.html:
In January 1948, between the partition vote and independence, Golda Meyerson set out for the United States to raise money. A common account holds that the new state was built and defended mainly on its own resources. Its founding leader described it differently. That winter the largest single pre-state fundraising effort took place not in Palestine but across the United States, and David Ben-Gurion credited it with making the state possible.

The effort began with a failure. After the November 1947 vote, the Jewish Agency's treasurer, Eliezer Kaplan, went to the United States to raise $7 million and did not succeed. The Jewish Agency represented the Jewish community of Palestine, and Ben-Gurion proposed going himself. The Agency's executive sent Golda Meyerson instead, later known as Golda Meir, then acting head of the Agency's political department. She left in January 1948. [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:reformjudaism_golda]

Her opening came through an established network. Henry Montor, executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal, pressed the Council of Jewish Federations to give her a speaking slot at its assembly in Chicago. Montor was no newcomer to this work. Three years earlier, in 1945, he had gathered 17 wealthy businessmen to meet Ben-Gurion at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment, a meeting that earlier chapters of this book connect to the arms network. [cite:jta_golda_1948] One organizer thus linked the fundraising of 1948 to the arms network of 1945.

The response was rapid. Reports put the early total at about $25 million in the first month. Chicago's Jewish federation took out a $5 million loan and handed it to her. She went on to about twenty cities and returned on 19 March 1948 with a reported $50 million. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m] [cite:jewishpress_golda_25m] By one comparison in the sources, that sum was several times Saudi Arabia's oil revenue for 1947. These are reported figures, and should be read as such.

The money went largely to weapons, including purchases from Czechoslovakia, the supply line taken up later in this part of the book ([scene:cz_s01|the Czech arms]). [cite:jwa_golda_50m] That link matters. It ties a fundraising campaign among American federations and appeals directly to the rifles and aircraft that reached the new state in its first months.

Ben-Gurion's own verdict is on record. He wrote in his diary that her success was "the only ray of light," and he said that history would record that there was "a Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible." [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:yu_golda_archives] His words credit the donors' money. It was raised through a federation-and-appeal network built up since the 1920s, which, through Montor, overlapped with the arms network.

The narrower point the sources support is this. In the decisive months before independence, the new state's ability to arm itself depended heavily on funds raised abroad through named American organizations, and its leaders said so at the time.

sections.h: The Arms Network in Operation
sections.html:
Late in January 1948, on a New Jersey dock, a crate marked "used industrial machinery" split open and spilled explosives. By then the network born at the Sonneborn meeting had been running for more than two years. It was not a plan on paper. It moved real weapons, real aircraft and real money through front operations and transit countries, and it did so before US authorities had pieced together enough of the picture to act.

A common belief holds that American law enforcement knew nothing of any organized Jewish-American effort to arm the Haganah before 1948, and that Israel's founding war was armed only by Israel's own government. The record supports neither half of that belief. Purchases were funneled through "neutral" countries, including Czechoslovakia, Panama, Mexico, Canada and France, before they reached Haganah operatives. [cite:mexico_arms] Academic research on the network documents trucks, radios, aircraft parts and weapons components routed this way specifically to defeat the US and British arms embargo on Palestine. Mexico was among the named transit points, and its role was not incidental. [cite:mexico_arms] The sources establish the pattern and the countries. They do not provide a full ledger of each shipment's route or size.

The most elaborate single operation belonged to Al Schwimmer, a veteran of the US Army Air Transport Command. Schwimmer bought roughly 30 surplus American warplanes. To move them, he built a fictitious Panamanian carrier, Lineas Aereas de Panama, and flew the aircraft via Panama, Brazil and Casablanca toward Israel. For months the scheme evaded both the FBI and the State Department. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] This was not loose, improvised smuggling. One man created an entire airline, with a name and a registration, to carry military aircraft across several countries under the eyes of two federal agencies. The sources do not explain how the airline kept its cover so long; they document its existence, its scale and its outcome.

The network's cover did not fail because of a breakthrough investigation. It failed because of an accident. By the end of January 1948, that crate labeled "used industrial machinery" broke apart while being loaded onto a freighter in New Jersey, and explosives spilled across the dock. It was one of 76 identical crates bound for Palestine. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] The spill, not detective work, is credited with giving US authorities their first concrete evidence of the smuggling network. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] That does not prove the authorities had no suspicions beforehand. The narrower point is that this accident supplied the first hard evidence.

The legal consequences came later and lasted for decades. Nine men involved in the network were tried in a Los Angeles federal courthouse in 1950. Schwimmer was convicted under the US Neutrality Act and lost his American citizenship. Charlie Winters served 18 months in prison for selling two B-17 bombers to the operation. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] Schwimmer went on to found Israel Aerospace Industries. President Bill Clinton pardoned him in 2001, and President George W. Bush posthumously pardoned Winters in 2008. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] The sources dwell on these two, the best documented of the nine. They do not give every defendant's charges or sentence.

Taken together, the routes, the airline, the dock accident and the trials reveal a network that was organized, international and sustained. It worked against US law, not with official American support. And it shows that the arming of the future state was well under way long before May 1948. The Haganah's supply lines through the Americas and Europe were one track of preparation. Another ran through Washington itself, where the question of who would sit in the White House when the decisions came due had already been settled by chance and by a party convention, as the next chapter describes.

sections.h: "Czechoslovak Arms Saved the State"
sections.html:
In 1948, the guns that defended the new state of Israel came from the communist East. Many readers assume the United States armed Israel from its founding. It did not. Washington kept an arms embargo in place, and the government willing to sell to the Jewish side was communist Czechoslovakia, acting with Soviet consent. The American-Israeli arms relationship came years later. In the first year, the decisive supplier was the Soviet bloc.

The pipeline opened before the state existed. On 14 January 1948, the Jewish Agency, which represented the Jewish community of Palestine, signed its first arms contract with Czechoslovakia. The deal was coordinated through "Secretariat D" of the state engineering-works holding. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:wiki_operation_balak] The date matters for two reasons. It came four months before independence. And it came before the UN Security Council's arms embargo, Resolution 46, of 17 April 1948. Czechoslovakia itself became a communist state in the February 1948 coup, and from then on its sales went forward with Stalin's consent. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] The decision fits Soviet diplomacy in the same months, which backed partition and granted the new state its first de jure, or full legal, recognition ([scene:so_s01|Moscow's early support]).

The most striking deliveries came by air. Through Operation Balak, a secret airlift ran from May to August 1948 between Ekron and the Žatec airfield west of Prague, code-named "Zebra." The planes carried arms, ammunition and personnel. They also carried fighters: the Avia S-199, a Czech-built derivative of the German Messerschmitt Bf 109, dismantled and crated inside C-46 and C-54 transports. About 25 were delivered, and they formed 101 Squadron. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:machal_avia_s199] The airlift did not stay secret. A defector exposed the Zebra base, and Washington pressed the United Nations to have it shut. Operations moved to Nikšić in Yugoslavia.

More weapons came by sea. They included some 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles and heavy weapons, many of them first produced for the Wehrmacht. In a 1952 report, the Czechoslovak Foreign Minister, Viliam Široký, put the receipts from the sales at almost $14.5 million. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] Part of that money came from the American fundraising of early 1948 described in the previous chapter.

The Western powers were not neutral bystanders. Britain supplied aircraft and training to the Arab air forces, while the United States kept its embargo in place. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] The result was the reverse of the later alignment. In 1948 the communist bloc armed the new state, and the United States declined to.

The new state's founding leader left no doubt about how he weighed these shipments. In 1968, Ben-Gurion said: "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely." [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] It was one man's verdict, given twenty years after the fact.

The Soviet bloc's role was neither sentimental nor lasting. Within months, according to the same sources, it began shipping the same kind of weapons toward the Arab side. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] The pipeline of 1948 reflected a brief convergence of interests, not a permanent alliance. The military bond with the United States that later defined Israel's arms supply did not yet exist.

sections.h: Plan Dalet: The Document and the Argument
sections.html:
On 10 March 1948, as Britain prepared to withdraw from Palestine, the general staff of the Haganah, the largest pre-state Jewish armed force, issued an operational plan. For decades a familiar account held that Palestinians left their homes in 1948 of their own accord, at the urging of Arab leaders, before any Jewish forces acted. This document stands squarely in the way of that account, and its existence is not in dispute. What historians dispute is what it was for.

Plan Dalet, in Hebrew Tochnit Dalet, or Plan D, was the operational plan for the period before and after the British withdrawal. Its village provisions covered operations against villages inside and near the territory to be held. Brigades were to encircle and search them. Where they met resistance, they were to destroy the village, "setting fire to, blowing up, and planting mines in the debris," and to expel the population beyond the borders of the state. Villages were to be garrisoned or demolished according to their strategic position. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] Put simply, the plan told commanders to hold villages that submitted, and to destroy those that resisted and expel their inhabitants.

The text is a primary document, and historians agree on what it says. Working from the same archives, they disagree about its purpose. The disagreement falls broadly into two readings, with others in between.

The first reading treats the plan as a master plan. Walid Khalidi set it out in a 1961 essay titled "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine." Ilan Pappé developed it in his 2006 book The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] In this view the document was the blueprint for deliberately removing the Arab population from the territory of the Jewish state.

The second reading belongs to Benny Morris, whose archival work documented the expulsions of 1948 in detail. Morris reads Plan Dalet as a military plan to secure territory and lines of communication before the Arab states invaded. In his account, its village provisions gave local commanders discretion, which they used in some places and not in others. Expulsions were decided locally rather than ordered from the center. The outcome was produced by war and by decisions at brigade level, not by a single master plan. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] Other historians stand between these two positions.

The disagreement is narrower than it first appears. Neither reading supports the older account of a purely voluntary departure before any Jewish military action. Morris, whose reading is the less sweeping, is also the historian whose research documented the expulsions in detail. The dispute is about design and cause. Did the text produce the depopulation by intention, or did it supply the frame within which local commanders made it happen?

The plan was carried out in April and May 1948. Operation Nachshon, the fall of Haifa, Jaffa and Safed, and the depopulation of several hundred villages belong to those weeks. They are taken up in the chapters that follow ([scene:s10|independence and the Nakba]), where the reader can judge how closely events fit the document.

This book records the text and the competing readings. It does not resolve an argument the record itself has not resolved. What is settled is the document's language, its date and its authorship by the Haganah general staff. What remains open, among serious historians, is the intent behind it.

sections.h: Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy and Tantura
sections.html:
In April and May 1948, in a village west of Jerusalem, on the road to Mount Scopus and on the coast, civilians were killed in numbers that still shape memory of that year. Two opposite simplifications have grown up around these killings. One holds that no massacres happened. The other holds that only one side suffered them. The documents support neither. They also show how such a record is made: much of what is now known surfaced over decades, and a good deal of it came from Israeli historians, students and veterans themselves.

Deir Yassin was a village west of Jerusalem. On 9 April 1948 it was attacked by the Irgun and Lehi, two underground Jewish militias, supported by the Haganah, the pre-state Jewish armed force, and the Palmach. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75] For decades the death toll was given as 254. Current scholarship puts it at about 110, generally within a range of 107 to 120. Many of the dead were women, children and elderly people. A Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies in a cave. The historian Benny Morris wrote that the killings were followed by mass Arab flight. Material on Deir Yassin in Israeli military archives remains classified, so the record is still incomplete. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The downward revision of the toll is itself part of the history: the larger figure was cited for decades before scholarship narrowed it.

Four days later came a killing on the other side. On 13 April, Arab forces attacked a convoy bound for Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus. They killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses. The attack was a reprisal for Deir Yassin. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The two events are bound together in time and in cause. An honest account cannot tell one without the other.

Tantura shows how slowly some parts of the record came to light. The Alexandroni Brigade captured the coastal village on 22 and 23 May 1948. A master's thesis by Theodore Katz recorded testimony of killings after the village had surrendered. Veterans sued him for libel, and he retracted. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura] The matter did not end there. In the 2022 Israeli documentary Tantura, veterans in their nineties described killings and a mass grave near what is today the popular Dor Beach. A document shown in the film acknowledges that soldiers dug a mass grave. Other veterans deny that any massacre took place, and the number killed cannot be established. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura] What stands on the record is testimony from participants, a document about a grave and continuing denials. There is no firm count.

Taken together, the three episodes defeat both simplifications. Massacres did happen in 1948. In the same weeks they were committed against Arab villagers and against Jews. The Deir Yassin killings came amid the two-sided civil war that preceded the invasion by the Arab states ([scene:s09b|the two escalations]), and in Morris's account they were followed by mass Arab flight.

How this evidence emerged deserves notice. Scholars corrected a death toll. A student's thesis was retracted under legal pressure, then echoed years later by veterans speaking on camera. Archives remain partly closed. The record of 1948 is still being written, and much of it has been written by Israelis examining their own history.

sections.h: Independence, the Nakba and the Czech Guns
sections.html:
At 4 p.m. on May 14, 1948, hours before the British Mandate expired at midnight, David Ben-Gurion declared the establishment of the State of Israel. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] Within eleven minutes the United States granted de facto recognition, a timing arranged by Clark Clifford over State Department objection. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The Haganah became the Israel Defense Forces, and the Mossad was established the following year. War with the neighboring Arab states began. Two familiar accounts of what followed have shaped memory of 1948: that Palestinians left of their own accord on the instructions of Arab radio, and that America created and armed Israel. The record contradicts both.

The second can be dealt with briefly, since the arms pipeline is traced earlier in this part of the book ([scene:cz_s01|the Czech arms]). The United States imposed an arms embargo on all parties to the 1948 war. Truman's recognition was political; the embargo stayed in place. [cite:morasha_czech_arms] The weapons came from communist Czechoslovakia, with Soviet permission: ex-German Mauser rifles, Messerschmitt Bf 109G fighters and ZK 383 submachine guns, flown by C-54 airlift from Žatec airfield in Operation Balak. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_shipments] Ben-Gurion credited them with saving the state. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] Moscow's motive was the same anti-British calculation that had shaped its vote on partition, and Soviet-Israeli relations shifted markedly in the following years.

The first account needs more. Between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians were displaced in the war of 1947 to 1949; Benny Morris estimates 700,000 and Walid Khalidi 750,000. About 500 villages were depopulated or destroyed, and Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) documents each one by name. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] [cite:walid_khalidi_all_that_remains] Palestinians call these events the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe." Much of the documentation comes from Israeli historians, among them Morris, Ilan Pappé, Tom Segev and Avi Shlaim.

The record names specific episodes.
