At Deir Yassin in April 1948 ([scene:ma_s01|the massacres of 1948]), according to Yehuda Slutsky's official Haganah history, the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages to spread panic. Many families in those villages fled in the weeks that followed. Ben-Gurion later noted in his diaries that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight. In July 1948, at Lydda and Ramla, approximately 50,000 civilians were expelled on Yitzhak Rabin's written orders, without Irgun or Lehi involvement. [cite:morris_1948] The broader scholarly record describes a mix of causes, village by village: direct military expulsions, massacres and the fear they spread, and the collapse of Palestinian society under war. Ilan Pappé argues in The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine (2006) that Plan Dalet meets the UN definition of ethnic cleansing. Morris, who stands politically to Pappé's right and does not use the same term, nevertheless documents the same operational facts. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] On that comparison, one account in the sources holds that the debate is over the term, not the facts. The sources also record a disagreement about intent, discussed in the chapter on Plan Dalet. Walid Khalidi and Pappé read the plan as a blueprint for deliberately removing the Arab population. Morris reads it as a military plan whose village provisions left expulsions to local commanders rather than ordering them from the center. Both readings belong to their authors; neither is settled.

The radio story itself was tested in 1961. The Irish journalist Erskine Childers went through the BBC monitoring records, which had transcribed Middle Eastern broadcasts throughout 1948, looking for the alleged evacuation orders. He published his findings in The Spectator: [cite:spectator_childers_1961]

There was not a single order, or appeal, or suggestion about evacuation from Palestine from any Arab radio station, inside or outside Palestine, in 1948. There is a repeated monitored record of Arab appeals, even flat orders, to the civilians of Palestine to stay put.

Decades later, Morris reviewed the archives and found no evidence for the broadcasts in Israeli, Arab or British records. [cite:decolonizepalestine_childers] Childers's finding is narrow. It does not explain every individual departure, but it removes a blanket explanation that the broadcast record does not support.

The territorial figures show what the war decided. Before 1948, Jewish ownership, bought parcel by parcel over decades, amounted to under a tenth of Mandate Palestine; the sources give figures of roughly seven and 9.8 percent. By the 1949 armistice, about 78 percent of Mandate territory was under Israeli control, against the roughly 55 percent allocated by Resolution 181. The difference was made not by purchase but by war and displacement.

Ben-Gurion stands at the center of both halves of this record. He led a community that included Holocaust survivors to statehood against invading armies. He was also the executive authority over a founding that included the expulsions. Both are documented, much of it in Israeli sources. The same holds for the wider frame. The Zionist claim that Europe's Jews needed a place of safety after 1945 was not false. The cost of meeting it fell on Palestinians, who bore no responsibility for Europe's crimes.

Two further details complete the founding year. Jewish communities had lived alongside Arab populations across the Muslim world for over a millennium, from Baghdad's community of 140,000 to Damascus, Cairo, Sana'a and Fez. It was not a utopia, and pogroms occurred. The exodus of roughly 850,000 Jews from Arab lands between 1948 and 1972 had multiple documented causes, including active Israeli and Jewish Agency recruitment operations. [cite:morris_righteous_victims] And on October 28, 1948, the Provisional Council adopted as the state flag the Magen David, the Star of David, between blue stripes, the design of the 1897 Zionist Congress at Basel. It placed the ancient Menorah on the state seal. [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] [cite:wjc_flag_unveiled_1948]

The displacement was never resolved. UN Resolution 194 of December 11, 1948 affirmed a Palestinian right of return. It has never been implemented; Israel has refused it on the grounds that it would end the Jewish demographic majority. The descendants of the displaced, registered with UNRWA, number some 6 million today, most of them stateless. [cite:morris_1948]

sections.h: Who Recognizes a Nation?
sections.html:
On May 14, 1948, eleven minutes after Israel declared its independence, one man in Washington decided that the United States would recognize it. He did so by press release. Some remember American recognition as an act of Congress. It was not. The decision belonged to a single office.

The constitutional basis is a short clause. Article II, Section 3 provides that the President "shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers." [cite:const_art2s3] In Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015), the Supreme Court held that this clause gives the President the exclusive power to recognize foreign sovereigns. [cite:scotus_zivotofsky] Read through that ruling, the power Truman used in 1948 was the President's alone.

Truman used it on the day of the declaration. Eleven minutes after Israel's proclamation, he announced de facto recognition, acceptance of the new government as a working reality, in a short press release. [cite:truman_recognition] Full legal, or de jure, recognition followed on January 31, 1949. In the interval, as an earlier chapter noted, the Soviet Union became the first state to extend full legal recognition, on 17 May 1948 ([scene:so_s01|Moscow's recognition]).

Congress had no vote on the question. Its role was indirect: resolutions of support, appropriations, and the Senate's confirmation of ambassadors, including the first American ambassador to the new state. These were real powers. None of them decided whether the United States would recognize Israel. That choice was made in the White House.

It was also made against the written advice of the government's own senior officials. The Secretary of State, the Joint Chiefs, the Defense Secretary and the CIA had all advised against it ([scene:ore_s01|the CIA's warning]). Their warnings, from the State Department, the Pentagon and the newly created intelligence agency, are traced earlier in this part of the book. Truman overruled them.

The constitutional point gives the story of 1948 its shape. Because recognition rested with the President alone, months of argument over partition, over trusteeship, and over oil and strategy came down in the end to one decision-maker. Advisers could warn, Congress could pass resolutions and advocates could press their case. Only the President could decide.

sections.h: The Actual Military Balance of 1948
sections.html:
On July 1, 1948, with the war still raging, an American government report tried to count the armies in the field. Two popular stories about the military balance of that war circulate side by side. The more familiar holds that Israel was a tiny, vastly outnumbered nation that defeated overwhelming Arab armies through sheer will. The second, told in reply, holds that Israel won only because international sympathy, not real capability, tipped the scales. The military record supports neither. It shows a balance that shifted during the war, in stages, and ended close to the reverse of where the underdog story begins.

That July report is the most useful single document, because it was written while the fighting went on. The sources describe it in one place as a CIA report and in another as a State Department report. It put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000 in total, with about 35,000 used for active operations. It also stated that the Arab armies were stronger than Israel in artillery and tanks at that point, while fielding a wide variety of small arms. [cite:frus1948_military_situation] A report written before anyone knew the outcome carries a credibility that later reconstruction cannot fully match. Its limit is that it is a snapshot of one moment, not an account of the whole war.

Historians describe the whole war in two distinct phases. From the invasion on May 15 until the first truce in June 1948, documented accounts describe Israeli forces as initially inferior in both numbers and arms. That early disadvantage was real, and the record does not dismiss it. After the truce, new recruits and arms supplies, including the Czech shipments described earlier in this part of the book ([scene:cz_s01|the Czech arms]), allowed Israel to seize the initiative decisively. One historical anthology states that for most of the rest of the war, excluding that initial period, "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization." [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948]

By the later stages the reversal was plain in the numbers. Documented accounts state that Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly 2 to 1. The Arab states reinforced their own forces as the war went on, but historians document that they never matched the pace of Israeli growth in men and arms. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] That final advantage does not mean the outcome was inevitable or easy. It means the war's end looked very different from its opening weeks.

Why, then, has the image of overwhelming odds proved so durable? Part of the answer lies in its sources. Many of the most widely repeated figures for the "tiny, outnumbered Israel" account trace back to estimates from John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion during the war. Historians who have worked on the documented order of battle note that, as commander of one of the fighting armies, Glubb had a direct and plausible incentive to inflate Israeli numbers and play down Arab ones. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] This is a reason for caution, not proof of deliberate falsification. But it is a caution rarely mentioned when his figures are cited as neutral fact.

Set against the full record, both popular versions fail. The underdog story holds only for the war's opening weeks, and even there it leans on one interested commander's disputed figures. The sympathy story fares no better. It has to ignore a dated military reversal, the arms deliveries that came with it, and a final 2 to 1 advantage that owed nothing to international goodwill and a great deal to logistics, organization and weapons that arrived and were used.

sections.h: Three Militias Become One Army
sections.html:
On May 14, 1948, the new state of Israel inherited not one army but three armed organizations: the Haganah, the largest pre-state Jewish armed force; and the Irgun and Lehi, two underground militias. Turning them into a single national force took four months. At two points it took force.

The legal step came first. On 26 May 1948, twelve days after the declaration of independence, David Ben-Gurion's provisional government issued an order establishing the Israel Defense Forces. The order outlawed any other armed force and required the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi to merge into the new army. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] On paper, that settled the question. In practice, it set up a test.

The test arrived by sea in June 1948. The Irgun brought an arms ship, the Altalena, to the coast, carrying weapons it meant partly for its own units. Ben-Gurion refused to let the cargo bypass the new army. On 22 June, IDF units under the command of Yitzhak Rabin shelled the ship off the Tel Aviv beach. Sixteen Irgun members and three IDF soldiers were killed. The Irgun's separate units were then disbanded. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] Within a month of the army's creation, the principle was fixed: weapons arriving for the state would pass through the state's own forces. The shelling did not end the political career of the Irgun's commander, Menachem Begin. He became prime minister in 1977.

The second confrontation came in Jerusalem. On 17 September 1948, members of Lehi assassinated the United Nations mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte. The government declared Lehi a terrorist organization and arrested its members. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] Here too the story did not end with the arrests. In February 1949 the detained members were released under a general amnesty. One of Lehi's three leaders, Yitzhak Shamir, became prime minister in 1983. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination]

These events close a line that runs through this book's account of the road to 1948, from the paramilitary groups of the Mandate, Britain's rule over Palestine, to the army of a sovereign state. The pre-state undergrounds had carried out operations described in earlier chapters, among them the attack on Deir Yassin by the Irgun and Lehi with Haganah and Palmach support ([scene:ma_s01|the massacres of 1948]). After independence the question changed. It was no longer what these groups would do against the British or against Arab forces. It was whether the new state would tolerate armed organizations it did not control.

By September 1948 the answer was no. Within four months of its founding, the state had established its monopoly on armed force, by order, by shelling and by dissolution. Yet the sequel ran the other way. Within thirty-five years, the leaders of both absorbed undergrounds had held the office of prime minister. The record of these months is one of absorption rather than simple suppression. The state brought the militias under its control, by force where necessary, and over the following decades brought their leaders into its highest office.

chapters.label: Stage Six
chapters.title: Consolidate and Account
chapters.intro:
The declaration of May 1948 ended one story and began another. In the years that followed, the new state consolidated what the war had produced. More slowly, it was made to account for it. This stage follows both tasks. It traces the state's relationship with Washington through an election year, a loan, a formal recognition and a threatened change of policy. It traces the laws that turned wartime flight into permanent title. It goes to the conference at Lausanne, where return and borders were negotiated and left unresolved, and to the single paragraph of a United Nations resolution on which every later negotiation would turn.

It also steps back. The same week in December 1948 that produced the modern human-rights order also produced the refugee resolution. This stage asks what that order could do for the people already displaced, and what it could not. It traces how the flight of 1948 was explained to Western readers, and how long the archives took to correct that account. Finally, it closes the books on the years before the state: who paid, through which channels, who was tied to whom by what documented link, and what the record can and cannot show about money and politicians.

One question runs through every section. Once the state existed, what did its founding actually rest on, and what did it leave unsettled?
chapters.outro:
By the early 1950s the new state had secured its position on several fronts at once. In Washington it had won de jure recognition, full legal recognition, in January 1949 and a $100 million loan from the Export-Import Bank, and it had turned aside a presidential warning that was never enforced. At home, the Absentees' Property Law of 1950 had placed refugee property in the hands of a state Custodian. The law reached even citizens classed as "present absentees," estimated by 2001 at about 200,000, while military rule kept the displaced from going back. In the immigrant camps, the treatment of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries had opened a wound the state would acknowledge with "regret" only in 2021.

Abroad, the refugee question had hardened. Lausanne had failed over which should come first, peace or return. Resolution 194 had been adopted, reaffirmed, and read in two opposite ways. The new human-rights order counted the displacement of about 711,000 people, fed them and debated their fate. But it placed them outside the main refugee convention and gave them no court. In the West, the story that they had fled on orders would stand until the archives opened.

And the books on the years before the state could now be closed. The record showed mass private giving, documented budgets and defense channels, a connected American network, one documented case of money changing a decision, and an apparatus built over fifty years before the state was declared.

sections.h: Truman After the Money: Retreat, Pledge, and a Threat Not Kept
sections.html:
American recognition in May 1948 did not settle Washington's policy toward the new state. Over the next two years Harry Truman's decisions shifted, sometimes in Israel's favour and sometimes against it, and the dates of those shifts are the best guide to what drove them. Two accounts of the period circulate. One says that once the donors had paid, Truman did whatever Israel wanted. The other says money had nothing to do with it. The dated record supports neither.

The first decision of the summer cut against the new state's supporters. On 25 June 1948 Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act "with very great reluctance," saying that it "discriminates in callous fashion against displaced persons of the Jewish faith." [cite:truman_institute_dpact] He did not leave it there. He pressed Congress for two years, until the act was amended in 1950. [cite:wjc_dpact]

That same summer, Truman privately wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the partition lines, and he was troubled by its refugee policy. He pressed neither point. The historian John Judis documents that Truman backed away in part because his nearly broke whistle-stop campaign needed $100,000 from two donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The fuller story of that transaction belongs to [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg].

The pull of the campaign showed again in September. On 21 September 1948 Secretary of State Marshall endorsed the plan of the murdered UN mediator, Bernadotte, which would have given the Negev to the Arab side. On 28 September the White House aide Clark Clifford was upset that Marshall had approved it without the President's endorsement, and the camp of Truman's opponent, Thomas Dewey, tried to exploit the episode. [cite:jvl_clifford_bernadotte] [cite:djn_marshall_bernadotte_1948] Truman backed away from the plan.

On 24 October 1948, ten days before the election and two days after a statement by Dewey, Truman went further. He quoted the Democratic platform's pledge of full recognition and of revising the arms embargo "to accord to the State of Israel the right of self-defense." He also told government agencies to speed up Israel's loan applications. [cite:ucsb_truman_oct24_1948] On 29 November he assured Weizmann that Israel would keep the Negev.

The pledges were then kept. An Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was set aside for Israel, and on 31 January 1949 the United States granted de jure recognition, full legal recognition of the state. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:docsteach_dejure_1949]

Then the pressure returned. On 28 May 1949, while talks were under way at Lausanne, Truman had a secret note delivered to David Ben-Gurion. It said the United States was "seriously disturbed" by Israel's position on territory and refugees. It said Israel should offer territorial compensation for land it held beyond the partition lines. And it warned that if Israel kept rejecting the UN resolution of December 1948, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable." [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] Israel rejected the demands in June. The threatened revision never came. In May 1950 the United States joined Britain and France in the Tripartite Declaration on the region.

Laid out by date, the sequence has a clear shape. The retreat from the Bernadotte plan and the October pledges came just when money and votes were most needed. After the election Truman both delivered and pushed back, and then did not enforce his own warning. That is neither a president who did whatever he was asked nor one untouched by his campaign's finances. What the documents establish is timing, and one moment in which a historian names financial need as part of the reason a president stopped pressing a point he cared about.

sections.h: Abraham Feinberg: A Donor, a Campaign, and a Decision
sections.html:
Abraham Feinberg's name is missing from most popular accounts of 1948. The usual explanation of Truman's support for Israel rests on personal conviction and on political calculation about Jewish voters in general. In that account, financial need never changed a specific decision. The record contains one case in which it did, and Feinberg stands at its centre.

Abraham "Abe" Feinberg was born in 1908 and raised in the Bronx, and he made his fortune in hosiery. From 1945 until 1968 he played a significant role, mostly behind the scenes, in relations between the United States and Israel. He was a confidant and key financier to three presidents: Truman, Kennedy and Johnson. He was also one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute, the arms-buying network formed in 1945. He died in 1998. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis] [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb]

The 1948 campaign brought him to the centre. Truman's campaign was broke, and Thomas Dewey was widely expected to make him a one-term president. Truman needed $100,000, a very large sum in 1948, to pay for a whistle-stop tour through the Midwest. Feinberg and the jewelry magnate Ed Kaufmann led the fundraising that produced that amount at that moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] Feinberg later summed up his path to influence in his own words: "My path to power was cooperation in terms of what they needed — campaign money." [cite:prnewswire_feinberg_fbi]

The historian John Judis ties that money to a specific decision. In mid-1948 Truman wanted Israel to stop seizing territory by force beyond the UN partition lines, and he was personally "disgusted" by Israel's refugee policy. He reportedly said that Jews had turned their own story on its head by denying Palestinians the right of return. Judis documents that Truman abandoned these impulses in part because he needed the $100,000 from Feinberg and Kaufmann for the tour at that exact moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman]

The claim should be stated with its limits. It is a historian's sourced account, not an inference from general goodwill. It names a donor, a sum, a moment and a policy objection that was dropped. It also says "in part." Judis does not argue that money was the only reason Truman stopped pressing. The wider record of the period, examined in [scene:mn_s02|the question of money and politicians], shows other documented forces behind American policy that involved no payment at all. What the Feinberg case establishes, on Judis's account, is that financial dependence did, at least once, change a specific decision.

Feinberg's role did not end with the campaign. In 1952 US authorities ordered him to register as an agent of a foreign principal over Israel Speaks, a publication he ran. He shut it down rather than register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, the law requiring agents of foreign principals to register. [cite:israellobby_feinberg_fbi] According to Avner Cohen's history Israel and the Bomb, from 1958 Ben-Gurion secretly made Feinberg his chief coordinator for raising private American money for Israel's clandestine nuclear weapons program. He told his staff simply to "call Abe." [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb]

Read together, these episodes describe something more lasting than a single campaign gift. Feinberg was a fixture across three administrations, connected to the arms network of 1945, to the campaign of 1948, and to the nuclear program from 1958. Truman's recognition of the state, eleven minutes after its declaration, sits inside this same wider financial relationship. On the record, this is not a story about money in the abstract. It is a named donor, a precise figure and a dated decision, documented as such.

sections.h: The Absentees' Property Law: Citizens Declared "Absent"
sections.html:
The war of 1948 uprooted hundreds of thousands of people. The fighting did not, by itself, make their loss of property permanent. A body of law passed after the war did that. The familiar account holds that Palestinians who stayed inside Israel in 1948 kept their homes and land as full citizens. For a large number of them, the law said otherwise.

In March 1950 the Knesset, Israel's parliament, passed the Absentees' Property Law, 5710-1950. It built on an emergency regulation of 1948 on absentee property. The text is blunt. All absentees' property is vested in a government-appointed Custodian of Absentees' Property. Every right an absentee held passes automatically to the Custodian. Anyone holding absentee property must hand it over. And the property is vested even if the absentee's identity is unknown. [cite:un_absentees_property_law_text] Anyone found living on such property, including its original owner, was breaking the law. [cite:wiki_present_absentee]

Everything turned on one word. An "absentee" was anyone who had left his usual home during the war, whether for areas outside Israeli control or for anywhere else. That covered the refugees beyond the new borders. It also covered tens of thousands of Arabs who had simply moved from one village to another inside Israel. Afterward they were registered as citizens. They were issued identity numbers. They could vote and stand for the Knesset. In law they were absent; in fact they were citizens living in the country. They came to be called "present absentees," and they could not reclaim their property. [cite:wiki_present_absentee]

Their numbers were not small. By 2001 the present absentees were estimated at about 200,000 people, nearly 17 percent of Israel's Arab citizens. Half the populations of the two largest Arab towns in Israel are internally displaced. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day] [cite:cornell_bilsky_absentee_law]

The objection from abroad came early. In April 1949, before the permanent law existed, the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, the body charged with brokering a settlement, proposed a preliminary step: "suspension of the application of the Absentee law until the final peace settlement." Arab delegations argued that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens. Israel did not suspend it. The 1950 law made the arrangement permanent. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949]

The law did not work alone. From 1948 to 1966 Israel's Arab citizens lived under military rule, which restricted where they could go. Together the two kept internally displaced citizens from physically returning to reclaim their homes, a subject the next part of this book takes up in its own right. Salman Abu-Sitta estimates that more than 1,000 square kilometres were expropriated from Arab citizens between 1948 and 2003; the figure is his own estimate. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day]

The law remains in force and has been applied in East Jerusalem. Its method is simple to state. In everyday speech, "absentee" kept its ordinary meaning. In law, it was stretched to include people who had never left the country. The flight of 1948 is told elsewhere in this book. This law shows how that flight became permanent state ownership, and how it reached even those who stayed. The same questions of refugees and property were also on the table at [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

sections.h: Human Rights Were Born the Same Week
sections.html:
In the second week of December 1948, the UN General Assembly wrote the founding texts of modern human rights. In those same days, the Palestinian refugees were being counted. It is sometimes assumed that the new human-rights system examined the displacement and passed judgment on it. The chronology tells a different story. The parts of the system that might have judged what happened did not yet exist.

Before 1948 there was no worldwide system of human-rights treaties. The League of Nations' Permanent Mandates Commission reviewed Britain's administration of Palestine, but there was no treaty of individual rights and no court to enforce one. The International Committee of the Red Cross worked under the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions of 1929. Its delegate Jacques de Reynier entered Deir Yassin on 11 April 1948 and reported what he found. That was a record, not a judgment.

Then, in a single week of December 1948, the General Assembly adopted three instruments. On 9 December it adopted the Genocide Convention. [cite:w_genocideconv] On 10 December it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, by 48 votes to 0 with 8 abstentions. Article 13(2) of the Declaration reads:

Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country. [cite:un_udhr]

On 11 December came Resolution 194, on the return of refugees and compensation for those not returning. The modern rights order was written in the very days the Palestinian refugees were being counted. The UN Conciliation Commission later put their number at about 711,000.

The wording of Article 13(2) is not in dispute. Its application is. Palestinians cite it alongside Resolution 194. Israel has argued that neither creates a binding right of return for descendants. [cite:un_udhr]

What the international system did offer, it offered as relief. The General Assembly created UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestine refugees, in December 1949, and it began work in May 1950. UNRWA provides schools, health care and relief to registered Palestine refugees. Its mandate is relief and works. It was not given the task of resettlement, of legal protection, or of securing return. [cite:unrwa_who]

The next instrument set Palestinians apart. The 1951 Refugee Convention, in Article 1D, excluded people already receiving protection or help from another UN agency. Because Palestinian refugees had UNRWA, they fell outside the protection system that covers other refugees, and outside the mandate of the UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, to find lasting solutions. [cite:w_refconv] The very fact that they were receiving relief put them in a category of their own.

And there was no court. The International Criminal Court did not exist in 1948. Its founding treaty, the Rome Statute, was adopted in 1998 and came into force in July 2002, with no reach backward in time. Palestine joined in 2015, which is why the Court's jurisdiction begins in that era and not earlier. [cite:w_romestatute]

The sum is plain. The displacement of 1948 was documented by the Red Cross, counted by a UN commission, addressed in a General Assembly resolution, and relieved by an agency created for it. It was debated. It was never judged, because the institutions that might have judged it were either not yet built or not given the task. How the displacement was explained to the public in the meantime is the subject of [scene:np_s01|the next section].

sections.h: The Right of Return: What Resolution 194 Says, and How Each Side Reads It
sections.html:
On 11 December 1948 the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution whose eleventh paragraph is still argued over today. The "right of return" it is said to contain is read in sharply different ways. Two simple versions are common. One holds that international law guarantees every refugee's descendant a return. The other holds that the resolution behind the claim means nothing. The text itself is short, and both sides cite it. The argument is over what it requires.

Resolution 194 (III) was adopted on that December day. Its paragraph 11 resolved that

the refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date

and that compensation should be paid for the property of those choosing not to return. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194] The General Assembly has reaffirmed the resolution every year since 1949. [cite:wiki_res_194]

How the resolution was first received is less tidy than either side's present position suggests. Arab states and Palestinian representatives at first rejected it, because accepting it implied accepting Israel. Palestinians now cite it as the foundation of the right of return.

Israel stated its reading early. Ben-Gurion told the UN conciliators that the clause "live at peace with their neighbours" made return conditional on peace with the Arab states. [cite:unispal_194_survey] Critics of the Palestinian reading add three points. General Assembly resolutions are recommendations, not binding law. The text says refugees "should be permitted" to return, not that they must be. And the return of several million descendants would end Israel's Jewish majority. [cite:unwatch_194]

Supporters of the Palestinian reading answer that the right rests not on Resolution 194 alone but on broader international law. They also point to Israel's own admission to the United Nations in 1949, which came with an assurance from Abba Eban that Israel would honor resolutions 181 and 194. [cite:wiki_res_194]

Both readings are documented, and this book does not settle between them. What can be said is where each puts its weight. The Israeli reading rests on the conditional clause and on the legal standing of a General Assembly resolution. The Palestinian reading rests on the yearly reaffirmation, on wider legal principle, and on Israel's own assurance at admission. Each side quotes the same sentence and stresses a different part of it.

In practice the result has been unbroken deadlock. The talks at [scene:lau_s01|Lausanne] in 1949 broke down on this question, with Israel offering return only within a final peace and the Arab states demanding return first. More than fifty years later, at Camp David in 2000, it was still unresolved. Every negotiation in between has run into the same paragraph. The most lasting disputes of 1948 were not only about land and armies. They were also about how a few lines of text, adopted that December, would be read.

sections.h: Lausanne, 1949: Where Return and Borders Were Negotiated, and Failed
sections.html:
In April 1949, a few months after the fighting, the refugee question came before a formal negotiation at Lausanne. Two opposite accounts of what happened there are still repeated. One says Israel never offered anything on refugees. The other says the Arab states refused every offer. The United Nations' own report on the talks supports neither. It shows two sets of conditions, each arranged in an order the other side would not accept.

The forum was the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine, created by Resolution 194 in December 1948 to help the parties reach a settlement. It convened talks at Lausanne from 27 April to 12 September 1949. The Arab delegations refused to negotiate directly with Israel, so the Commission shuttled between the parties. On 12 May they signed the Lausanne Protocol, which took the 1947 partition map as a basis for discussion. [cite:wiki_lausanne_1949] [cite:pij_lausanne]

The positions were set out early. The Arab states demanded that Israel first accept the return of refugees under Resolution 194, and they wanted the 1947 partition lines. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_israel_studies_peace] Israel held that the Arab invasion had nullified the partition plan and that refugees could be dealt with only inside a final peace. Israel first floated annexing Gaza along with its refugee population; Egypt refused.

Then came the offer. On 3 August, according to the Commission's own progress report, Israel offered to accept the return of 100,000 refugees, which would have brought its Arab population to a maximum of 250,000. The offer was made "only as an integral part of a general and final peace settlement." [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:jvl_ccp_fourth_report] The Arab delegations called it contrary to Resolution 194 and to the Protocol. Israel later withdrew it. The Commission's report also records Israel blocking a committee on orange groves owned by refugees. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report]

The conference ended in September without agreement. The United States had already sent Ben-Gurion a secret warning in May. Now it told Israel it might revise relations over the deadlock. What became of that warning is traced in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's post-election policy].

The shape of the failure explains why it lasted. Israel would discuss return only after peace. The Arab states would discuss peace only after return. Each side's sequence was the reverse of the other's, and neither moved. The offer of 100,000 shows that Israel was ready to put a number on the table. The conditions attached to it, and the Arab rejection of those conditions, show why the number never became policy. With no agreement, roughly 700,000 refugees remained refugees.

That is why Lausanne matters. It was not the last negotiation on the question. But it was the one at which the refugee problem stopped being a consequence of the war and became a permanent feature of the conflict. The question it failed to settle has outlived every negotiation since, and in the end it turns on how one reads a single paragraph of Resolution 194.

sections.h: Where Palestinians Went: A Diaspora Older Than the Flight of 1948
sections.html:
Two Palestinian migrations are often run together. The first began in the 1870s, under Ottoman rule, and carried families to Latin America. The second was the flight of 1948, which carried refugees to neighbouring Arab lands. A common assumption holds that Latin America's Palestinian communities are made up of 1948 refugees who were welcomed with open doors. The familiar version ends there. The record contradicts both halves of it.

The emigration to the Americas began in the 1870s. Most of the early migrants were Christian families from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour. Because they travelled on Ottoman papers, they were long called "Turcos." [cite:palquest_sv]

Chile holds the largest Palestinian community outside the Arab world, with estimates commonly running into the hundreds of thousands. In Santiago, the football club Palestino was founded in 1920; as Club Deportivo Palestino it plays in the national first division. [cite:w_palchile] [cite:w_palestino]

El Salvador's community is estimated at roughly 70,000 to 100,000 people, overwhelmingly of Bethlehem origin. It is described as the third-largest in Latin America, after Chile and Honduras. By the same account, El Salvador's Bethlehem-descended population is several times larger than Bethlehem's own population today. [cite:palquest_sv]

The doors were not open. In 1921 El Salvador declared Arabs and Chinese to be "pernicious" races, a documented act of exclusion. The country's elites looked down on the "Turcos" as peddlers. The community built its standing in commerce in spite of that discrimination. [cite:palquest_sv]

In time it reached the top of national politics. El Salvador has had two presidents of Palestinian descent. Antonio Saca won in 2004, defeating another candidate of Palestinian descent, Schafik Handal. Nayib Bukele won in 2019. His paternal grandparents emigrated from Jerusalem and Bethlehem in the early twentieth century, and his father became a well-known imam. [cite:palquest_sv] [cite:jweekly_bukele] Bukele himself is pro-Israel, a reminder that descent does not decide a politician's position. [cite:jweekly_bukele]

The refugees of 1948 were a different population, with a different date of departure and a different legal status. Roughly 700,000 people displaced that year went mainly to Jordan, including the West Bank, and to Lebanon, Syria and the Gaza Strip. There, from 1950, they were registered by UNRWA, the UN relief agency for the refugees described in [scene:ud_s01|the section on human rights].

Keeping the two apart matters for both histories. To treat the Ottoman-era emigrants as refugees of 1948 erases what they actually did: they left under an empire, met formal discrimination, and built communities that eventually produced heads of state. To treat the refugees of 1948 as part of an older, settled diaspora erases what happened to them: a displacement that remains unresolved. The two migrations began in the same land. They did not begin for the same reason.

sections.h: The Yemenite Children Affair
sections.html:
Between 1948 and 1954, families living in Israel's immigrant transit camps say their babies were taken from them. The young state's treatment of its own newcomers is part of the founding record, and this episode has been fought over inside Israel for decades. A common view holds that the founding generation treated all Jewish immigrants alike. The record of the camps, and of the children who disappeared from them, complicates that view.

Jews who arrived from Arab and Muslim countries after 1948 were often placed in transit camps, the ma'abarot, shantytown settlements for new arrivals. According to the Times of Israel, these immigrants were largely sidelined by the European-born leadership of the ruling Labor party. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021]

The affair began in these camps and the clinics that served them. Families, mostly from Yemen but also from the Balkans, North Africa and elsewhere, say that between 1948 and 1954 their infants were taken from camps and clinics. Doctors told the parents their children had died, but would not give them bodies or death certificates. The families allege that the babies were given to Ashkenazi families, Jews of European origin, in Israel and abroad. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] The children who vanished this way are counted in the hundreds.

The state investigated more than once. Three official inquiries, the first in 1967, concluded that most of the children had died of disease. [cite:arabnews_stolen_babies] That did not end the dispute. The newspaper Israel Hayom later published documents that, it said, pointed to possible organized involvement by state bodies. [cite:israelhayom_yemenite] As described, those documents show a possibility, not an established finding. The official inquiries and the families' accounts remain in conflict.

The government's formal answer came in February 2021. The cabinet approved NIS 162 million, about $50 million, in compensation, with about 1,050 families eligible. Its decision stated that the government "regrets" the events and recognizes the families' suffering. [cite:tps_yemenite_2021] [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] Prime Minister Netanyahu called the affair one of the most painful in the state's history and asked that it be taught in schools. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021]

The families' organizations were not satisfied. The decision, they said, lacked the essential element: an official apology and an acceptance of responsibility. [cite:toi_yemenite_2021] That gap between regret and responsibility is the heart of the matter. The compensation acknowledged suffering. It did not accept responsibility for what had happened.

The affair belongs in an account of 1948 and its aftermath for a reason beyond the individual cases. It is documented evidence of a hierarchy inside the new state: an Ashkenazi establishment, and Mizrahi immigrants, Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, placed in camps under its administration. Readers raised in Israel often learn this part of the record late. It sits beside the laws governing the state's Arab citizens, described in [scene:ap_s01|the Absentees' Property Law]. Together they show that building the state meant deciding how different groups of its people would be treated, and that those decisions were not the same for all.

sections.h: From AZEC to AIPAC
sections.html:
AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, is often thought to have appeared suddenly in the 1950s as a new, independent lobbying group with no earlier history. The familiar version stops there. The institutional record does not. It shows an unbroken line of descent from the wartime American Zionist Emergency Council, or AZEC. It also shows a federal foreign-agent case along the way, and that case must be stated precisely, because it concerned a successor body, not the original one.

The American Zionist Emergency Council, built under Abba Hillel Silver in 1943, did not dissolve after statehood. In 1949 it was renamed the American Zionist Council and registered as a tax-exempt nonprofit. [cite:azec_powerbase] This was an ordinary continuation, not the founding of a new organization.

The foreign-agent question arose more than a decade later. On 21 November 1962 the Internal Security Section of the Justice Department, under Attorney General Robert Kennedy, ordered the American Zionist Council to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The department alleged that the Council had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency over the preceding eight years. [cite:azc_fara_doj] The order was aimed at the 1949 successor, not at the 1943 body. It was an allegation against one organization at one time, later withdrawn, and it should not be read back across the whole lineage as one continuous violation.

The Justice Department did later withdraw its demand. In 1963 the Council's lobbying work was split off into a newly restructured organization, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. AIPAC was set up to run solely on private American donations, and on that basis it maintained that it was not a foreign agent. [cite:aipac_wiki]

The sequence is short, and every step is documented: a wartime council, a new name in 1949, a foreign-agent order in 1962, its withdrawal, and a restructuring in 1963. Together these steps answer the question of where AIPAC came from. It was not a new creation without a past. It was the lobbying arm of an organization whose roots ran back to the campaign of the 1940s, reorganized after a federal challenge so that its money came from American donors alone. The wider network that AZEC belonged to is mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network map].

sections.h: How the Flight Was Told: "They Left on Orders" Until the Archives Opened
sections.html:
For more than a decade after 1948, the dominant Western account held that the Palestinians had left voluntarily, on the orders of Arab leaders, and that this had been established at the time. Parts of what happened were indeed reported promptly. But the explanation that took hold for the mass flight was not supported by the documents, and it took some forty years for the documents to displace it.

Some events were known almost at once. The killings at Deir Yassin in April 1948 were reported in Western newspapers within days. They were documented by the Red Cross delegate who entered the village. News of the massacre spread through Arab Palestine, and the historian Benny Morris records it as a major accelerant of flight. [cite:w_morris_birth]

Objection was public, and some of it came from prominent Jewish figures. On 4 December 1948 a group that included Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook published a letter in The New York Times condemning Menachem Begin's new Herut party. The letter cited Deir Yassin and called the party fascist in its methods. [cite:w_arendt_letter] It stands as a documented Jewish objection at the time, printed in America's paper of record.

Yet the explanation that became standard in the West ran the other way. Arab leaders, the story went, had broadcast orders by radio for civilians to leave. In the 1950s this became the usual explanation in Western and Israeli official accounts. Its effect was to place responsibility for the refugee problem on the Arab states.

The familiar version stopped there. The record did not: the broadcasts had been monitored, so the claim could be tested. In May 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers published "The Other Exodus" in The Spectator. He reported that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of Arab broadcasts in 1948, including the BBC's. He found no evacuation orders. He found appeals to stay. His article set off a long public dispute, with claims and counterclaims running for weeks in the letters pages. The Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi had made the same case, from Arab sources, in 1959. [cite:w_childers]

The decisive correction came from Israel's own records. In 1988 Benny Morris published The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem, drawing on newly opened Israeli military and state archives. He concluded that the main causes of flight were military attack, expulsion and fear. Some local Arab commanders, he found, had ordered women and children evacuated, but there was no general Arab order to leave. Later editions of his work found more expulsion orders. [cite:w_morris_birth]

How the account changed matters as much as where it ended. The early version was a political narrative the documents did not support, and the documents that corrected it were Israeli state archives, not an adversary's claims. The correction has limits. Historians still disagree about intent and planning, including the role of the military plan known as Plan Dalet. But mainstream scholarship no longer defends the account that the refugees simply left on orders.

The forty-year gap is itself part of the history. The explanation that took hold in the 1950s was checked against the monitoring records only in 1961, and against Israel's own archives only in 1988. The same distance between a founding story and its documents is the subject of [scene:pn_s01|seven founding narratives, checked].

sections.h: How Israel Was Sold to Americans
sections.html:
Between 1945 and 1948, Americans were given a case for a Jewish state. It is often assumed that they backed Israel because it was a proven strategic ally. The familiar version stops there. The documents do not. The case made to the American public at the time rested on quite different grounds. The strategic argument came later, after a long interval, and against the earlier opposition of the national-security establishment.

The first ground was refuge. The central argument of 1945 to 1948 was humanitarian: some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe, and the Holocaust behind them. Earlier parts of this book document that crisis in detail.

The second ground was religious. For Christian supporters, a Jewish state in Palestine fulfilled restorationist belief, the conviction that the Jews would be restored to the land, a current this book traces back to 1839. The third ground was political: the new state was presented to Americans as a democracy.

What the case did not rest on, in 1948, was American strategic interest. The national-security establishment argued the opposite. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs, the Defense Secretary and the CIA all warned that backing the new state would harm American interests. They were overruled. At the founding, Israel was not supported as a strategic ally. The strategic professionals regarded support as a liability.

The publicity of the period also carried a hostile picture of Arabs. Pro-Zionist material leaned heavily on the Grand Mufti's wartime collaboration with Hitler, a real and documented episode, and used it as a broad brush. That should be kept apart from what came much later. The organized, well-funded anti-Islam network in the United States is documented mainly from the 2000s, building on currents that emerged after 1967 and after 1979. [cite:cap_fear_inc] Anti-Arab framing was present in 1948. The industry did not yet exist.

The strategic case arrived a generation after the founding. The argument that Israel was a strategic asset grew after its victory in 1967. It was formalized under President Reagan, who called Israel a strategic asset and signed a strategic-cooperation agreement in 1981.

The order of events matters for how the relationship is understood today. Israel was first presented to Americans in terms of refuge, scripture and democracy. The relationship is often defended now in terms of alliance and security. The second set of terms was not available in 1948, and the people whose job was to judge American security interests at the time said so in writing. Reading today's framing back into the founding misdescribes both periods. It is one of several founding narratives examined in [scene:pn_s01|seven narratives, checked].

sections.h: Did Money Buy the Politicians?
sections.html:
In mid-1948 Harry Truman's campaign was nearly broke, and the question of what money did to American policy on Palestine has been argued ever since. It is usually answered in one of two ways. Either Zionist money bought Congress and the White House, or money played no part at all. Both answers treat a bundle of separate claims as one. Pulled apart, the claims stand on very different evidence, and one of them cannot be settled either way.

The first claim is that there was organized political pressure. This is documented in detail. The record includes the local committees of the American Zionist Emergency Council, the movement's chief lobbying body in the United States; its letter and telegram campaigns; its book America and Palestine; the 1944 party platforms; and the Wagner–Taft resolution. Much of it survives in the movement's own files. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]

The second claim is that money changed a specific decision. This is documented once. The historian John Judis records that in mid-1948 Truman stopped pressing Israel over territory and refugees in part because his campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann. The full case is set out in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg].

The third claim is that members of Congress were systematically paid before 1948. This cannot be proved or disproved, because the records that would decide it were never required to exist. Until the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, the governing law was the Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925. It required disclosure mainly from party committees working across several states, not from candidates. It carried few penalties. It left enforcement to Congress, which rarely enforced it. It was riddled with loopholes, and candidates' donors were largely hidden until 1971. [cite:wiki_fcpa_1925] [cite:sage_fec_history] [cite:crs_campaign_finance] Without disclosure records, any claim that particular legislators were paid is unsupported. So is any claim that they were not.

The fourth point is that other documented forces pushed the same way without money. They include the moral urgency of the Holocaust years; concentrations of Jewish voters in states such as New York; sincere Christian restorationism, the belief that the Jews should be restored to Palestine, going back to 1839; Henry Wallace's personal Zionism; and the 1922 Lodge–Fish resolution, which is credited to lobbying with no payment documented.

The opposing record belongs here too. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, and they were overruled. The pressures that beat them are documented as political. A financial one is documented only in the single case above.

The result is a finding with a visible gap in it. What can be shown is an organized, well-funded political movement with direct access to decision-makers, and one documented case of money shifting a decision. Wider claims of bought politicians are not in the record. That silence is itself a finding. It is evidence neither of innocence nor of guilt. It reflects a legal regime under which the evidence never had to be kept.

sections.h: Who Paid for It All? The Funding Ledger
sections.html:
For decades two explanations of how the movement was paid for before 1948 have circulated. One says it ran on a few wealthy patrons. The other says it ran on secret government money. The familiar versions stop there. The documents do not. They show organized private giving on a mass scale, increasingly American, sustained over decades. Throughout this section, amounts are given as they stood at the time and, where the source allows, in today's dollars.

The movement's permanent fund was Keren Hayesod, its central fundraising arm. From April 1921 to December 1929 it raised $20.1 million worldwide, about $370 million today. More than half, $11.0 million, came from the United States. The next largest sources were South Africa ($1.5 million), Germany ($0.98 million), Romania ($0.88 million), Britain ($0.88 million), Poland ($0.82 million) and Canada ($0.74 million). [cite:jta_kh_decade] Over its first twelve years, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised. [cite:jta_kh_12yr] Before 1948 the fund paid for immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works. [cite:jvl_kh]

The scale changed with the United Jewish Appeal, the American umbrella campaign formed in 1939. It raised more than $124 million between 1939 and 1945, and $100 million in 1946. [cite:raphael_uja] In 1947 it raised about $110 million. [cite:cambridge_solidarity] In 1948 it raised a record $150 million from more than a million contributors in 4,950 communities. [cite:jta_uja_1948] That campaign was described as the largest non-government humanitarian campaign in American history. [cite:jta_uja_1948] [cite:cambridge_solidarity] Across 1946 to 1948 the three campaigns came to about $360 million, or about $5.2 billion today.

Where the money went needs care. Of the 1948 total, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe, and $10.4 million to resettling refugees in the United States. [cite:jta_uja_1948] Roughly half went to Palestine, about 43 percent to relief in Europe and about 7 percent to the United States. To count the whole sum as funding for Israel would overstate it; much of it fed Holocaust survivors in Europe. In today's dollars, measured by the consumer price index of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the 1948 campaign comes to about $2.0 billion and its Palestine share to about $1.0 billion. [cite:bls_cpi]

The conversions follow a stated method. Each amount is multiplied by the ratio of the 2025 consumer price index, 321.943, to the index for the year in question. That is the same method the government's own inflation calculator uses. [cite:bls_cpi] Sums in pounds are first converted at the exchange rates of the period, and values before 1913 are approximate.

Arms were bought through separate channels, and they are harder to total. The purchases ran through front companies. Estimates of the cost of Czech arms run from about $14.5 million to about six times that. Golda Meyerson's fundraising tour brought in about $50 million, which went largely to weapons. The government of Somoza's Nicaragua supplied $3 million in letters of credit. [cite:israelaffairs_italy] These are ranges, not a total.

The ledger has an honest limit. No audited grand total exists, and some streams overlap, so they are shown separately rather than added together. Even so, the shape is clear. The bank, the land, the immigration and the arms were built over half a century on giving that came from around the world, grew increasingly American, and by 1948 was drawn from more than a million individual donors. That does not fit the picture of a handful of patrons, a point taken up again in [scene:pn_s01|seven founding narratives, checked]. How the operating budgets and the defense money worked is the subject of [scene:gf_s02|the next section].

sections.h: Charity for an Army: Budgets, Defense, and Britain's Bill
sections.html:
In 1939 the American consul in Jerusalem filed a report on a budget. It offers one of the first clear views of how the movement paid for its defense. The familiar account says the pre-state army was funded in secret, by unknown means, and that Britain ran Palestine on the cheap. The record is more specific on both counts. The operating budgets were reported at the time. Defense money ran through named channels. And Britain itself put a figure on what holding the country cost.

The budgets can be followed from that year. After the Zionist Congress, the consul reported that the budget of the Jewish Agency, the movement's executive body in Palestine, had been set at £720,000, about $74 million today. Of that, £100,000 was for settling refugees and £80,000 for "the Jewish security service (defense)." [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget] Defense, in other words, was a budget line from at least that date.

The American share grew fast. In 1944 the Jewish National Fund, the movement's land-buying arm, spent $10.8 million raised in the United States, and the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod spent $14.9 million, a combined $25.7 million. The United Palestine Appeal's budget for 1945 was $35.3 million. [cite:djn_1945_upa] In 1946 the Agency said it had received $12 million from the United States the year before. It sought a budget of $56 million, about $0.93 billion today. [cite:djn_1946_budget]

Defense money had its own channels. In 1938 the Jewish National Council, the representative body of the Jewish community in Palestine, created Kofer HaYishuv. This was a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, meant to fund central security and expand the Haganah, the community's underground militia. [cite:w_kofer] Ten years later the link between charity and defense was stated openly in the United States. In June 1948 a community campaign advertisement in Detroit told donors that "the United Jewish Appeal is the official American agency for aid to Haganah," and that the only channel for such aid was the local Allied Jewish Campaign. It also warned that collecting money for dissident militias was fraud. [cite:djn_1948_haganah] Charity and defense ran through the same pipe, and the campaign said so.

The other side of the ledger was Britain's. Under the Mandate, Britain's administration of Palestine, the civil budget rose from £P1.9 million in 1922–23 to £P3.2 million in 1934–35. [cite:horowitz_1937] The garrison cost £1.5 million in 1923–24. [cite:league_report_garrison] By the British government's own end-of-Mandate statement, the military forces in Palestine cost the British taxpayer about £100 million in 1945–47, about $6.7 billion today. Parliament debated keeping some 80,000 to 100,000 soldiers there. [cite:hmg_termination_1948] [cite:hansard_1947_08] About 750 British soldiers and police were killed over the period. [cite:nam_palestine]

The resulting picture is substantial but not complete. The operating budgets, the defense levy, the charity channel and Britain's cost are all documented. No audited total of the Haganah's budget is publicly available, and this book does not supply one. What can be said is that the defense effort was not financed by unknown means. It was paid for partly through a published budget line, partly through a local levy, and partly through American campaigns that called themselves the official channel of aid. Britain, for its part, was paying heavily, by its own account, to hold the territory in the Mandate's final years.

sections.h: The Network Map, 1897–1948
sections.html:
The American pro-Zionist effort of the half-century before 1948 is sometimes described as a loose crowd of unconnected sympathizers. The record describes something more structured. It shows a set of organizations tied to one another by founding, funding and coordination, reaching outward to named legislators, White House aides and donors. This section maps those ties by their distance from the centre and names the kind of each tie. It maps only documented organizational, political and financial relationships. It asserts no tie on the basis of identity.

At the centre stood the Jewish Agency and the World Zionist Organization, under Weizmann and Ben-Gurion. They set the movement's goals. A Justice Department order of 1962 alleged that the Jewish Agency funded the American Zionist Council, the postwar successor of the wartime lobbying body; the department later withdrew its demand that the Council register. [cite:azc_fara_doj]

One step out were the bodies tied directly to that centre by organization. The American Zionist Emergency Council, or AZEC, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, ran the national campaign. The Zionist Organization of America had reached 147,000 members by 1918. Hadassah completed this first circle. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]

A second step out were bodies that those organizations created or coordinated. The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine were both organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has called them "hardly autonomous." Henry Montor ran the United Jewish Appeal. The Sonneborn Institute, with its front company Materials for Palestine, was set up at Ben-Gurion's meeting in 1945, linking fundraising to arms. [cite:hnn_clark_truman]

The third step reached the political and financial endpoints. In Congress they included Senator Robert Wagner, chairman of the American Palestine Committee, and Senator Robert Taft, co-sponsor of the Palestine resolution; Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III, sponsors of the 1922 resolution; and Representative Sol Bloom, chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee and a target of telegram campaigns. [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation] In the White House they included the aides David Niles, Clark Clifford and Max Lowenthal, and Truman's friend Eddie Jacobson, all of whom carried the Zionist case to the President. [cite:wiki_david_niles] Among donors they included Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann, whose $100,000 for Truman's 1948 campaign is documented, and the 1948 tour that raised about $50 million through Montor's network.

Two loops stand out in this structure, and they are the map's clearest finding. The first might be called the commitment loop. AZEC collected legislators' statements of support, printed them in its book America and Palestine, and mailed the book to every member of Congress. It then used the book to press for votes and platform planks. Those produced new statements, which fed the next round. Public statements became leverage for more statements.

The second is the Montor loop. Henry Montor gathered the donors for the 1945 Sonneborn meeting, out of which the arms network formed. Montor then secured Golda Meyerson's platform for 1948, and her tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms. One fundraiser's network ran from the arms meeting of 1945 to the tour of 1948.

The map does not show a single chain of command, and it should not be read as one. Some ties were organizational, some political, some financial, and the degree of control varied. What it does show is that the effort was not a loose crowd of sympathizers. It was a connected structure, built over decades, whose links can be named and sourced. Its successor organizations are traced in [scene:s07g|From AZEC to AIPAC].

sections.h: Seven Founding Narratives, Checked
sections.html:
Many stories about Israel's founding are taught as settled history. This section gathers seven of them and sets each beside the documented record presented elsewhere in this book. Six are familiar parts of the founding account. The seventh comes from the opposite direction, and it is included on purpose: the standard that checks the founding slogans must also check the conspiracy myths about who paid.

The first is the slogan "a land without a people for a people without a land." The familiar version stops there. The count does not. Britain's own census of 1922, taken two years into the Mandate, recorded 757,182 people, about 11 percent of them Jewish. The slogan did not describe the country.

The second holds that Palestinians left because Arab leaders told them to. The monitored broadcasts of 1948 showed no general evacuation order, and Israel's own archives point to attacks, expulsions and fear as the main causes of flight. That correction is traced in [scene:np_s01|how the flight was told].

The third is the image of a miracle against impossible odds. A CIA assessment from 1948, and later research, describe a war fought in two phases that Israel ended with roughly a two-to-one advantage in manpower. The victory was real. The odds at its end were not those of the familiar image.

The fourth holds that Israel was born of the Holocaust. The program, the British pledge and the Mandate all came before Hitler, by between 11 and 37 years; the dates 1896, 1917, 1920 and 1922 mark them. The Holocaust sped up support for a state. It did not create the program.

The fifth holds that Israel accepted partition, the Arabs rejected it, and the Arabs then started the war. The vote did split as described. But the fighting began as a two-sided civil war months before the Arab armies entered.

The sixth holds that the land was bought fair and square. In 1947 about 7 percent of the land was Jewish-owned. Purchases were made legally from absentee owners. But under Ottoman land law those purchases evicted the tenant farmers who worked the land, and later confiscations followed, among them those under the absentee property law of 1950.

The seventh comes from the other side: the claim that the Rothschilds, or a few Jewish bankers, paid for it all. The documented money came overwhelmingly from mass small-donor giving, with more than a million American contributors in 1948 alone. Edmond de Rothschild, the Paris Rothschild, did fund early colonies, but he opposed Herzl. The founding was not bankrolled by a handful of financiers, as the ledger in [scene:gf_s01|who paid for it all] shows in detail.

Taken together, the seven checks do not add up to a single verdict. Some founding claims are simply contradicted by the record, as with the empty land and the orders to flee. Others are partly true but misleading as usually told, as with the partition vote, the legal land purchases and the military victory. And the myth of a few bankers fails just as the slogans do, against the same kind of evidence. The record corrects in every direction. That is what makes it worth trusting.

sections.h: Fifty-One Years From a Bank to a State: The Whole Sequence, Step by Step
sections.html:
In 1897 a congress at Basel set a goal; in 1948 a state was declared. A common account treats Israel's creation as a sudden response to the Holocaust and to a postwar decision at the United Nations. Laid end to end, the record shows something else: a sequence built over five decades and across two continents, each step resting on the one before. The movement did not start cold and turn hot in 1947.

The first layer was money and land. In 1897 the Basel Congress set the goal. In 1899 the Jewish Colonial Trust was founded, a bank chartered in London and funded by small shareholders. In 1901 the Jewish National Fund began buying land that was never to be resold. In 1902 came the Anglo-Palestine Bank. Between 1912 and 1918 an American machine took shape: Hadassah; Brandeis, with access to President Wilson; and the Zionist Organization of America, at 147,000 members. In 1917 came the Balfour Declaration, Britain's pledge, addressed to Lord Rothschild. In 1920 came Keren Hayesod, the movement's central fund.

The second layer was political and monetary. In 1921 came the Weizmann–Einstein tour, and a $5 million tour that met President Harding. In 1922 Congress endorsed Balfour through the Lodge–Fish resolution. In 1927 a Palestine pound managed from London was introduced. In 1929 non-Zionist American money joined an enlarged Jewish Agency. In 1932, and again in 1941 and 1942, Christian committees were organized from the Zionist political office. In 1933 the Haavara transfer agreement was concluded.

The third layer was mobilization. In 1942 the Biltmore program committed the movement to a commonwealth. In 1943 AZEC built its lobbying machine. In 1944 the movement's aims entered both party platforms. In 1945 the secret Sonneborn meeting created an arms network. In 1948 Golda Meyerson's tour raised about $50 million, Czech arms were bought, and banknotes were printed in New York.

Beneath all of this lay older foundations: the British and Ottoman layers of administration, a Christian restorationist lobby dating from 1839, and the Rothschild colonies dating from 1882.

Seen whole, the sequence changes what 1948 means. The familiar version stops at the Holocaust. The documents go further back. The Holocaust transformed the urgency, the politics and the moral case for a state. But the record shows that it did not create the apparatus. The bank, the land fund, the American fundraising and lobbying machine, the congressional endorsement and the arms channels had been assembled over the previous half-century. When the moment came, the instruments already existed. The state was not improvised in two years.

This summary draws on sections throughout this chapter, among them those on the electricity monopoly [cite:wiki_israel_electric], on foreign agents before there was a state [cite:djn_bergson_fara_1944], and on the question "Has the Vatican Taken More Concrete Action Elsewhere?" [cite:gandhi_poland_solidarity]. None of the steps listed here is an inference; each is sourced in its own section. What this summary adds is the order, and the order is the argument. A state that the familiar account presents as a beginning appears in the documents as the completion of a long build, a point made another way in [scene:oc_ch03|the mechanism, in plain terms].

sections.h: Built Before It Was Declared: The Mechanism in Plain Terms
sections.html:
On 14 May 1948 the state of Israel was declared. The familiar statement is that Israel was created in 1948, and as a statement about the declaration, it is accurate. As a statement about when the state's machinery came into being, it misleads. By the time the world watched the state declared, its working parts had been running for decades.

A simple comparison makes the point. Picture a restaurant on the night of its grand opening. The opening is real, and it is the first moment most people notice the place. But the kitchen was built in 1899. The land was bought in 1901. The health permit was granted in 1922. The marketing team had been working the neighbourhood since the 1940s. Everything that made the opening possible happened before the sign went up, and most of it happened out of public view.

Each part of the comparison stands for a documented institution. The kitchen is the financial base: the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Anglo-Palestine bank, set up between 1899 and 1902. The land is the permanent holdings of the Jewish National Fund, the movement's land fund, begun in 1901 and held in perpetuity. The permit is the Mandate, Britain's charter to govern Palestine, which in its Article 4 in 1922 recognized a "Jewish agency" and so gave the movement's agency legal standing. The marketing team is the American political machine of the 1940s, the American Zionist Emergency Council, which mapped Congress district by district. [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress] [cite:jvl_palestine_arab_congress] [cite:jerusalemstory_arab_executive]

Each was in place before May 1948, and each had been running for years when the state was declared on 14 May. The declaration was the first line most people were shown. It was not the first line of the program.

That is the sense in which the state was set running before it was declared. The phrase describes the documented sequence; it adds no claim to it. The institutions and their dates are those set out in [scene:us_s08|the whole sequence, step by step]. What the comparison adds is a way of seeing why 1948 can look like a beginning, when the record shows it as the end of a fifty-year build.
